t.mednik hill mining landscape@50.4,13.1:
Mědník is a small, steep hill on the Czech side of the Ore Mountains, or Krušné hory, the range that forms the border between Bohemia and Saxony. It rises above the village of Měděnec, whose name, like the hill's, comes from the Czech word for copper. For centuries, miners tunnelled into the hill for copper and iron ore, and the hill is now part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, inscribed by UNESCO in 2019 as a cross-border site.

At the top stands a small Baroque chapel of the Immaculate Conception, and from there the view stretches over the high plateau of the Ore Mountains and down into the valley of the Ohře. The old mine workings can be visited in season; the Mariánská mine adit offers guided tours. The surrounding landscape is the result of centuries of mining: spoil heaps, shafts and the remains of the settlements that grew up around them.

The Ore Mountains have a melancholy beauty. In the twentieth century, Sudeten German communities were expelled after the war, many villages emptied, and pollution from coal burning in the basin below killed forests on the ridges. Much has recovered, but the sense of a frontier landscape remains.

The riding is excellent. The road climbing from Klášterec nad Ohří up to Měděnec and on toward Kovářská and the border crossing at Vejprty winds through forest and over the high plateau, at around eight hundred metres and more, with good bends and views. On the plateau, the roads are open and fast, crossing meadows and spruce forest, while the climbs from the Ohře valley on the southern side are steep and twisting. Weather changes quickly up here: fog, rain and cold are common, and winter brings snow; this is a ski area.

Klášterec nad Ohří, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, food and a château with a porcelain museum. The plateau villages are small, so fill up below. Czech roads require a vignette on motorways, but not on these mountain roads. The local beer, as anywhere in Bohemia, is excellent and cheap; try it with goulash and dumplings after a day in the hills.
t.palaces and parks of potsdam and berlin@:
Potsdam lies just outside Berlin, in a landscape of lakes, rivers and woods along the Havel, and for over two centuries it was the summer residence of the Prussian kings and German emperors. Frederick the Great built the palace of Sanssouci here in the 1740s, a single-storey Rococo palace above terraced vineyards, where he wanted to live without worries, as its name suggests. His successors added more palaces, gardens and follies, and today the ensemble, together with sites in Berlin, forms one of Germany's largest UNESCO World Heritage sites.

The Park Sanssouci is vast, with the main palace, the New Palace, the Chinese House, the Orangery and the Roman Baths among its buildings. Frederick is buried on the terrace of Sanssouci, next to his dogs, as he wished, and visitors leave potatoes on his grave, in honour of his promotion of the crop in Prussia. The New Garden, on the shores of the Heiliger See, has the Cecilienhof Palace, where Truman, Stalin and Churchill, later replaced by Attlee, met in 1945 for the Potsdam Conference to decide the fate of post-war Germany.

The Glienicke Bridge, which links Potsdam to Berlin over the Havel, was on the border between East and West during the Cold War and was used for exchanges of spies, earning it the nickname Bridge of Spies. Potsdam's old town includes a Dutch quarter of red-brick houses built for Dutch craftsmen in the eighteenth century.

The riding around Potsdam is flat but pleasant. The roads along the lakes and through the forests of Brandenburg are quiet and scenic, especially toward Werder, famous for its fruit orchards and blossom festival, and toward Caputh, where Albert Einstein had a summer house. Traffic in Potsdam and Berlin is heavy, and the cities have a lot of cobblestones and tram rails, which can be slippery when wet.

Potsdam has every service, and Berlin is close by. Local food includes Brandenburg asparagus in spring and fish from the lakes. Late spring and early autumn are the best times to visit the parks.
t.rother berg mining landscape@50.5,12.8:
Schwarzenberg, in the western Erzgebirge, is a town of steep streets, slate roofs and a castle and church perched on a rock above the Schwarzwasser river, and the hills around it are riddled with old mine workings. The Rother Berg, the red mountain, takes its name from the iron ore that colours its soil, and it is one of the components of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, the cross-border UNESCO site listed in 2019. For eight centuries, miners in these mountains dug for silver, tin, iron, cobalt and later uranium, and their work shaped not only the landscape but the culture of the whole region.

Around the Rother Berg you can find traces of shafts, spoil heaps and old mining paths in the forest, and the nearby village of Pöhla has a visitor mine, a former tin and iron mine with huge underground chambers. The mining culture lives on in the traditions of the Erzgebirge: the wooden Christmas decorations, candle arches called Schwibbögen that once lit the miners' way home, nutcrackers and smoking men, and the parades of miners in their black uniforms during the Advent season. Schwarzenberg's Christmas market is one of the most atmospheric in the region.

The riding here is genuinely good. The Erzgebirge is a long, gently tilted range, with roads that climb from the valleys through spruce forest to the high plateau along the Czech border, with tight bends, steep gradients and changing surfaces. From Schwarzenberg, routes lead south to Johanngeorgenstadt and across the border into Bohemia, or east to Oberwiesenthal and the Fichtelberg, at 1,215 metres the highest mountain in eastern Germany. The weather is cooler and wetter than in the lowlands, with snow lingering into spring on the heights and mist common in autumn. Weekends bring many motorcyclists, and some popular stretches have speed controls.

Schwarzenberg has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, and the surrounding villages have traditional inns. Local dishes are hearty mountain food: potato dumplings, Buttermilchgetzen, a potato cake made with buttermilk, and the Christmas stollen. A ride across the border is easy, as there are no controls, and the Czech side offers cheaper fuel and beer, as well as spa towns like Karlovy Vary within easy reach.
t.the adgb trade union school@52.7,13.5:
In the pine woods just outside Bernau, north of Berlin, a cluster of yellow brick buildings steps down a gentle slope toward a lake, and it is one of the purest expressions of Bauhaus architecture anywhere. The Federal School of the General German Trade Union Federation, known by its German initials ADGB, was designed by Hannes Meyer, the second director of the Bauhaus, with Hans Wittwer, and built between 1928 and 1930 as a training college for union officials. Every detail, from the arrangement of the dormitory wings in staggered blocks to the glass corridor that runs down the slope, was designed to encourage community, light and a healthy life. It was added to the UNESCO Bauhaus site in 2017.

The school had a short life in its original use. In 1933 the Nazis seized the trade unions and took over the buildings, using them for their own training purposes, and after the war it became a school for the East German unions. After German reunification, it fell into disrepair, but it has been carefully restored and now serves as a training centre, with guided tours offered on certain days. The visitor centre explains the history and the ideas behind the architecture.

The riding around Bernau is pleasant but unspectacular, with flat roads through pine forests, lakes and villages of the Barnim region. The Schorfheide-Chorin biosphere reserve to the north is a large area of forests, lakes and wetlands, with quiet roads and the Gothic ruins of Chorin Abbey, and the Grumsin beech forest, another UNESCO site, is nearby. Traffic around Berlin can be heavy, but once you are out in the countryside, the roads are quiet and well surfaced, though cobbled stretches and tree-lined avenues are common in Brandenburg, and the trees can be unforgiving.

Bernau, about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and a medieval town wall that is one of the best preserved in the region. Local food includes Brandenburg classics like potato soup, fish from the lakes and the gherkins of the Spreewald, further south. Lake Liepnitz, near Wandlitz, has clear water and is a popular spot for swimming in summer.
t.grumsin@53.0,13.9:
North-east of Berlin, the last ice age left behind a landscape of hills, hollows and lakes, shaped by glaciers that advanced and melted back again. In one corner of it, between Angermünde and Joachimsthal, lies the Grumsin forest, a beech wood that has been left largely undisturbed for a long time. It is part of the UNESCO site of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, inscribed as one of Germany's contributions in 2011. Old beeches tower above a forest floor scattered with fallen trunks, small ponds and bogs, and in spring the canopy glows a fresh, translucent green.

The Grumsin lies within the Schorfheide-Chorin Biosphere Reserve, a vast area of forest, lakes and farmland that was once a royal hunting ground and later a favourite retreat of the East German elite. Today it is a haven for wildlife: cranes breed in the wetlands, their calls echoing across the fields in spring and autumn, white-tailed eagles nest near the lakes, and beavers have returned to the rivers.

Chorin Abbey, a few kilometres south, is a beautiful ruin of red brick, a Cistercian monastery built in the Gothic style typical of northern Germany, and in summer it hosts concerts in its roofless nave. Nearby, at Niederfinow, two enormous boat lifts raise and lower ships between the Oder-Havel canal and the Oder valley, one of them built in the 1930s and a newer one opened recently. Watching a ship rise in its giant water-filled tank is strangely mesmerising.

The riding here is relaxed. Roads run through forests and farmland, past lakes and villages, many of them lined with old trees forming long avenues, beautiful but unforgiving if you leave the road. Some minor roads are still cobbled, which can be rough and slippery when wet. Traffic is light, but wildlife, especially deer and wild boar, crosses frequently, particularly at dawn and dusk. Summers are warm and dry, winters cold, and autumn brings beautiful colours and morning mist.

Angermünde, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try fish from the lakes, smoked or fried, or a plate of local potatoes with quark and linseed oil, a Brandenburg classic, in a village inn.
t.karlovy vary@50.2,12.9:
Legend has it that Emperor Charles IV was out hunting in the forests of western Bohemia in the fourteenth century when a stag he was chasing, or in some versions one of his hounds, fell into a pool of scalding water, and that is how the hot springs of Karlovy Vary were found. Whatever the truth, the town that grew up around them bears his name, Karlsbad in German, and by the nineteenth century it had become one of the most fashionable spas in Europe, visited by tsars, composers, poets and the cream of European society. In 2021, it became part of the UNESCO listing of the Great Spa Towns of Europe.

The town fills a narrow, winding valley along the Teplá river, lined with grand hotels, villas and colonnades painted in pastel colours. The springs are free to taste, and visitors stroll along the colonnades sipping the warm, mineral water from special porcelain cups with a spout. The hottest spring, Vřídlo, shoots a column of steaming water into the air inside a modern hall. The town is also known for Becherovka, a herbal liqueur, for its crisp spa wafers, and for its international film festival, held every summer, when the streets fill with stars and film buffs.

The riding around Karlovy Vary is excellent. The roads that climb out of the valley into the hills are steep and twisty, with good surfaces, and the forests of the Slavkov Woods to the south and the Ore Mountains to the north offer endless options. The road up to Boží Dar, on the German border, climbs high into the mountains, with long curves and great views. The Ohře valley, west of the town, is also scenic, with castles and rock formations. Traffic is moderate, but busy in summer and on weekends.

Karlovy Vary, with fifty-two thousand inhabitants, has all services, including fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels. The centre is mostly pedestrianised, so park outside and walk. Try svíčková, beef sirloin in a creamy vegetable sauce with dumplings, or a plate of goulash with a Czech beer. Pick up a box of spa wafers as a souvenir, and if you are brave, try the mineral water: it is an acquired taste.
t.luther s birthplace@51.5,11.6:
Martin Luther was born in Eisleben on 10 November 1483, and by an odd twist of fate he died here too, in 1546, while on a visit to settle a dispute between the counts of Mansfeld. The house where he was born was rebuilt after a fire in the seventeenth century and became one of the first museums in Germany dedicated to a single person. Together with the house where he died and the sites in Wittenberg where he lived and taught, it forms the UNESCO site of the Luther Memorials in Eisleben and Wittenberg, listed in 1996. The museum tells the story of Luther's family, his childhood and the beginning of the Reformation, and it has been extended with modern exhibitions.

Eisleben is a small town in the Mansfeld Land, a region shaped by copper mining for over eight hundred years. Luther's father was a miner and smelter, and the landscape around the town is dotted with conical slag heaps, the legacy of centuries of mining. The town itself has a pleasant old centre, with the market square, the churches of St Andreas, where Luther preached his last sermons, and St Peter and Paul, where he was baptised.

The riding around Eisleben is gentle, with rolling hills, fields and small villages. To the west, the Harz mountains rise, offering some of the best riding in central Germany, with winding roads through forests, valleys and over passes, and the Brocken, the highest peak, looming over everything. The Selke and Bode valleys are particularly scenic, with cliffs, castles and tight bends. Traffic is light, but watch for wildlife, especially deer and wild boar, and be aware that the Harz roads are popular with bikers and closely monitored by police.

Eisleben, with twenty-four thousand inhabitants, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Order a bowl of Soljanka, the sour, spicy soup that is still a fixture in eastern Germany, or a plate of Thuringian sausages with sauerkraut and mustard. The Süßer See, a lake east of town, has a lakeside path and places for a break, and in summer you can swim there. Halle, about thirty kilometres away, is a larger city with more options for food and accommodation.
t.annaberg frohnau mining landscape@50.6,1:
Silver built Annaberg. In the late fifteenth century rich silver ore was found in the Erzgebirge, the Ore Mountains on the border between Saxony and Bohemia, and a town was founded almost overnight in 1496 to house the miners. Within a few decades Annaberg was one of the largest towns in Saxony, and its wealth paid for the St. Annenkirche, one of the most beautiful late Gothic hall churches in Germany, with slender pillars branching into a star-ribbed vault like the trunks of trees.

The mining landscape of Annaberg-Frohnau is part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, a cross-border site recognising eight hundred years of mining. In Frohnau, the Frohnauer Hammer, an old hammer mill powered by water wheels, is one of the oldest technical monuments in Germany and still demonstrates how iron and copper were worked. The famous mathematician Adam Ries, whose arithmetic books taught generations of Germans to calculate, lived and worked in Annaberg, and his house is now a museum.

The Erzgebirge is excellent riding country. The roads wind over the high plateau and through deep valleys, with forests, meadows and small towns, and the climbs to the Fichtelberg, the highest summit in Saxony at 1,215 metres, and across the border to the Klínovec in the Czech Republic, offer fine views and bends. The B95 runs through Annaberg, linking Chemnitz with the Czech border. Surfaces are generally good, but winters are long and snowy, and the season starts late here. Expect cooler temperatures than in the lowlands.

Annaberg-Buchholz has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the market square, with the church above it, is lively. The Erzgebirge is famous for its wooden toys and Christmas decorations, especially nutcrackers and candle arches, which reflect the traditions of mining families, and the Christmas markets here are magical. Local food includes potato dishes and hearty stews. The Pöhlberg, a basalt hill above the town, has a viewing tower and a restaurant, and a great view over the Erzgebirge.
t.berlin modernism housing estates@52.5,13:
Most World Heritage sites are palaces, cathedrals or ruins. Berlin got onto the list in 2008 with flats. The Berlin Modernism Housing Estates are six residential developments built between 1910 and 1933, among them the Hufeisensiedlung in Britz, shaped like a horseshoe around a pond, the Gartenstadt Falkenberg with its bright colours, the Weisse Stadt in Reinickendorf and the Siemensstadt estate. Architects such as Bruno Taut, Martin Wagner and Walter Gropius designed them to give ordinary working families light, air, green space and decent bathrooms at a time when many Berliners lived in dark, cramped tenement blocks around courtyards.

The point here in Kreuzberg is a city marker rather than one of those estates, a starting place among streets that show exactly what the reformers were reacting against: dense nineteenth-century blocks, back courtyards and busy avenues. From here the estates are spread out across the city, Britz to the south-east, Falkenberg to the far south-east, Siemensstadt and the Weisse Stadt to the north-west, so seeing them by bike is a satisfying urban tour.

Riding in Berlin is flat, busy and full of surprises. Cobblestones appear on older streets, tram tracks in the east, and cyclists everywhere, often on paths that cross your line at junctions. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, parking is a puzzle and the speed limits are generally enforced. On the plus side, the city's wide avenues and grid of streets make navigation straightforward, and the estates themselves are calm, leafy places where the bike can rest at the kerb while you walk.

Fuel, food and coffee are never far away. Kreuzberg itself is famous for its cafés, Turkish bakeries and döner stands, and for a mix of cultures that makes lunch an adventure. Close by you have the Landwehr Canal, the remains of the Anhalter Bahnhof and the Topography of Terror documentation centre, a sobering stop on the site of the former Gestapo headquarters.

Visit the estates in spring when the gardens bloom and the colours of Taut's façades glow against the green. Walk through the Hufeisensiedlung and imagine a family moving in from a cramped tenement in 1927, opening a window onto trees and sky for the first time. That is what the idealists of the Weimar years were building for.
t.jachymov mining landscape@50.4,12.9:
The word dollar comes from this small town in the Ore Mountains. In the early sixteenth century, the silver mines of Jáchymov, then called Joachimsthal, were among the richest in Europe, and the coins minted here were called Joachimsthaler, shortened to thaler, which became daler and eventually dollar. The town grew rapidly, with thousands of miners, and it is now one component of the World Heritage inscription for the Erzgebirge mining region, shared between the Czech Republic and Germany. Its later history is darker and stranger.

The mines also produced pitchblende, a mineral that Marie Curie used to isolate radium and polonium. In 1906, Jáchymov opened the world's first radon spa, where patients bathe in radioactive water, and it still operates today. After the Second World War, the communist regime used political prisoners to mine uranium for the Soviet nuclear programme, in brutal labour camps around the town. The Red Tower of Death, a building near Ostrov where ore was processed, is a memorial to those who suffered, and a trail through the forest leads past the remains of the camps.

The riding in the Ore Mountains is excellent. The road from Ostrov climbs through Jáchymov to Boží Dar and the border with Germany, with curves, forests and views, and Klínovec, the highest peak in the Czech side of the range, at over twelve hundred metres, has a ski area and a lookout tower. Across the border, Oberwiesenthal and the Fichtelberg are close. The tarmac is decent on the whole, and traffic is light except in the ski season. Weather in the mountains is cool and changeable, with fog, rain and snow from autumn to spring.

Jáchymov has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Ostrov, about seven kilometres away, is larger. Czech food is hearty: roast pork with dumplings and cabbage, goulash, svíčková, beef in cream sauce, and excellent beer. The spa hotels in Jáchymov have restaurants. Visit the town, walk to the mining museum in the old mint, and then follow the trail to the camp remains; the contrast between the beauty of the mountains and the history of suffering is striking, and it stays with you.
t.freiberg mining landscape@50.9,13.3:
Silver was found near Freiberg in 1168, and within a few decades the town had become one of the richest in Saxony. For eight centuries, miners dug ever deeper into the hills, and the wealth they brought up paid for churches, palaces and the splendours of Dresden. Freiberg's Bergakademie, founded in 1765, is the oldest mining university in the world still operating, and its mineral collection is one of the finest anywhere. The town and its mining landscape are part of the Erzgebirge mining region listed by UNESCO, shared between Germany and the Czech Republic.

The old town is beautiful, with a medieval street plan, Renaissance houses and the cathedral of St Mary, whose Golden Gate, a richly carved Romanesque portal, and tulip pulpit are masterpieces. The cathedral also has two organs built by Gottfried Silbermann, the great organ builder of the eighteenth century. Visitors can go underground in the mines, such as Reiche Zeche, where the university still trains students, and see the tunnels and workings of centuries.

The riding in the Ore Mountains is very good. South of Freiberg, the roads climb toward the Czech border, with curves, forests and mining villages, and the Silver Road, a tourist route, links the mining towns of the region. The B101 runs through the area, and minor roads offer quieter alternatives. The asphalt holds up well, but there are cobbles in old towns. Weather in the mountains can be cool and wet, with snow in winter. Traffic around Freiberg can be heavy at peak times, but the mountain roads are calm.

Freiberg covers fuel, food and a bed for the night. Saxon food is hearty: sauerbraten, marinated beef, potato soup, dumplings and cakes, such as Eierschecke, a layered cake with custard and quark. Freiberger beer is a local brand. Visit the cathedral to hear the Silbermann organ if a recital is on, then go underground in a mine. Riding out of town, you will see the old mining heaps and shafts in the landscape, the traces of a story that shaped the region for eight hundred years.
t.garden kingdom of dessau worlitz@51.8,12:
In the late eighteenth century, a small German principality decided to remake its entire landscape as a work of art. Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz of Anhalt-Dessau, inspired by travels in England and by the ideas of the Enlightenment, created a vast network of parks, gardens, palaces and estates along the Elbe and Mulde rivers, combining beauty, education and agriculture. The result, the Garden Kingdom of Dessau-Wörlitz, is one of the earliest and largest landscape gardens in continental Europe, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

The heart of it is Wörlitz Park, laid out around a lake with canals, islands, bridges and buildings in many styles. Wörlitz Palace, built in the 1770s, is considered the first neoclassical building in Germany. The Gothic House, with its pointed windows and stained glass, is one of the earliest Gothic Revival buildings on the continent. And on an island in the lake stands an artificial volcano, the Stein, which could be made to erupt with fireworks, alongside a copy of a Roman villa. Small hand-pulled ferries carry visitors across the canals, part of the charm.

The parks lie in the Middle Elbe floodplain, now a biosphere reserve, with meadows, oak forests and old river channels. The area is home to beavers, which have made a remarkable comeback here, as well as storks and many other birds. Dessau, a short ride west, is famous as the home of the Bauhaus, the influential school of art and design, whose buildings are also listed by UNESCO.

The riding in the area is flat and easy, with straight roads through farmland, forests and villages. The roads along the Elbe, especially on the dike tops, offer views over the river and the floodplain. Traffic is light, but cyclists are common, especially on the Elbe cycle route. Surfaces are generally good, though some minor roads are cobbled or rough.

Wörlitz is a small town with cafés, restaurants and accommodation; for fuel, Dessau or Oranienbaum are more reliable. Try a local fish dish from the Elbe, or a slice of cake in a garden café. Spring and early summer are the best seasons, when the parks are green and full of flowers. Summer can be hot, and mosquitoes along the river can be fierce.
t.zatec@50.3,13.5:
The smell gives Žatec away in late summer. The fields around this small town in northwestern Bohemia are planted with hops, tall green vines climbing up wires on wooden poles, and when harvest comes in August, the air fills with their resinous, slightly bitter scent. Saaz hops, named after the German form of the town's name, have been prized by brewers for centuries for their fine aroma, and they are a key ingredient in Czech pilsner lagers. In 2023, UNESCO inscribed Žatec and the Landscape of Saaz Hops, recognising the town's hop warehouses, drying kilns, packing houses and the surrounding hop gardens as a unique agricultural and industrial heritage.

The town itself has a well-preserved old centre with a Gothic church, a baroque square and narrow lanes, and the streets around it are lined with tall hop warehouses, their small windows designed for ventilation. The Hop Museum explains the history of the crop and its processing, and the Temple of Hops and Beer, with a lookout tower and a hop astronomical clock, is a quirky attraction. Žatec was a largely German-speaking town until 1945, when the German population was expelled after the Second World War, a painful chapter that is still part of local memory.

The roads around Žatec run through the Ohře river valley and the rolling hop country, with gentle curves, good surfaces and light traffic. The hop gardens make a striking sight from the saddle, especially in summer when the vines are at full height. Head north toward the Krušné hory, the Ore Mountains, and the roads climb into forests and old mining country, with steep gradients and more technical bends. The Ore Mountains straddle the border with Germany and form part of the UNESCO Erzgebirge mining region, with old silver mines and mining towns. Weather here can be cold and wet, even in summer, so pack layers.

Žatec is a town of roughly twenty thousand people with fuel, shops, restaurants and pubs. It would be a crime to visit without trying the local beer, so if you are finished riding for the day, settle into a pub and order a fresh lager brewed with Saaz hops, along with hearty Czech food like roast pork, dumplings and sauerkraut. Walk the old town, visit the Hop Museum, and breathe in the scent of the fields. It is a place where agriculture and culture are inseparable.
t.the former school of applied art@51.0,11:
Weimar is a small city with a very large place in German culture. Goethe and Schiller lived and worked here, Liszt composed and taught, Nietzsche spent his last years here, and in 1919 the national assembly that created Germany's first democratic constitution met in the theatre, giving the Weimar Republic its name. That same year, the architect Walter Gropius founded a new art school in the city, merging the academy of fine arts with the school of applied arts, and called it the Bauhaus. The school building designed earlier by the Belgian architect Henry van de Velde, along with the main building of the art academy, became its home. These buildings, together with the Haus am Horn, are part of the UNESCO serial site of the Bauhaus and its sites, inscribed in 1996.

The van de Velde building is a fine example of early modernism, with large windows, clean lines and touches of Art Nouveau, and it is still used by the Bauhaus University. The Bauhaus itself stayed in Weimar only until 1925, when it moved to Dessau under pressure from conservative politicians, but its ideas about design, architecture and craft spread worldwide. The Bauhaus Museum in Weimar presents its history, and the city also has the Goethe House, the Schiller House, the Duchess Anna Amalia Library and much more.

For riders, Weimar is a compact city with cobbled streets in the old town and limited parking, so it is best to leave the bike on the edge of the centre and walk. The surroundings offer gentle riding through the Ilm valley, with small villages, parks and castles, and the Thuringian Forest, about an hour to the south, has some of the best motorcycle roads in central Germany, with winding climbs through dense forests. The Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, on the Ettersberg hill just north of the city, is a sobering visit and an essential part of understanding Weimar's history.

Weimar has fuel, food and accommodation, as you would expect of a city of over sixty thousand people. Try a Thuringian bratwurst, grilled over charcoal and served in a roll with mustard, or the local dumplings. Walk past the van de Velde building, visit the Bauhaus Museum, and then wander through the park on the Ilm to Goethe's garden house. It is a city where culture is everywhere, and the Bauhaus is only one chapter.
t.lauta mining landscape@50.7,13.1:
Marienberg was laid out in 1521 as a planned silver town, with a vast square market place and streets set in a grid, an idea of urban order that was new in this part of Europe. Lauta, today a district of Marienberg, lies among the old mine workings, spoil heaps and shafts that fed that wealth, and it is one of the components of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, the cross-border World Heritage Site shared by Saxony and the Czech Republic and inscribed in 2019.

The Ore Mountains have been mined for eight centuries: silver first, then tin, cobalt, uranium and other metals. Mining shaped everything here, from the towns and their churches to the forests, which were cut for fuel and timber, and the many ponds and ditches built to supply water power. In Lauta you can see the traces of this activity in the landscape, with mounds, hollows and old buildings, and the Pferdegöpel, a reconstructed horse-powered winding machine, shows how ore was hauled to the surface.

The region is also famous for its craft traditions. When mining declined, miners turned to woodcarving, and the Erzgebirge became the home of nutcrackers, smoking men, candle arches and Christmas pyramids, now sold all over the world. In December, the towns come alive with Christmas markets and miners' parades.

The riding is excellent. The Ore Mountains form a long ridge along the Czech border, with roads that climb from the valleys to the high plateau, through forests and villages. Curves are plentiful, traffic is light outside towns, and the views from the ridge are wide. In winter, snow covers the high ground for months, and the roads can be icy. The best riding season is from May to October.

Marienberg, two kilometres away, has fuel, and its huge square is lined with cafés. Nearby Wolkenstein has a castle on a rock above the Zschopau valley, and the valley road itself is a lovely ride. Local food is hearty: potato dishes, dumplings and, in winter, Stollen. A ride across the border into the Czech side of the Ore Mountains, with its own mining towns and landscapes, makes a fine extension.
t.ehrenfriedersdorf mining landscape@50.6,:
Tin, not silver, was the business of Ehrenfriedersdorf. For around eight hundred years miners dug into the Sauberg hill above this small Erzgebirge town for tin ore, and the Ehrenfriedersdorf mining landscape, with its shafts, spoil heaps, ponds and ditches, is one of the components of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region World Heritage Site. The Sauberg visitor mine lets you go underground into galleries worked by generations of miners, and the hard hat, the damp cold and the drip of water make the history very physical.

Water was the key to mining here. To drain the mines and power the machinery, miners built reservoirs and long ditches that collected rain and snowmelt from the hills, and some of these ponds survive as peaceful lakes in the forest today. The landscape around the town, with its patchwork of forest, meadow and old mining sites, has a gentle, slightly melancholy charm.

Just outside town, the Greifensteine are a group of granite towers rising out of the forest, a natural landmark with a viewpoint on top and an open-air stage below, where plays and concerts are performed in summer. Geyer, a few kilometres away, has the Geyersberg Binge, a huge collapse crater left by centuries of mining, and Thum and Annaberg-Buchholz are close. Annaberg's St Anne's church, one of the finest late Gothic hall churches in Saxony, was paid for by silver, and Adam Ries, the arithmetic master whose name every German knows from the phrase nach Adam Riese, lived and worked in the town.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads wind through the hills, forests and villages, with short climbs and descents and plenty of curves. Traffic is light outside the towns, and the views from the higher points reach far across the mountains. The Zschopau valley to the east has a particularly nice road. Winter is long and snowy, and the riding season is roughly from May to October. Mornings can be foggy in the valleys.

The town itself, one kilometre away, has fuel, as do Thum and Geyer. Look out for Buttermilchgetzen, a potato pancake made with buttermilk, and hearty soups. A visit to the mine followed by a walk up the Greifensteine makes a good half-day break from the bike.
t.wohnstadt carl legien@52.5,13.4:
Bruno Taut liked colour, and in Berlin in the late 1920s, he used it to make social housing feel joyful. The Wohnstadt Carl Legien, built between 1928 and 1930 in Prenzlauer Berg, is a large estate of apartment blocks arranged around green courtyards that open onto the street, with facades painted in bright, contrasting colours: yellow, red, blue and green, the balconies and window frames picking out the patterns. It was named after Carl Legien, a leader of the German trade unions, and it was built by a union-affiliated housing association to provide light, air and greenery for working families. It is one of the six Berlin Modernism Housing Estates listed by UNESCO in 2008.

The estates were built during the Weimar Republic, when Berlin was booming, and they were a response to the dark, overcrowded tenements of the nineteenth century. Taut and other architects of the time, like Martin Wagner, believed that good design could improve people's lives, and the estates were among the most advanced housing of their time. Today, they are still lived in, and still feel fresh and humane. Walking through the courtyards, you can see why.

Prenzlauer Berg itself is one of Berlin's most popular districts, with cafés, shops, restaurants and parks, and its tree-lined streets and restored nineteenth-century buildings make it a pleasant place to explore. The Kulturbrauerei, a former brewery turned cultural centre, and the Mauerpark, along the former route of the Berlin Wall, are nearby.

Riding in Berlin is a test of patience, with heavy traffic, cobblestones, tram rails and many cyclists. The city has a low emission zone, the Umweltzone, but motorcycles are exempt from the sticker requirement. Parking is easier for motorcycles than for cars, and you can usually find a spot on the pavement or in a designated area.

For riding outside the city, head north toward the lakes and forests of Brandenburg, where roads wind through pine forests, past lakes and villages, with gentle curves and little traffic. The Schorfheide and the Uckermark, to the north-east, are particularly beautiful, and the beech forest of Grumsin, part of the UNESCO-listed ancient beech forests of Europe, lies in this area.

Prenzlauer Berg, a district of nearly a hundred and fifty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. Try a currywurst from a street stand, or one of the many international restaurants of the district, and enjoy a coffee in a café on the Kollwitzplatz.
t.marianske lazne@50.0,12.7:
Goethe fell in love here when he was already in his seventies. In the summer of 1821 and the years that followed, the poet spent his holidays in Marienbad, the spa town now known as Mariánské Lázně, and fell for Ulrike von Levetzow, a young woman of nineteen; his proposal was declined, and on the journey home he wrote the Marienbad Elegy, one of his most moving poems. The town was then at the height of its fame as one of the great spas of Europe, visited by kings, emperors and artists, from Edward VII of Britain to Chopin and Kafka.

Mariánské Lázně lies in a valley in western Bohemia, surrounded by forested hills, and the town is built around a park, with grand hotels, villas and spa buildings in elegant styles. The centrepiece is the Colonnade, a long cast-iron gallery built in the 1880s, where guests walk while sipping the mineral water from the springs. In front of it, the Singing Fountain dances to music several times a day. The town is one of the Great Spa Towns of Europe, listed by UNESCO in 2021, along with Karlovy Vary and Františkovy Lázně nearby.

For riders, western Bohemia offers good, varied riding. The roads through the Slavkov Forest, a protected landscape of forests, meadows and peat bogs between Mariánské Lázně and Karlovy Vary, are winding and quiet, with good surfaces. To the east, the Teplá monastery, a large Premonstratensian abbey, is worth a visit. To the north, the road to Karlovy Vary leads through the forest to another famous spa town, and beyond, the Ore Mountains, on the border with Germany, offer more winding roads through forests and mining towns.

Motorways in the Czech Republic require an electronic vignette for cars, but motorcycles are exempt. Speed limits are enforced, and police checks are common, especially near the German border.

Mariánské Lázně, a town of over fourteen thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the spa wafers, oplatky, large, thin wafers filled with sweet cream, sold warm from stands in the town, and a glass of Becherovka, the herbal liqueur from Karlovy Vary. For a meal, try roast duck with red cabbage and dumplings, a classic Bohemian dish. And take a sip of the mineral water at the Colonnade, as Goethe did, though you may find the taste an acquired one.
t.house with balcony access peterholzstr@5:
Hannes Meyer, the second director of the Bauhaus, believed that architecture should serve the needs of the people, not the egos of architects, and the five apartment buildings he designed with Bauhaus students in Dessau-Törten in 1929 and 1930 are an expression of that belief. The Laubenganghäuser, houses with balcony access, are three-storey brick buildings with external walkways along the facades giving access to the apartments, a cheap and efficient way to provide affordable housing for workers. The buildings on Peterholzstraße were added to the UNESCO listing of the Bauhaus and its sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau in 2017.

The Bauhaus was founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919 and moved to Dessau in 1925, where Gropius designed the famous Bauhaus building, a landmark of modern architecture, with its glass curtain wall and asymmetric wings. Nearby, the Masters' Houses, where the teachers, including Kandinsky, Klee and Feininger, lived, are also open to visitors. In Törten, the Bauhaus also built a housing estate of small row houses designed by Gropius, and the Konsum building, a shop and apartment block.

Dessau lies at the confluence of the Mulde and the Elbe, in Saxony-Anhalt, and the surrounding area is part of the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, a UNESCO site, a landscape of parks, gardens and palaces created in the late eighteenth century by Prince Leopold III of Anhalt-Dessau, inspired by the English landscape garden. The park at Wörlitz, with its lakes, bridges, temples and palace, is one of the finest of its kind in Europe.

For riders, the area offers flat, easy riding through farmland, forests and floodplains, with gentle curves and little traffic outside the towns. The Middle Elbe Biosphere Reserve, along the river, has meadows, oak forests and beavers. Further south, the Harz mountains offer more challenging roads.

Dessau, a city of over seventy thousand people about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The region's cuisine is hearty and simple: try a plate of Soljanka, a sour soup of East European origin popular in eastern Germany, or roast meat with potato dumplings and red cabbage. And as you ride past the plain brick buildings of Törten, take a moment to appreciate the idealism behind them, a belief that good design should be for everyone.
t.mikveh@51.0,11.0:
In 2007, during construction work near the Krämerbrücke in Erfurt, archaeologists uncovered a medieval ritual bath, a mikveh, beside the river Gera, which had been forgotten for centuries. It dates from the thirteenth century and was used by the city's Jewish community until the pogrom of 1349, when the community was destroyed during the panic of the Black Death. It is now protected and can be visited on guided tours. Together with the Old Synagogue and the Stone House, a medieval residence, the mikveh forms the Jewish-Medieval Heritage of Erfurt, listed by UNESCO in 2023.

The Old Synagogue is one of the oldest surviving synagogue buildings in Europe, with parts dating back to around 1100, and it survived because, after 1349, it was converted to a warehouse and later a dance hall and restaurant, its original use forgotten. Today it houses a museum, and its basement displays the Erfurt Treasure, a hoard of gold and silver jewellery, coins and other objects buried by a Jewish merchant during the pogrom and found in 1998, including a rare medieval Jewish wedding ring.

Erfurt is the capital of Thuringia, a city of churches, towers and half-timbered houses, and its old town is one of the best preserved in Germany. The Krämerbrücke, a medieval bridge lined with inhabited houses and small shops, is one of the city's landmarks, and the cathedral and the church of St Severus stand side by side on a hill above the Domplatz, reached by a broad flight of steps. Martin Luther studied at the university here and became a monk in the Augustinian monastery.

For riders, Erfurt is a gateway to the Thuringian Forest, a range of forested hills to the south, with excellent roads winding through valleys, over ridges and past small towns and villages. The Rennsteig, an old ridge path, runs along the crest, and roads crossing it, such as those around Oberhof, Schmiedefeld and Ilmenau, offer superb riding. Closer to Erfurt, the countryside is flat to rolling farmland, with good roads but less excitement.

Erfurt, a city of over two hundred thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. Thuringia is famous for its sausages, the Thüringer Rostbratwurst, grilled over charcoal and served in a bread roll with mustard, sold at stands all over the city, and for its potato dumplings, Thüringer Klöße. Grab a sausage on the Domplatz and enjoy it with the view of the cathedral.
t.jewish medieval heritage of erfurt@51.0,:
Erfurt is a compact, well-preserved medieval city in central Germany, and for hundreds of years it was home to one of the most important Jewish communities in the Holy Roman Empire. The Old Synagogue, with parts dating back to about 1100, is one of the oldest surviving synagogue buildings in Europe, and a ritual bath, or mikveh, uncovered in 2007 beside the Gera river was found in remarkably good condition. UNESCO listed the Jewish-medieval heritage of Erfurt in 2023, recognising the buildings as testimony to a community that thrived and then suffered.

The story is painful. In 1349, during the Black Death, the Jewish community was attacked and many were killed, and the survivors' property was seized. A hoard of medieval silver and gold, hidden by a Jewish owner at the time of the pogrom, was found in 1998 during building work and is displayed in the Old Synagogue. The city's other heritage is also rich: the Krämerbrücke, a stone bridge from the fourteenth century lined with timber-framed shops and houses, the cathedral and the church of St Severus on their hill above the main square, and the university where Martin Luther studied.

Riding in the old town is a matter of cobbles, tram lines and narrow streets, and much of the centre is closed to traffic, so park at the edge and walk. The surrounding country of Thuringia is lovely, with rolling farmland, forested hills and the Hainich, a large beech woodland that is another UNESCO site. The roads in the region are generally good, with moderate traffic and pleasant bends, and a ride to the Thuringian Forest to the south is a good day out. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.

Erfurt has fuel at every approach road, and the old town is full of cafés and restaurants serving Thuringian specialities, including the grilled sausage called Rostbratwurst, dumplings with roast meat, and a good local beer. The synagogue museum has fixed opening hours, so check before visiting, and allow an hour or two. Wander the lanes along the Gera at the end of the day, when the half-timbered houses glow in the evening light.
t.gartenstadt flakenberg@52.4,13.6:
On the southeastern edge of Berlin, near the Dahme river, a few streets of small houses are painted in colours so bold that locals nicknamed the place the paint-box estate. This is the Gartenstadt Falkenberg, or Falkenberg Garden City, designed by the architect Bruno Taut and built in the years just before the First World War. Taut believed that colour could improve ordinary lives, and so he gave the terraced houses facades of deep blue, red, ochre and green, with gardens, tree-lined lanes and a central square. It was an early experiment in affordable housing for working families, and UNESCO included it in 2008 among the Berlin Modernism Housing Estates.

The estate's story is a human one. Cooperative housing groups financed it, and the first residents were mostly workers and craftsmen who wanted a garden and fresh air in place of the crowded tenements of inner Berlin. The colours faded and were painted over during the following decades, and in the late twentieth century careful restoration brought back Taut's original scheme. Walking the lanes today, you notice how small and neat the houses are, and how generous the greenery is, with fruit trees and hedges between the plots.

For a motorcycle, this is a city ride with some pleasant surprises. The southeastern districts of Berlin, around Grünau, Bohnsdorf and Altglienicke, are quieter than the centre, with lakes, woods and rowing clubs along the Dahme, and the roads are good and often lined with trees. Expect cobbles on side streets, tram tracks and cyclists, and note the airport nearby, with its aircraft noise and traffic. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and on a sunny afternoon the colours of the houses glow.

Grünau and Altglienicke have fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, and there is a good choice of bakeries and small restaurants in the neighbourhood. Berlin specialities such as currywurst, doner kebab and a glass of Berliner Weisse beer are within easy reach. Visit on foot, respect the privacy of residents, and keep the bike on the main street, because the lanes are narrow and the estate is still a home.
t.museumsinsel@52.5,13.4:
The northern tip of an island in the Spree in the middle of Berlin holds five museums that between them cover about six thousand years of human history. The Museumsinsel, or Museum Island, grew out of a decision in the nineteenth century by the kings of Prussia to build a cultural centre in the heart of the capital, and the buildings, in neoclassical and neo-baroque style, were added one by one until the 1930s. UNESCO listed the ensemble in 1999. Among the treasures are the Pergamon Altar, the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, and the bust of Queen Nefertiti, which sits in the Neues Museum.

The story of the island is also the story of Berlin's twentieth century. The museums were bombed in the Second World War, much of their collections moved or lost, and the buildings left damaged in East Berlin for decades. After reunification a long rebuilding programme, led by the architect David Chipperfield for the Neues Museum, brought them back, and the contrast between old stone and new restoration is part of the interest. Next door, the huge cathedral and the Lustgarten add to the mass of the place.

Riding to and around the island is a matter of urban patience. The centre of Berlin has wide avenues such as Unter den Linden, trams with slippery rails, cobbled side streets and heavy traffic, and parking close to the museums is difficult. Motorcycle bays exist in the area, but you may do better to park a little further away and walk. Traffic lights are strict, and cyclists and scooters can appear from any direction. Weekday mornings are busier, and a quiet Sunday morning is a gentler time to ride through the centre.

Fuel stations are few in the very middle of the city, so top up on the outskirts. The district around the island has countless cafés, bars and restaurants, ranging from simple snack stalls to grand dining rooms, and the Hackescher Markt area nearby is lively in the evening. Book timed tickets in advance for the busier museums, and allow at least a morning, since one building alone can occupy a couple of hours.
t.mines of rammelsberg@51.8,10.3:
The two belong to the same story. The Upper Harz was one of the great silver and lead mining districts of Europe, and its engineers built an astonishing network of ponds, ditches and tunnels to bring water to the wheels that drove the pumps and hoists. That water system is part of the UNESCO listing, which took in Rammelsberg and Goslar in 1992 and was later extended to cover the Upper Harz. Today the ponds look like natural lakes, and it takes a moment to realise that someone dug every channel by hand.

Clausthal-Zellerfeld is a town of around fifteen thousand at some 600 metres, and it has the largest wooden church in Germany, the Marktkirche. The building is a huge, light and surprisingly warm interior, and the town has a technical university with roots in the mining academy. Winters are long, snow often lasts into March, and in summer the streets are busy with Harz walkers. For riders, there is fuel here, plenty of cafes and a base from which to make the plateau loops.

The riding is great in the right season. The Harz plateau is a place of spruce forest and open clearings, with well-surfaced roads that climb through bends and descend to river valleys. B242 and B241 are the main routes, with quieter roads to Wildemann and the Innerste valley, where forest falls steeply to a little river. Fog is common, and so is wet leaf mulch after autumn storms. A good tip is to wait for a clear morning after rain, when the whole forest smells of resin and wet earth. In summer it is a few degrees cooler than the plains, which can be a relief.

Around the town, the old mining ponds such as the Oderteich are worth a detour, with reflections of the spruce in still water. Stop for a coffee in Zellerfeld and look at the cut stone of the old administrative buildings. This is a landscape made by labour, and once you notice the ditches running along contours, you start to see them everywhere.
t.schneeberg mining landscape@50.6,12.6:
Schneeberg is a mining town high in the Erzgebirge, the Ore Mountains, which divide Saxony from Bohemia, and its history is written in silver, cobalt and uranium. A silver rush in the late fifteenth century made the town rich, and the church of St. Wolfgang, a huge Gothic hall church with a Cranach altarpiece, was the proud result. Later the miners found cobalt, which was used to colour glass and porcelain a deep blue, and Saxony became the world's main supplier of that pigment. In the twentieth century came the Wismut company, a Soviet-German enterprise that mined uranium on a massive scale in the nearby valleys, leaving scars and also the radon spa at Bad Schlema. UNESCO listed the Erzgebirge mining region, including Schneeberg, in 2019.

The riding is a reason of its own. The Ore Mountains give you rolling uplands, spruce forest and open farmland on plateaus around 600 metres, with long, well-surfaced roads and many small villages. Between Schneeberg and the Czech border there are plenty of gentle bends, and over the ridge, at Boží Dar and Abertamy on the Czech side, mining history continues into the next country. The B169 and B93 carry heavier traffic, but the lanes in between are quiet. Snow can linger into April, and fog is frequent.

Schneeberg is a town of some sixteen thousand, so fuel, food and cafes are available, with Zschorlau and Bad Schlema close. Look for the old Bergmann habit in the town. Miners' parades with uniforms and lamps are still part of local festivals, and the Christmas season here is full of wooden candle arches, pyramids and nutcrackers, since woodcarving was how miners earned money when the mines failed. There is also a surprising amount of baroque architecture, since the town burned in 1719 and was rebuilt.

Allow an hour for the church and square, and then ride out to one of the old mine sites in the woods. Heaps of waste rock, stone-lined adits, and small ponds mark the old workings. Autumn, when the spruce is dark and the birches bright, makes a good time. Bring a jacket, because even summer evenings turn cool.
t.mines of rammelsberg and historic town o:
Goslar is a small city at the northern edge of the Harz, and it is hard to overstate how much money and power sat here in the Middle Ages. The Rammelsberg hill, just south of the town, held a vast body of silver, lead, copper and zinc ore, and mining went on for about a thousand years, until the mine closed in 1988. The Ottonian and Salian emperors built their palace in Goslar because the silver paid for it. The imperial palace, the Kaiserpfalz, still stands in a big, over-restored form on the edge of the old town. UNESCO listed the mine and the old town together in 1992, and in 2010 the Upper Harz water system was added to the same site.

The town centre is a joy on foot, with crooked half-timbered houses, slate-clad facades, a market square with a glockenspiel that performs scenes from mining history, and streets that tilt like boats. The Rammelsberg itself is open as a museum, and you can take a tour underground, which is cold and damp and feels like a proper working mine. Goslar has more than forty thousand people, so fuel, parking and a decent meal are not a problem, and the nearby towns of Langelsheim and Bad Harzburg add to the choice.

Riding around Goslar is varied. To the north the land is flat and open, with fields stretching to the horizon. To the south the Harz climbs quickly, and roads such as the one up the Okertal valley offer wooded gorges, tight bends and sheer rock walls. Harz roads are generally well made but narrow, with wet leaves, mist and the occasional deer to watch for. It is busier on summer weekends and quietest in early autumn. For a dramatic climb, go up toward the Brocken region from Bad Harzburg, where the weather can differ sharply from the lowlands.

Spend an hour in the old town, then find a cafe in the market square. The local beer and a sausage of the Harz variety is a simple lunch. If you have time, take the mine tour and see where the wealth of the empire actually came from. After a morning of limestone and slate, the contrast of a hot drink and warm bread is hard to beat.
t.town of inde@25.9,-105.2:
In the high desert of northern Durango, between mountain ranges and dry basins, the town of Inde lies along the old silver road that ran from Mexico City to Santa Fe in New Mexico. The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior Land, was in use from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth, carrying silver, mercury, supplies, settlers and missionaries over 2,500 kilometres, and the Mexican sections were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2010. Inde was a stopping point on that road, with a church, a plaza and the haciendas that supplied the mining camps.

The town today is small, quiet and low-built, with adobe walls and a plain church, and it has fewer than seven hundred people. The old haciendas of the area, including the former hacienda of the Limpia Concepcion, tell the story of the great estates, with their chapels, granaries and walls, built to produce food and animals for the mines and to protect themselves from raids by the Indigenous peoples who resisted the Spanish. Now, many are in ruins, with beautiful adobe and stone arches slowly returning to earth.

The land is the Chihuahuan Desert, a country of mesquite, yucca, agave and creosote bush, with mountains on the horizon and a vast sky overhead, and it is silent except for the wind. In spring after a wet winter, the desert flowers, and in the evening, the light turns the hills purple and gold. Summers are very hot, with powerful thunderstorms in July and August, and winters can be cold, with frost at night. The best seasons are spring and autumn.

Riding here is about distance. The paved roads are long and straight, with little traffic, a decent surface and few services, and the dangers are cattle on the road, potholes, and fatigue. Carry water, food and a spare can of fuel, because villages are small and petrol stations are far apart. Santa Maria del Oro, about fifteen kilometres away, has several thousand people and the most reliable services in the immediate area, but the larger towns are further away. Avoid riding at night, and tell someone your route. If you are lucky, you may find a family selling cheese or burritos at a roadside stall.
t.the house in which luther died@51.5,11.5:
Martin Luther was born in Eisleben in November 1483 and died there in February 1546, which is either a neat symmetry or a joke the town has never tired of telling. He had travelled to his hometown in the winter of 1546 to settle a quarrel between the counts of Mansfeld, and he fell ill and died in a house near the market square after a few days. The building is now a museum, and the Sterbehaus, the house in which he died, holds items from the last days of his life, with a room where he is believed to have breathed his last. His birth house is a few minutes' walk away, and both are on the UNESCO list.

The town, officially named Lutherstadt Eisleben, sits on the edge of the Harz foothills in Saxony-Anhalt, in a region that was once rich in copper. Mining in the Mansfeld area had been a major industry for centuries, and Luther's father worked in it, which is why Luther grew up in a family tied to the mines. The market square has a statue of Luther, and St Andrew's church, where his body lay before it was taken to Wittenberg, has a pulpit from which he preached.

The riding here is quiet and modest. Roads run through low, rolling farmland, with fields of wheat and sugar beet, old mining tips and and the Süßer See, a lake, to the east. Traffic is light except in the town centre, and the countryside has a post-industrial, thoughtful feel. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and there are few crowds except around Luther anniversaries and the Reformation festivals.

Eisleben has around 24,000 people and has everything you need, with fuel, shops, and restaurants around the market. For food, a plate of Thuringian-style sausage or a bowl of bean soup is easy to find. Allow an hour for the museum. The house is a reminder that the great turning point of European history began with quarrels and sermons in places much like this, and the quiet streets here carry the weight of that story without making a fuss.
t.upper harz water management system@51.8,:
Mining needed power, and in the Upper Harz the power came from rain. The silver, lead and copper mines around Clausthal and Zellerfeld went deeper over the centuries, and the water wheels that pumped and hoisted needed a steady supply high on a plateau with no big rivers. So miners, over about seven hundred years, built a network of reservoirs, ditches and tunnels that gathered every drop of rain and snowmelt and channelled it to the wheels. Many of the ponds and ditches were made between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, and a large part still holds water, which is why the system is on the UNESCO list.

What you see on the ground is quieter than the idea. A dam with a grassy crest, a pond with spruce on its banks, a narrow ditch tracing the contour of a hillside with a path alongside. The ponds look like natural lakes, and many are used for swimming or fishing now. The ditches are easy to miss unless you know to look for a thin line of water winding through the forest. The Oderteich, a big dam from the early eighteenth century, is the best known, and the Dammgraben and Sperberhaier Damm are among the ditches that walkers follow.

Clausthal-Zellerfeld, a town of about 15,000 people only a kilometre away, was the mining capital, and has a good mining museum, a technical university that grew from the old mining academy, and one of the largest wooden churches in Germany, the Marktkirche zum Heiligen Geist. It is a practical stop for fuel, bakeries and a bed. The old tradition shows in the greeting Glück auf, which locals still use.

The riding is classic Harz. Roads climb over the plateau through spruce forest, with gentle curves, some tighter bends on the descents to Goslar and Osterode, and the occasional view down onto the flatlands. Many of the spruces have died in recent dry years, and large cleared patches show where bark beetle damage has opened the landscape. Weather matters: fog and drizzle are common, snow can arrive early and linger on the high ground, and winter closes some minor roads. Late May and September are generally the best months. Try a Harzer cheese if you dare, or a plate of Schmalzbrot with a coffee in town.
t.classical weimar@51.0,11.3:
Weimar is small, about 65,000 people, and for a few decades around 1800 it was the cultural capital of the German-speaking world. Goethe moved here in 1775 at the invitation of the young Duke Carl August, and stayed for most of his life. Schiller came later, Herder and Wieland were already in town, and together they made the little court a place where poetry, philosophy and theatre were taken very seriously. The Goethe house on the Frauenplan and Schiller's house nearby are open to visitors, and the Park an der Ilm, a landscaped garden along the river, has Goethe's garden house. The UNESCO listing covers these and other buildings of the era.

Weimar has other layers. The Anna Amalia Library, a rococo hall of books that was damaged by fire in 2004 and restored, is a sight in itself. In 1919 Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus here, the school of design that changed architecture and furniture across the world, and the same year a national assembly met in the German National Theatre to draw up the constitution of what became known as the Weimar Republic. Not far outside town, on the Ettersberg, lies the site of the Buchenwald concentration camp, a sober reminder of what followed, and a memorial there is open to visitors.

Riding to Weimar from the surrounding Thuringian countryside is easy and pleasant. Gentle roads run through farmland, small woods and villages with church spires, with a long view over the Ilm valley. It is not a technical ride, and traffic in town can be dense, with cobbles in the old centre. Park on the edge and walk, since everything is close. Erfurt, the state capital, is about 20 km west.

Practicalities are simple. Weimar has fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and plenty of rooms. The food to try is the Thuringian Rostbratwurst, grilled over charcoal and served in a roll with mustard, and the Zwiebelmarkt, the onion market in early October, is a colourful festival. Spring, when the park is in leaf, and autumn, with its golden trees, are the best times. A late afternoon walk in the Ilm park, with a coffee at one of the cafés near the market square, is a fine way to end a ride.
t.gro siedlung britz@52.4,13.5:
From above, the Hufeisensiedlung, the Horseshoe Estate, looks like a giant horseshoe wrapped around a pond, and from the ground it looks like something rarer, a housing project that people actually love. It was designed by Bruno Taut and Martin Wagner between 1925 and 1930 for a cooperative, as part of the effort in Weimar-era Berlin to give working families light, air and gardens instead of the dark tenements of the nineteenth century. Rows of low terraced houses with their own small gardens curve around a central green, and the façades are painted in strong colours, notably a long blue wall. It is one of six Berlin housing estates that UNESCO listed together in 2008 as examples of modern housing reform.

Taut was a believer in colour as a social tool, and the estate's reds, blues and whites give it a lively, cheerful feel that has survived decades of restoration. Walk through the courtyards and you find details like the garden gates, the doors, the staircases, each designed with care. Many of the houses are still occupied by tenants and owners, so be respectful and stay on the public paths. There is an information point in one of the buildings for visitors.

Britz lies in the south of Berlin, in the Neukölln district, close to the Britzer Garten, a large park laid out for a garden show in 1985, with lakes and a windmill. The riding here is city riding, with wide avenues, tram lines in places, cobbled sidestreets and heavy traffic at rush hour. Weekends are calmer, and the green areas offer a pleasant contrast. Tempelhof Field, the former airport, is close and open as a park, where cyclists and kite fliers gather on the old runways.

Fuel and supplies are easy to find in Berlin, with plenty of stations along the main roads and shops in the shopping streets of Neukölln. Nearby Gropiusstadt, a huge high-rise estate designed in the 1960s, shows a different approach to the same housing problem. For food, a Berlin currywurst or a döner kebab is the obvious snack, and the area has many Turkish and Arab cafés. A coffee and a stroll around the horseshoe is a gentle way to spend an hour.
t.mosquee sidi yeti@33.7,10.9:
Djerba is the sort of island where you can ride for an hour and never see anything higher than a date palm. The mosque of Sidi Yati sits on the flat interior, a short run from Erriadh, which is the nearest proper town, with Midoun and the capital Houmt Souk a little further out. Everything here is low, white and thick-walled, and the mosques follow the same rule: buttressed, squat, almost fortress-like, with small windows and none of the soaring minarets you might expect from the mainland.

There is a reason they look defensive. Djerba has been raided and occupied by a long list of visitors, from Normans and Spaniards to corsairs, and the island's old Ibadi community built its places of worship to be both prayer halls and refuges. Ibadism is a branch of Islam distinct from Sunni and Shia, and Djerba is one of the few places where it still shapes everyday life. The island's traditional settlement pattern, scattered farmsteads and village mosques spread across the countryside rather than packed into one centre, earned a UNESCO listing in 2023, and this is exactly the landscape that listing is about.

For the rider it means unhurried going. The roads are narrow, mostly sound, and crossed by scooters, donkeys, the occasional cart and dogs who have opinions about motorbikes. Olive groves and palms close in on both sides, with whitewashed walls marking property lines, and corners are gentle bends rather than anything you would call a challenge. Speeds stay low because the island demands it, and that suits the place. Midday heat in summer is heavy, so go early, or in the softer light of late afternoon when the lime wash turns the colour of warm butter.

Practicalities are easy. Erriadh, Midoun and Houmt Souk are all big enough to have fuel, and cafes serving mint tea or strong coffee are never far. Erriadh itself is worth a slow pass, since its walls are covered in murals from an art project that turned a quiet village into an open-air gallery. If you arrive by the Roman causeway or the ferry from the mainland, remember that Djerba has a long history as a place of trade, with a Jewish community at Hara Sghira that is among the oldest in North Africa. Take your helmet off at the mosque and look at how the buttresses are shaped. It is plain architecture, but it is plain architecture that has lasted.
t.goslar@51.9,10.4:
Goslar is the town where Harz mining became legend. For more than a thousand years, miners dug silver, lead, copper and zinc from the Rammelsberg hill just outside the town, and the wealth built an imperial city. Emperors of the Holy Roman Empire held court at the Kaiserpfalz, the great palace hall beside the old town, which was built in the eleventh century and rebuilt in the nineteenth. The Rammelsberg mine closed in 1988, after a thousand years of work, and UNESCO listed the mine and the old town in 1992, later adding the water management system of the Upper Harz.

The old town is a delight, with about fifteen hundred half-timbered houses, a market square with a town hall, and narrow lanes of slate-roofed houses. On the market square a clock chimes with a little parade of miners, and the cafes serve Harzer Kase and local beer. Goslar is also the home of Gose, a sour, salty beer named after the river that runs through the town, which is now fashionable again.

The town stands on the northern edge of the Harz, and for riders it is a gateway to a very good area. Roads climb south into the mountains, through spruce forests, to Altenau and Clausthal-Zellerfeld, and east through the valley of the Oker. The Brocken, the highest peak of the Harz, is further east. The roads are well surfaced, with long bends and gentle climbs, and the forests, many damaged by bark beetle in recent years, give wide views. Weather in the Harz can be cold and foggy even in summer.

Goslar has about forty-three thousand people, and fuel stations are easy to find on the edge of town, with Langelsheim, a smaller place, a short way along the road. It makes a good place to fill up before you go into the hills, where stations are fewer. Autumn colours are lovely, and winter brings snow to the high roads. Take an hour to walk through the old town before you set off. The town rewards slow looking.
t.luther memorials in eisleben and wittenb:
Wittenberg is a small town on the Elbe that changed Europe. In 1517, an Augustinian monk and professor of theology named Martin Luther took on the sale of indulgences, and the debate that followed became the Reformation. Tradition says he nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of the castle church, though historians still argue about whether he actually used a hammer. What is certain is that he sent them to the archbishop and that printers spread them across Germany within weeks.

The town is full of Luther. He lived in the old Augustinian monastery, now the Lutherhaus, the largest museum of Reformation history in the world, and he is buried in the castle church, with his friend Philipp Melanchthon nearby. He preached in the town church, where the altarpiece was painted by Lucas Cranach, and Cranach's house and workshop stand in the main street. UNESCO listed the Luther memorials in Wittenberg and Eisleben, the town where he was born and died, in 1996.

The setting is flat and gentle. The Elbe flows past meadows and old floodplain woods, and the roads around the town run through farmland and pine forest. The riding is easy, with straight roads, good surfaces and moderate traffic. The Fläming hills to the north have a few more curves, and the Dessau-Worlitz garden kingdom lies a short ride to the west. In spring and autumn, the light on the river is soft, and in summer the meadows are alive with birdsong.

Wittenberg has about thirty thousand people, and fuel, food and rooms are all easy to find. The old town is compact and mostly pedestrian, and the main street is lined with colourful renaissance houses. Cafes are plentiful, and the beer gardens under the chestnut trees fill up on warm evenings. Allow an afternoon for the museums, and an evening for the cafes. It is easy to walk the old town in a couple of hours.
t.melanchthon s house@51.9,12.7:
Wittenberg had two giants, and Philipp Melanchthon was the quieter one. Born in 1497 in Bretten, in southwest Germany, he came to Wittenberg at twenty-one to teach Greek at the university, and he stayed for forty-two years. He was a brilliant scholar, a shy man with a gentle manner, and he became Luther's closest collaborator. Luther was the preacher and fighter, and Melanchthon was the thinker and writer. He drafted the Augsburg Confession of 1530, the founding statement of the Lutheran church, and he reformed the German school system so thoroughly that he was called the Teacher of Germany.

His house stands in the old town, a short walk from the Lutherhaus. It was built in the 1530s, a fine renaissance building with a stepped gable, and Melanchthon lived here with his family until his death in 1560. The house is now a museum, and visitors can see his study, his library and the rooms where students and visitors sat around his table. It was listed with the other Reformation sites by UNESCO in 1996.

The setting is a calm one. The town lies on the Elbe, with meadows and woods beside the river, and the riding around it is relaxed, along flat, straight roads through farmland and pine forest. Pratau, a small village a few kilometres away, is on the river road. Rides from here go to the Bauhaus trade union school at Bernau, a masterpiece of modernist architecture, and to the great collegiate church, where Melanchthon is buried next to Luther.

Wittenberg has about thirty thousand people, so fuel and food are not difficult. Cafes line the main street, and the beer gardens under the trees are pleasant on a summer evening. The university where he taught still exists, as part of the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg, and its old buildings are a quiet place to stroll. Autumn is lovely, with soft light and mist on the river. Slow down, and read the inscriptions on the houses.
t.house with balcony access mittelbreite 1:
In the 1920s, the German architect Walter Gropius was asked to design housing for working families, and he approached it as an experiment in how to build well and cheaply. The Bauhaus school had moved to Dessau in 1925, and Gropius used the opportunity to build a whole estate at Torten, on the southern edge of town, with rows of simple concrete houses designed for mass production. A few years later, in 1930, he built a block of balcony-access houses nearby, in which flats were reached by open walkways on the outside rather than by internal stairs, a design that saved space and money.

The balcony-access houses at Torten are among the sites that make up the UNESCO World Heritage listing of the Bauhaus and its sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau, inscribed in 1996. The flats are small and efficient, with clean lines, big windows and flat roofs. Some visitors find them austere, but at the time they were a radical attempt to give ordinary people good light, air and a bit of comfort. The house at Mittelbreite is part of that world.

Dessau itself is a flat, green city on the Elbe and Mulde rivers, with about seventy-seven thousand people. The Bauhaus building, with its glass facade and workshop wing, stands in the middle of town and is the star of the story, and the Masters' Houses, where Gropius, Klee and Kandinsky lived, are set among pine trees. The countryside nearby holds the Garden Realm of Dessau-Worlitz, a landscape of English-style parks and little palaces that was among the first of its kind in Germany.

The riding is flat and easy, with straight roads through farmland, riverside meadows and pine woods, and the surface is good. The Elbe floodplain forest is a biosphere reserve, with oak woods and beavers. Fuel and food are plentiful in Dessau, with Vockerode a small village on the river. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild air and soft light. Allow time to walk through the estate, and notice how well it has aged.
t.muskauer park park muzakowski@51.5,14.7:
Muskau Park straddles a river and a border. The Neisse flows through it, and since 1945 it has been the frontier between Germany and Poland, which means that half the park lies in Bad Muskau and the other half in Leknica. Visitors walk across a reconstructed bridge from one country to the other, with no checks, and pass from the German part of the park to the Polish part in a few minutes. UNESCO listed the park as a joint site in 2004.

The park was created by Prince Hermann von Puckler-Muskau, a nobleman, writer and garden designer, who began work on it in 1815. He spent a fortune turning the estate into a landscape of meadows, trees, water and views, shaped to look as natural as possible, and when his money ran out he sold the estate and moved to Branitz, near Cottbus, where he built another park. He wrote a book on landscape gardening and travelled widely, and he was a famous character. A kind of ice cream, layered with chocolate, strawberry and vanilla, is named after him in Germany.

The Neues Schloss, the palace in the centre of the park, was damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt, and it houses a visitor centre and exhibitions. Paths wind among old oaks, along the river and over little bridges, and you can walk for hours. The town of Bad Muskau has a spa tradition, with peaty water, and the smaller Polish town of Leknica has cheap shops and cafes.

Riding here is gentle, with quiet roads through pine forest and heath, and the surface is generally good. To the south, the Jizera Mountains rise on the Czech border, with winding roads, and to the south-west lies Dresden, about a hundred kilometres away. Fuel is easy in Bad Muskau, and often cheaper on the Polish side, so check the price. Spring is lovely, when the trees are bright green, and autumn brings gold. A cup of coffee on the terrace is a good start to the day.
t.luther hall@51.9,12.7:
