Wittenberg's Luther Hall is a big, plain, slightly forbidding building, and that is part of its charm. It began as the Augustinian monastery where Martin Luther lived as a friar, and after the Reformation it became his family home, given to him and to his wife Katharina von Bora, a former nun who ran the household with considerable firmness. You can picture a crowded place: students at the table, guests, children, a brewery's worth of hospitality. Luther taught at the university here, preached in the town church, and, according to tradition, nailed his ninety-five theses to the door of the Castle Church in 1517. Wittenberg thus became one of the places where the modern world was argued into being.

Getting here is easy and gentle. The town lies on the Elbe in the flat open country of Saxony-Anhalt, with the Fläming hills to the north and the Dübener Heide to the south. Roads are wide, quiet and often lined by old avenues of trees, a feature of this part of eastern Germany that gives long straights an odd, cathedral-like shade. There are almost no real corners, so this is relaxed riding, with the wind as the main variable. A spring or autumn day, with low sun across the fields and the smell of ploughed earth, suits it best.

Wittenberg is a proper town of around thirty thousand people, so fuel, food and coffee are never a worry. The old centre is long and straight along the main street, with colourful Renaissance houses, among them the homes of the painter Lucas Cranach, who also served as mayor and ran an apothecary and a printing business. Park at the edge, walk the cobbles, and take your time with the big brick church at either end of the old town.

Pratau and Teuchel, the villages nearby, are quiet, small and rural, useful for a peaceful stop beside the river dike. The Elbe cycle path runs along the water here, and on a warm day you will share the flood plain with plenty of cyclists. It is a gentle place, with a deeply serious history behind it.
t.siedlung schillerpark@52.6,13.3:
Siedlung Schillerpark is a block of red-brick housing in Berlin's Wedding district, and it is easy to ride straight past without grasping what it is. It was designed by Bruno Taut, one of the great figures of German modernism, and built in the later 1920s as the first of the new housing estates that Berlin's reform-minded councils and cooperatives raised to give working families light, air and a balcony. Today it sits among the six Berlin Modernism Housing Estates on the UNESCO World Heritage list. It is modest in scale, with long brick walls, rounded corners, small balconies and clear colour, and its calm is the point.

The estate takes its name from the Schillerpark next door, a green square of old trees and lawns, named after the poet Friedrich Schiller. Wedding itself is a district with a working-class history, once a heartland of the German left, and still lively, multicultural and a bit rough around the edges, with a food scene that ranges from currywurst to Turkish bakeries. It is a good place for a quick lunch, and the nearby streets are full of the sort of cafes where nobody will mind boots and a helmet.

Riding in Berlin is mostly about patience. The roads are wide, but traffic and tram tracks demand attention, especially in wet weather when the rails get slick. Cobbled sections are still around in the older streets. Berlin is a city of cyclists, and bike lanes sometimes appear without warning at the edge of your lane. Parking a motorbike is easy and often free on the pavement edges, as long as you leave room for pedestrians. Fuel is no problem anywhere in the city.

Allow time to walk around the buildings rather than just look from the saddle. The details are in the stairwells, the doors and the colour accents, which Taut chose with care. This is one of those places where the idea matters more than the monument: decent homes, for ordinary people, done beautifully.
t.mosquee welhi@33.8,10.8:
The little mosques of Djerba look like fortresses that have turned to prayer. Whitewashed, with thick sloping buttresses, small domes and short squat minarets, they stand among olive groves and date palms across this flat Tunisian island, and they belong to a particular faith, the Ibadi branch of Islam, whose followers settled here in the early centuries after the Arab conquest and developed a distinctive local tradition.

Djerba entered the UNESCO list in 2023, not for any one monument but for its whole settlement pattern, with farms, villages, mosques, markets and wells scattered over a landscape without rivers. Everything depended on rainwater, stored in underground cisterns, and the houses, called menzels, stand on their own plots surrounded by walls, with olive trees, palms and vegetable plots. It is a dispersed, tidy, sun-bleached world.

Erriadh, the nearby village of some fourteen thousand people, has an unusual double character. It contains the Ghriba synagogue, one of the oldest in North Africa and a place of annual pilgrimage by Jews from many countries, and since 2014 it has also been a gallery of street art, called Djerbahood, with murals by artists from around the world on the whitewashed walls. The mixture of faiths and art suits an island where Jews, Muslims and Christians lived side by side for centuries.

Riding in Djerba is easy and slow. The island is flat, the roads are good, and the speed is set by scooters, trucks and sleepy dogs. Fuel is plentiful in Houmt Souk and Midoun, and every village has a shop for water and bread. The wind can be strong, and in summer the heat is fierce, so ride early and rest at midday. Spring and autumn are best.

Try a brik, a crisp pastry filled with egg and tuna, and strong sweet mint tea, preferably under an olive tree.
t.zone cotiere inhabitee@33.9,10.7:
Most of Djerba is cultivated, and then the cultivation stops. On the island's northern shore, where the olive groves and palm gardens run out, a strip of shallow sea, salt flat, sand and scrub stretches along the coast with hardly a building on it, and this is the uninhabited coastal zone that the island's heritage listing includes in its protected landscape. In 2023, UNESCO recognised Djerba for the way its people shaped a territory without rivers or springs, and the empty shore is part of that story, because it shows what the settlers started with and what they chose to leave alone.

The edge of the island is a place for birds. Flamingos, herons, spoonbills and waders feed in the shallows, particularly in winter and on migration, and the mudflats at low tide glitter in the light. The air smells of salt and seaweed, and the horizon is huge and level. There are fishing methods here that are very old, including traps of palm fronds set in the shallows, and fishermen walk out at low tide to check them.

The nearest town is Houmt Souk, the island's capital, about ten kilometres away, with a population of about sixty thousand, with a bustling market, a small fort, Borj el Kebir, at the harbour, and a Tower of Skulls, built in the sixteenth century, that is a reminder of the island's Mediterranean wars. Fuel, food and repairs are there. Small roads lead toward the coast, often ending in sand or at a fisherman's shack, and surfaces can be rough, so a gentle pace and a small bike are best.

The island is connected to the mainland by a causeway, said to date from Roman times, and by a short ferry. The Mediterranean wind, the sirocco in summer, can be searing, and in winter, storms can sweep in from the north.

Spring, with wildflowers, and autumn are the best seasons. Take water, a hat and binoculars. Do not drive on soft sand or salt flats without local advice, because bikes sink and tides rise. Dine on grilled fish in Houmt Souk, and look for the island's famous octopus.
t.zone temlel@33.8,11.0:
Midoun is the second town of Djerba, and Temlel lies just beside it, a rural zone of walled plots, olive trees, palms and whitewashed houses in the east of the island. It is the kind of place that a guidebook would skip, and yet it is exactly what the island's World Heritage listing is about. In 2023 UNESCO recognised Djerba as an outstanding example of how a community lived on an island with no rivers, by dividing the land into small family holdings, each with its well, its cistern, its olive press or oven, and its orchard, grouped in neighbourhoods called houmas, around a mosque and a market.

Walk or ride the lanes and you see the walls of palm trunks and mud, the arched doorways, the domed cisterns on rooftops and the careful rows of olive trees, many of them centuries old. Djerba has been known for its olive oil since antiquity, and the groves still make a living for many families. The island is said to be the land of the lotus eaters in Homer's Odyssey, where Odysseus's men forgot their homes, which locals will gladly mention with a smile.

Midoun has the fuel stations, cafes and shops, and its weekly market on Friday is lively, a good place to buy pottery, woven baskets and spices. The tourist hotels line the beaches further north-east, and the roads between them and the villages are busy in summer with taxis, buses and quad bikes. Away from the coast, the lanes are quiet, narrow and often unpaved.

Riding here is gentle and flat. Watch for sand on the road, hidden junctions, and dogs, goats and children. Summer is hot, around thirty-five degrees in August, so mornings and evenings are best. Winter is mild but can be wet and windy. Spring brings flowers among the olive groves, and autumn is sweet and calm.

Try fresh bread baked in a clay oven, olive oil poured over it, with a glass of mint tea.
t.mosquee louta@33.7,10.9:
In the central and southern parts of the island, among olive groves and sandy lanes, stand small whitewashed mosques of the Ibadi tradition, with thick walls, simple domes and sometimes a short minaret and an outer stair. Some were built as places of refuge, with storerooms and wells inside, to serve scattered communities in times of raids, and others as neighbourhood mosques for a cluster of farms. Together they are among the features for which the island of Djerba was added to the UNESCO list in 2023.

Ibadism is a very early branch of Islam, neither Sunni nor Shia, with roots in the first century of the faith. Its followers have lived in Djerba for more than a thousand years, along with communities in Oman and parts of the Algerian Sahara, and their mosques are modest, austere buildings with little decoration, an expression of the movement's emphasis on simplicity. Visitors should remember these are working places of worship, and non-Muslims are usually welcome only to look from the outside, or in specific circumstances.

The countryside around is Djerba at its most traditional, a flat, sunny landscape of olive trees, date palms and low whitewashed walls, with windmills and wells here and there. The nearest town is Midoun, about twelve kilometres away, which has fuel, shops and restaurants. Roads in the interior are narrow and sometimes sandy, and you share them with scooters, farm carts and wandering sheep.

Part of the pleasure of Djerba is its potters, particularly in the southern village of Guellala, where families have been making clay jars and pots in the same way for generations. You can watch the potters at work, and buy pieces to take home, though a bike has limited luggage space.

The Mediterranean climate is mild, with hot summers and short wet winters. Spring is the best time, with wildflowers, and October is warm and quiet. The wind can blow strongly, especially in winter, so a windproof layer helps. If you stop at a roadside stall, try a handful of fresh dates or a glass of palm sap, which is sold in the morning.
t.zone khazroun sedghiene guecheine@33.8,1:
Khazroun, Sedghiene and Guecheine are the kinds of names that appear on a heritage dossier and nowhere else, and they refer to zones of the island's countryside that make up one part of the World Heritage listing. Djerba was inscribed by UNESCO in 2023 as a cultural landscape, and the list names several zones, each a patch of the traditional pattern in good condition.

They lie in the east-central part of Djerba, a few kilometres from the town of Midoun, in a flat, dry, farmed landscape with sandy soil. The pattern is the same everywhere: a scatter of family compounds, each walled, each with its well and cistern, olive trees, palms, small fields for barley and vegetables, and sometimes a small private oratory. Lanes wind between the walls, edged by prickly pear and agave, and every few hundred metres stands a whitewashed mosque or a shrine to a local holy man, a marabout, with a small dome.

What strikes the visitor is how quiet and orderly it all is. There are no big towns in the countryside, only a loose weave of homes and gardens, held together by shared water, shared markets and shared mosques. In the past, the men of Djerba often migrated to work as traders in other parts of Tunisia and abroad, and women ran the farms, which helped to shape the island's culture. The traditions of weaving, pottery and olive oil, along with the Berber language, which is still spoken by some communities, survive in the island's villages.

For riding, the lanes are flat and slow, shared with scooters and the occasional goat. Midoun has fuel and food, and the island is small enough that nothing is far away. Sand blows across the tarmac, so take care on bends. Summer heat is intense, and August nights stay warm. Spring and autumn are better.

Try the island's lamb, slow-cooked with spices, and the sweet pastries made with dates and honey. A cup of tea, thick with sugar and mint, is the standard welcome.
t.oranienburg@52.8,13.2:
Oranienburg is a town on the Havel river, a short way north of Berlin, and it carries two very different histories side by side. On one side there is the palace, built in the seventeenth century for Louise Henriette of Orange, the Dutch-born wife of the Elector of Brandenburg, who gave the town its name. It was the first baroque palace in Brandenburg, and its Dutch influence is seen in the proportions and brick. The town became known as Oranienburg, the castle of Orange, and the palace now houses a museum and gardens.

On the other side is a darker chapter. In 1936 the Nazi regime opened the Sachsenhausen concentration camp at the town's edge, and tens of thousands of prisoners died there. The site is now a memorial and museum, and a visit is sober, serious and well worth the time. Many people combine it with a trip from Berlin, and the surrounding town carries the memory in quiet ways. Allow a few hours and treat the visit with the gravity it deserves.

As a starting point for a ride into the Ruppiner Land, this is a handy exit from the capital. North of the town, the roads fall into a rhythm of straight, tree-lined avenues, a typical feature of Brandenburg, with old chestnuts, limes and cherries standing at the roadside. Sandy soil, pine plantations and glittering lakes fill the landscape, and the pace is calm. Surfaces are generally good, though some are patched, and avenues can be dappled with light that hides potholes. Traffic is light on weekdays and busy on summer weekends as Berliners head for the water. Spring and early autumn are pleasantly mild.

The ride continues to Neuruppin, the home town of the writer Theodor Fontane, and on to Rheinsberg, where Frederick the Great spent happy years as crown prince in a small lakeside palace. Oranienburg has fuel stations, a supermarket and cafes, and the suburban train line to Berlin makes it easy to leave a car. Leegebruch, a smaller town nearby, has basic services. Top up here before heading out, as pumps thin out in the forest.
t.mosquee imghar@33.7,10.7:
Djerba's mosques look like small fortresses, which is more or less what they once were. Imghar, in the interior of the island, is one of the group of Ibadi mosques whose whitewashed walls, thick buttresses and low domes give them the air of a farmhouse that has been trained for war. Ibadism is a branch of Islam that predates the Sunni-Shia split, and it survives today mainly in Oman, parts of North Africa and here on Djerba, where it has shaped the island's culture for over a thousand years.

The mosques were built to serve a scattered farming community, with each hamlet, or menzel, having its own place of prayer, and some of them doubled as schools, courts and refuges. Walls are plain, with few windows, and the interior is a cool, dim hall of low vaults supported on heavy pillars, unadorned and quiet. The simplicity reflects a puritan tradition, and many mosques have a small minaret that looks more like a watchtower. Some have underground prayer rooms for use in summer heat, and many are still in use. Non-Muslims are usually not admitted to the interior, so respect the signs and enjoy the architecture from outside.

The ride across the island is flat and easy, along roads lined with palms, olives and whitewashed walls, past small farms and tiled houses. Surfaces are generally good, but the roads are narrow, and locals ride scooters without helmets and drive fast. The wind from the sea can be strong, and sand blows across the road in some places. Be careful at roundabouts, and in the heat of midday expect to see few people on the street. Djerba is small enough that every point is within an hour of any other, so you can ride a loop of several mosques in a day.

Fuel is easy, with stations in the main towns, and the island's capital, Houmt Souk, is the best place for repairs and food. Erriadh, fourteen kilometres away, is a larger village with cafés and a lively market. Try a plate of couscous with fish, or brik, a fried pastry filled with egg, followed by a glass of strong, sweet mint tea.

Spring and autumn offer pleasant temperatures; midsummer can be fiercely hot.
t.eglise saint nicolas@33.9,10.9:
Houmt Souk is the island's main town, a place of whitewashed arcades, small squares and a busy fishing harbour, and the church of St Nicolas gives it a reminder that Djerba has never been exclusively one thing. The island has been home to Muslim, Jewish and Christian communities for centuries, and its location on the trade routes of the central Mediterranean brought Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs, Normans, Spaniards and Ottomans. In 1560, a Spanish and allied fleet was defeated nearby by an Ottoman force under Dragut, and the victors built a tower of the skulls of the dead beside the harbour, which stood until the nineteenth century. A monument now marks the site.

The old town has a covered souk, with stalls selling leather, silver jewellery, pottery, spices and sponges, and the craft workshops are as much a pleasure to watch as the goods are to buy. The fort of Borj el Kebir, at the water's edge, is a well-preserved Ottoman and Spanish structure with a small museum. Cafés around the harbour serve fresh fish, and the fishermen unload their catch in the early morning.

Riding in town requires patience. The streets are narrow, with traffic and pedestrians in the souk area, and parking is limited. A good rule is to park outside the old centre and walk. On the surrounding roads, watch for scooters that appear from side streets without warning, and for sand on the surface after a windy day. Sun and heat in summer are intense, and drinking water is worth carrying.

Fuel stations are numerous, and the town has everything from supermarkets to garages, as it is the commercial heart of an island of some one hundred and fifty thousand people. The airport is not far, and the causeway at El Kantara, a Roman-built link to the mainland, is an easy half-day ride to the south-east.

Evenings, when the light softens and the arcades fill, are when the old town feels most alive.
t.mosquee guellala@33.7,10.8:
Guellala is a potters' village, and has been for as long as anyone can remember. The clay beneath the hills of southern Djerba is a fine, pale material that fires to a warm terracotta, and the workshops around the village shape it into jars, plates, oil lamps and large amphorae, still using techniques similar to those of Roman times. Potters work at wheels in open yards, stack their wares to dry in the sun, and fire them in kilns fuelled with olive wood, and visitors can stand and watch. A small museum about local culture lies a short drive away.

The Mosque of Guellala belongs to the island's group of Ibadi places of worship, whitewashed and heavily built, and the contrast between its plain walls and the colourful pottery workshops is part of the pleasure of the village. The village sits on an upland ridge at the south end of the island, and from there you can look out over olive groves, palm trees and fields toward the sea, and on a clear day you can see the Tunisian mainland as a low line on the horizon.

The roads around Guellala are among the best for riding on Djerba, with gentle bends, mild gradients and light traffic. The coast road along the southern shore passes beaches of pale sand, some quiet, some busy with hotels. Surfaces are good but sandy at the edges, and in the summer months the heat can reach forty degrees, so rest in the shade at midday. Keep an eye out for goats, donkeys and the occasional camel, which are used for tourist rides near the beaches.

Fuel is available in Erriadh, about eleven kilometres away, or in Houmt Souk, so top up before heading south. Cafés in the village sell mint tea and pastries, and small restaurants serve fish grilled over charcoal.

Buy a piece of pottery if you can, although the bigger jars are too awkward for a bike, and small bowls and lamps pack better.
t.mosquee medrajen@33.9,11.0:
The east of Djerba is the island's holiday coast, with long beaches, a line of big hotels and the busy market town of Midoun just inland, but the older island is not far behind. The Mosque of Medrajen, in the countryside between Midoun and the sea, belongs to the group of fortified Ibadi mosques that dot the interior, and it reminds visitors that the island was farmland and olive groves long before it was a resort.

Midoun, with about thirty-two thousand people, is the island's second town, and on Friday its weekly market fills the streets with stalls selling vegetables, spices, fabric, pottery and animals. Locals come to buy and sell, and visitors can browse and bargain in a good-natured way. The town also has a small museum of folk art and traditions, and cafés where men play cards and drink tea.

The coast road is a long ride, flat and straight, with palms and low white houses on one side and the sea beyond the dunes on the other. Beaches are broad and white, with shallow, warm water, and the Mediterranean here is gentle. The flip side of the resort strip is traffic, with tourist coaches, rental scooters and quad bikes, and the roads can be busy in high season, so look out for sudden stops and turns. Inland, in the olive groves, the lanes are quieter, sandy at the edges and often shaded by palms. In midsummer, afternoon heat is harsh, and wind can lift sand across the road.

Fuel and services are easy to find in Midoun, which has stations, banks and workshops. Restaurants along the coast serve grilled fish, and in the town you can find simple places selling brik, lablabi chickpea soup and fresh bread. The sweet shops sell makroudh, date-filled semolina pastries, and the best are warm.

Go in the shoulder seasons, April to May or October, when the weather is warm and the beaches are less crowded.
t.mosquee mthanya@33.7,10.8:
Mthanya is another of Djerba's fortress mosques, tucked among olive groves and low white houses south of Erriadh, and like its neighbours it is built for strength rather than show. The island has dozens of these Ibadi mosques, and UNESCO recognised them in 2023 as part of the cultural landscape of Djerba, along with the farm hamlets, the markets and the water systems that make this island such a distinct human habitat.

Erriadh, the nearest big village, is a good place to see how the island's communities have lived side by side. Its old name was Hara Sghira, the Small Quarter, and it has been home to a Jewish community for many centuries. Close by stands the Ghriba synagogue, one of the oldest in Africa, which draws pilgrims from across the world each spring, and its blue-tiled interior glows in the light that filters through the windows. The village has also become known for street murals, painted by artists from around the world on the whitewashed walls, which give a modern flavour to the old streets.

Djerba itself has an old tradition of legend. In Homer, the Lotus-eaters lived on an island where visitors who ate the lotus forgot their homes, and the Greeks identified that island with Djerba, which gave the place a reputation for hospitality and for forgetting time. You can believe it on a warm afternoon with a glass of tea in the shade.

The riding is easy and flat, along quiet country roads shaded by palms and bordered by prickly pear. Surfaces are good, though patched, and sand drifts across the road in places. Local drivers are quick and inclined to overtake in the wrong places, so keep to the right and stay alert at junctions. The island is small, and getting lost is not much of a risk, though signs are not always clear.

Fuel is easy in Erriadh and in Houmt Souk, and the hotels and guesthouses are plentiful. Try fresh dates, olives and olive oil from local farms, and the island's spicy harissa.

Spring brings blooms in the gardens and mild days, making it a fine time to visit.
t.strausberg@52.6,13.9:
Strausberg is the last proper town before Berlin turns into Brandenburg, and it knows how to be useful. It sits on the shore of a long lake, the Straussee, about thirty kilometres east of the capital, with the S-Bahn running straight in, and about twenty-six thousand people live here. The medieval centre kept a stretch of its town wall and the brick gothic Marienkirche, and the little ferry across the lake, the Strausberg ferry, is one of the nicest short crossings in the region. The town also runs one of the smallest tram networks in Germany, a single line that has served for a century.

The place had a more serious role in the recent past. During the Cold War, the headquarters of the East German Ministry of National Defence stood on the edge of town, and the area was a closed military district, with barracks and an airfield. Those days have gone, and today the lakeside is a place for walking, rowing and cafés, and the town functions as a commuter suburb with a pleasant setting.

From here, the ride east leads into the Märkische Schweiz, the Brandenburg Switzerland, a hilly nature park of beech woods, small lakes and glacial ridges that is a favourite for Berliners at weekends. The name is generous, since the hills are low, but the landscape of rolling ground, forests and still water after the pancake flatness around Berlin is a real contrast. Buckow, the little spa town in the middle, was the home of the playwright Bertolt Brecht and the actress Helene Weigel, whose summer house is open to visitors. Roads are narrow, curving between lakes and trees, and the surface is generally good, with some old cobbled stretches in villages.

Strausberg is a good place for fuel, supermarkets and bakeries before leaving the city's orbit, since villages in the park have fewer services. Weekends in summer are busy with cyclists and families, so early starts are rewarded. The best seasons are spring, when beech leaves turn fresh green, and autumn, when the forests glow copper. Stop for coffee by the water and a slice of cake before heading east.
t.ribnitz damgarten@54.2,12.4:
Ribnitz-Damgarten is really two towns that were stitched together by a river. The Recknitz, sluggish and brown as it slides toward the Saaler Bodden lagoon, was for centuries a border: Ribnitz belonged to Mecklenburg, Damgarten to Pomerania, and the two places looked across the water with different rulers and different habits. They merged only in 1950, and the bridge that joins them is still the most important thing in town. It sits on the old main road to the Baltic coast, at the neck of the Fischland-Darß-Zingst peninsula, so nearly everyone riding toward the beaches has to pass through.

The town's best-known attraction is the German Amber Museum, in a former convent. The Baltic produces the finest fossil resin in the world, formed in forests that stood here over thirty million years ago, and pieces of amber with ancient insects trapped in them are the star exhibits. After storms in winter, amber still washes up on the beach, and local hunters walk the strandline with torches. A short way out of town, the bird park at Marlow has a big collection of exotic species and is popular with families.

For the ride, the interest begins as the road crosses onto the peninsula. The B105 runs along a thin strip of land between the Baltic and the Bodden lagoons, through beech and pine forest, past thatched cottages and artists' villages. The roads are flat and generally in good condition, with long, easy bends. Summer weekends bring slow queues of holiday traffic, so ride midweek or early in the morning if you can. In October the area fills with cranes, as tens of thousands gather in the lagoons on their way south, a great sight at dawn.

With seventeen thousand people, Ribnitz-Damgarten has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and smoked-fish stalls, so it is a sensible place to top up before the peninsula, where services are thinner and prices higher. Try smoked fish with potatoes, and sea buckthorn drinks, a local speciality. The wind off the Baltic can be fresh, and the light, especially at the end of the day, is clear and silvery.
t.eutin lake road@54.1,10.6:
Eutin is a small town that carries itself like a larger one, thanks to a history of bishops and dukes. For centuries it was the seat of the prince-bishops of Lübeck, who made the place their country residence, and later it belonged to the Dukes of Oldenburg. Their legacy is a moated castle beside the Großer Eutiner See, with a landscaped park around it, and a town centre of cobbled lanes, a market square and brick gabled houses. The composer Carl Maria von Weber was born here in 1786, and every summer an opera festival is staged on the lake in his honour, with the castle gardens as a backdrop.

The lake road is the point. It runs through the region known as Holsteinische Schweiz, or Holstein Switzerland, a name that makes locals smile a little, since the highest point, the Bungsberg, reaches just over a hundred and sixty metres. But what the hills lack in height they make up for in variety. This is glacial landscape, shaped by ice-age moraines that left behind a jumble of small hills, hollows, lakes and boggy valleys. The roads wind between them, through beech woods, past reed-fringed water and along tree-lined avenues, with views of the lakes opening between the trunks. For northern Germany, it is rich, rolling riding, with short, tight curves in the woods and gentle grades.

The surface is mostly good, but many of the lanes are narrow and tree-shaded, so patches of moss, damp leaves and fallen twigs can catch you out after rain. Cyclists and walkers share the roads in summer, particularly around Eutin and Malente, and the lake is a popular place for sailing and swimming. Early mornings are best, when the water is still and the mist drifts across, and the autumn colours in the beech woods are superb.

Eutin is known as the Rose Town, because of its gardens, and it has a population of around seventeen thousand, so fuel, bakeries and cafes are no trouble. A slice of cake in the market square, with a view of the lake, is the traditional way to spend an hour. The coast of the Baltic, with its seaside resorts, is only a short ride east, so a lake-and-sea day is easy to put together.
t.hamburg@53.5,10.0:
Harburg is the part of Hamburg that most visitors never see, and that is its charm. It sits on the south bank of the Elbe, across the water from the centre, and for centuries it was a separate town in another state, a port, a manufacturing centre and a river crossing in its own right. Today it is a district of Hamburg with a university of technology, old warehouses converted into offices and an inner harbour with a mix of rusted cranes and new apartments. Beyond lies the Harburg Hills, a low wooded ridge, and then the heathland of Lower Saxony.

Riders who come back to Hamburg from the heath know the end of the day well. The roads from the Lüneburg Heath run north through pine woods and farmland and into the suburbs, and then come the Elbe bridges, with the vast container port spread out on either side, a steel landscape of gantry cranes, stacked boxes and ships that are bigger than any building you have ever seen. The Köhlbrand Bridge, a long cable-stayed span, carries traffic high above the harbour at night, and the lights below are an unexpected pleasure. The traffic is heavy at rush hour, so plan your return time.

Hamburg is Germany's second city and its biggest port, and the harbour has shaped its character for a thousand years. Merchants of the Hanseatic League made the city rich, and the title Free and Hanseatic City is still in its official name. The people are known for a dry, reserved humour and an indifference to weather, and there is a local saying that there is no bad weather, only the wrong clothes. A Fischbrötchen, a bread roll with pickled herring or smoked salmon, is the standard quick lunch.

Fuel is plentiful in Harburg and on the main roads in and out. Parking is tight in the centre, so look for garages on the edge. The best time to ride the heath is late summer, when the heather blooms purple, and the best time to see the port is at dusk, from the harbour promenade, when the lights come on and the ferries cross in the dark.
t.church of st wiperti@51.8,11.1:
Quedlinburg is a town that survived by being overlooked. It escaped the worst of the wars and the building booms, and so it has more than thirteen hundred half-timbered houses, from the late Middle Ages to the nineteenth century, packed into a tangle of cobbled lanes at the foot of the Harz mountains. UNESCO listed the town in 1994, and walking through it, you feel as though you have fallen into a picture book of a German town, with leaning facades, carved beams and window boxes.

The church of Saint Wiperti sits a short way from the castle hill, and its crypt is one of the oldest in Germany. It dates from the tenth century, and the story of the place goes back to the time of the Ottonian kings, the dynasty that founded the Holy Roman Empire. Henry the Fowler, the first of them, died in 936 and was buried on the castle hill above, and his widow Mathilde founded a community of canonesses there that became one of the richest and most powerful convents in the realm. Wiperti is simpler, a place of stone and quiet, with a low crypt where the vault rests on short columns. Step inside, and the air is cold and the sound muffled, and you can well believe it has been a place of prayer for a thousand years.

The road from here leads east toward Naumburg, with its great cathedral and its famous statues of the founders. The Harz foothills around Quedlinburg are easy riding, with gentle bends, tree-lined avenues and fields of wheat and rapeseed. Nearby, a spectacular rock ridge called the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, runs for kilometres across the landscape in a line of jagged sandstone, with a path along the top. Further south, the Harz proper has tighter roads and forest, with the Brocken rising above, and the narrow-gauge steam railway puffs around its flanks.

Quedlinburg has nearly twenty-three thousand people, with fuel on the edges and plenty of cafés and restaurants in the centre. Try a Harz specialty such as a hearty sausage dish or a slice of the local cake, and the town is also known for seeds and flower breeding, with big seed companies in the area. Cobbles in the old town are rough, so park outside and walk. Advent markets are popular, and the town is packed at weekends in December, so choose a weekday in spring or autumn for the best light.
t.hamburg@53.6,10.0:
Hamburg opens up to the water. The Elbe runs through the city, the port covers a large chunk of it, and the harbour front is a long working landscape of cranes, container ships, tugs and ferries, with the sound of horns carrying across the water at night. The old warehouse district, the Speicherstadt, is a block of red-brick buildings on oak piles, built in the 1880s and now partly part of a UNESCO listing, with canals running between them and gabled facades reflecting in the water. Next to it, the HafenCity is a modern district whose centrepiece is the Elbphilharmonie, a concert hall in the shape of a glass wave on top of an old warehouse, opened in 2017 after many delays and a scandalous overrun in costs.

The city has a mix of moods. The Reeperbahn is a famous street of bars, clubs and theatres in St Pauli, where the Beatles played in their early years, and on a Sunday morning, the fish market opens at dawn and is a place of loud stalls, hot coffee and people coming home from the night before. The Alster, two lakes in the middle of town, is surrounded by fine villas and parks, where sailing boats cross the water in summer. Churches such as the Michel, with a green copper tower, dominate the skyline, and the old tunnel under the Elbe, built in 1911, still lets pedestrians walk under the river.

From Hamburg, the ride goes north-east toward Lübeck, the old Hanseatic capital, with a Gothic brick centre and its Holstentor gate. The road passes through the farmland of Schleswig-Holstein, flat, open and often windy, with brick villages, thatched farmhouses and long avenues. It is a relaxed ride, with moderate traffic and a good surface, and the sea is never far. In the city itself, traffic is heavy, parking is difficult, and a few tunnel and bridge routes can be blocked by incidents, so allow time for the Elbe crossings.

Fuel is easy outside the centre and on the main roads. Eat a fish roll on the quayside or a plate of Labskaus, a salty mash of corned beef and potato, and have a coffee in a harbour café. Summer is the high season, but spring and autumn are quieter, with sharp light on the water. Rain can arrive at any moment, so a waterproof layer is not optional.
In 1919, in a small and rather provincial city best known as the home of Goethe and Schiller, an architect called Walter Gropius opened a school that changed the look of the modern world. The Bauhaus aimed to unite art and craft, to bring painters, sculptors and designers into the workshop and to design for ordinary people, and in Weimar it attracted teachers such as Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky and Oskar Schlemmer. The school moved to Dessau in 1925 after local political pressure, and then to Berlin, until the Nazis closed it in 1933, but in those fourteen years it set the course for modern architecture, furniture and graphic design.

The UNESCO listing covers several sites in Weimar and Dessau. Among them is the Haus am Horn, a small experimental house built for the Bauhaus exhibition of 1923, a compact cube with a central living room lit from above and a kitchen designed for efficiency. It stands in a park on the edge of town, plain and bright, and shows what the young designers thought a modern home should look like. The main school building, a larger structure designed by the Belgian architect Henry van de Velde, now belongs to the university, and the city also has the Bauhaus Museum, opened in 2019.

Weimar itself is a city of paradoxes. It was the centre of German classical literature, with the homes of Goethe and Schiller, the park along the Ilm river and the Anna Amalia Library, and it gave its name to the republic of 1919. About eight kilometres north, on the Ettersberg hill, lies the site of the Buchenwald concentration camp, a sobering memorial that shows how close the highest culture can lie to the darkest barbarism. Many visitors combine both visits in a single day, and they should leave time.

The roads around the city run through gentle Thuringian countryside, rolling fields, small woods and villages with brick-red roofs, and the surface is generally good. Weimar has about sixty-five thousand people, with fuel on the main roads and a wealth of cafés. Try a Thuringian bratwurst from a stall on the market square, grilled over charcoal and served in a bun with mustard. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the onion market in October fills the streets with braided onions and music.
t.historic centres of stralsund and wismar:
Stralsund and Wismar were two of the great ports of the Hanseatic League, the trading alliance that dominated the Baltic in the Middle Ages, and UNESCO lists their old centres together. Both are built of brick, because there is no stone on the north German plain, and both have the high Gothic churches and gabled merchants' houses that tell of a wealth built on herring, grain, timber and salt. Stralsund sits on the Strelasund, the narrow strait that separates the mainland from the island of Rügen, and it is the larger and more dramatic of the two.

The church of Saint Mary, with a tower rising about a hundred and four metres, was for a short time in the seventeenth century the tallest building in the world, after a spire was added in the mid-1600s, though lightning later destroyed the top and the roof was rebuilt. Its brick bulk dominates the skyline. In the old market, the Town Hall has a decorative gabled facade pierced with round windows, a trick to reduce wind pressure, and it is a good example of north German brick Gothic at its showiest. In 1628, Stralsund held out against the army of Wallenstein, who famously said he would take it even if it were chained to heaven. He failed.

The harbour is a pleasure for walkers, with the three-masted sailing ship Gorch Fock moored at the quay and a big modern aquarium, the Ozeaneum, behind. From the town, a long bridge carries the road across the strait to Rügen, the largest German island, where chalk cliffs and beech forests lie at Jasmund. This is where the ride heads, in the direction of the Danish island of Møns Klint, which shares a geology of white chalk. Roads in the region are flat and straight, with long avenues of lime trees and wind that can be fierce on the coast.

Stralsund has almost sixty thousand people, with fuel on the edge of town, plenty of cafés and fish restaurants, and small hotels in the centre. Try a fish roll with pickled herring, or fried plaice with potatoes. The bridge to Rügen can be busy in summer, and a queue is likely on Friday evening, so go early. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear light on the water, while summer weekends are packed with holidaymakers.
t.schwerin residence ensemble@53.6,11.4:
Schwerin Castle looks too much like a fairy-tale to be real, and in a sense it is not quite old enough: the present building, a mix of Renaissance, Gothic and French chateau styles, was built in the mid-nineteenth century for the Grand Duke Friedrich Franz II, who wanted a palace that looked like something from the Loire. It stands on an island in the Schweriner See, a large lake that stretches away in all directions, linked to the town by a causeway and a bridge, and the whole ensemble is reflected in the water on a calm evening. Today it houses the parliament of the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

UNESCO listed the residence ensemble, the castle with its gardens, the nearby buildings and the palace park, as an outstanding example of nineteenth-century historicism, a time when architects borrowed freely from the past. The gardens include a baroque canal, a neat orangery and a grotto, with tall old trees and swans on the water. A short walk away, the cathedral is the highest church in the region, a brick Gothic building whose tower, rebuilt in the nineteenth century, rises to about a hundred and seventeen metres, and from its gallery you can see the lake and the countryside for miles.

The old town is small and pleasant, with narrow streets, half-timbered houses and a market square, and a lakeside promenade where people walk at the weekend. The lake is the fourth largest in Germany, with eleven islands and quiet shores, where cyclists, swimmers and sailors take over in summer. The ride goes on to Wismar, the other Hanseatic city, with its great brick churches, and the road across the countryside is easy, with gentle bends, avenues of trees and fields of rapeseed.

Schwerin has nearly a hundred thousand people, with fuel stations on the main roads and plenty of cafés near the castle. Local food includes fish from the lake, such as smoked eel and zander, and the region's famous sea buckthorn drinks. Parking in the old town is limited, so leave the bike at a car park near the lakeside and walk. In July the castle hosts open-air concerts and a festival, and the town fills with visitors. May and September are quieter and the light is soft, and winter fog on the lake gives the whole place an air of mystery.
t.leipzig@51.3,12.4:
On Monday evenings in the autumn of 1989, thousands of people gathered at the Nikolaikirche in Leipzig after the prayers for peace and walked around the ring road with candles, chanting that they were the people. The East German state could have sent in the tanks, and did not, and within weeks the Berlin Wall had fallen. Leipzig is proud of that, and rightly. The church still stands in its quiet square, with a classical interior of slender palm-like pillars in pastel colours, and a plaque outside records the demonstrations.

The city's older fame is musical and commercial. Johann Sebastian Bach spent the last twenty-seven years of his life here as cantor of the Thomaskirche, writing and directing music for the choir, the Thomanerchor, which still sings there on Fridays and Saturdays. Mendelssohn and Schumann also worked in the city, and Wagner was born here. As a trading city, Leipzig held a major fair from the Middle Ages, and the arcaded passages in the centre are the descendants of the merchants' courtyards. Auerbachs Keller, a cellar restaurant, appears in Goethe's Faust as the place where Mephistopheles amuses the students with wine and tricks, and a pair of bronze figures at the entrance tell the story.

Outside, the Monument to the Battle of the Nations, a massive stone colossus completed in 1913, marks the site of Napoleon's defeat in 1813. South of the city, old open-cast lignite mines have been flooded to form a chain of lakes, and the new lake district is a popular place for cycling, sailing and swimming. The roads around Leipzig run flat and straight through farmland, with plenty of avenues of trees and long views, and the riding gets better to the south and west, where the land begins to roll toward Saxony's hills.

Leipzig has more than half a million people, with fuel stations throughout, a lively café scene and a growing reputation among young people. Try Leipziger Allerlei, a vegetable stew with crayfish tails, and the local sour beer called Gose, which tastes of salt and coriander. Traffic is heavy on the ring road, and trams use the centre, so mind the rails in wet weather. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and the festival of lights in October draws crowds.
t.kiel@54.3,10.1:
Kiel is a city that faces the water in every direction. It sits at the head of the Kiel Fjord, a long inlet of the Baltic, and at the eastern end of the Kiel Canal, which cuts across the base of the Jutland peninsula to the North Sea and is the busiest artificial waterway in the world by ship traffic. Cargo ships, tankers and ferries pass in a line, and from the high bridges you can watch giant vessels slide past apparently at roof level. The canal was opened in 1895, and for its size and importance it deserves more visitors than it gets.

The sea shaped the city's history. Kiel was a German naval base for a century, and the sailors' mutiny of 1918 here sparked the revolution that ended the German Empire. In the Second World War it was bombed so heavily that most of the old centre vanished, so the modern city is mostly postwar, with a sensible but plain look. What you will enjoy is the waterfront, with its ferries to Norway and Sweden, the promenade, the harbour with old sailing ships, and the beaches of the fjord, which are used for swimming from May to September.

Sailing is the big thing. Every June, Kiel Week turns the whole fjord into a festival of regattas, with thousands of boats, music stages and street food, the largest sailing event in the world, and the city hosted the Olympic sailing competitions in 1936 and 1972. At Laboe, across the fjord, a tall brick tower serves as a naval memorial, and the old submarine U-995 sits on the beach as a museum. The view from the tower over the water is wide and good.

The riding is flat to gently rolling, with roads around the fjord and into the farmland of Schleswig-Holstein, where fields of rapeseed shine yellow in May and roadside avenues of old beech create tunnels of green. Wind off the Baltic is often strong, and sudden showers come in from the sea. Fuel stations are plentiful, and the city has about two hundred and thirty thousand people. Fish is the thing to eat, with a Fischbrötchen from a harbour stall or a plate of fried herring. Spring and early autumn are best, and Kiel Week is wonderful but crowded, with hotels full for weeks.
t.the former school of art@51.0,11.3:
Henry van de Velde was a Belgian painter turned designer, and he is the reason Weimar has a building that looks like the future of 1906. The Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar brought him here to reform the local art and craft school, and in 1904 he designed a new school building for it, a plain, bright structure with big windows, clean lines and a staircase of studied elegance, in the Art Nouveau style that Germans call Jugendstil. When Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919, he merged it with this school and took over its building, so the walls that housed one tradition passed to the next with hardly a change of paint.

The two periods are linked by one idea, that design should serve life rather than decoration, and the same building witnessed both. Inside, light floods in through the north-facing studios, and the staircase, with its curved balustrade and stained walls, is an object lesson in how to be modern without being cold. Students such as Oskar Schlemmer painted murals here, and one of them, painted on the staircase, was destroyed by the Nazis in the 1930s, then restored after the war. The building is part of the Bauhaus University today, and parts of it can be visited on guided tours.

Weimar is a gentle city for a rider on foot, with a compact old town and a park running along the Ilm river. Goethe's house stands on the Frauenplan, the library of Duchess Anna Amalia has a rococo hall whose books survived a serious fire in 2004, and the cafés on the market square serve Thuringian cake and strong coffee. Thuringian dumplings, known as Klöße, appear on every menu with roast meat and red cabbage. The surrounding countryside is calm and rolling, with fields, orchards and wooded hills, and roads that run through small villages with red roofs and church towers.

Parking in the centre is tight, so leave the bike on the edge and walk. Weimar has about sixty-five thousand people, with fuel on the ring road and in the surrounding villages. Weekends in summer are busy with tour groups, and the best time to enjoy the town is a weekday morning in spring or autumn, when the light is soft and the streets are quiet. The Onion Market in October is lively and worth a detour.
t.berlin motorcycle escapes@53.2,14.4:
This is the Lower Oder Valley National Park, the only floodplain national park in Germany, and one of the wildest corners of the country. In spring the river floods the meadows, turning them into a shallow, glittering lake, and the dykes become islands. Birds arrive in huge numbers: cranes, geese, white-tailed eagles, black storks and corncrakes, whose rasping call is heard on summer nights, and beavers have returned to the channels.

The old town of Gartz, on the western bank, has a medieval gate and a church with a tall tower, and a quiet, unspoilt air. A few kilometres south, Schwedt, a larger town of about thirty-eight thousand people, has a more industrial story. It grew in the 1960s around an oil refinery at the end of the Druzhba pipeline, which supplied much of eastern Germany with fuel, and its wide boulevards and tall blocks are a legacy of that period. Before that, Schwedt was a centre of tobacco growing, thanks to Huguenot refugees who planted tobacco in the Uckermark in the seventeenth century, and some old drying barns still stand in the villages.

The riding here is gentle and spacious. The roads run along the dykes and through the polders, with long, open views of the river and Poland beyond, and the atmosphere is calm. The surface varies from smooth asphalt to old, bumpy brick and patchy repairs, and in places the road narrows and becomes a single track. Wind from the east can be strong, and mist often hangs over the meadows in the morning and evening. The border with Poland is open, and a bridge or ferry crossing is easy, with a different landscape on the other side, though you should carry your papers.

Schwedt has fuel, supermarkets, cafes and everything else a rider might need, and it is the best place to fill the tank, because the villages along the river are small and have few services. Gartz has a bakery and a couple of simple places to eat. Try a plate of smoked fish or a serving of local potato dishes, and give yourself time for a stop at one of the dyke-top viewpoints in the evening, when the cranes come in to roost.
t.plauer see@53.5,12.3:
Plau am See sits at the western end of the Plauer See, the third-largest lake in Mecklenburg after the Müritz and the Schweriner See, in the heart of the lake district that stretches across the north-east of Germany. The town of nearly six thousand has a small old centre, a harbour, and a lift bridge over the river Elde that is a local landmark, and it is a sensible stop for fuel, ice cream and a swim. Malchow, about fifteen kilometres to the east, has seven thousand people and sits on an island between two lakes, joined to the shore by an old swing bridge.

The lake district was left behind by the glaciers, which scooped out hundreds of basins and left ridges of sand and gravel between them, so that the country is a patchwork of water, reedbeds, pine and beech woods, and flat farmland. Many of the lakes are linked by canals and rivers, popular with houseboat holidaymakers in summer, and the shores are lined with campsites and small beaches. The water is mostly clean and fairly warm in July and August, and local swimmers use the shallow public beaches, some with a small fee in season.

For a rider, this is easy, restful country. The roads here are flat and mostly straight, lined with old avenues of lime and chestnut trees, with the lake appearing now and again through the trunks, and there is little traffic outside the holiday months. The surface can be rough in places, with patches of brick or cobbles in villages, and the avenues mean heavy shade and wet leaves in autumn. Nothing here is thrilling, but the light and space are the reward, and the long straight stretches suit a relaxed day with swimming stops.

Birdlife is rich: cranes gather in autumn, sea eagles nest near some of the lakes, and cormorants and herons are common on the shoreline. For food, smoked fish is the local speciality, along with fried fish rolls and, in autumn, game and mushrooms. Wasps and mosquitoes can be annoying near the water on summer evenings. Fuel is available in Plau and Malchow, but the roads between have few stations.
t.nordhausen@51.5,10.8:
Nordhausen is a town of some forty-four thousand people on the southern edge of the Harz, the biggest place for a wide area, and it carries a heavy history that deserves a pause. In the last years of the Second World War the Nazis built a huge underground factory in the nearby Kohnstein hill, where V-2 rockets were assembled by prisoners from the Mittelbau-Dora camp, and thousands died of hunger, disease and brutality. The Dora memorial and museum at the site is a serious, sober place, open to the public. In April 1945 the town itself was destroyed in air raids, and most of the old centre was lost.

Today Nordhausen has a modern town centre, a handful of surviving old buildings, and a long tradition of distilling grain spirit, with the Nordhäuser Korn sold across Germany. It makes a good place to fill up and eat before heading into the hills. To the south, the Kyffhäuser, a low wooded ridge rising above the plain of the Goldene Aue, is the destination for the hairpin ride: a road with bends and gradients unusual for this part of Germany, climbing to a massive stone monument to Emperor Wilhelm I with the legend of the sleeping Barbarossa beneath. According to the story, the red-bearded emperor sleeps within the mountain, and will return when the ravens stop circling.

The country around is known as the Südharz, with gypsum karst landscapes, sinkholes, clear springs and beech woods, and a gentle, rolling character. Roads are generally good, curving over wooded hills and through village streets, and the Kyffhäuser section is the real highlight, though it is short. The traffic is mild except in the town itself, and weekend bikers from Thuringia and Lower Saxony make the hills busy on dry days.

Practically, use Nordhausen or one of the small towns for fuel and bring a layer in spring and autumn, when the hills are cooler than the plain. There is a tram network in the town, with rails to watch for in the wet. Summers are warm and sometimes humid, and thunderstorms form over the Harz in the afternoon. Autumn light on the beechwoods is good.
t.sankt andreasberg bends@51.7,10.5:
Sankt Andreasberg is a small town of two thousand at roughly six hundred metres in the Upper Harz, a mining place that has lived on silver, in one way or another, for five hundred years. The lodes were worked from the sixteenth century, and the Grube Samson, a mine here, is famous for its water-driven ore hoist, which kept working until the 1900s and is preserved as a museum, an astonishing piece of engineering from the age of waterwheels. You can still see the old ditches and ponds that fed the mines across the hills, many of them now loved by walkers.

The town sits on a ridge among spruce woods, with the high Harz plateau around it, and the weather is a thing in itself: it is often foggy, wet or snowy for much of the year, and a summer day can start with cloud and finish with sun. Braunlage, about five thousand people, lies a few kilometres to the north-east and is the nearer place for fuel, lunch and a bigger choice of shops; the Wurmberg, Lower Saxony's highest peak at about 970 metres, rises next to it. The spruce forests on these slopes have been badly damaged by bark beetle and drought in recent years, and large areas stand grey and open, a landscape unfamiliar to those who knew the dark woods.

The riding is among the best in northern Germany. The road from Sankt Andreasberg runs across the plateau and drops through bends into valleys, with a good surface, plenty of corners and wide views when the sky is clear. Weekends bring many bikers, especially from Hamburg and Hannover, and police checks and speed cameras are used, so ride with common sense. Be careful with wet leaves, mud, and fog, and with the sudden cold at height, which can make a May morning feel like March.

Food in the Harz means hearty things: Harzer cheese, which is sharp and smelly; Schmorbraten; Kassler; and in autumn, game with mushrooms; with strong coffee and cake in the cafés. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the traffic is light. The old mining paths and ponds are a good excuse for a short walk.
t.stolberg harz old road@51.6,11.0:
Stolberg is a tiny half-timbered town of about fourteen hundred people in a narrow valley on the southern edge of the Harz, so well preserved that people often call it a museum in itself, with houses leaning against each other along the main street and a castle on the hill above. It was the seat of the counts of Stolberg, whose line ran for centuries, and the birthplace of Thomas Müntzer, the preacher and radical leader of the Peasants' War of 1525, who was executed after the battle of Frankenhausen not far to the south.

The place is on a quiet road through the Südharz, which is an unusual landscape of limestone and gypsum karst, with caves, sinkholes and clear streams, among beech woods and orchards. Rottleberode, a short way along, is a small village that has a show cave, the Heimkehle, one of the largest gypsum caves in Germany, with a lake inside. On the hill above Stolberg stands the Josephskreuz, a wooden cross-shaped tower designed in the 1830s and built to a plan by the architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, which gives views across the hills on a clear day.

For riders the roads here are narrow, winding and often empty, and the old roads climbing from the valley give a sense of the Harz without the weekend crowds of the main roads. Surface quality varies, with some patches and gravel on the bends, and the climbs are short but steep, so it is no place for hurry. The nearest bigger towns with fuel are Nordhausen and Sangerhausen, each some twenty to thirty kilometres away, so fill the tank before you turn off.

Sangerhausen has a famous rose garden, the Europa-Rosarium, with thousands of varieties, a lovely detour in June. The area is also known for its sausages and for Harz honey, and the villages have small inns with simple, filling food. Spring brings blossom on the orchards, autumn a haze of woodsmoke and yellow beech leaves. Mornings in the valley can be cold and misty, but the sun quickly gets into the hills.
t.schwerin castle lakefront@53.6,11.4:
Schwerin Castle looks like a fairy tale that got out of hand. Golden domes, turrets, bay windows and gilded ornaments crowd a small island in the middle of Lake Schwerin, joined to the town by a bridge, and at dusk the whole thing is reflected in the water in a way that makes people stop their cars. The building seen today is largely a nineteenth-century neo-Renaissance reconstruction, made for the grand dukes of Mecklenburg-Schwerin on the site of a medieval fortress, and it now houses the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as well as a museum. The castle and its gardens are part of a World Heritage ensemble inscribed in 2020.

The castle even has a resident ghost, the Petermännchen, a small friendly spirit said to haunt the cellars and guard the castle's treasures. His likeness appears on souvenirs around town. A short walk from the water, the old town has brick Gothic churches, the cathedral with its tall tower, and the Schelfstadt district, a quiet quarter of baroque half-timbered houses laid out in the eighteenth century. In summer the lakeshore fills with strollers, sailors and ice cream sellers, and boat trips cross the water to small islands.

Riding out from Schwerin is easy and relaxed. The city is the capital of a region of glacial lakes, rolling farmland and long avenues of old lime and chestnut trees, which make a green tunnel overhead on warm afternoons. The roads are quiet and mostly flat, with few severe curves, but with plenty of pleasant gentle bends round the lakes, past manor houses and brick churches with squat towers. The area is dotted with Herrenhäuser, manor houses built by the landed gentry, many now hotels or museums, and with fields that glow yellow with rapeseed in late spring. Wismar, the old Hanseatic port on the Baltic, is about thirty kilometres north and makes an easy and rewarding target.

Schwerin is a city of nearly a hundred thousand, so fuel, parking and meals are no trouble, and the cafes around the old market square are good for a rest. Be careful on the avenues, where tree roots can lift the tarmac and deer cross at dusk. Look out for smoked fish, regional specialities such as Mecklenburg duck with red cabbage, and in summer the cold fruit soups. In autumn and spring, mist rising off the lakes is beautiful but can be slippery, so ride gently until the sun has dried the road.
t.sternberg lake roads@53.7,11.8:
Sternberg is a small town of about five thousand in the Mecklenburg lake country, east of Schwerin, on a lake of the same name in a landscape of low hills, reedbeds and rolling farm fields. The Sternberger Seenlandschaft is a patchwork of water left behind by the last ice age, and the lakes here are quiet, clear and good for swimming in summer, with small public beaches and shady shoreline spots. Wismar, the old Hanseatic port on the Baltic, lies to the north, and Gägelow, the other village on the list, is one of its suburbs.

The town has a long history that includes some dark episodes. In 1492 it was the site of a trial in which Jews were accused of desecrating the host, and a number were burned, a persecution that left a lasting stain; the medieval parish church still stands in the middle of town, a big brick building typical of the region. Like much of Mecklenburg, the area is dotted with brick Gothic churches, manor houses and estates, and the Baltic coast and its cities, Wismar and Rostock, lie within reach.

For a rider the pleasure is calm. Roads here are long, flat and straight, with old avenues of lime and chestnut trees, quiet villages, and a surface that varies between smooth new asphalt and cobbles or patchwork in places. The corners are few, and the draw is the swimming and the light: ride in the morning, swim at midday, and wander on in the evening when the air cools. Wind comes off the Baltic and can be steady, and thunderstorms in summer are sudden. Watch for deer and wild boar at dusk, and for farm traffic.

Fuel is available in Sternberg, though small stations close early, and in the larger towns nearby, such as Schwerin to the west and Wismar to the north. Eat smoked fish, fried herring, and in late summer plum cake and sweet cherries from the roadside stalls. Cranes gather on the fields in autumn, and their calls carry a long way. The water warms up by midsummer, and shallow swimming places suit a quick stop.
t.gustrow old town meal@53.8,12.2:
Güstrow is a town of thirty-one thousand in central Mecklenburg, and one of the best places in the region to walk around for an hour with a coffee in your hand. It was once a ducal residence, and in the sixteenth century the dukes built a splendid Renaissance palace here, one of the finest in northern Germany, with decorated gables, a big courtyard and an Italian-influenced design. The old centre, with its market square, brick gothic houses and half-timbered corners, is compact and pleasant, and the cathedral, a vast brick church from the thirteenth century, rises above the roofs.

The artist who made Güstrow famous was Ernst Barlach, the sculptor and writer, who lived and worked here from 1910 until his death in 1938. His angel, a bronze figure hovering with closed eyes, hangs in the cathedral, made in 1927 as a memorial to the dead of the First World War. The Nazis removed it as degenerate art and melted it down, but a cast had been secretly kept, and a replica now hangs in its place. Barlach's studio house and workshop beside the lake are open as a museum, and the Inselsee, a large lake at the edge of town, makes a pleasant place to stroll or swim in summer.

This is a stop for food and a short wander, not for corners. The surrounding country is flat to gently rolling farmland with avenues of old trees, and the roads are straight and quiet, with views over fields of rape, which blaze yellow in May, and maize in late summer. Surfaces are variable, with patches of cobbles in the villages, and there are often farm vehicles. Wind from the Baltic can be strong across the open land.

Fuel and supermarkets are easy to find, and restaurants around the market square serve regional dishes such as fish from the lakes, duck with red cabbage, and rhubarb cake. Park on the edge of the old town and walk in, as the cobbled streets can be slippery in the wet. Spring and early autumn are the pleasantest seasons, and the long summer evenings are good for a late meal. The palace courtyard hosts concerts in summer.
t.stralsund@54.3,13.1:
Stralsund's skyline tells you at once that this was a rich merchant town. Red-brick Gothic gables, pointed spires and the enormous bulk of the Marienkirche, whose tower rises more than a hundred metres, crowd the old town island, which is surrounded by water and linked to the mainland by causeways. In the Middle Ages, Stralsund was one of the leading members of the Hanseatic League, the trading alliance that dominated the Baltic, and together with Wismar its old town is a World Heritage site. In the harbour, the three-masted Gorch Fock I, a sail training ship, is moored, and the Ozeaneum, a striking modern museum of sea life, stands beside it.

The ride out is the draw, because from here you cross to Rügen, Germany's largest island. For years the only link was the Rügendamm, a causeway and bridge built in the 1930s, but a high new bridge opened in 2007 and carries the main traffic across the Strelasund. In the summer holidays the approach roads can back up for kilometres, so cross early or late, or in the shoulder seasons. On the island, the roads wind through low green hills, fields of rape and wheat, and avenues of old trees, with glimpses of blue sea.

Rügen has the famous chalk cliffs of the Jasmund peninsula, white walls that rise over the Baltic and are topped with beech forest, among them the Königsstuhl, a viewing point at about a hundred and eighteen metres. The painter Caspar David Friedrich made them a symbol of German Romanticism in the early nineteenth century. Seaside resorts such as Binz, with grand white villas along the promenade, and the little town of Putbus, a planned classical town of white houses built round a circular plaza, are well worth a look. The Baltic water is cold and shallow, and the beaches in the resorts are wide and sandy, with wicker beach chairs called Strandkörbe to shelter from the wind.

Fuel and food are no problem in Stralsund, a city of nearly sixty thousand, with stations on all main roads, and on Rügen the main towns have supplies, though prices rise in the summer. A fish sandwich, a Fischbrötchen, filled with herring, smoked salmon or crab, is the standard Baltic lunch, and best eaten at the harbour. The wind from the sea is brisk, so a windproof layer is wise, even in July, and sudden showers can drift in off the water.
t.hamburg south@53.5,10.0:
Harburg, on the southern bank of the Elbe, is the part of Hamburg that visitors usually skip, which makes it a good place to leave from. The district grew up around an inner harbour and a long tradition of industry, and today it holds a mix of old brick warehouses, a technical university and the modern bridges and motorways that thread over the great river. A short way north, the port of Hamburg, one of the largest in Europe, spreads over islands and docks, with cranes standing against the sky and container ships passing so close to the river's edge that they seem to float over the roofs. On the far side, the Elbphilharmonie, a glass concert hall built on a brick warehouse and opened in 2017, shines like a crystal wave.

South of the river, the land begins to rise, but only gently, into the Harburg hills and then onto the Lüneburg Heath, a sandy plain of heather, juniper and birch woodland. The heath is at its best from mid-August to mid-September, when the heather blooms purple across the open ground, and flocks of Heidschnucken, the grey, horned heath sheep, graze between the trees. The highest point is the Wilseder Berg, at 169 metres, a modest summit by any standard but a favourite with walkers. The roads that cross the heath are quiet and gently curving, shaded by oaks and pines, and the little brick villages have thatched farmhouses and old stone walls.

Further east, the Göhrde forest and the Wendland, a region near the old inner German border, have unusual round villages, called Rundlinge, in which farmhouses stand in a circle around a central green, a layout inherited from Slavic settlers of the Middle Ages. The Elbe valley here is wide and quiet, with dykes, meadows and the occasional ferry across the water. Riding on these small roads is slow, pleasant and rewarding, though the surfaces can be rough after winter, and deer are a constant danger.

Services around the start are no trouble, with large stations in Harburg and the neighbouring town of Seevetal, plenty of food options and parts shops. Once into the heath and the Wendland, stations are rarer, so fill up beforehand. Weather off the North Sea can change quickly, with wind and showers, so keep a waterproof handy. In autumn, early morning fog on the heath is atmospheric, though it deserves caution.
t.krkonose mountain@50.0,14.9:
The title of this stop is a mountain range far to the north, but you are in the rolling farmland of central Bohemia, east of Prague, around the small town of Kouřim. The Krkonoše, the Giant Mountains on the Polish border, lie more than a hundred kilometres away, and this is the quiet, gentle country you cross on the way home. The land is a mixture of fields, orchards and woodland, with long views across the plain and the occasional church spire.

Kouřim itself has an unusual claim. On a hill above the town stands an early medieval hillfort, a great ring of earth ramparts that was one of the main centres of the Slavic tribes before Prague rose to dominance, and it was still important in the tenth century. Below it, the town keeps a market square and a Gothic church with a high tower. A short walk from the centre is a skansen, an open-air museum of village buildings, with wooden cottages, barns and a windmill brought from villages across central Bohemia, so that you can walk through the countryside of a century ago.

The surrounding region is a patchwork of agriculture and forest, with a mild climate and fertile soil, and the villages are quiet. Near Kostelec nad Černými Lesy, the forests belong to a school forest used for teaching and research, and old oak and beech trees stand beside the paths. In spring the orchards blossom, and in late summer the combine harvesters work the cereal fields from dawn to dark.

For a rider finishing a long day, this is an easy landing. The roads are flat or gently rolling, with moderate traffic and a good surface, and the villages are so close together that you drop speed limits every few minutes. Speed cameras and police checks are common in Czech towns, so keep an eye on signs. Český Brod, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafes, and Kostelec nad Černými Lesy has a few small places to eat. Try a plate of svíčková, beef in cream sauce with dumplings, and a glass of local beer, and be in Prague by dark.
t.prague bohemia@50.7,14.4:
The country is one of volcanic hills, sandstone rocks and mixed woods, the western edge of the Lusatian region. Cone-shaped basalt peaks rise from the farmland, and the lower slopes are patched with orchards and small fields. It is lovely and little visited, and you will often have the roads to yourself.

Česká Lípa, with nearly forty thousand people, has plenty of fuel and food, and a neat old centre with a Gothic Augustinian monastery and a handsome square. The town sits at the edge of the Kokořín and Lusatian landscapes, and it is a natural base for a few days of exploring. The nearby Máchovo lake, near Doksy, is a famous spot for swimming and boating, and the sandstone rocks and forests around it have a romantic, mysterious character.

For a rider, the roads here are enjoyable and varied. They wind through the foothills of the Central Uplands, climbing to small passes and descending to quiet villages, with views of volcanic cones and distant ridges. The surface can be patchy, and bends are often tight and blind, with farm traffic and cyclists. In summer the hills are green and the air is warm, and in autumn the beeches and oaks are a blaze of colour. Fog fills the valleys on cold mornings and burns off by midday.

The area was long home to a mixed Czech and German population, and the old half-timbered houses, known as Umgebinde, are a distinctive feature of the region. Many have been restored, and a few small museums tell the story of the weavers and glassmakers who once lived here. Fuel is easy to find in Česká Lípa, but the smaller villages have little, so fill up beforehand. A bowl of garlic soup and a dark beer in a village pub is a good way to end a day.
t.melnik river@50.4,14.5:
Mělník stands on a spur above the meeting of two rivers, and the meeting is the thing. The Vltava, which has run north from the Šumava through Prague, joins the Labe, the Elbe, here, and from the terrace of the castle you can watch the dark Vltava slide into the paler Elbe and the two flow away together towards Germany and the North Sea. It is a very Czech view: flat fields, a long bridge, a few white churches, and orchards on the slopes.

The castle belongs to the Lobkowicz family, who have owned it, on and off, for several centuries, and it is open to visitors, with a wine cellar and a collection of paintings and furniture. The wine matters here, because Mělník is the centre of the Bohemian vineyards, a small region of south-facing slopes where vines have been grown for a thousand years. Tradition credits Saint Ludmila, grandmother of Saint Wenceslas, with planting the first vines, and Emperor Charles IV is said to have introduced Burgundy grapes in the fourteenth century. The wines are mostly dry whites and light reds, and a dry white goes well with fish.

In the old town, the Church of Saints Peter and Paul has an ossuary in its crypt, where the bones of some fifteen thousand people, dug up to make room for new burials, are arranged in neat patterns on the walls. It is macabre, quiet and oddly beautiful, and opening hours vary. Around it, the main square holds cafes, a town hall and a well, and the lanes lead down to the river through gateways in the old walls.

The ride here is a gentle one: low hills, vineyard lanes, small villages and long views over the river plain, with light traffic and decent roads. The most scenic route follows the river bank and passes under the castle, and you can stop at the bridge to watch the barges. Mělník has about nineteen thousand people, so fuel, shops and places to eat are all on hand. Try a glass of local wine with a plate of cold meats and cheese in a vaulted cellar. Early autumn, during the grape harvest and the wine festival, is the best time to be here.
t.wismar harbour food@53.9,11.5:
Wismar is the Baltic port that spent a century and a half as a piece of Sweden, and it still shows. Between 1648, when the Peace of Westphalia handed it to the Swedish crown, and 1803, when it was pledged to Mecklenburg, the town was a fortified Swedish outpost, and two stone heads at the harbour entrance, the so-called Swedish Heads, are a reminder of the time.

The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed together with Stralsund in 2002 for its Hanseatic architecture. Brick Gothic is the language here: huge red churches with tall towers, steep gabled merchant houses and a vast market square, one of the biggest in northern Germany, with a handsome pavilion in its centre, the Wasserkunst, which once supplied the town's drinking water. The church of St Nicholas, with its enormous nave, stands as a symbol of the wealth of the Hanseatic League.
