The harbour is the place for lunch. Fish rolls, called Fischbrötchen, are sold from small boats and kiosks along the quay, filled with herring, smoked salmon or crab, and eaten on the spot with a view of the fishing boats. A few small ferries and sightseeing vessels leave from the quay, and the sea air is a welcome change after the day's riding. The nearby coastline has long, quiet beaches and a few small seaside resorts.

For a rider, Wismar is the end of a long, flat ride through Mecklenburg's lakes and fields. The roads are straight and the wind can be strong, with a good chance of a headwind on the way out and a tailwind on the way back, or the other way around. The surface is generally good, and the avenues of old trees that line many of the roads are lovely in the early summer. Fuel is available in town, and Hornstorf, a village to the south, has little. Come in the evening, when the brick glows red and the harbour is quiet.
t.gettorf road@54.4,10.0:
Gettorf is a small town on the Schwansen peninsula, a few kilometres inland from the Baltic, with about six thousand inhabitants and all the basics a rider needs: fuel, a bakery, a supermarket and a handful of cafes. Everything here is gentle, rolling and green, and the sea is never far away.

Schwansen is the land between the Eckernförde Bay and the Schlei, a low peninsula of farms, manor houses and hedgerows. The hedgerows are the local trademark: the Knicks, earth banks planted with hazel, hawthorn and blackthorn, which divide the fields and give the landscape a patchwork look. They shelter birds and small animals and break the wind, and in spring the blossom along the lanes is lovely. The roads between them are narrow, winding and well shaded, and a ride along them is pleasantly slow.

The surface is generally good, but expect agricultural traffic, especially at harvest time, and keep an eye out for mud on the bends after a farm vehicle has passed. The bends are gentle and blind, with the hedges close, so it pays to ride a little cautiously. The best time is a calm morning in early summer, when the rapeseed is in yellow bloom and the air smells sweet. The wind off the sea can be strong, and the weather changes quickly, so carry a jacket.

Nearby Eckernförde has a fine harbour and a long beach, and is known for its smoked herring, the Kieler Sprotten and other fish dishes. A little way inland, the Hüttener Berge, a low range of wooded hills, is a nature park with small lakes and forest tracks. The Kiel Canal, one of the busiest artificial waterways in the world, runs not far to the south, and the great ships that glide past the fields look strangely out of place. Kiel itself, a short ride south-east, is the region's capital, with a big harbour and a lively waterfront.
t.probstei villages@54.4,10.4:
The name comes from the provost of the convent at Preetz, who once held the land and drew rent from its farmers. The villages are strung along the lanes at the edge of the fields, with brick farmhouses, village churches and long avenues of trees.

It is an easy, relaxed place to ride, with flat roads, light traffic and wide views over the fields. The bends are gentle, and the surface is generally good, with a few rough patches on the back roads. The wind blows hard on the open land, so be ready for it, and the sky seems huge. In summer, the fields are full of ripening barley and wheat, and the air smells of hay and the sea. There is little shade, so carry water.

The coast is not far, and the beaches at Wendtorf and Laboe are a favourite with the locals. Next to it lies U-995, a Second World War submarine that visitors can walk through, an eerie reminder of how cramped life was on board. The Kieler Woche, the great sailing festival in June, fills the fjord with white sails and draws crowds from all over Europe.

Fuel is available at Laboe and in the larger towns around Kiel, and there are also several cafes and restaurants on the coast. Many serve fresh fish, including smoked eel and herring, and the local speciality of Kieler Sprotten, small smoked sprats. In the evening the sea turns silver and the ships glide into the fjord with their lights on. It is a pleasant, uncomplicated place to wind down at the end of a day.
t.hohwacht bay@54.3,10.7:
Hohwacht Bay is a wide curve of the Baltic coast in eastern Holstein, with a long, sandy beach, low dunes and shallow, gentle water that warms quickly in summer. The land here is flat and green, with the sea on one side and the rolling hills of Holstein Switzerland on the other, and the light has that clear, northern quality that painters love.

For swimmers, this is one of the more pleasant stretches of the German Baltic. The beach is sandy and the water is shallow, so it warms up in July and August, and families flock to it. There are cafes and ice-cream stands, and in the evening the sun sinks into the sea, turning the sky orange and pink. Out of season the beach is almost empty, and the gulls and wind are the only company. The air carries the smell of salt and seaweed, and the waves leave long lines of amber-coloured weed.

The roads around the bay are quiet and pleasant, running between fields of rapeseed and wheat, with old brick farms and small villages. Bends are gentle, and the surface is generally good, with the occasional rough patch. In summer the traffic near the beaches can be heavy, with cars and caravans queuing for the car parks, so go early or late. A cycle path follows the coast, and cyclists are common, so give them room.

Lütjenburg, six kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket and a pleasant old centre with a market square. Close by is Panker, a manor estate with a distinctive yellow house, known for its horses and a hill with a viewing tower called Hessenstein, from where you can see the Baltic and the hills. The country is full of manor houses, many of them still working farms, and the local cheese and smoked fish are excellent. Fuel is easy to find in Lütjenburg, and the best advice is to bring a towel and an appetite.
t.osterode@51.7,10.3:
Osterode am Harz lies on the south-western edge of the Harz mountains, at the point where the hills flatten out into the fields of southern Lower Saxony. It is a practical, friendly town of about twenty thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and several places to eat, a sensible spot to refuel the bike and yourself.

The Harz was Germany's great mining country, and the evidence is everywhere. Silver, copper, lead and iron were dug here for centuries, and a clever system of ponds, ditches and tunnels was built to power the mine pumps with water, a network that UNESCO recognised in 2010. Osterode was never a mining town on the scale of Clausthal or Goslar, but it was a trading and processing centre, and the old timber houses recall that prosperity. The Söse river runs through town, and a reservoir in the hills above supplies drinking water.

The riding in this corner of the Harz is excellent. From Osterode, the roads climb in tight, shaded bends through spruce forest, with the road surface generally in good shape and the traffic light on weekdays. The ride to Bad Lauterberg and Herzberg runs along the southern edge, with gentle curves and views across to the Thuringian hills, while a short ride north reaches the high Harz plateau with its cool, misty air. The Harz suffers from bark beetle damage, and large areas of dead spruce are slowly being replaced with mixed woodland, so you will see bare slopes and fresh planting.

Local food is hearty: Harzer Käse, a sharp sour-milk cheese, and wurst, with a cold beer. Herzberg am Harz, ten kilometres away, has a castle and a quiet old centre, and is where the little Sieber stream comes down to the plain. This stop is a good end to a day in the hills, with a short, easy ride to the plain and a bed for the night. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for the Harz roads, when the air is clear and the crowds thin.
t.preetz old town@54.2,10.3:
Preetz is a lake town in the green middle of Schleswig-Holstein, and its old town squeezes between the Schwentine river and a pair of small lakes. Kiel is just fifteen minutes away, but Preetz has its own pace.

The old town has one of the oldest institutions in the region: the convent of Preetz, founded in 1211 as a Benedictine house for noble women. After the Reformation it became a Protestant foundation for unmarried ladies of the Schleswig-Holstein nobility, and it still operates today, with a church of impressive size standing beside a quiet cloister. The convent once owned most of the land to the east, and it gave its name to the Probstei, the district of farming villages that its provost ruled. You can walk around the grounds, and the church is open for visits outside services.

For riders, Preetz is a handy start or finish. The roads that radiate from it head towards the Holstein lakes, small, winding and lined with beech woods and meadows, with the surface generally good and the traffic light on weekday mornings. Bends are gentle and often hidden by the trees, so it pays to keep a steady pace. The Kellersee and the Plöner See, the biggest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, are within easy reach. In autumn, the beech woods turn a rich copper, and mist rises from the lakes at dawn.

Fuel is available at the edge of town, and there are bakeries and cafes around the market, including a good one for a slice of plum cake and a mug of coffee. Schellhorn, a village a little over a kilometre away, has a pleasant lake shore. The region is known as Holstein Switzerland, a name given by nineteenth-century visitors who found the rolling hills and lakes reminiscent of the Alps, though the highest point is barely a hundred and seventy metres. The comparison is flattering, but the countryside is lovely in its own right.
t.hamburg south@53.4,10.0:
Harburg was its own town for most of its history, and some residents still say so. Standing on the south bank of the Elbe, across the great river from Hamburg, it grew up as a Hanoverian and later Prussian harbour town, with its own castle, canal and industries, until the Greater Hamburg Act of 1937 swallowed it into the city. The old inner harbour has been reborn as a district of offices and cafes, and the technical university stands on a former industrial site. It is a rougher, more honest part of Hamburg than the lakeside villas of the north.

The industries tell the story. Rubber, oil mills, shipyards and chemical works lined the harbour for a century, and their chimneys and warehouses still give the waterfront an edge of grit. Behind the town, the Harburg Hills rise in a wooded ridge, and then the country opens out into the Lüneburg Heath, the great sandy plain of heather, juniper and birch that stretches south and east. The heath is at its best in August and September, when the heather blooms purple and bees, shepherds and hikers come out. The highest point, the Wilseder Berg, rises to 169 metres, and it is the highest point of the heath.

A ride towards the Harz starts with the practical business of getting out. The Elbe tunnel and the motorway interchanges south of Harburg are congested, especially at rush hour and on summer Fridays, and sorting out the lanes can be tricky. Once past Seevetal and Stelle, the roads open up, and the heath roads are straight, quiet and lined with old oaks and half-timbered farms, which makes for relaxed riding. Wind is the main danger, and sudden fog in the early morning is common in autumn.

Fuel is easy here, with several stations in Harburg and Seevetal, and the bakeries open early. A Franzbrötchen and a coffee from a harbour bakery is a good start, and a plate of Heidschnucken lamb, from the heath sheep, makes a good dinner later. Late summer is the best season, though spring and autumn are fine, and a day of heather and big skies is a good way to start a longer journey south.
t.wernigerode overnight edge@51.8,10.8:
Wernigerode calls itself the colourful town of the Harz, and it is no exaggeration. The old centre is a jumble of half-timbered houses in reds, greens and ochres, with carved beams and crooked upper floors, and the town hall at its heart looks like something from an illustrated book, with two pointed towers and a steep gable. It lies at the northern edge of the Harz, with a hilltop castle looking down from the slope and the high plateau of the Brocken in the distance.

The castle, a nineteenth-century fantasy of turrets and battlements built on older foundations, is a good example of romantic historicism, and the view from its terraces over the town and the plain is worth the climb. Below it, the Harz narrow-gauge railway, with its steam engines, runs from the town station up to the Brocken, the highest point in northern Germany at 1,141 metres. The trains are a living museum, and a trip to the summit on a clear day, with steam drifting past the spruce trees, is a delight. Tickets are sold at the station, and the line also runs to Nordhausen.

For a rider, Wernigerode makes an excellent night stop. The roads to the Harz plateau, towards Schierke and Elend, wind up through dense spruce woods in tight bends, with the Brocken looming above. The surface is generally good, but it is shaded and slow to dry, and fog and low cloud can come in quickly. In winter, snow and ice make these roads hazardous, and the high Harz can be closed by drifts.

The Harz was divided by the border between East and West Germany for forty years, and Wernigerode lay on the eastern side. The Brocken itself was a restricted military zone, topped by Soviet and East German listening posts, and was closed to the public until 1989. The scars of that time have mostly faded, but the border zone is now a green belt, with a hiking path along the old patrol road. In the evening, try a dish of Harz game with a dark local beer, and enjoy the walk through the lamplit lanes before bed.
t.torfhaus harz high point@51.8,10.5:
Torfhaus is a scattering of buildings on the high road across the Harz, at about eight hundred metres, where the road crosses a wide, boggy plateau of moor and spruce. There is no village here to speak of, just a car park, a few places to eat and the visitor centre of the Harz National Park, and its popularity comes from a view: from the edge of the plateau you look east across a broad valley to the Brocken, 1,141 metres high and bare on top, the highest peak of the Harz. Altenau, six and a half kilometres away, and Bad Harzburg, nine, are the nearest towns for fuel.

The road is the B4, which climbs from Bad Harzburg in a series of long bends and straights through dense forest. It is a good, fast road, with a smooth surface and a limit enforced by cameras in places, and on a weekday morning it is an enjoyable climb. At weekends, it fills with day-trippers and traffic can be dense. The weather can be extreme: the Harz plateau is one of the foggiest and wettest places in Germany, with snow lying from November well into spring, and even in summer, mist and drizzle are common.

The Brocken is the stuff of legend, the mountain where witches are said to gather on Walpurgis Night, the thirtieth of April, in Goethe's Faust and in older folklore. The Brocken also gives its name to a strange optical effect, the Brocken spectre, in which a walker's shadow is cast on mist, ringed by a halo. In the Cold War, the area was a sensitive border zone, and Torfhaus was the last stop in West Germany before the barbed wire; from here, you could look across to the East German listening posts on the summit.

The moors around the settlement are among the most important in the region, and a boardwalk path leads across the Torfhaus Moor, with sundews, cotton grass and peat pools. In clear weather the walk is a quiet pleasure. Hot chocolate and soup are available from the little cafes.
t.goslar high road@51.9,10.4:
Goslar is a thousand years old and looks every year of it. The old imperial city lies at the northern foot of the Harz, and its centre is a miniature of medieval Germany: steep slate roofs, half-timbered houses, narrow lanes, and a market square with a golden glockenspiel that, at set hours, acts out scenes from the town's mining history.

For several centuries, Goslar was one of the most important places in the German empire. The emperors held court here in the Kaiserpfalz, a vast palace built in the eleventh century and heavily restored in the nineteenth, whose great hall is still impressive and decorated with wall paintings. The wealth that supported it came from the Rammelsberg, a mountain just outside town where silver, copper and lead were mined for nearly a thousand years, until the mine closed in 1988. Today the old mine is a museum and, with the old town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For a rider, Goslar is a natural gateway to the high roads of the Harz. From the town, the road climbs towards Hahnenklee and Clausthal-Zellerfeld in a series of long, forested bends, with the surface good and the traffic light on weekdays. Spruce woods and mining ponds line the route, and the landscape has a feeling of age, as if the mountains had been worked for so long that they have become part of the human world. In autumn, the larches turn gold among the dark firs.

The old town has a good choice of cafes and restaurants, and a plate of Harz specialities, perhaps roast game or sausage with sauerkraut, goes well with a Gose, a sour, salty beer that was brewed in Goslar for centuries and is now sold in many bars. Langelsheim, seven kilometres away, is a smaller town with more modern amenities. If you can, take a walk through the old streets before the day trippers arrive, and listen for the church bells. The old town is largely pedestrian, so find a car park on the edge and walk in.
t.bad doberan minster@54.1,11.9:
Bad Doberan has one of the finest brick Gothic churches in Europe, and it was built by monks. The minster, the Doberaner Münster, was the church of a Cistercian abbey founded in the twelfth century, and the present building, finished in the fourteenth century, is a tall, plain, pale-red brick basilica whose clear lines and soaring interior are the essence of the Baltic Gothic style. The abbey was dissolved at the Reformation, but the church survived, and the dukes of Mecklenburg were buried inside. Its stained glass, carved altars and a huge cross from the Middle Ages are still there.

The town around it is a curious mix. Bad Doberan, with about eleven and a half thousand people, was the summer seat of the Mecklenburg dukes, who in 1793 founded Heiligendamm, the first seaside resort in Germany, a few kilometres up the coast. The resort grew into a collection of white neoclassical villas along the shore, called the white town by the sea, and the dukes' love of the water shaped the area. Germany's oldest racecourse is here, too, dating from the early nineteenth century.

What makes the trip a pleasure is the Molli, a narrow-gauge steam railway that has run between Bad Doberan, Heiligendamm and the seaside town of Kühlungsborn since 1886. The little train, with its tall chimney and its whistle, runs straight through the streets of the town, and it is a sight you remember. For a rider, it also marks the start of the Kühlung hills, a low wooded ridge along the Baltic coast with narrow, curving roads through beech forest, with views over the sea from the top. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends.

Fuel and food are easy in Bad Doberan, with several stations and bakeries, and the seaside towns have smoked fish stalls, serving herring in a roll with onions. Summer brings crowds to the coast, and the sea breeze keeps temperatures mild, though the water is cold, and September is a good month, with fewer people. Wind off the Baltic can be strong, so wear a good jacket, and take care on the coast road where cyclists and holidaymakers are numerous.
t.schwerin castle sight@53.6,11.4:
Schwerin castle is a fairy tale in brick and gilt, and it is built on an island. The palace of the Mecklenburg dukes stands on a small island in the Schweriner See, linked to the town by a bridge, with turrets, towers and a golden dome reflected in the water. The present building, a romantic mix of Renaissance and Gothic styles, was built in the middle of the nineteenth century to a design that drew on the French chateaux of the Loire, and it is now the seat of the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. UNESCO listed the castle and its gardens in 2020.

The setting is the thing. The city of about ninety-six thousand people lies among seven lakes, with woods and meadows running to the edge of the old town, and the Schweriner See, the fourth largest lake in Germany by area, stretches north for kilometres. The castle gardens, laid out in the formal baroque style with canals and terraces, give way to a landscaped park with old trees, and the walk around the lake on a summer evening is one of the nicest in northern Germany. The legend of the Petermännchen, a little ghost who haunts the castle and looks after its treasures, is told to children and visitors alike.

The roads that bring a rider here are quiet and gentle. The Mecklenburg lake district is a glacial landscape of low hills, lakes, reed beds and beech woods, with straight roads between the villages and long tree-lined avenues of lime and chestnut. The surface is mostly good, and traffic is light, though tractors and cyclists are common. In late summer the fields are golden, and the birdlife on the lakes, including cranes and sea eagles, is rich.

Schwerin has fuel and every kind of service, and the old town, with its narrow lanes around the cathedral, has cafes and restaurants. The brick Gothic cathedral has a tall spire, which you can climb for a view across the lakes. Try a plate of smoked eel or fresh pikeperch from the lake, and a local beer. The Altstadt and Schelfstadt districts are pleasant to walk through, though cobbles and tram tracks need care. May to September is the best season.
t.kyffhauser serpentines@51.4,11.1:
Kyffhäuser is a modest range of wooded hills on the border of Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, just rising out of the Goldene Aue plain, and it is soaked in legend. The hills are low, but they stand alone above the flat plain, so the views from the top are remarkable.

The legend is that Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who died on crusade in 1190, is not dead but sleeping inside the mountain, his beard growing through a stone table, waiting for the day Germany needs him. In the nineteenth century this story was bound up with German nationalism, and in the 1890s a huge monument was built on the ridge, a tower about eighty metres high topped by a statue of Emperor Wilhelm I, with a stone figure of Barbarossa at its base. The monument is vast and rather forbidding, and the view from the top, across the Harz, the Thuringian Basin and the plains, is excellent.

The road itself is a good one, narrow and curved, climbing through forest with a series of hairpins and a surface that is generally smooth. Traffic is modest, apart from weekends, and the bends are tight enough to be fun and open enough to see around. Beware of damp leaves in autumn and of ice in the shade, which lingers in winter. The nearby reservoir at Kelbra is popular with birdwatchers, and thousands of cranes gather there in autumn on their way south.

Bad Frankenhausen has a very different monument: the Panorama Museum, which houses an enormous circular painting, by Werner Tübke, of the Peasants' War battle fought there in 1525, when Thomas Müntzer's army was destroyed. The town also has a church tower that leans more than the tower of Pisa, owing to subsidence in the old salt-bearing ground. Fuel and food are available in Bad Frankenhausen, and the old salt spa there is still in use.
t.preetz old road@54.2,10.3:
Preetz sits on a narrow neck of land between two lakes, the Postsee and the Lanker See, in the part of Schleswig-Holstein that the Germans call Holsteinische Schweiz. Holstein Switzerland is a generous name for a landscape whose highest points barely scratch a hundred metres, but the glaciers of the last ice age did leave behind something lovely here: a jumble of lakes, ridges, beech woods and little roads that follow every fold. Preetz is the gateway, a small town of about sixteen thousand people with a proper market square and a calm, practical air.

The town grew around a Benedictine convent founded in the thirteenth century, and the monastery church by the lake is still the quiet heart of the place. The community later became a noble ladies' foundation, which is the sort of odd survival you find a lot in northern Germany. It is worth ten minutes if the church is open. The surrounding streets are all red brick, low roofs and bicycles and on a warm day you are more likely to notice the ice cream queue by the water than any monument.

For a rider the appeal of this start is what lies in every direction. The lanes run gently up and down over glacial hills, with bends that are mostly tight and tidy rather than fast, and the surface is generally good, though farm tractors leave mud and crop remnants around harvest time. Stay alert at the many junctions where hedges block the view. Weekends in summer bring cyclists and cars looking for the lakes, so early starts pay off, and the best light comes in the evening when the fields turn gold and the water goes still. Spring, with rapeseed blooming bright yellow, is when the area looks most like a postcard, although the wind off the Baltic can still be cold.

Fuel is no problem: Preetz is large enough for stations and supermarkets, and nearby Raisdorf adds more choices on the road toward Kiel. Cafes around the market square serve coffee and cake in the German manner, which suits a lazy morning before you head out. The Baltic is only about twenty kilometres north, and you will smell it in the air when the breeze turns, a salty, seaweedy note that always means the day is going to be open and bright.
t.uelzen hundertwasser station sight@53.0,:
Uelzen's railway station is the most unexpected thing in Lower Saxony. Friedensreich Hundertwasser, the Austrian artist who hated straight lines, redesigned it for the Expo 2000 world's fair, and the result is a riot of golden onion domes, wobbly floors, ceramic columns in every colour and trees growing from the roof. Walking through the building is free, and you do not need a train ticket.

Hundertwasser believed that buildings should be alive, with grass on the roof, windows of different sizes and floors that dance. The station is one of his last works, and he died in 2000, just before the Expo. Inside, the uneven floors give the odd sensation of being a little drunk, and the lavatories are famously a work of art in themselves. The town around it is otherwise a quiet, practical place of brick houses and long streets, a farming centre for the sugar-beet and potato lands of the eastern Heath.

Uelzen has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and it is a good place to eat before heading into the heath. The region is known for its heather, which blooms in August and September, covering the sandy hills in purple, and for its heath sheep, the grey-horned Heidschnucken, whose meat is a regional dish. The roads out of town run through pine woods, over open heath and past low farmsteads, flat and gentle, with long straights and sudden bends around a village. The surface is generally good, and the traffic is light.

The Elbe-Lateral Canal runs close to Uelzen, a modern waterway built to carry barges north to the Elbe, and you can watch the big ships pass. The churches and the old centre have a pleasing, brick-built look, and a market takes place in the square. Wrestedt, seven kilometres away, is a small village with little to offer. If you have time before the train arrives, wander through the little park. Eat slowly, and let the strange colours of the station settle in your mind.
t.quedlinburg@51.8,11.1:
Quedlinburg is one of the best preserved medieval towns in Germany, with roughly thirteen hundred half-timbered houses, a number that is hard to believe until you have walked its streets. The whole old town, with the castle hill and the abbey church, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1994. The houses date from the fourteenth to the nineteenth centuries, and many have been restored with care.

The history is older than the houses. In the tenth century, Quedlinburg was a favourite residence of the early German kings of the Ottonian dynasty, and Henry I, who founded the dynasty, is said to be buried in the crypt of the collegiate church of St Servatius, on the hill above the town. For centuries an abbey for noble women stood here, with powerful abbesses who sometimes ruled as princesses. The Romanesque church, with its massive twin towers, is a fine example of the style, and the church treasury holds a few precious relics.

The old town is a delight to walk, with cobbled lanes, a handsome market square with the town hall and a statue of Roland, and a number of small museums. Among them is a museum devoted to Lyonel Feininger, an American-German painter and Bauhaus teacher who loved the town. Quedlinburg was also known for seed growing, and a huge acreage of flowers and vegetables once surrounded the town. The poet Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock was born here in 1724.

For riders, Quedlinburg is the end of a day in the Harz, reached by quiet roads along the northern edge of the hills, through farmland and small villages. The roads are gentle, with a surface that is mostly good and traffic that is light, apart from the tourist season. Fuel is on the edge of town, and it is best to leave the bike in one of the car parks outside the historic core. In the evening, the old streets are lit by lamps, and the sound of church bells carries across the roofs. Weddersleben, four and a half kilometres away, is a village with little for a visitor.
t.bad oldesloe@53.8,10.4:
It has about twenty-four thousand inhabitants, fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and the main road passes right through, so it works well as a fuel stop on the journey between the two great Hanseatic cities. The motorway runs a few kilometres west, but the old road is more interesting.

The town grew rich on salt. Brine springs rise here, and the salt works provided a living for centuries, in competition with nearby Lüneburg and Lübeck. The town added the title Bad, meaning spa, to its name when it became a brine bath, and visitors came to take the waters in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The salt works have gone, but a pleasant spa park and a museum recall the trade, and the Trave runs through the town in a pretty, tree-lined course.

For a rider, the road to Bad Oldesloe from Hamburg runs through gently rolling farmland, with sections of avenue lined with old trees, and the surface is generally good. The speed limit changes frequently, and speed cameras are common near the town, so keep a watch. It is a convenient stage on a day that heads towards the Baltic coast or the lakes of Holstein, and the surrounding countryside is pretty in a quiet way: hedgerows, small woods, and meadows full of cattle.

The Trave is a small, winding river that begins in the Holstein hills and flows through Bad Oldesloe and Lübeck to the Baltic at Travemünde. Along the way, it passes through reed beds and wet meadows that are rich in birds, and canoeists enjoy the quieter stretches. Rümpel, a village three and a half kilometres away, is a small place with a few houses and a church. Fill up here and have a coffee before setting off.
t.lubeck old road@53.9,10.7:
Lübeck is the queen of the Hanseatic League, and from the old road in you can see why. The brick skyline of seven church spires rises from an island in the Trave, with the great Holstentor gate, built in the fifteenth century and so heavy that it has sunk into the soft ground, standing guard at the western entrance. The whole old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and with over two hundred thousand people around it, the city has everything a rider could want: fuel, restaurants, shops and a lively old centre.

For centuries Lübeck controlled the trade of the Baltic. Merchants brought salt from Lüneburg, which was shipped east, and returned with furs, wax, timber and grain from Russia and Scandinavia, and the wealth of those merchants is written in the brick gables of the old town. The Buddenbrooks house on Mengstraße, now a museum, recalls the novel by Thomas Mann, who was born here and made the city's merchant families famous in literature. His brother Heinrich and the novelist Günter Grass are also connected to the city.

Food is a pleasure. Lübeck marzipan, made from almonds and sugar, has been famous since the nineteenth century, and the shop and cafe of Niederegger on the market is a must for sweet-toothed visitors. The Lübecker Rotspon, a red wine that is matured in the city's cellars, is another local product, and the old inns serve Labskaus, a sailor's dish of corned beef, potatoes and beetroot, topped with a fried egg and a pickled herring. The Hospital of the Holy Spirit, a huge medieval hospice with a painted hall, is worth a look.

Riding in is easy, along the Trave from the north or through the leafy suburbs. Park near the Holstentor or the station, and explore on foot, because the old town is an island and busy with traffic. Stockelsdorf, four kilometres away, is the nearest suburb. If you stay for the evening, the spires are floodlit, and the reflections in the river are fine. It is a lovely place to end a day, and a good place to eat well.
t.lubeck@53.9,10.7:
At the northern edge of the city, in the district around Stockelsdorf, the road leads to the Baltic coast, and the ride begins here, heading north-east through the forests and fields of Ostholstein towards Travemünde, Timmendorfer Strand and the sea.

The city's cathedral, begun by Henry the Lion in 1173, stands at the southern end of the old town, and the Burgtor gate is on the north side, just before the road leaves the town. The brick Gothic of Lübeck's churches, especially St Mary's, which served as a model for many churches around the Baltic, is the first sight of a style that you will see again and again on the coast, in Wismar, Stralsund and as far as Tallinn. The Salzspeicher, the old salt warehouses beside the river, are a reminder of how the city grew rich.

The Baltic coast road, which the Germans call the Ostseestraße, is a mixed pleasure. The first stretch is a flat road through farmland, with the sea hidden behind the dunes, and the resort towns along the coast are crowded in summer. But the roads inland, among the hedges and rolling fields, are much quieter and more pleasant. The best time to ride is in the evening or early morning, when the light is soft and the roads are empty.

Travemünde, at the mouth of the Trave, is the seaside district of Lübeck, with a long beach, a casino and the four-masted barque Passat, which is moored there as a museum ship. Ferries to Scandinavia and the Baltic states leave from the harbour, and the ships coming and going are a fine sight. A walk on the beach promenade, with an ice cream and the sea breeze, makes a good way to start the day.
t.schonkirchen@54.3,10.2:
Schönkirchen is the kind of place that rarely gets a mention in guidebooks, a commuter village of about six thousand people east of Kiel, spread along a ridge of farmland a few kilometres from the Baltic. Everything you need is here: a fuel station, a bakery, a supermarket and a few places to eat. It makes a calm start or finish for a day that avoids the busy city.

What makes it useful is its position. Kiel lies just to the west, a port city of nearly a quarter of a million people that grew up around its fjord, a long narrow arm of the Baltic reaching deep into the land. The shipyards that build submarines and warships still line the shore, and ferries to Norway and Sweden leave from the quays beside the city centre in the evening, big white ships gliding out past the sailing boats. The Kiel Canal, opened in 1895 and now the busiest artificial waterway in the world by ship numbers, begins in the north of the city at Holtenau, and you can watch freighters pass through the locks.

East of Schönkirchen, the land gives way to open fields and small villages, with the Baltic never far away. Roads run straight between hedgerows, then bend sharply around a farm or a church, so it is a landscape that rewards attention and a relaxed pace. The surface is generally good, though farm traffic leaves mud on the bends in harvest season. The wind off the sea is a constant, and the clouds move fast, so a layer is useful even in summer.

In the last week of June, Kiel hosts Kieler Woche, the biggest sailing festival in the world, when the fjord fills with thousands of boats and the city fills with music, food stalls and crowds. Accommodation is scarce then, and traffic is heavy, so book early or avoid it. In quiet times, a ride through the villages and along the coast, with a stop for fresh fish at a harbour kiosk, is a fine way to spend a day.
t.molln lake town@53.6,10.7:
Mölln is the town where Till Eulenspiegel is said to have died, and the town has never let anyone forget it. The medieval trickster, a figure from German folk tales who made fools of everybody he met, is supposedly buried near the church of St Nicolai, and a gravestone with an owl and a mirror is a favourite photograph spot. The tales are of uncertain origin, but the town is proud of the legend, and you will find owls and mirrors on souvenirs, fountains and signs. It gives the little lakeside town a sense of humour that many places lack.

Mölln lies on a chain of lakes in the Herzogtum Lauenburg, a gentle landscape of glacial hills and water that feels more Scandinavian than central European. The Stadtsee in the middle of town has a pleasant promenade, and the old centre climbs a small hill with cobbled lanes and half-timbered houses. Salt used to travel along the Old Salt Route from Lüneburg to Lübeck, and Mölln was one of the stations on the way, which is partly why it has such an old and handsome centre. About eighteen thousand people live here, so you will find fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places for coffee and a Fischbrötchen.

The riding around town is quietly enjoyable. Roads wind between lakes and beech woods, with many sections shaded by old trees, and the surface is generally good. The corners are short and smooth rather than demanding, and there are a lot of villages with 30 km/h zones, so patience is useful. Traffic is moderate, with the heaviest flow on summer weekends when Hamburg residents head for the lakes. Beyond Mölln the Schaalsee biosphere region lies to the east, a protected area of clear water and quiet villages along what used to be the border between East and West Germany, and the landscape there is particularly peaceful.

Early autumn is lovely, when mist hangs over the lakes in the morning and the beeches turn copper. The smell of the place is wet leaves, still water and woodsmoke, and the air always feels cooler than it does in the city, thirty or forty minutes to the west. A short walk along the lakeshore before you set off, or when you come back, is a good way to end the day. You will not need to look hard for a bench and a view.
t.selent lake shore@54.3,10.4:
Selent is a village of about thirteen hundred people, and its lake, the Selenter See, is the second largest in Schleswig-Holstein, a long glacial basin of roughly twenty-two square kilometres. Nothing here is grand. The shores are low and wooded, reed beds line the edges, and there are good places for birdwatching, with grebes, swans and cormorants common. It is a quiet bit of Holstein Switzerland where the main events are the arrival of the wind, the colour of the water and the occasional sailing dinghy.

The village itself is small but has a real history. Selent has an old manor, Gut Selent, and the surrounding estates were part of the dense network of noble properties that shaped the landscape of eastern Holstein for centuries. The big country houses, the long lime avenues leading up to them, and the red-brick farm buildings all belong to the same story. The area is largely agricultural, with wide fields of rapeseed, wheat and maize under big skies. The Baltic is not far to the north, and on a clear day the air has a tang of salt that makes the place feel more open than inland Germany.

For motorcyclists, the roads around the lake are an easy pleasure. They are mostly narrow, with gentle bends, short climbs and shady tunnels of trees, and traffic is light except at weekends in high summer. Watch for farm vehicles and cyclists, and slow down in the villages, where speed checks are common. The best riding is in the early morning or late afternoon when the sun is low and the shadows long. Spring and autumn have fewer visitors, and the light on the water is excellent then.

There is no big fuel infrastructure in Selent, which is a village, so fill up beforehand. The nearest town with a good choice of stations and supermarkets is Lütjenburg, about ten kilometres away, with around fifty-eight hundred inhabitants and a pretty old centre. Hohwacht, on the Baltic coast beyond it, is a seaside resort with beach cafes and fish rolls, a natural next stop. In Selent itself you can usually find a bakery and a cafe on a good day, though hours vary, so do not plan your lunch around it. The lake is best enjoyed with a flask of coffee and an unhurried ten minutes on the shore.
t.boknis eck viewpoint@54.6,10.1:
Boknis Eck is a headland on the coast of the Eckernförde Bay, on the Baltic side of Schleswig-Holstein, and the first thing you notice is how low everything is. The land at this point stands only a few metres above the sea. It is a coastline of small cliffs, beaches strewn with flint and boulders left by the glaciers, and long views across the water toward Denmark. The sea off Boknis Eck is also known to marine scientists, who have run a time series station here since the 1950s, measuring temperature, salinity and nutrients in the bay.

The coast road toward Damp and Waabs leads through a countryside of sandy fields, hedges and scattered farms, and the speed here is not about corners but about rhythm. The roads are quiet and the surface is mostly good, with a wind that can be strong and cold even in summer, so check the forecast for the Baltic before heading out. The Schlei inlet, a long narrow fjord-like arm of the sea, lies to the north, and the road to Kappeln follows it for part of the way. Damp has a big holiday complex and a long beach, and is busy in summer; Waabs and its surroundings are quieter.

The history of the area belongs to the borderland between Denmark and Germany. Schleswig was long contested, and many of the villages here still have both Danish and German associations. Not far away lies the Viking settlement of Haithabu, a trading town in the early Middle Ages, and the Danewerk, its protective earthwork. This corner of the country has seen a lot of arguing over who belongs to whom, and mostly it has settled into a relaxed mix. Smoked fish, Fischbrötchen and Matjes are the food to look for along the coast.

For fuel, go to Kappeln, a town of nearly ten thousand people about fourteen kilometres away, or Eckernförde to the south, since the nearby villages are small. A thermos and a windproof layer are more important than anything else here. The light is clear and clean, the air smells of salt and seaweed, and the horizon is huge. If you come on a still evening in summer, the sunset over the bay is a fine reason to linger at the viewpoint a little longer than you planned.
t.bad segeberg@53.9,10.3:
Bad Segeberg has a hill that should not be there. The Kalkberg rises out of the flat Holstein plain like a stray piece of the Alps, a block of limestone pushed upward by an underground salt dome, and on its flank there is an open-air arena where, every summer since 1952, the Karl May Festival has staged Wild West adventures with real horses, stuntmen and fireworks.

The Kalkberg also contains a cave system that is the largest bat hibernation site in Germany, with tens of thousands of bats, including several rare species, that spend the winter there. The caves are protected and closed to visitors in the cold months, but you can join guided tours in summer. The quarry that once cut into the hill has been turned into the performance venue, and the town's old brick houses and its lake, the Segeberger See, make a pleasant place to wander.

The riding around Bad Segeberg is easy and enjoyable. Roads run through the rolling country of central Holstein, with beech woods, small lakes and hedgerows, and the traffic is light outside the festival season. When the festival is on, the town is crowded and the roads clog with coaches, so avoid the Saturday evenings in July and August. The surface is generally good, and bends are gentle, with a few tighter turns around villages.

To the north, the lakes of Holstein Switzerland begin around Plön and Eutin, and to the south the road leads to Hamburg through the quiet farmland of Stormarn. Klein Rönnau, a village close by, has a small museum of rural life. Try a plate of Holsteiner Katenschinken, a smoked ham, in one of the old inns, and take a walk around the Segeberger See before you set off. In autumn the beech woods are glorious, and the lake mists linger over the water until mid-morning.
t.kiel west@54.3,10.1:
Kiel is a city with a fjord at its heart, and the west side is where you most feel the practical, working character of the place. The Kiel Fjord cuts deep inland, giving the city a sheltered harbour, and the Kiel Canal begins at its western edge, so the neighbourhoods here are tied up with ships, locks and shipyards. This was the home of the German Imperial Navy in the nineteenth century, and the sailors' revolt in 1918 that helped end the First World War started here. The city was bombed almost flat in the Second World War, which is why so much of the centre is plain postwar architecture rather than old brick.

Today Kiel is a university city of about two hundred and thirty thousand people with a lively waterfront, and every June the sailing event called Kieler Woche fills the harbour with boats and the streets with music and food stalls. If you leave to the west you pass through Kronshagen and Mönkeberg, suburbs that are mostly residential, and the first part of the ride is urban, with traffic lights, cyclists and commuter flows. Allow a bit of time for the first few kilometres and do not expect much until you clear the ring road.

Once outside the city the landscape opens into farmland and woods, with roads that pick up gentle curves and small climbs, and the Baltic sea air makes the whole place feel fresh. The surface is generally fine. The wind can come in sharply off the water, so layers are useful. A short walk along the fjord before you set off is a pleasure on a clear morning, with ferries and sailboats crossing the water and the smell of salt and diesel rising off the quay. The Kiel Canal crossings, by bridge or small ferry, add a bit of variety to the ride.

Fuel is everywhere in the city, with stations on every main road, so fill up and eat a proper breakfast before you leave. Fish rolls are the local fast food, and a Fischbrötchen with a coffee on the waterfront is a good way to start. Plan to leave early on weekends in summer, when the city fills with visitors and the roads toward the coast can be slow. The reward comes after the first half hour: lakes, hedgerows, small villages with brick churches, and a big sky that belongs entirely to the north.
t.hamburg east edge@53.6,10.2:
Nobody writes songs about the east side of Hamburg, and that is part of its charm as a starting point. Out here the city thins into Stormarn, a district of hedgerows, low brick villages and big sky, and the places on the map, Stapelfeld, Barsbüttel and Glinde, are the sort of towns that exist mainly so that people have somewhere to sleep within reach of the harbour. Glinde has about sixteen thousand people and a good supply of supermarkets and petrol stations, and Barsbüttel is not far behind, so there is no need to worry about fuel before you leave.

What you get in exchange for the lack of drama is access. The motorway to Lübeck is close, but you do not have to take it. Small roads head off toward the Sachsenwald, a large old forest to the south-east that was once Bismarck's estate, and the little river Bille winds through meadows on the way. The hedgerows here are the typical Schleswig-Holstein knicks, earth banks planted with hazel and blackthorn, which have divided the fields for centuries and give the lanes their narrow, enclosed feel. Corners are short and often blind, so keep a little in reserve, particularly when a tractor appears with a trailer wider than the road.

Nearby Ahrensburg has a Renaissance moated castle, white and red with a tidy reflection in its pond, that is worth a detour if you have time before the day begins. The surrounding country was shaped by the ice age and the local brick tradition, and you can see that in the farm buildings and the churches. The air in summer smells of cut grass and rapeseed, and in autumn of ploughed earth and woodsmoke. Cyclists use these lanes heavily at weekends, so a calm pace pays off.

The best time to leave is early morning, when the commuter flow is still building toward the city and the road east is almost empty. Evenings are good for the return, with the sun dropping behind you and the lights of the city glowing on the horizon. This is not a place for photographs or long visits, but it is a practical, friendly kind of start where you can check your tyres, buy a roll and a coffee, and set off with a full tank and a clear head.
t.celle old town sight@52.6,10.1:
Celle is a town that was almost forgotten and so was saved. It sits on the Aller river at the southern edge of the Lüneburg Heath, a handsome ducal residence of seventy-one thousand people, and its old town escaped the bombing of the Second World War, leaving hundreds of half-timbered houses in perfect shape, with carved beams, painted inscriptions and gables leaning over the cobbles.

The dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg lived at the castle in the centre of town for centuries, and its Baroque theatre, the oldest in Germany still in use, remains a lively place. A sad story is attached to the castle: Caroline Matilda, the young queen of Denmark, was exiled here in 1772 after a court scandal, and died of fever three years later at the age of twenty-three. The castle is open to visitors, and her rooms are among the sights.

Celle is also a horse town. The state stud, founded in 1735, breeds Hanoverian horses, and each autumn its stallions are paraded in a famous show in the stud's yard, drawing crowds from across Germany. The countryside around the town is flat and green, with riding stables beside the roads, and the horses are as much part of the landscape as the pines.

For riders, Celle makes a good stop for lunch or a night, with a good choice of cafes and restaurants around the square, and a pleasant walk along the Aller. The roads north and east, through the heath and the Aller valley, are quiet and flat, with long straights, an occasional bend around a village and sandy verges. The surface is mostly good, but watch for sand on the corners. Adelheidsdorf, six kilometres away, has fuel and a small centre. In late summer the heather flowers, and the whole area glows purple, and if you can, time your visit for August or September.
t.luneburg@53.3,10.4:
Salt made Lüneburg, and the town looks as though it knows it. For more than a thousand years the brine springs under the old town were boiled down into white gold, which was carted to Lübeck and shipped across the Baltic to preserve herring, and the profits built a city of tall brick gables, grand merchant houses and a town hall that grew by accretion across six centuries.

The salt that made the city also threatens it. The ground has sunk in places, as the brine was pumped out, and a few streets near the old salt works lean at odd angles, with houses tilting and church towers bent. The effect is surreal and charming, and it adds to the sense of an old town that is constantly shifting. The old harbour district, with its brick crane and its gabled warehouses, is the prettiest corner, and a cafe by the water is a good spot for a coffee.

Lüneburg is also the gateway to the Lüneburg Heath, a wide landscape of sandy hills, junipers and purple heather that is one of the best known in Germany. The heather blooms in late August and September, and the heath sheep, the Heidschnucken, graze among the shrubs. The town's cuisine reflects that: roast Heidschnucke, buckwheat cakes with local cranberries, and heather honey. The roads around the heath are straight and quiet, with the surface mostly good and the traffic light, and a ride at dawn, with mist over the heather, is a memorable experience.

Reppenstedt, four kilometres away, is a large village with supermarkets and fuel. The Elbe is a short ride to the north, with its dike roads and ferries, while to the south the heath rises gently towards the Wilseder Berg, the highest point in the region. The old town is partly pedestrian, so leave the bike on the edge and walk in. In the evening, the brick glows in the low sun, and the lanes fill with students from the university. Stay for dinner, and linger.
t.old and new towns of quedlinburg@51.8,11:
Quedlinburg is a town that looks as if someone forgot to demolish it, and the result is a delight. More than a thousand timber-framed houses survive in its old centre, representing every century from the fourteenth to the nineteenth, and the lanes between them are so narrow and so cobbled that a motorcycle feels like an intruder. UNESCO listed the town in 1994 as an outstanding example of a medieval European town, and the claim is hard to argue with. It sits at the northern edge of the Harz mountains, with the rounded forested hills on the horizon to the south and the flat Saxon lowlands to the north.

The town's history goes back to the tenth century, when Henry the Fowler, the first king of the East Frankish realm, was buried here in 936, and the collegiate church on the castle hill, a Romanesque building of grey stone, still holds his tomb. The hill, called the Schlossberg, gives a fine view over the roofs, and the church treasury includes some famous medieval pieces that were once stolen at the end of the Second World War and later recovered. The streets also hold the house of the poet Klopstock, born here in 1724, and a good many small cafes, galleries and wine bars.

The riding around Quedlinburg is varied. To the south the Harz offers winding roads through spruce and beech forest, with a good number of bends and gentle climbs toward the Brocken, northern Germany's highest peak. To the north the plain gives long, easy stretches with little traffic. Cobbled streets in the old centre call for care in the wet, and parts of the centre are pedestrian or have access restrictions, so park at the edge and walk. Weekends in summer and the Christmas season bring crowds.

With about twenty-three thousand people, the town has several petrol stations on its ring roads, and the centre has plenty of places to eat, mostly serving hearty German food and the local beers. The light is best in the evening, when the stone and timber turn warm, and the smell of wood smoke and baking drifts through the lanes. Spend an hour on foot before you ride on; the town rewards slowness better than almost anywhere in the region.
t.zone 1 burgkloster aegidienstrasse@53.9,:
Lübeck's old town is an island, wrapped in the arms of the river Trave and its canal, and you cross water to reach almost every part of it. The island was the capital of the Hanseatic League, the trading alliance of north German and Baltic cities that dominated the sea for centuries, and the wealth of those merchants is visible in the seven great church spires that fill the skyline. UNESCO listed the old town in 1987, and unlike many cities, it has the feel of a place still in use rather than a museum.

The Burgkloster, near the north end of the island, was a Dominican monastery founded in the early thirteenth century on the site of an earlier castle, hence the name, which means castle monastery. After the Reformation it became a courthouse and prison, and today the surviving brick halls are part of a museum complex alongside the European Hansemuseum, which tells the story of the trading network. Just along the road is the Aegidienkirche, a Gothic church named for St Giles, in a quiet quarter of old merchant houses and narrow passageways called Gänge, courtyards hidden behind the street front where artisans once lived.

The streets in this part of Lübeck are cobbled and tight, and it is a place to park the bike and walk. The traffic around the island is busy, with one-way systems and bridges that tend to bunch up at rush hour. Expect restrictions in the centre, and look for official motorcycle parking at the edge of the old town. The mood in the evenings is warm, with brick walls turning orange in the low light and gulls wheeling over the canal.

Lübeck is famous for marzipan, and the shop with the best known name sells it in every shape, so a small box in the pannier is a respectable souvenir. Thomas Mann, who wrote Buddenbrooks about the city's merchant families, was born here, and the politician Willy Brandt grew up here too. With more than two hundred thousand people, the city has fuel on its main arteries, and Bad Schwartau and Stockelsdorf are good for supermarkets and stations on the way out. The coast, with the long beaches of Travemünde, is only about twenty kilometres away, and the air has a salty edge when the wind comes from the Baltic.
t.town of valle de allende@26.9,-105.4:
Valle de Allende is a quiet town in the high desert of southern Chihuahua, set in a broad valley at about 1,500 metres, with green orchards and fields along the river and bare brown hills beyond. The population is around four thousand, and the place feels more like a country crossroads than a tourist stop. It is a base for a ride that heads south into the mountains toward Indé, across a landscape that has been shaped by mining and ranching for four centuries.

The region owes its existence to silver. Parral, a bigger city about twenty-seven kilometres away, grew rich from the mines in the seventeenth century and has the colonial streets to show for it. It is also the town where the revolutionary general Pancho Villa was shot in his car in 1923, and a museum in the town tells his story. Allende's valley fed that mining boom with grain and fruit, and its old haciendas and churches still stand, with adobe walls the colour of the hills.

The ride itself is a study in empty space. Roads in this part of Mexico run long and straight over high plains, then twist through rocky gaps and across dry creek beds, with few other vehicles. The surface varies from well-kept highway to patched tarmac with potholes, and stray cattle and goats are a hazard, especially at dusk. Topes, the speed bumps at village entrances, appear without warning, and you should slow down for each one. Weather is dry for most of the year, with rain from July to September, when afternoon storms can flood arroyos in minutes.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Valle de Allende has a Pemex station in all probability, but supplies in small towns can run out, so fill up in Parral, where services are better. Carry cash in pesos, since cards are rarely taken in the villages, and some water. Tortillas, cheese from the Chihuahuan Mennonite colonies, and roasted meat are a common lunch, and a small family restaurant is the best bet. Mornings are crisp, afternoons hot, and the stars at night are astonishing.
t.rheinsberg lakes@52.6,13.9:
Strausberg is a lakeside town at the eastern edge of Berlin's commuter belt, and the last stop on one of the city's suburban railway lines. It is set on the Straussee, a long, narrow lake that bends through the middle of the old town, and its medieval centre keeps some stretches of town wall and a church, with a pleasant promenade on the waterfront. A little ferry in summer crosses the lake, a pleasant way to see the town from the water. Rehfelde, a smaller village nearby, and Petershagen add a few pretty corners.

The ride that finishes here is named after Rheinsberg, a lake-studded town about ninety kilometres to the north-west, in the Ruppin country. Rheinsberg is where the young Frederick the Great, then crown prince, spent some of the happiest years of his life in the 1730s, playing the flute, reading philosophy and writing letters to Voltaire. The pink palace on the lake is a lovely sight, and the writer Kurt Tucholsky made the town the setting of a light novel in 1912. Reaching it from Berlin means long roads through pine forest and lake country, with lines of old trees along the road.

The country around Strausberg is easy and quiet. Flat and rolling roads run through fields of rye and sunflowers, with lakes and forest glimpsed between the trees, and the Märkische Schweiz, a low hilly nature park with beech woods, begins a short ride to the north-east. Roads are generally smooth, with cobbled stretches in some villages and tree-lined avenues. Deer cross at dusk, and in summer, the roadside is bright with poppies and cornflowers.

Strausberg has about twenty-seven thousand people, and fuel, food and rooms are easy to find. The town has cafes by the lake, and a plate of smoked fish with a cold beer on the shore is a good ending. Traffic into Berlin is heavy at rush hour, so a late start suits the city better.
t.scharmutzelsee@52.7,12.9:
Nauen is a small town in the Havelland, on the flat country west of Berlin, with a secret claim to fame: radio. In 1906 a transmitter station opened here, among the fields, and it became one of the first in the world to send signals across the globe. The station grew into a huge installation, with steel masts and long wire arrays, and parts of it are still preserved, making it the oldest radio station of its kind still standing. A museum tells the story, and the old masts rise above the fields.

The country around is gentle and wide. This is the Havelland Luch, a low, damp plain of meadows, ditches and reed beds, drained in the eighteenth century under Frederick the Great, and today a haven for birds. White storks nest on rooftops here, and the nearby village of Linum, some twenty-five kilometres to the north, has long been known as a stork village, with dozens of nests every spring. In autumn, thousands of cranes stop to feed in the fields on their way south, and their calls carry far across the open land.

The label points to Scharmützelsee, a big lake south-east of Berlin, so the route ends here at the other side of the city, a long loop. Roads in the Havelland are straight and quiet, with avenues of old lime and chestnut trees, and the surface is mostly good, with some cobbles in villages. The wind can be strong across the open plain, particularly in autumn. Brieselang and Paulinenaue, small places nearby, have a few shops and cafes.

Nauen has about seventeen thousand people, so fuel, groceries, bakeries and rooms are easy to find. Local farm shops sell asparagus in spring and potatoes and apples in autumn. Early summer mornings, with mist over the meadows, are the best time to be here. Beware of tractors on the narrow lanes and of deer at dusk.
t.lusatia lakes@52.3,13.9:
Here the forest begins to close in on Berlin. Grünheide, a village of about seven and a half thousand, sits between the Peetzsee and the Werlsee, and its streets run among tall pines. It has become better known in recent years because the electric car maker Tesla opened a large factory in the forest on the edge of town in 2022.

The label points to Lusatia, the lake district about a hundred kilometres to the south-east, where huge open-cast lignite mines, Tagebau in German, are being turned into lakes. The ride there shows an extraordinary landscape of raw cuts in the earth, giant excavators and new water, a place that is changing before your eyes. Back here, the contrast is soft, with sandy soil, birch and pine, and the smell of resin on a warm day.

Riding in this region is simple and pleasant. Roads run straight through the woods, with long avenues of old trees and a surface that is mostly good, though sand can drift across the lane in places. Cobbles still appear in villages. In dry summers, forest fire danger is high, and signs at the roadside show the daily level. Deer and wild boar cross at dawn and dusk, so slow down. Cyclists and walkers use the lakeshore paths in good numbers.

Spreenhagen has fuel and a few shops, and Grünheide has a couple of cafes and a petrol station, with larger services in Erkner, a short ride west. The lakes are popular for swimming, and the best way to end a hot day is a plunge in the Peetzsee. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with cooler air and fewer crowds.
t.muritz national park@52.7,13.5:
Bernau is the old walled town on the northern edge of the Barnim plateau, and it carries a surprising weight of history for a place that most Berliners know as the end of a railway line. Its medieval wall, with stretches still standing and a few towers, encloses a small centre of brick churches and old houses, and local legend says it was saved in 1432 when the women and children of the town poured boiling beer over Hussite attackers. The story has been told so often that a beer festival in July is named for it.

The label points to the Müritz National Park, a big expanse of lakes and forest more than a hundred kilometres north, where the ride has been all day, so this is the end of a very long loop. In Bernau the contrast is gentle, with a quiet old town and quick links back to Berlin. Just outside, an unusual sight stands among the trees: the former trade union school, built between 1928 and 1930 by the Bauhaus director Hannes Meyer, a clean group of buildings that UNESCO added to the World Heritage list in 2017.

The riding around here is easy. The Barnim is a low, rolling plateau of glacial deposits, with farmland, pine woods and small lakes, and the roads run in long, calm lines between villages. Surfaces are mostly good, but cobbled sections still turn up in older streets and some rural lanes. Buch, to the south, belongs to Berlin and holds a large hospital campus with old brick buildings in a park. In late summer, the smell of cut hay and warm pine drifts through the lanes.

Bernau has about thirty-five thousand people, with fuel, shops and cafes in the centre, and the villages nearby, like Rüdnitz, have a bakery or two. Weekday traffic on the main road into Berlin is heavy at rush hour. For a meal, a plate of local fish or game in a beer garden under old trees is the way to go, with a glass of the town's beer to follow.
t.spreewald canals@52.7,13.7:
The Barnim plateau looks plain until you ride it. East of Bernau and north of Berlin, it is a broad swell of land left by the glaciers, with fields of rye and rapeseed rolling to the horizon, small woods of pine and oak, and tidy villages built around churches made of fieldstone, the rough granite boulders that the ice dropped across the whole region.

The label points to Spreewald, a maze of canals and wooded islands more than a hundred kilometres south-east, where the roads end at the water and boats take over. The ride from there to here swaps that waterworld for a sea of fields, and the contrast is part of its charm. Local roads are smooth, wide and almost empty, often lined with avenues of lime, chestnut or maple that give long stretches of shade. In some villages, the old cobbles still run through the centre, and they can be slippery in the rain.

Werneuchen, a small town with a brick church and a broad market place, was home in the twentieth century to an airfield, and later became known for the sunflower fields and wind farms that cover the land nearby. In July, the sunflowers bloom in huge yellow blocks, and in late summer the cranes gather on the stubble in the evenings. In winter the plateau is bleak and windy, with snow blowing across the road, and the low sun gives a pink light.

Fuel is easy, since stations line the main roads to Bernau, and Werneuchen has a few shops. Village inns serve plain fare, usually pork or fish with potatoes, with beer from a nearby brewery. Be careful of deer on the roads at dusk, and of farm machinery during harvest, when tractors fill the lanes and mud drops from their tyres.
t.barnim forest@52.8,13.0:
Neuruppin is where Fontane was born, and the whole region still feels like one of his books. Theodor Fontane, the great novelist and travel writer of nineteenth-century Prussia, came into the world here in 1819 and later spent years walking through the Mark Brandenburg, recording its castles, lakes and villages in his Wanderings, a work that made the sandy north a place of literary pilgrimage.

Neuruppin, a town of about thirty-two thousand, was rebuilt in a grid after a great fire in 1787, and that planned layout, with wide streets and classical houses, has a calm elegance. The architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, who designed much of Berlin, was born here in 1781, and his statue stands near the church. Lake Ruppin, a long narrow lake, runs along the town's edge, with a lakeside promenade and a boat service in summer. Kremmen, a smaller town to the south-east, has an old medieval wall and a long street of brick houses, and Lindow lies among woods and lakes.

The label points to the Barnim Forest and Werbellinsee, which lie to the east, and the ride covers much of the same country, passing woods, lakes and long quiet roads. Surfaces are generally good, though cobbles appear in the villages, and tree-lined avenues are common. In autumn, mist lies over the lakes in the morning, and cranes call from the fields. Deer, wild boar and the occasional elk can be on the road at night.

Kremmen has fuel and a few places to eat, and Neuruppin has a full range of services. Local specialities include smoked fish from the lakes and Ruppin's famous picture sheets, colourful prints made in the nineteenth century. A late afternoon walk along the lake at Neuruppin, with the light turning gold, is a pleasant way to finish a ride.
t.flaming skate@52.2,13.8:
Storkow is a small town on a lake in the Dahme-Seenland, south-east of Berlin, with a castle at its heart. Burg Storkow, a medieval fortress first recorded in the thirteenth century and rebuilt over time, stands beside the water, with towers and a gate, and the old town around it is a neat cluster of brick houses and a church. The Storkower See, with reeds and a swimming beach, lies right beside, and to the south, the huge lake called Scharmützelsee, the second-largest in the region, is only a few kilometres away.

The land here is a mix of pine forest, sandy heath and lakes left by the glaciers, and it has the quiet of a place that has not changed much. Wendisch Rietz, a village on the Scharmützelsee, is a popular spot for sailing and swimming, and smaller villages such as Reichenwalde sit among the trees. The area is a favourite weekend destination for Berliners, who come to swim, cycle and eat smoked fish by the lake, so roads can get busy on sunny Saturdays.

The label points to the Fläming Skate, a loop of smooth tarmac for skaters in the Fläming hills to the south-west, and this finish lies on the way back to Berlin from the south-east. The riding is relaxed, with straight roads through pine woods, smooth bends around the lakes, and a lot of shade. Surfaces are generally good, with cobbles in the villages and occasional sand at the edges. Wild boar and deer appear at dusk, and in dry summers the forest fire danger is high.

Storkow has about nine and a half thousand people, with fuel, shops, cafes and a couple of guesthouses. A plate of smoked eel or whitefish, a local speciality, with a cold beer at a lakeside kiosk, is a good way to end the ride. Spring and autumn are quieter, and the lakes shine in the low light.
t.uckermark@52.4,13.1:
Few places make a better last stop than the quiet lanes beside Potsdam's South-Western Cemetery. Stahnsdorf, a town of about thirteen thousand people, is known for its great wooded cemetery, laid out in 1909 as a burial ground for Berliners, with winding paths, tall trees and elaborate Art Nouveau monuments.

Many famous people lie there. The film director F. W. Murnau, who made Nosferatu, is buried at the cemetery, as are the artist Heinrich Zille, known for his sketches of working-class Berlin, and the painter Lovis Corinth. The place has the feel of a park more than a graveyard, with rhododendrons, mossy stones and birdsong, and an evening visit when the sun comes low through the pines is deeply peaceful. Entry is free, and visitors should walk quietly.

The label points to the Uckermark, a region of rolling hills and lakes to the north-east, about a hundred kilometres away, where the ride began, so the day ends with a long return to the south-west. The roads here are quiet and tree-lined, with smooth bends through woods and past small lakes. Cobbled sections still appear in old streets, and cyclists are very common on the paths along the Teltow Canal. In autumn the forest glows with yellow and rust.

Nearby, Potsdam is only a few kilometres away, with its palaces and parks, and Wannsee, with its big lake and beaches. Fuel, food and rooms are easy to find, and Stahnsdorf has bakeries and a few simple restaurants. A bowl of soup in a village inn after a day on the road, with the smell of woodsmoke outside, is a good end. Be careful of deer on the roads at night.
t.potsdam havel@52.5,12.9:
The land is flat and watery, with the Havel winding through meadows, reed beds and shallow lakes, and the old fishing town of Ketzin sits on its bank, with a small harbour, a church and a ferry across the river. The air smells of mown grass and mud, and herons stand in the shallows.

Next door lies the Döberitzer Heide, a former military training ground that is now a huge wilderness area, closed to farming for more than a century. Heath, sandy hills, birch and pine make a landscape unlike the rest of the region, and herds of Przewalski's horses, bison and red deer roam freely, grazing the grass and keeping the scrub in check. Guided walks and a few marked paths allow visitors in, but the best views are from the edges. Close by, at Elstal, stand the remains of the 1936 Olympic Village, where athletes lived during the Berlin Games, and some buildings have been restored.

The label links this finish to Potsdam and the Havel, the lakes and palaces to the south, and the ride from there to here follows narrow lanes beside the river. Roads in the Havelland are flat and quiet, with avenues of old trees, and the surface is mostly good, with some cobbled stretches in villages. In spring, white storks return to nest on rooftops, and in autumn, cranes pass over in long lines.

Fuel is available on the main roads, and Wustermark and Dallgow have shops and bakeries, with Ketzin offering a few cafes by the harbour. Smoked fish from the Havel is the local treat. Take care on the narrow lanes at dusk, when deer come out to feed.
t.lehnin abbey@52.6,13.7:
Werneuchen is not on anyone's list of famous places, and that is part of its charm. It sits on the Barnim plateau northeast of Berlin, a town of a little under eight thousand people surrounded by wide, open farmland, big skies and the thin line of a tree-lined road that always seems to run straight to the horizon. The ride that ends here has spent the day around Lehnin Abbey on the other side of the capital, so this is the long loop home, a different Brandenburg from the pine country in the west.

The land is flat enough that weather arrives in plain sight. On a windy day the crosswind across the fields can lean a loaded touring bike over more than you would expect, and in late summer the harvest brings dust, straw and slow combines. Early evening is kind: the light turns copper, skylarks and swallows work the verges, and the sandy soil gives off a warm, dry smell. The surface is decent, though many of the side roads are narrow and have been patched so often that the repairs form a pattern of their own.

Altlandsberg, a few kilometres south, is a good example of what the area has to offer. It is a small walled town with a castle and a compact old centre that was shaped by landowners who wanted to impress, and it is a pleasant place to park and walk for a quarter of an hour. Werftpfuhl is a quiet village nearby, mostly of interest for the way it shows how commuter belt and farmland now sit side by side.

For fuel and food you are well served. Werneuchen has filling stations, supermarkets and a handful of bakeries and snack bars, and Altlandsberg offers a more relaxed cafe stop if you want to sit for a while. A rider can get a decent coffee and a slice of cake almost anywhere here for a modest sum.

Brandenburg's quiet roads can feel repetitive to some, but they have a loose, unhurried quality that rewards a steady throttle hand. At the end of a day of abbey walls and wooded lanes, this is a gentle way to bring the engine down to idle.
t.markische schweiz@52.7,13.5:
Wandlitz is the kind of place that has a famous lake and a notorious past. The Wandlitzsee, a clear glacial lake on the Barnim plateau north of Berlin, draws Berliners for swimming and sunbathing in summer, and the lakeside has a beach, cafes and a path around the water. But for forty years, a small enclosed settlement nearby, the Waldsiedlung, housed the leading members of East Germany's Politburo, behind a fence in the woods, with their own shop and doctor. The East German people called it the ghetto of the leaders.

The countryside here is the Barnim Nature Park, a low plateau of forests, lakes and fields left by the ice sheet, with pine plantations and old beech woods. It is a pleasant mixture, with sandy paths, meadows and wet hollows where cranes feed. Bernau, with its medieval town wall, lies a few kilometres east, and the villages in between have field-stone churches. The old Schorfheide forest, a former royal hunting ground, stretches further north.

The Märkische Schweiz, named in this stop's label, is a hilly district further east around Buckow, where the playwright Brecht kept a summer house. Here, closer to Berlin, the riding is simpler but enjoyable. Roads run through pine forest with long straight sections and gentle curves, and some stretches have avenues of old trees. The surface is smooth on main roads, uneven on minor ones, and cyclists are everywhere on summer weekends. Take care at junctions with bicycle paths. Wildlife is a hazard at dawn and dusk, and the forest roads can be damp and covered with needles.

Practically, Wandlitz has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, with a cluster of cafes around the lake, and Bernau, with about thirty-five thousand people, has a full range of services. Gasthäuser serve local food, including smoked fish from the lakes, and in summer ice cream stands do a roaring trade. The lake is a good place for a break, with benches and a shaded promenade. The S-Bahn reaches Bernau, and Wandlitz has a regional train to Berlin, so a one-way ride and train return is easy.
t.buckow lake bend core@52.6,14.1:
The road bends around the Schermützelsee here, and the bends are the point.
