Buckow lies in a hollow of the Märkische Schweiz, where glaciers once carved a long channel and filled it with water, and the road follows the lake shore in a series of turns that make a welcome change from the straight lines of the Brandenburg plain. Beech woods climb the slopes, and the water flashes between the trunks.

Buckow itself is small, with about sixteen hundred people, but it has been a resort since the nineteenth century, when Berliners took the little narrow-gauge railway out from Müncheberg to spend the summer in villas along the shore. The railway is long closed, but the station buildings and some of the villas remain, with their carved balconies and shady gardens. The town retains a gentle, slightly faded charm, like a seaside resort with the sea replaced by a lake.

For riders, this is one of the most enjoyable roads east of Berlin. The curves are tight enough to be fun and open enough to be safe, the surface is generally good and the traffic is light on weekdays. Watch for gravel and leaves on the corners, especially in autumn, and for cyclists, who love this road as much as you do. Weekends in summer bring crowds, so it is best to ride early or on a weekday.

In the village, you will find a couple of cafes and a baker, and in summer a kiosk at the lakeside sells ice cream and drinks. A smoked fish roll from one of the stands is a classic.

The best light is in the evening, when the sun drops behind the western ridge and the lake goes still. If you are lucky, you will have the lake road to yourself, with only the sound of the engine and the evening birds.
t.schermutzelsee@52.6,14.1:
The water here is the point. Schermützelsee is the largest lake in the Märkische Schweiz, a long, clear glacial channel that runs alongside Buckow, and in summer the shore is dotted with small beaches, jetties and boat hire stations. The water is clean and refreshingly cool, edged with reeds and beech woods, and on a hot day it is hard to resist.

Swimming is straightforward. There is a public beach near the centre of Buckow, with a grass area and a kiosk, and quieter spots along the shore where locals slip in from the bank. The lake is deep in the middle, so be careful if you plan to swim out, and keep in mind that the water takes a while to warm up in spring. Boats and pedal boats can be hired in season, and a small passenger boat makes tours of the lake.

The setting is tranquil. The hills rise gently around the water, with villas and old trees along the shore, and in the early morning the lake is almost still, with mist lifting off the surface. In autumn the beeches turn copper and gold, and the reflection doubles the colour. Winter is quiet, with a skin of ice sometimes forming near the shore, and the village is a calm place for a hot drink.

For riders, the road to the lake is a pleasure in itself, winding through woodland and past small farms. Be careful about leaving kit unattended on the beach, as in any popular spot, and bring a towel, because you will not find one at the water. Fuel is in Müncheberg, about eight kilometres away.

If you go in high summer, aim for the morning or the late afternoon, when the day-trippers are fewer. A swim, a smoked fish roll and an hour in the shade make a very good break.
t.neuhardenberg palace roads@52.6,14.2:
Neuhardenberg is a village on the edge of the Oderbruch, and its palace has an unusual story of renaming. The estate was called Quilitz until 1814, when the Prussian king gave it to his state chancellor, Karl August von Hardenberg, as a reward for his service in the reform era and the wars against Napoleon, and Hardenberg renamed the place after himself. The great architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel redesigned the palace and built the church in the village, a pale, clean-lined building that is among his best small works. In East Germany the village was renamed again, as Marxwalde, and it kept that name until 1990.

The palace today is a cultural centre and hotel, with concerts, readings and exhibitions in its rooms, and a restaurant and cafe in the grounds. The park around it, laid out in the English landscape style, is open, and there is a path beside the village pond. The village is small, about three thousand people, and the main street has the quiet of a place that was once important and is now content.

For riding, the surrounding roads are an easy pleasure. The route from Müncheberg and Seelow runs across the open plateau with long views, passing through villages with avenues of cobbles and old lime trees, and the occasional dip toward the marshes of the Oderbruch. Surfaces are generally good, although some of the older avenues have uneven stretches, and the cobbled village streets are slippery after rain. Farm traffic and combine harvesters appear in late summer. Cranes, white storks and hawks are frequent. Morning light on the fields is beautiful.

Practically, there is a fuel station in Neuhardenberg itself and more in Seelow and Letschin, though it is wise not to rely on small stations being open late. The palace restaurant is the best place for a proper meal, and the village has a bakery and a small shop. Parking is easy in front of the palace. A short walk in the park and a look inside the Schinkel church take about an hour and make a pleasant break. Weekends bring day visitors, so a weekday is quieter.
t.neuruppin lakefront@52.9,12.8:
Neuruppin is where Theodor Fontane was born, in 1819, in the pharmacy his father ran on the main square, and he began his famous walking tours of Brandenburg with the county around the town. The architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, who would shape so much of Berlin, was born here too, in 1781. For a town of thirty-two thousand people, that is quite a pair of local boys.

The town lies on the long, narrow Ruppiner See, a lake that stretches several kilometres north-west, with a promenade, boat landings and cafes along the shore. It is a calm, handsome town with a grid of wide streets, and the lakefront is the natural place for lunch. Most restaurants have terraces overlooking the water, and fish is the safe choice: zander, smoked eel or fried perch, with potatoes and a cold beer or a glass of local wine.

The riding to and from Neuruppin is gentle, through the lake district of the Ruppiner Land, with pine forest, reed beds and small villages. The roads are well surfaced and the traffic is light outside the town, and the lake views appear in fragments between the trees. If you want a longer day, Rheinsberg, with its palace on a lake, lies about twenty-five kilometres north. It was the home of the young Frederick the Great when he was crown prince, and the place where he is said to have been happiest.

Practical matters are easy: fuel and supplies are available in town, and parking near the lake is straightforward on weekdays. At weekends in summer, the waterfront fills with families and cyclists, so go early if you want a table.

The light on the lake in the late afternoon is lovely, a soft silver that suits the calm of the town. Sit with a coffee, look across the water and think of the boy from the pharmacy who ended up writing the great novels of the Mark.
t.rheinsberg palace@53.1,12.9:
Rheinsberg is where a prince became a king, or at least learned to think like one. Frederick, the Prussian crown prince later called the Great, spent four happy years here, from 1736 to 1740, in a palace on the shore of the Grienericksee, away from his violent father, with books, flute music, friends and the philosophers he corresponded with. He had the architect Knobelsdorff remodel the building, and the result is a pale, graceful Baroque and early rococo palace, with a double-winged courtyard facing the water. Later he spoke of this period as the happiest of his life.

The palace was also the setting for a famous light novel. In 1912, the young journalist Kurt Tucholsky published Rheinsberg, a Picture Book for Lovers, a little comedy about a weekend away that became a classic. Today the palace houses a museum with its restored interiors, and the park has lawns, trees, a long terrace by the lake and a number of small buildings and sculptures. The little town, with a population of about nine thousand, has a cobbled centre and a few pretty streets.

For riders, Rheinsberg is the highlight of a gentle lakes ride. The roads from Neuruppin and Lindow run through avenues of old trees, beside lakes with swans and reeds, and through quiet villages. The surface is generally good, with some rough patches near the village edges, and the bends are mild. Traffic is light except on summer weekends, when cyclists and day trippers arrive. In spring, the avenues are dusted with blossom, and in autumn the woods turn gold. Mist often lies on the water in the early morning.

Practically, the town has a fuel station, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes, and several restaurants near the palace serve fish from the lakes and traditional Brandenburg dishes. Parking for motorbikes is easy near the palace entrance, and a stroll through the park is a pleasant way to take a break. Lindow, with about three thousand people, is the next town in one direction and has a small fuel station, but check hours. An afternoon here, with a coffee in the park and the lake shining, is worth the detour.
t.stechlinsee@53.2,13.0:
Few lakes in Germany have as strong a hold on the imagination as the Stechlinsee. It is deep, nearly seventy metres, and so clear that you can see far down through the water, with a bed of white sand and a ring of beech forest around the shore. Fontane made it the setting for his last novel, Der Stechlin, in which the lake is said to stir whenever something great happens in the world, a kind of seismograph of history. It is a beautiful idea, and standing on the shore you can almost believe it.

The lake lies north of Berlin, in the lake district around Fürstenberg, and its clean water is partly an accident of history. For decades, East Germany ran its first nuclear power station on the shore of a neighbouring lake, using Stechlinsee water for cooling, and the plant shut in 1990. Today the lake is a protected nature reserve and a research site for freshwater ecology, and its water is among the cleanest in the region.

Swimming is possible at the village of Neuglobsow, where a public beach has a jetty and a kiosk, and the water is cold and crystalline. The village also has a small glass museum recalling the glassworks that once operated nearby, and a few cafes serving smoked fish and cake. In autumn the beeches turn copper, and a walk around part of the lake is a pleasure.

The ride here is mostly through forest on quiet roads, with gentle curves and occasional cobbles in the villages. Be careful on wet leaves in autumn and for wild boar and deer at dawn and dusk. Fuel is available in Fürstenberg, about eight kilometres away, and it is wise to fill up before you head out into the forest.

Come on a weekday in early summer or in September, when the water is warm enough to swim and the crowds have thinned. Sit by the water and listen to the wind in the beeches. It is a place that rewards stillness.
t.bernau fuel escape@52.7,13.6:
Bernau is the gate to the north-eastern forest, and the way to use it is to be out of Berlin before the city notices you have gone. The B2 and the A11 both start here, with the S-Bahn line running alongside, and the stations around the edge of town are where commuters and weekend riders cross paths. With almost thirty-five thousand people, Bernau has everything a rider might need: fuel, bakeries, supermarkets and a bike shop or two.

North of the town, the Barnim plateau rolls toward the lakes. Wandlitzsee and Liepnitzsee are half an hour away, and beyond them the great pine and beech forests of the Schorfheide begin. The land was shaped by glaciers, and every few kilometres the road dips into a hollow with a small lake or a stream, then climbs back to open farmland. Surfaces are generally good, and the corners are gentle, which makes for easy, relaxed riding.

Bernau has a historical side that is easy to overlook if you are in a hurry. The old town wall is remarkably intact, with a brick tower called the Pulverturm, and a museum in the old executioner's house. The town holds an annual festival in summer commemorating the legendary Hussite siege of 1432, with costumes, music and a lot of beer, which the story says played a part in the victory.

If you are heading north, the early morning is best. The traffic on the B2 builds quickly after seven, and by eight it is a steady stream of vans and commuters heading the other way. Leave before that and you will find the road clear and the light low and golden across the fields.

Fill the tank, buy a coffee and a roll, and have a look at the old wall. It takes ten minutes and tells you something about how long people have been defending this little patch of the Mark.
t.chorin monastery@52.9,13.9:
Few ruins in Germany are as quietly impressive as Chorin. The monastery was founded in the late thirteenth century by Cistercian monks, who moved here from a less suitable site nearby, and they built it in the red brick that is the signature of north German Gothic. The west gable is a masterpiece, a tall wall of brick with delicate tracery, blind windows and slender pinnacles, standing against the sky. The roofless church, the cloister and the remaining monastic buildings sit beside a small lake, the Amtssee, and the setting among woods and meadows feels remote even though Berlin is only an hour away.

After the Reformation, the monastery was dissolved and decayed, serving as a quarry and farm. In the nineteenth century, Karl Friedrich Schinkel and others helped to save what was left, and the ruins became a romantic landmark. Every summer the Chorin Music Summer fills the ruins with concerts, and sitting in the old church under the open sky while a quartet plays is memorable. The surrounding region is the Schorfheide-Chorin biosphere reserve, a landscape of ancient beech woods, lakes and fields, famed for its cranes, sea eagles and black storks.

For a rider, the roads around Chorin are a treat. The route from Eberswalde, about eight and a half kilometres away, climbs gently through beech forest, with the surface in generally good condition, and the lanes toward Britz and the Werbellinsee are quiet and twisting. Avenues of old trees line many stretches, and the dappled light makes it hard to read the road, so take it slowly. Wildlife is frequent, including deer and boar, and cyclists fill the roads on summer weekends. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Chorin village has about two and a half thousand people, a cafe near the monastery and a few small shops, but fuel is available in Eberswalde, with about forty thousand people and a full range of services. Parking by the monastery is straightforward, and the entry fee is modest. The cafe serves cake and coffee, and a walk around the lake takes half an hour. Allow time to sit in the cloister and listen to the quiet.
t.werbellinsee shoreline@52.9,13.7:
The Werbellinsee is a long, deep, glacial lake in the Schorfheide, about ten kilometres from end to end, and its shoreline is one of the loveliest in Brandenburg. Beech forest comes down to the edge, the water is clear and dark, and the road runs along it in places so close that you can smell the water. Joachimsthal lies at its northern end, and Eberswalde, a good-sized town of about forty-two thousand, is a short ride to the south.

The Schorfheide has been a hunting ground for centuries, first for the Hohenzollern princes, later for Nazi leaders and then for the rulers of East Germany. A hunting lodge on the lake, Hubertusstock, served as a retreat for East German officials, and its guests included international statesmen. Today the area is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and parts of its ancient beech forest, such as the Grumsin, are listed as World Heritage. The deer have outlasted all their hunters.

For a rider, the shoreline road is a quiet pleasure, winding through the trees with occasional glimpses of the lake. The surface is mostly good, though patched in places, and the speed limit is low near the villages. Weekdays are calm, and weekends bring cyclists and families to the beaches. In summer, the water is clean and cool, and public beaches at several points allow swimming.

Fuel is not on the lake, so fill up in Eberswalde or Britz before you go. There are small restaurants and a few kiosks, and in season a smoked fish stand near the water. Carry some cash, as card payments are not always accepted in small places.

The best light is in the morning, when mist hangs on the water and the sun comes through the beeches in long rays. In autumn, the leaves turn copper and gold, and the reflection on the lake is double. It is a place to slow down.
t.schorfheide forest roads@52.9,13.6:
Schorfheide is the forest that has hosted more rulers than any other in Germany. Hohenzollern electors hunted here, Hermann Göring built a vast estate called Carinhall in the woods, naming it after his first wife, and the leaders of East Germany kept their own hunting lodges, all in the same pine and beech. Carinhall was blown up in 1945 and little remains, but the forest itself is intact, and it is one of the largest continuous woodlands in the region.

The roads that run through it are long, straight, tree-lined and quiet. Pines and beeches crowd the verge, and in places the branches meet overhead. The surface is mostly good, with some patched sections, and the corners are gentle, which makes it ideal for easy, meditative riding. Cobbles show up in the villages, and sand can blow across the road near open heath. In spring and autumn, mist often lies in the hollows, and the light filtering through the trees is lovely.

Wildlife is part of the draw. Red deer are numerous, and in September and October the stags roar during the rut, a sound that carries through the forest at dusk. Wild boar, foxes and, increasingly, wolves are present, though you are far more likely to meet a deer on the road than anything else. Cranes feed in the clearings in autumn, and white-tailed eagles nest in the old trees near the lakes.

Practical matters need some thought. Villages such as Marienwerder are small and have few services. Carry water and some food, and keep a spare layer, because the forest is cooler than the open land.

Go early on a weekday, switch off the engine for a few minutes and listen. The silence is full of small sounds, and it is one of the best things about riding here.
t.bernau@52.7,13.6:
Bernau keeps its medieval wall. Most German towns lost theirs to the nineteenth century, but here a long stretch of the brick-and-fieldstone circuit survives, with the Pulverturm, the Steintor and the grim little Hungerturm still standing, and you can walk almost the whole circle in half an hour. Legend says the wall saved the town from the Hussites in 1432, and an annual festival with costumes keeps the story alive, whatever the historians say. About thirty-five thousand people live here now, and the old centre, with its large Gothic church of St Marien, sits quietly behind a commuter-belt outer ring.

The other surprise on the edge of town is a school. In the late 1920s, the trade-union federation built a training school in the woods, designed by the Bauhaus director Hannes Meyer, a low, calm complex of glass and brick with covered walkways. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2017 as part of the Bauhaus sites, and the restored building is open for visits. Together with the old wall, it makes Bernau a smaller and more interesting stop than the S-Bahn timetable suggests.

The land around is the Barnim plateau, glacial and gently rolling, with forests of pine and oak, small lakes and the villages of Rüdnitz and Panketal in the surrounding countryside. Riding here is unhurried. The main road toward Eberswalde and the Schorfheide is smooth and quick, and the lanes off it twist through woods with patches of cobbled surface in the villages. Cyclists fill the roads at weekends, and wild boar and deer are about at dusk. A morning in early summer, with the light coming through the pines, is the best time.

Practically, Bernau has everything. Fuel stations ring the town, supermarkets and bakeries are in the centre, and several cafes sit near the market square, serving coffee, cake and, in warm weather, local ice cream. Parking near the wall is easy, and there is a bike-friendly culture, so you will see plenty of other riders. It is a fine place to finish a day on the Schorfheide and Werbellinsee roads, with the S-Bahn waiting to carry you home if the bike needs a rest.
t.lubbenau fuel and food@51.9,14.0:
Lübbenau is the front door to the Spreewald, and the first thing it will tell you is that this is a landscape of water. The Spree breaks up here into hundreds of small channels, called Fließe, that wind between meadows and alder woods, and for centuries the only way to reach many farms was by flat-bottomed punt. Tourists still glide through on long wooden boats pushed with poles, and the postman used to deliver by boat in the old days.

The town has about seventeen thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and a good run of bakeries are easy to find. The old centre sits near the harbour where the punts start, and the restaurants around it serve the dishes the region is proud of: Spreewald gherkins, which carry a protected name, with linseed oil and boiled potatoes, smoked or fried fish, and horseradish in everything. A few pancake and cake places do a thriving trade at the weekend.

This is also the edge of Sorbian country. The Sorbs, a Slavic minority who have lived in Lusatia for more than a thousand years, keep their own language, costumes and customs, and in some villages the road signs are bilingual. In spring, Sorbian women paint Easter eggs in intricate patterns, and in some villages girls wear the traditional headdress on feast days.

Riding here is gentle. The roads are flat and straight, with the occasional bridge over a channel, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is thick on summer weekends, when coaches and cyclists crowd the lanes near the harbour, and it is better to arrive early. Avoid the middle of the day if you can. In the early morning, mist hangs over the water and the light turns the alders gold.

A boat ride costs a modest sum and takes you into a world with no engines. It makes the road feel loud afterward.
t.burg spreewald canal core@51.8,14.1:
Burg is the heart of the Upper Spreewald and one of the most Sorbian places you will find in Brandenburg. The village, with about four and a half thousand people, goes by its Sorbian name, Borkowy, on bilingual signs, and the wooden houses with their carved gables and steeply thatched roofs stand beside canals that serve as streets. Here the water is the main road. Punts carry visitors between farms, and a surprising number of locals still keep their own boats.

The Spree arrives from the south and splits into a labyrinth of channels, and the area is a UNESCO biosphere reserve. The woods are mostly alder, growing right in the water, and in autumn the leaves fall and float along the surface. Small meadows between the channels are mown by hand in places, because machines cannot get in. Kingfishers, otters and beavers live in the quieter channels, and white storks nest on the village rooftops.

For a rider, the roads around Burg are narrow, flat and slow, with low speed limits and bridges that creak. This is not a place for speed but for gentle cruising, and you will often share the road with cyclists, who outnumber cars on a summer weekend. The surface is generally good, though bumpy at the bridges, and it can be slippery after rain. Parking in the village is limited, so be patient.

There are restaurants by the canals serving fish, potato dishes and the famous gherkins, and a few bakeries selling Sorbian pastries. Fuel is not in the village, so fill up in Vetschau, about seven kilometres away, or in Lübbenau. A traditional Spreewald lunch is plain and filling, and tastes better after a morning on the road.

Early morning and evening are the best times, when the village is quiet and the light on the water is golden. In winter, the canals sometimes freeze, and the locals skate between the farms, a scene that looks like a Dutch painting. It is a place that asks you to slow down.
t.straupitz windmill sight@51.9,14.1:
The windmill at Straupitz is a Dutch-style tower mill, a plump, whitewashed thing with a turning cap and four long sails, standing at the edge of a Spreewald village that otherwise looks as if it belongs in an illustrated children's book. It is a working museum these days, and the sails creak in a good breeze. It is only part of the reason to stop. A few hundred metres away stands the village church, built in the 1820s and 1830s to a design of Karl Friedrich Schinkel, a big, round-arched brick building with a surprising grandeur, sometimes called the cathedral of the Spreewald.

Straupitz belongs to the Sorbian, or Wendish, country, the home of a Slavic minority that has lived in Lusatia for over a thousand years. Place names appear in two languages on the signs, and in some villages older women still wear the elaborate folk costume and headdress on feast days. The cuisine is distinctive. Spreewald gherkins, sold in jars everywhere, are famous, and a plate of boiled potatoes with quark and linseed oil is a local dish worth trying at least once.

The landscape is flat and watery. The Spree splits here into a maze of small channels, with alder carr, wet meadows and little farms on raised mounds, and in summer the whole area is full of green light. The roads are straight and quiet, with avenues of old oaks and poplars, and the bends come when the road meets a channel. The surface is generally good, though in places it has the patched look of a road that floods. Mist and midges are common near the water, and cyclists fill the lanes at weekends, so give them room. Spring and early autumn are lovely.

Practically, Straupitz has a small shop and an inn, and the nearest fuel is in Burg, about nine kilometres away, with more at Lübbenau. Neu Zauche, closer by, is a tiny village. Take cash, because some places do not take cards. A visit to the windmill and church takes an hour, and the nearby cafes sell gherkin rolls and cake, which makes a good lunch for riders short on time.
t.schwielochsee@52.0,14.2:
Schwielochsee is a broad, shallow lake south-east of Berlin, where the Spree widens out before continuing north, and it is among the larger natural lakes in Brandenburg. The shoreline is a mix of reeds, pine woods and small villages with sandy beaches, and the water is warm enough in summer for easy swimming. It is a lake for holidays rather than drama, and none the worse for that.

The surrounding country is quiet, flat and half-forgotten. To the south lie the heaths and the former lignite landscapes of Lusatia, and to the north the forest of the Dahme-Heideseen. The nearest towns are small: Friedland, with about thirty-six hundred people, lies a little to the south, and Beeskow, sixteen kilometres away, has a medieval castle and a town wall. Both have fuel and basic services, and Beeskow is the better place for a proper meal.

Riding here is easy and unhurried. Roads run along the lake edge and through the pine forest, mostly smooth and empty, with the occasional sandy patch near the shore. The curves are mild and the traffic light. In summer, the weekends bring campers and caravans to the lakeside sites, and you will want to avoid the main road toward the camping areas on a Friday evening.

A swim stop is simple. Several villages have public beaches with a small kiosk or a restaurant, and in the afternoon the water is warm and clear. Bring a towel and a little cash, as card payment is not universal here. After a swim, a plate of fried fish and potatoes tastes better than it has any right to.

The light over the lake in the evening is a soft, flat gold, and the reeds go dark against the sky. It is an excellent place to slow down at the end of a long day, with the smell of woodsmoke and warm sand drifting across the shore, and no one in a hurry.
t.lubbenau@51.9,14.0:
Lübbenau is the gateway to the Spreewald, and the first thing you notice is the quiet that comes from a town where half the traffic moves by punt. The Spree breaks into a lace of channels here, called Fließe, with flat-bottomed boats, the Kähne, gliding between banks of alder and willow, and the old harbour in the centre is the place where visitors board. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, farmers poled their vegetables and mail along these waterways, and some villages were only accessible by water. The rich soils grow cucumbers, horseradish and onions, and the gherkins have become a regional symbol.

The town is about seventeen thousand people, with a Baroque palace and park that was the seat of the Counts of Lynar, and a pleasant old centre with a church, a small museum and cafes. The Spreewald is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and it supports otters, white storks, kingfishers and a surprising number of dragonflies. The air is humid and smells of wet wood and pond weed, and in early mornings, mist hangs on the water and the world seems far away.

For riders, this is flat-country riding, easy and calm. The roads between Lübbenau, Lübben and the villages are straight with avenues of old trees, and the main hazards are cyclists, who flock to the cycle paths along the canals, and farm vehicles. The surface is mostly good, though the narrow lanes through the villages may be patched and flooded after heavy rain. Expect crowds at the harbour in July and August, when day-trippers arrive in coaches. Spring, with the blossom, and early autumn, with the mist, are the better seasons. In winter, the canals sometimes freeze, and locals skate along them.

Practically, the town has fuel stations on the approach roads, supermarkets, bakeries and a good choice of restaurants serving fish, potatoes with linseed oil and the inevitable gherkin. Parking near the harbour is limited at weekends, so arrive early. Lübben, nearly ten kilometres north, is the other main town of the Spreewald, with a lovely old town on an island in the Spree. If you have time, take a boat trip, because the canals are best seen from the water.
t.bad belzig castle hill@52.1,12.6:
Above the little spa town of Bad Belzig, on a low hill with a view across the Fläming, stands Burg Eisenhardt, a medieval castle that has survived better than most in Brandenburg. Its round keep, nicknamed the Butterturm, rises over the walls, and the castle's courtyards and bastions hold a museum and a youth hostel. The hill itself was a lookout for centuries, guarding a trade route across the heath. The town below has about twelve thousand people and a pretty, cobbled centre, with timber-framed houses and a market square, and the castle gives it a faintly storybook air.

The Fläming is a ridge of glacial moraine that runs through western Brandenburg and into Saxony-Anhalt. At about two hundred metres it counts as high country here, and the ridge supports oak and beech forest, heath and farmland, with a patchwork of small villages. A few kilometres away, the hill of Hagelberg was the site of a battle in 1813, in which Prussian forces beat a French army during the Napoleonic Wars. Wiesenburg, a smaller town to the west, has a castle and a big landscape park with rare trees and a lake, well worth a visit.

For riding, this is some of the best country near Berlin. The roads roll gently over the moraine, with long, curving straights, avenues of cherry trees that blossom in April, and views over fields and woods. The surface is mostly good, and the villages have a quiet charm, with thatched barns and old churches. Traffic is light, and the hazards are the usual ones of boar, deer and tractors. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. In summer, heat on the open ridge can be strong, and in winter the north wind is bitter. Fog gathers in the hollows.

Practically, Bad Belzig has a fuel station, supermarkets, bakeries and several cafes and restaurants, as well as a thermal spa that makes a good place for a soak after a long day. Niemegk, with about two thousand people, has smaller services. The castle is open daily in season, and a climb of the keep gives a fine view. Parking at the foot of the hill is easy, and the walk up takes a few minutes. Bring cash for the village cafes.
t.wiesenburg park roads@52.1,12.5:
Wiesenburg lies on the northern edge of the Hoher Fläming, a ridge of low hills, forest and heath south-west of Berlin that counts as the highest ground for a long way around. The town has about five thousand people and a small palace with a landscape park, laid out in the English style, where old and unusual trees stand in wide lawns and a stream winds through. The park is open to visitors and is a pleasant place for a short walk.

The Fläming is a quiet landscape. Pine and oak woods cover the slopes, sandy fields and heaths lie in the hollows, and villages are small and far between. The ridge was shaped by glaciers, which left behind a pattern of hills and valleys that rolls gently to the horizon. Avenues of old trees line many of the roads, and cobbled sections are common near villages. The area is a nature park, popular with walkers, cyclists and riders on horseback.

For a motorcyclist, the roads are some of the best in this part of the country. They are narrow, winding and well surfaced, with bends that are gentle enough to flow and tight enough to keep you awake. Traffic is very light, especially on weekdays, and you may go a quarter of an hour without seeing another vehicle. Watch for gravel and leaves on the corners, and for farm machinery in harvest season.

Fuel and food are in Wiesenburg, which has stations and a few restaurants and bakeries. A railway runs through the town, and the old station is a reminder of its past as a junction. If you need a larger town, Bad Belzig, about ten kilometres away, has everything, including a hospital and a medieval castle.

Autumn is a good time here. The beeches and oaks turn red and gold, and the heath is purple in late summer. In spring, the fields are green and the forests fill with birdsong. It is a place that rewards a slow, unplanned ride, with a stop wherever the view or the smell of the woods tempts you.
t.rabenstein castle photo@52.0,12.6:
Burg Rabenstein is one of the best-preserved medieval castles in Brandenburg, standing on a wooded hill in the Hoher Fläming, and it looks every bit like a child's picture of a castle: a round keep, stout walls and a pointed roof rising from the trees. It dates back to the twelfth or thirteenth century, and it has been a lookout, a family home, a ruin and, in modern times, a museum and a venue for events. Falconry displays have long been a feature, and the site has an owl and eagle collection that draws families in summer.

The setting is the reason to stop for a photograph. The castle sits above a village, and the approach road climbs in a gentle curve through beech forest, with a view of the walls appearing and disappearing between the trunks. In autumn the leaves turn gold around it, and in winter, with frost on the branches, it looks like something from a fairy tale.

The Hoher Fläming is one of the highest parts of the region, though high is relative: the Hagelberg, the summit of the range, is about two hundred metres, and was the site of a battle in 1813 in which Prussian troops beat a French force. The hills and forests around the castle are criss-crossed by quiet roads, cobbled lanes and avenues of lime and oak, and they are among the most pleasant riding in the area. Surfaces vary, and the cobbles can be slippery when wet.

Niemegk, a smaller town, is closer and has the basics. The castle has a cafe and a small restaurant, though hours vary, so do not rely on it.

The best time is a clear morning on a weekday, when the car park is empty and the light is low on the walls. Walk up to the gate, look at the stonework, and breathe the smell of old wood and damp stone. It is a small journey into the Middle Ages.
t.strausberg lakes edge@52.6,13.9:
Strausberg has two things you do not often find together: a long, beautiful lake and an extremely unusual railway. The Straussee stretches several kilometres through the town, with a promenade, a small passenger ferry that crosses it in a few minutes, and wooded shores that make you forget that Berlin is just beyond. The little ferry is a pleasure in itself, a cheap and slightly absurd way to cross water.

The other curiosity is the Strausberg railway, an electric tram line that runs through the town and has done so since the early twentieth century, still operating today as a local line. Together with the S-Bahn, which connects the town to central Berlin, it gives Strausberg an unusual transport heritage. The old town is small, with a remnant of its medieval wall, a gate tower and a Gothic church, and is worth a short walk.

With nearly twenty-seven thousand people, Strausberg has all the services you might want: fuel stations on the main road, supermarkets, bakeries, cafes and restaurants along the lake. It is a good place to start a ride, being only about thirty kilometres from the centre of Berlin and a gateway to the Märkische Schweiz and the Oderbruch. The roads east are quiet and the scenery improves quickly.

The ride along the lake edge is gentle and slow, with low speed limits and a fair number of pedestrians. Further on, the roads open up, with tree-lined avenues, long straights and gentle curves. The surface is good, and the main hazard is farm vehicles and the occasional pothole.

Come early on a weekend if you want the lakefront to yourself. The light on the water at dawn is soft and silver, and the first ferry crosses with almost no passengers. Have a coffee at the quay, take in the view, and then head east. The best of the day is still ahead of you.
t.buckow and schermutzelsee@52.6,14.1:
Buckow tends to be remembered for one house. In 1952 the playwright Bertolt Brecht and the actress Helene Weigel acquired a modest villa on the shore of the Schermützelsee, with a garden running down to the water, and used it as a summer retreat until Brecht's death in 1956. It is now a small museum, set among old trees, and the rooms keep a sense of the plain, slightly austere taste of its owners. Brecht wrote the Buckow Elegies here, short poems of great simplicity, looking at the lake and the trees.

The town is a small resort in the Märkische Schweiz nature park, with sixteen hundred residents and an old-fashioned air. Villas from the late nineteenth century line the roads, built when Berliners began to treat the lake and its hills as their own Swiss holiday. There is a spa park, a clutch of cafes and a boardwalk along part of the shore. In summer, the town fills up with visitors, and the smell of grilled sausages and smoked fish drifts through the streets.

The lake itself is the draw for swimming and walking, and you can circle it on foot in a few hours. The woods on the slopes are mostly beech, with oak and pine on the drier ground, and in spring the forest floor is covered with wood anemones. Buckow's position in a hollow between wooded hills makes it feel sheltered, and the air is noticeably fresher than in Berlin.

Riding into Buckow from the west gives you a descent through the beech woods, with the lake appearing suddenly between the trees. Roads are generally good, with some tight bends and occasional patches of gravel or leaves. Fuel is in Müncheberg, eight kilometres away, and should be bought before you arrive. In the town, a handful of bakeries and cafes provide the basics.

Early mornings and weekdays are quiet, and the lake is a mirror. It is a pleasant place for a slow lunch and a swim, and a reminder that even a modest landscape can inspire a lot of poetry.
t.neuhardenberg palace plain@52.6,14.2:
The Oderbruch is a landscape made by a king's order. In the middle of the eighteenth century, Frederick the Great had the marshy valley of the Oder drained and diked, turning a swamp into some of the richest farmland in Prussia, and he invited settlers from across Europe to farm it. The villages that sprang up have a regular layout, with a single long street and a church in the middle, and the fields run in straight lines to a flat horizon.

The land has seen heavy history. In April 1945, the Soviet army crossed the Oder and attacked the German positions on the Seelow Heights, a low escarpment above the plain, in one of the last great battles of the Second World War, and a memorial and museum at Seelow, about twenty kilometres south-east, tell the story. The great Oder flood of 1997 put the dikes to the test, and the villages still talk about the sandbag lines and the weeks of watching. In Letschin, nine and a half kilometres away, the young Theodor Fontane spent part of his childhood, when his father kept a pharmacy there.

Riding here is about space and light. The roads are straight and flat, with tall avenues of poplars and limes that give the landscape its rhythm, and wind sweeps in across the open fields with nothing to stop it. Crosswinds can be strong, and a headwind on a long straight is a test of patience. The surface is generally good, with occasional rough patches. In spring, the rapeseed turns the fields yellow, and in autumn, cranes pass overhead in loud flocks and storks gather before flying south. Evening light on the flat land is beautiful.

Practically, Neuhardenberg has fuel and a small shop, and Letschin and Seelow offer more. There is little shelter in a storm, so watch the sky. The palace restaurant in Neuhardenberg is good for a proper meal, and bakeries in the villages open early. Carry some cash for farm stands, which sell eggs, honey and vegetables in season. A slow evening drive here is a good way to understand why a king wanted this land.
t.oderbruch open road air@52.6,14.4:
Open sky is the signature of the Oderbruch, and Letschin sits in the middle of it. This is a polder, a stretch of marshland along the Oder that Frederick the Great had drained in the 1740s and 1750s, moving the river into a new channel and settling farmers from across Europe on the reclaimed land. The result is a flat, fertile plain, crossed by dykes and drainage ditches, with farms laid out in rows and a huge horizon.

Letschin has a particular link to Theodor Fontane. His father took over the village pharmacy in the late 1830s, when Theodor was a teenager, and the writer later looked back on the Oderbruch with real affection. There is a small memorial, and a sense in the village that the great writer is still part of the place. About five thousand people live in the municipality, with fuel and a few shops, and Seelow, twelve kilometres south, is the nearest larger town.

The history here is also heavy. In April 1945, the Seelow Heights, on the western edge of the Oderbruch, were the site of one of the last great battles of the war in Europe, when the Red Army broke through German defences on its way to Berlin. A memorial and museum at Seelow describe it, and the landscape still holds traces. Neuhardenberg, nearby, has a church designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel and a palace that is now a cultural centre.

For a rider, the Oderbruch roads are among the most open in the east: straight stretches along dykes, wide views and little traffic. Wind is the main factor, and the horizon seems enormous. The surface varies, and some roads have broken edges and ruts. In spring and autumn, cranes and geese fill the sky, and the sunsets can be spectacular.

Stop in a village, look across the fields and let the quiet settle. It is an unshowy landscape that grows on you.
t.muncheberg fuel window@52.5,14.1:
Müncheberg sits on the old trade road between Berlin and the Oder, the route that later became the Reichsstraße 1, running from Aachen all the way to East Prussia. Today it is the B1, still carrying freight and holidaymakers through the middle of the town, but beyond the main road the town is quiet. About seven thousand people live here, and it is a reliable place for fuel, with stations on the main road and supermarkets within a short distance.

The town has an unexpected specialism: agricultural science. A large research institute for agricultural landscapes is based here, with experimental fields on the plateau, and the town's place in the history of plant breeding goes back to the early twentieth century. That is why you see test plots of grain and unusual crops beside the road, tidily labelled. The medieval centre has a section of the old town wall, with towers and a gate, though the church was damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt.

Müncheberg is a good gateway to the Märkische Schweiz, whose lakes, hills and beech woods begin a few kilometres to the north. The roads between the two are some of the most enjoyable in the region, gently curving and well surfaced, with light traffic on weekdays.

A bakery or two in the centre sells good bread, and a handful of restaurants serve plain German dishes: schnitzel, potato dishes, fish in season. Prices are low. It is not the sort of town that tries to charm you, but the pace is relaxed and the people friendly.

Come early, when the market stalls are setting up and the light is low across the square. Take a moment to look at the old walls, buy a roll and a coffee, and fill the tank. The hills are waiting.
t.gransee backroads@53.0,13.2:
Gransee is a small town with a big memory. In 1810 the young Queen Luise of Prussia died suddenly at her family's summer residence, and her coffin was carried back to Berlin in a slow procession that rested overnight in Gransee. The town later raised a monument on the spot, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, a delicate cast-iron canopy that still stands in the market square, a rare piece of early German neo-Gothic metalwork. It is lovely and a little sad.

The town has about sixty-five hundred people and is surrounded by a rather well-preserved medieval wall, with a gate, the Ruppiner Tor, and a gunpowder tower among the surviving elements. Inside, the streets are quiet, with brick houses and a large Gothic church. It is an easy place for fuel, bread and a coffee, with stations on the main road and a few cafes in the centre.

The country around Gransee is the northern Brandenburg lake district, a blend of forest, farmland and water that stretches north to the Mecklenburg border. Backroads here are narrow and quiet, running between fields and lakes, with long tree-lined stretches and the occasional cobbled village. The surface is mostly good, and you will meet few cars on weekdays. It is leisurely riding, suited to a slow day and an open mind.

Wildlife is part of the pleasure. White storks nest on village rooftops, cranes feed in the fields in autumn, and herons stand in the ditches. Deer step out of the forest at dawn, so keep your speed down. In summer, the lakes are warm, and many have small public beaches.

From Gransee, Rheinsberg is about thirty kilometres north-west, and Zehdenick is closer to the south. Both are worth a visit, but there is no need to hurry. The charm of this region is that nothing is far and nothing is urgent. A day of wandering the backroads, with a stop at a lakeside cafe, is a fine way to spend a Sunday.
t.rheinsberg castle and lake@53.1,12.9:
Rheinsberg belongs to the water. The town sits on the Grienericksee, with the long Rheinsberger Rhin running out toward the Ruppin lakes, and it is surrounded by a chain of lakes and forests that forms one of the quietest corners of Brandenburg. The palace is the headline attraction, but the lakes explain why the prince Frederick, later the Great, found the place so restful. On a still summer evening, with swans on the water and the pale walls of the castle reflected in the lake, it is easy to understand.

North and east of the town, the landscape reaches a more austere beauty at Lake Stechlin, an exceptionally clear and deep lake that Theodor Fontane used as the title and setting of his last novel, Der Stechlin. A short distance from Rheinsberg, on a different lake, the German Democratic Republic built its first nuclear power plant, which ran from the mid-1960s until 1990, and the site is now being dismantled. It is an odd contrast, an experimental reactor beside a lake of sedge and water lilies. The town also has a tradition of pottery, and the local ceramics shops sell blue-and-white ware.

The riding is easy and pleasant. The roads from Rheinsberg to Lindow, Neuruppin and Gransee run through avenues of old lime and oak, beside lakes, with views of reeds and boats, and the bends are mild and the surface decent. Traffic is light on weekdays, and weekends bring cyclists and day-trippers. In summer, the lakeside roads are pleasant, and in autumn the woods turn gold and the mist lies on the water in the early morning. The hazards are deer and boar, especially at dusk, and wet leaves on shaded corners.

Practically, Rheinsberg has a fuel station, a supermarket, several bakeries and a few restaurants near the harbour, where smoked fish and fresh pike-perch are on the menu. Lindow, with just over three thousand people, is about sixteen kilometres away and has smaller services, while Großwoltersdorf is a village with little more than a shop. Take cash, since some small places do not take cards, and bring something warm for the evening, because the air off the lake cools quickly. A boat trip on the lake is a nice change of pace.
t.neuruppin lakefront food@52.9,12.8:
In 1787 a great fire destroyed most of Neuruppin, and the town was rebuilt on a grid, in a clean neoclassical style, with wide streets and a large parade ground. The plan, drawn up by royal officials, gives the place an unusual openness, and walking through it you can feel the order of the Enlightenment. The lake side of the town, however, kept its old character, and the lakefront is where you want to eat.

Neuruppin has about thirty-two thousand people and is the largest town for many kilometres, so it has all the services: fuel, supermarkets, bike shops and a hospital. The lakefront, along the Ruppiner See, is a promenade of cafes, ice-cream stands and restaurants with terraces, and boats of all sorts bob along the quay. There is a spa on the shore, using the local brine, and a pleasant beach in summer.

Food options are plentiful, and the best are the simple ones. Fresh fish from the lake, such as zander and perch, is served grilled or fried, with potatoes and salad. Smoked eel is a regional delicacy. Brandenburg also loves its asparagus in spring, its mushrooms in autumn and its plum cake in late summer, and most menus reflect the season. Prices are reasonable, and portions are generous.

The riding around the town is easy and pleasant. Roads along the lake and through the forest are well surfaced, with gentle curves and light traffic outside the holiday season. In July and August, the lakefront fills with visitors, and you may need patience to find parking. Weekday lunchtimes in spring and autumn are the best moments.

Take your time. Sit at a table by the water, order something fried, and watch the boats. The light on the lake changes through the afternoon, and the wind ruffles the surface. It is a good place to spend an hour doing very little.
t.kremmen moor roads@52.8,13.0:
Kremmen sits at the edge of a marsh, and the roads around it are a lesson in how the Mark Brandenburg was made. The ground here is the Rhinluch, a broad, low-lying fen of peat and sand that was drained, diked and farmed from the eighteenth century onward, and the word Luch means exactly that, a wet meadow.

The moor is a place for birds. In autumn, thousands of cranes gather in the fields of the Rhinluch to feed before moving south, and their calls carry for miles across the flat land at dawn and dusk. White storks nest on roofs and poles in the villages, geese pass overhead in long skeins, and in the wet meadows, lapwings and curlews still turn up. The landscape is subtle, with long horizons, rows of willows, canals and the smell of wet earth and cut grass. Mist often lies on the fields in the morning.

For riders, the moor roads are straight and level, with long views and the occasional causeway raised above the fen. Surfaces are patchy, with cracks and sinks where the peat has settled, so keep an eye out for bumps, especially after a wet spring. Wind can be strong, and rain squalls cross the plain quickly. The old brick-paved village lanes are slippery when wet. It is quiet riding, good for easing off the pace and watching the sky. Early morning and evening are the best times, when the light is soft and the cranes are active.

Practically, Kremmen has a fuel station, a supermarket, bakeries and a couple of inns, and Velten and Leegebruch, about twelve kilometres away, have larger services. Berlin is within an easy ride, and the regional train from Kremmen goes in. In the autumn, you can hear the cranes from the road, so stop the engine and listen. Keep the tank topped before heading out on the quieter roads, because there is little between villages.
t.konigs wusterhausen@52.3,13.6:
In December 1920 a group of postal engineers at Königs Wusterhausen broadcast a concert of carols and instrumental music from a hill outside town, and the sound went out across Germany. It is remembered as the country's first radio broadcast, and the hill, the Funkerberg, still carries a historic radio station and a museum of early broadcasting. Whatever the exact date, this was where German radio began, and the masts on the hill have been a landmark ever since.

The town has other claims on history. In the early eighteenth century, the Prussian king Friedrich Wilhelm I, known as the Soldier King, made the hunting lodge here his favourite retreat, and held his legendary Tobacco Colloquium, a sort of smoky evening club, in its rooms. The little palace is open to visitors. The Dahme river runs through the town, with a lock and a harbour, and the old railway junction ensures plenty of traffic.

With over thirty-two thousand people, Königs Wusterhausen is a busy commuter town and has everything: fuel on all the main roads, supermarkets, cafes, bakeries and a station for the S-Bahn into Berlin. It makes a good fuel stop for riders heading south into the Dahme-Seengebiet or the Spreewald, since the road beyond becomes quieter and the stations fewer.

Traffic through the town can be heavy, especially in the morning and evening, and the level crossings on the railway can hold you up. The ride south, however, is a pleasure, through forest and along lakes with gentle bends and long straights. In summer, the lakes around the town are busy with swimmers and boaters.

Fill the tank, take a coffee and look at the radio hill. It is a modest hill, but it has the right to be proud. If you ride south after that, notice how quickly the villages thin out and the pines close in; the last proper supermarket is behind you, and the lakes and canals of the Dahme country are ahead.
t.schlepzig forest water@52.0,13.9:
Schlepzig sits where the Spreewald stops being a tourist postcard and goes back to being forest. This is the Lower Spreewald, north of Lübben, where the Spree splits into slow channels beneath alder woods so dense that the light turns green, and the ground is more water than land. The trees grow in the wet, their roots arching above the surface, and in autumn the leaves float on the channels in drifts of orange.

The village is small, a string of farms and wooden houses along the water, and it keeps a quiet, working feel that you lose farther south. Locals still cut hay by hand on the wet meadows, store it on stilted barns and travel by boat. A canal-side inn or two serves the standard Spreewald plate of fish and potatoes, and a small museum recalls the traditional way of life. Lübben, about ten kilometres south, is the nearest town and the best place for fuel and shops, so tank up before you come.

Riding in this part of the forest is gentle and slightly strange. The road runs flat through the trees, with bridges over the channels and long stretches of shade. The surface is generally fine, but some stretches have roots pushing up the tarmac, and after rain the shaded corners stay damp long after the sun has dried everything else. Mosquitoes in summer are enthusiastic, so a shut visor is more than a safety measure.

What you notice most is the quiet. With the engine off, the forest comes alive with sounds: frogs, birdsong, the rustle of reeds, the occasional plop of a fish. Dragonflies skim the channels in summer, and in the evening bats appear over the water. If you see a flat boat moving silently between the trees, pushed by a man with a long pole, the scene could belong to a century ago.

Early morning is the best time, when mist lies between the trunks and the light is soft. Spring and autumn are less crowded than high summer, and winter brings a stillness that has its own appeal. Take your time and let the forest set the pace.
t.lubben old town@51.9,13.9:
Lübben is the stylish older sister of the Spreewald towns, a place of about fifteen thousand people on the river, with a small castle, a lively harbour and enough old streets to make a lunch stop feel like an event. The Spree comes in from the south in several arms, and the town grew up on the island between them, with water on every side.

Its most famous resident was a hymn writer. Paul Gerhardt, one of the great poets of German Protestantism, spent the last years of his life as pastor in Lübben and died here in 1676, and his hymns, such as the one beginning with the words about a head full of blood and wounds, are still sung in churches across Germany and beyond. A statue stands outside the church, and a small museum tells his story. Even if you do not know the hymns, the town has a pleasant air of old Lutheran seriousness.

For a food stop, Lübben is hard to beat in this region. The old town and the harbour have cafes and restaurants, many with terraces over the water. Spreewald specialities are everywhere: pickled gherkins, smoked fish, linseed oil with potatoes and quark, and pancakes with plum jam. A coffee and a slice of cake at the harbour, with punts gliding past, is an easy way to spend an hour. Fuel is available at stations on the edge of town.

Riding to and from Lübben is a flat, quiet matter, with roads through meadows and woods and the occasional wooden bridge. Weekends in summer bring cyclists and walkers in large numbers, so go slowly in the narrow lanes. Parking is easier on the edge of the old town than near the harbour.

A boat trip on the channels is the classic activity, and short tours leave from the harbour through the day. If you do not have time, a walk across the little bridges at the Schlossinsel will give you the flavour. The castle, a modest building with a tower, now houses a museum and a cultural centre, and the park around it is shady and calm.
t.burg spreewald@51.8,14.1:
Burg is where the Spreewald water becomes a thing you can touch. The village has canals on every side, and a number of small landing stages where people launch punts and canoes, and in summer the water is warm, shallow and the colour of tea from the alder roots. A swim here is a traditional pleasure, and several spots along the channels have been set aside with steps and platforms.

The water is gentle, slow-moving and fairly clear, with beds of water lilies near the banks and tiny fish that nibble your toes. It is not the sort of swimming where you cross a lake, more a case of lowering yourself in and floating among the reeds. Canoes and kayaks can be hired at several points, and paddling is a good way to see the quieter channels, where kingfishers, herons and the occasional otter go about their business. In the evening, the water turns copper and the mosquitoes come out, so bring repellent.

The village has a Sorbian heritage, and you can find traces of it in the architecture and in the language on the signs. Not far to the north-west, near Vetschau, stands the Slawenburg Raddusch, a reconstruction of a ring-shaped Slavic fortress from the early Middle Ages, with a museum telling the story of the settlers who first drained and farmed the marsh. It is an easy detour, and children enjoy it.

The ride into Burg is flat and straightforward, with bridges and gentle bends. Fuel is not in the village, so you should fill up in Vetschau, seven kilometres away, or in Lübbenau. There are small shops and restaurants in the village, and a lakeside sausage stand in summer. Carry cash.

Come on a weekday morning if you can. The water is clearer, the light is soft, and you may have the landing stage to yourself. A swim, a coffee and a bowl of gherkin soup make a very good midday.
t.beeskow river roads@52.2,14.2:
Beeskow is a small town on the Spree with a castle that has found a second life. Burg Beeskow, a medieval fortress of brick and fieldstone beside the river, was once a seat of local lords and later a prison and a granary. Today, it houses an art archive that holds thousands of paintings and sculptures commissioned by the East German state, a large and strange collection that gives a picture of the art of the old regime, and it also hosts concerts and exhibitions. The town around it, with about eight and a half thousand people, still has parts of its medieval wall, a Gothic church of St Marien and a market square with old houses.

The Spree flows slowly past, a broad and gentle river lined with reeds and willows, on its way from the Lusatian hills to Berlin. The land around is a mixture of forest, meadow and lakes, with pine woods on sandy ridges and wet hollows between. Tauche and Friedland, little villages near the town, are typical of the region. Further south, the river enters the maze of channels of the Spreewald, and to the west, the Scharmützelsee glitters through the trees at Bad Saarow.

As a ride, the river roads are relaxed and rewarding. The roads wind beside the Spree, through villages with half-timbered houses and brick churches, with avenues of lime and chestnut trees, and the bends are gentle. The surface is generally good, with rougher patches on the minor roads, and farm traffic is common. Cyclists use the riverside paths heavily on summer weekends. Fog lies on the river on cool mornings, and in autumn the woods turn gold. Spring is lovely, with blossom and fresh green.

Practically, Beeskow has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and a few inns and cafes by the castle and in the market square serve local food, including fish from the river and lakes. Parking by the castle is easy, and the courtyard cafe is a pleasant place for a coffee. The nearest larger town is Frankfurt on the Oder, a short ride east. It is wise to keep cash for small villages, and a rain jacket in the pannier is always a good idea.
t.konigs@52.3,13.6:
Königs Wusterhausen has two claims on history, one to do with a soldier king and the other with a radio mast. In the early eighteenth century, Frederick William I of Prussia, the Soldier King, used the hunting lodge here as his favourite retreat, and it was the setting for the Tobacco Collegium, an all-male evening society where he smoked pipes with his generals and played rough jokes. The squat little palace still stands beside the Dahme river and is open as a museum. His son, who grew up to be Frederick the Great, hated the place.

The radio story is more modern. On the Funkerberg, a low hill at the edge of town, Germany's first radio broadcast went out in 1920, a Christmas concert transmitted from the transmitter station, and over the following decades the hill became the centre of German broadcasting, with a forest of masts. Part of the site has been preserved as an industrial monument, and the old transmitter hall is open for tours. The town has about thirty-two thousand people, a pleasant historic core and a river harbour.

For riders, the area south-east of Berlin is easy, open country. The roads follow the Dahme valley and run through pine forest and fields, with lakes appearing between the trees and avenues of old trees lining the lanes. The surface is generally good, with rough patches where the old concrete peeks through, and the bends are gentle. Weekend traffic from Berlin can be heavy on the main road, so take quieter routes via Zeuthen and Schulzendorf. The ride south into the Spreewald is flat and easy, and mist hangs over the river in the early morning.

Practically, Königs Wusterhausen is a proper town, with fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and many cafes, and the S-Bahn line runs to Berlin, which makes it a handy place to finish a day. The palace has a cafe in its courtyard, and the harbour has restaurants serving fish. Parking near the station is easy, and the town centre is compact. Summer evenings by the river are lovely, with boats and swans drifting by and the smell of grilled sausages in the air.
t.zone hara sghira@33.8,10.9:
Hara Sghira means the little quarter, and for centuries it was the name of the Jewish village on Djerba's north coast, a few minutes from Houmt El Souk across flat olive and palm country. Today the modern town around it is called Erriadh, and it has two reputations. One is religious: the El Ghriba synagogue, which locals will tell you is the oldest in Africa, draws pilgrims every spring for a festival of candles and song, and visitors go through security checks at the gate, which is a sign of the troubled recent history rather than anything to be nervous about. The other is artistic, for in 2014 well over a hundred artists from dozens of countries covered the whitewashed walls of the village with murals, and the project, called Djerbahood, turned a sleepy street grid into an open-air gallery.

Walk the lanes slowly, because the paintings are the sort you notice at second glance: a giant figure folded around a door frame, patterns that continue across a corner, a face painted over a water tank. Some have faded in the island's sun, and new work appears. Whitewashed cubic houses, blue shutters and shaded courtyards fill the gaps, and a few cafes near the main square serve mint tea and strong coffee.

Djerba itself is as flat as a billiard table, which makes the riding easy and a little monotonous, with straight roads lined with olive groves and date palms, and the occasional herd of sheep. The pleasure is in the small lanes and the light. Wind is the main hazard, as gusts from the sea can push a loaded bike sideways, and sand drifts across the tarmac on bad days. Traffic is moderate, though scooters appear from side lanes without warning, and speed bumps in the villages are not always painted.

Fuel is easy: Erriadh is a town of about fourteen thousand people, and Houmt El Souk, the island's capital, is six kilometres away with petrol stations, shops and its harbour market. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when temperatures sit in the twenties, while August brings fierce heat and crowds at the beach resorts on the east coast.
t.mosquee tlakine@33.9,10.9:
Djerba is covered in small mosques, hundreds of them, and the visitor who sets out to find the quiet ones soon realises that you cannot ride more than a few kilometres without passing a whitewashed dome. Tlakine is one of those village mosques on the island's interior, set among olive and palm plantations between Houmt El Souk and the villages to the east. Most Djerbian mosques belong to the Ibadi tradition, a distinctive branch of Islam that survives in only a few places, including Oman, Djerba and parts of the Mzab in Algeria. The island's Ibadi community took refuge here when persecuted elsewhere, and built mosques that look more like fortresses than places of worship.

The shape is characteristic: thick walls, sloped buttresses, small windows, and a squat dome or a series of domes, all painted in lime wash that is renewed every year. Some had minarets, but many do not. The plain look is deliberate, since the Ibadis value simplicity, and several served as places of refuge when pirates raided the island in past centuries. Nowadays many are still in use, and a few have a small school attached for Koranic study. As a visitor you will often have to admire from the outside unless someone invites you in, and good manners say not to enter during prayer.

The riding here is easy and relaxed, with narrow tarmac lanes between stone walls, cacti and olive trees, and little traffic away from the main roads. Houmt El Souk, about seven kilometres away, is the island's main town, with more than sixty thousand people, and has all the fuel, cafes and shops you need. A good break is the covered market at its heart, where you can buy olives, dates, harissa and the island's famous sponges, and eat grilled fish near the harbour.

The best time is spring or autumn, when the sun is warm but kind, and the whitewash looks dazzling against a blue sky. Summer is hot, with temperatures often above thirty-five degrees by midday, so start early.
t.djerba testimony to a settlement pattern:
In 2023 UNESCO added Djerba to its World Heritage list under a title that sounds more like a university thesis than a holiday island: Djerba, Testimony to a Settlement Pattern in an Island Territory. What it means in practice is that the island has kept the way people have lived on it for centuries. Instead of one big town, families lived in scattered farms called menzels, each surrounded by its own fields, and villages grew around mosques, markets and cisterns. Rain is scarce here, so water was collected from the roofs and stored in underground tanks, and the layout of the land reflects that.

Riding through the area near Midoun, the largest town in the east, you see it clearly. Low whitewashed houses with flat or domed roofs stand in the middle of plots lined with palms and olives, joined by sandy lanes, and every few kilometres a small mosque appears with its domes and thick, buttressed walls. The island is almost flat, so the only landmark is the horizon, and the sea is never far. For all that it is not boring, because the details change constantly, from the colour of doors to the style of the walls.

The tarmac is mostly decent, but side roads can be sandy at the edges, so take care on corners, and watch for loose gravel where farm tracks meet the road. Wind blows steadily across the island, and in the afternoon it picks up. Mornings are best, with soft light and few other vehicles. Tourist traffic builds up near the resort strip along the east coast, where large hotels line the beach, but a few kilometres inland everything is quiet.

Midoun, two kilometres away, has about thirty thousand inhabitants and a good selection of cafes, small restaurants and petrol stations, and holds a lively weekly market. The island is joined to the mainland by a Roman causeway, still in use as a road at El Kantara, and Homer is said to have set the land of the lotus-eaters here, a charming idea for a place where nobody seems in a hurry. Plan for spring or autumn, with March to May and October to November the most comfortable.
t.mosquee sidi smain@33.9,10.9:
Close to the coast road on Djerba's north side, a few kilometres from Houmt El Souk, the mosque of Sidi Smain is one of many small religious buildings on the island, and like most of them it is better enjoyed as part of the landscape than as an isolated monument. Djerba is a flat island of olive groves, palm gardens and low white houses, and the mosques here come in two types: the large village ones with thick buttresses, and the small neighbourhood ones that look a bit like lime-washed cubes with a dome on top.

Houmt El Souk is the place to base yourself. The island's capital has a lively market, narrow lanes of whitewashed houses and a harbour where fishing boats unload octopus, which Djerba is known for. A fortress, Borj el Kebir, stands at the water's edge, dating from the fifteenth century and rebuilt by the Spanish, and in the sixteenth century a tower of skulls from a lost naval battle stood nearby. The town has more than sixty thousand people, so fuel, repair shops and a good lunch are within five minutes of the mosque.

Riding here is flat and easy. You leave town on small lanes between stone walls, passing gardens with fig trees, palm groves and prickly pear, and the road meets the sea on the north coast, with long, empty beaches and views toward the mainland. The risks are mostly sand on the tarmac, loose dogs in villages and unmarked speed bumps. Stay out of the soft edges where sand collects, and be aware that on windy days the gusts can push you off line.

Time your visit for spring, with blossom in the gardens, or autumn, with warm sea and softer light. In winter it can be surprisingly chilly and wet, and in July and August it is too hot to enjoy a long ride. For lunch, ask for a plate of grilled fish and a bowl of harissa, and finish with strong coffee at a cafe on the main square.
t.beartooth pass@45.0,-109.4:
Beartooth Pass reaches 10,947 feet, making it one of the highest paved roads in the United States, and it earns that reputation honestly. US 212 climbs out of Red Lodge, Montana, through a series of switchbacks and long sweeps of road cut into the face of the Beartooth Mountains, finally crossing a tundra plateau that looks more like Greenland than the American West. The broad top is treeless, dotted with small lakes and snow patches that last well into summer, and rock and sky meet in wide views. The journalist Charles Kuralt called it the most beautiful drive in America, and generations of riders have taken his word for it.

The road was finished in the mid-1930s and still feels like a feat of engineering. On the Montana side, it rises from the town in a famous set of hairpins, with big drops on the open side and few guard rails to calm the nerves. At the top, you are in the Absaroka-Beartooth Wilderness country, near Montana's highest peaks, including Granite Peak, which stands at just over 12,800 feet. In the alpine zone, you may spot marmots and pikas, mountain goats on the slopes and sometimes a bighorn sheep, and the flowers in July are unexpectedly bright against the grey stone.

The pass is only open when the snow allows, usually from late May until mid-October, and crews fight for every mile each spring. It can close at any time if a storm comes in, and snow has fallen on the summit in every month of the year. Dress for it: at the top, it can be thirty degrees colder than in town, and weather can swing from sun to sleet in an hour. Start early, because afternoon thunderstorms build over the high ground in summer, and lightning on an exposed plateau is not a risk anyone should take.

Services are thin. Fuel and food are in Red Lodge, a town of a couple of thousand, at the bottom of the east side, and in Cooke City on the far side, which keeps its own small supply. Do not count on anything at the top. Altitude can make you light-headed, so stop and breathe if you need to.

Many riders turn here and come back down the way they came, and the descent offers a second look at a view you had your back to on the way up.
t.neustrelitz@53.4,13.1:
Neustrelitz is a town built for a prince who wanted a new home. After a fire gutted the old hunting seat at Strelitz in 1712, the dukes of Mecklenburg-Strelitz moved to a site beside the Zierker See and, from the 1730s, laid out a baroque town in the shape of a star. Eight streets radiate from the market square, each ending in some small vista, and the geometry is still easy to see from the middle of the square. The palace burned in 1945 and was cleared away, but the park and orangery survive.

This is the heart of the Mecklenburg Lake District, a flat, glaciated country of reeds, pine woods and more than a thousand lakes, and the roads here are a different kind of riding from the Alps. Forget corners. The pleasure is rhythm: long avenues of lime and oak that arch overhead, small villages with red-brick churches, and glimpses of water through the trees. On a still morning in late summer the light on these roads is soft and golden. The surface is usually decent, though old cobbled stretches can appear in village centres and there are plenty of cyclists and tractors in season.

Just to the east lies Müritz National Park, a protected area of beech forest, bog and shoreline where sea eagles nest and, in October, thousands of cranes gather at dusk on the fields to roost. The sight and sound of them is one of the great autumn spectacles of northern Germany, and a reason to ride here late in the year, in warm gear.

Practical needs are easy. With over twenty thousand people, Neustrelitz has several fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and the lakeside harbour has cafes serving smoked fish. Further out the villages thin, and the next fuel can be a long way off, so tank up before you set out across the lakes. Wind is the main enemy: open fields give it free play, particularly in spring.

If you like riding that clears the head rather than the pulse, this is lovely, quiet country and rarely crowded outside July and August.
t.chihuahua@28.6,-106.1:
Chihuahua is the biggest city in Mexico's biggest state, and it is a long way from anywhere. Around 800,000 people live on a high desert plain at about 1,400 metres, with the Sierra Madre Occidental rising to the west, and the city has the businesslike feel of ranching and manufacturing country: wide avenues, big trucks, boots and hats that are not for show. Its cathedral, built in the eighteenth century from pink stone, dominates the main square, and Pancho Villa, who operated in this region during the Revolution, has a museum in the house where he lived. As the start of the Copper Canyon route, it is the place to sort out everything you need.

Fill the tank here and buy water and snacks, as the road west into the sierra passes through long, thinly populated stretches. Fuel stations and workshops are plentiful in the city, and less so as the road climbs. The route heads toward Creel and the canyons, through Cuauhtémoc, a town with a large Mennonite community whose families came from Canada in the 1920s and who farm the plains, make cheese and drive horse-drawn buggies. You will see men in overalls and women in long dresses at the roadside stalls, selling cheese and apples.

The riding opens with straight, fast highway across ranchland, where you can see rain falling a long way off. Then the land begins to fold, pine trees appear, and the road climbs toward the high country, with bends and views over forested ridges. Surface quality is generally fair on the main highway, and trucks are frequent, so overtaking needs thought. Winter can be bitterly cold and bring frost and snow at altitude, while summer brings strong sun and afternoon storms. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

The Copper Canyon itself is a network of gorges larger and in places deeper than the Grand Canyon, home to the Rarámuri, or Tarahumara, a people famous for running enormous distances in sandals. Chihuahua is where you can try regional food before the journey: machaca, dried shredded beef with eggs, chile con queso, and burritos in the style of the north. Get an early start, and before long the city will fall behind and the sierra will begin.
t.erzgebirge krusnohori mining region@50.4:
The word dollar comes from these hills.
