In the early sixteenth century, a silver rush at Joachimsthal, today's Jáchymov, made the town one of the largest in Bohemia, and the coins minted there, the Joachimsthaler, shortened to thaler, gave their name to currencies around the world. The Erzgebirge, or Krušné hory, the Ore Mountains on the Czech-German border, were mined for silver, tin, cobalt, iron and finally uranium for eight centuries, and the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2019.

Jáchymov has a darker chapter too. After 1945, the uranium mines were worked by forced labour, including thousands of political prisoners held in camps by the communist regime, to feed the Soviet nuclear programme. The Path of Hell, a memorial trail, tells their story. Long before that, Marie Curie had isolated radium from Jáchymov ore, and the town became the first radon spa in the world, which it still is today.

Up on the plateau around Abertamy and Boží Dar, the land is high, cold and open, with spruce woods, peat bogs and old mining scars: spoil heaps, collapsed shafts and the long ditches that carried water to the wheels that pumped the mines dry. Klínovec, the highest peak on the Czech side at 1244 metres, faces the Fichtelberg across the border. In winter, this is ski country; in summer, it offers excellent riding, with long, smooth roads through forest, wide views over the Ohře valley, and the steep, twisting descent from Boží Dar down to Jáchymov and Ostrov.

Weather here is a story in itself: mist, wind and cold can arrive even in summer, and snow can linger until late spring. Abertamy itself is famous, oddly, for glove making, which once employed much of the town. It is a small place, so fill the tank in Ostrov, Karlovy Vary or across the border in Johanngeorgenstadt. Try Czech classics like svíčková or goulash with dumplings in a mountain inn, and remember that Czech motorways require a vignette.
t.grunthal silver copper liquation works@5:
Down in the valley of the Flöha, on the edge of Olbernhau, stands an industrial village that looks almost too neat to be real: slate-roofed workshops, a hammer mill, workers' houses and a stout gatehouse, all enclosed within a wall. This is the Saigerhütte Grünthal, a works that separated silver from copper ore by a technique called liquation, and it is one of the best preserved sites of its kind in Europe. It forms part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, listed by UNESCO in 2019 for both the German and Czech sides of the range.

The works flourished from the sixteenth century, when silver from the Ore Mountains fuelled the wealth of Saxony, and it operated for hundreds of years. The copper hammer mill with its great water-driven hammers still works on demonstration days, and the thump of iron on metal echoing through the yard is a sound you will not forget. A few kilometres away, Seiffen is famous for its wooden toys and Christmas ornaments, the nutcrackers and smoking men that miners once carved in winter when the shafts were idle, and the village glows with candle arches in December.

The roads here are among the most enjoyable in eastern Germany. The Erzgebirge rises in long, wooded waves from north to south and then drops sharply into Bohemia, so the routes along the ridge and across the border are full of curves, crests and forest switchbacks. Expect patched surfaces, logging trucks and farm traffic, and in winter snow lies deep and long; this is one of Germany's colder corners. Motorcyclists from Saxony love the ride along the border road towards Seiffen and the descents into the Czech valleys.

Olbernhau has more than ten thousand residents, and fuel, bakeries and inns are easy to find. Try the local potato dishes and a slice of Eierschecke, the Saxon custard cake, with a coffee, and on a clear evening ride up onto the ridge for a long view across the hills into Bohemia.
In 2008, when parts of the old town of Dippoldiswalde began to subside, engineers investigating the problem found something nobody expected: a network of medieval silver mines running beneath the streets, dating back to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The tunnels contained remarkably well preserved wooden ladders, tools and even shoes, offering an unparalleled glimpse of mining at the start of the Ore Mountains' silver boom. These finds are part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region listed by UNESCO in 2019.

The mines themselves are not open to visitors, but the castle museum in town presents the discoveries in an engaging way, with reconstructions and original finds. Dippoldiswalde is a small town of around eleven thousand people on the Red Weisseritz river, at the northern edge of the eastern Ore Mountains, and its old centre, with a square, church and castle, is pleasant to wander. Just upstream, the Malter reservoir is a popular place for swimming and boating in summer, and the surrounding hills are covered in a mosaic of fields, meadows and forest.

For riders, the eastern Ore Mountains offer a fine choice of roads. South of town, routes climb gradually towards the ridge and the Czech border, through villages with half-timbered houses and long views. The road to Altenberg, a winter sports centre with a bobsleigh track, is particularly popular, and from there you can cross into Bohemia and descend towards Teplice and the Krupka mining landscape on the other side. Surfaces are generally good, but watch out for frost damage and gravel in spring, and logging trucks on forest roads. Winters here can be harsh, with heavy snow on the higher ground.

Dippoldiswalde has fuel stations, shops and restaurants. The narrow-gauge Weisseritztal railway, one of the oldest in Germany, runs through the valley, and you may hear its steam whistle echoing between the hills. Try a Saxon speciality like Quarkkeulchen, small fried pancakes made with curd cheese and potato, served with apple sauce, or a hearty Erzgebirge potato soup, and enjoy the view of the hills from a café terrace.
t.waldsiedlung zehlendorf@52.5,13.3:
Bright colours were a weapon for Bruno Taut. The architect believed that good housing could change people's lives, and in the 1920s he designed several large housing estates in Berlin for working and middle class families, with light, airy flats, gardens and shared green spaces. The Waldsiedlung Zehlendorf, better known as Onkel Toms Hütte, Uncle Tom's Cabin, after a nearby inn and the underground station, was built between 1926 and 1931 on the edge of the Grunewald forest, and Taut, working with other architects, painted the houses in strong reds, greens, blues and yellows, so that the estate glows among the pine trees. It is one of the great monuments of modern housing in Germany.

The estate is a pleasure to wander through, with its long terraces of houses following the curves of the streets, gardens full of flowers, and the pine forest always close by. The colours were restored in recent decades, after being lost under later coats of paint, and they give the place a cheerful, almost playful atmosphere. Nearby are the lakes of Krumme Lanke and Schlachtensee, popular for swimming and walking, and the vast Grunewald forest, with paths, lakes and the Teufelsberg, a hill made of wartime rubble, crowned by an abandoned American listening station.

For motorcyclists, there is a special connection here. Just to the north runs the AVUS, which opened in 1921 as one of the first roads in the world built exclusively for motor vehicles, and it was used as a racetrack for decades, with a steep banked curve at its northern end that saw some terrifying races in the 1930s. Today the AVUS is part of the city motorway, but its history still gives a thrill to anyone riding along it.

Riding in Berlin is generally easy, with wide streets, clear signs and relatively calm traffic by the standards of big cities, though cyclists, trams and cobbled streets demand attention. Zehlendorf is a leafy, prosperous district with fuel, shops and restaurants. To the south west, Potsdam, with its palaces and parks, is a short ride away, and the lakes of the Havel offer pleasant roads along the water. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters, and spring and early autumn are the best times for riding.
t.the castle church@51.9,12.6:
On 31 October 1517, according to tradition, a professor of theology named Martin Luther nailed a list of ninety five theses to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, challenging the sale of indulgences by the Catholic Church. Whether he actually used a hammer is debated by historians, but the theses spread rapidly across Germany and beyond, thanks to the printing press, and they sparked the Reformation, which transformed the religious, political and cultural life of Europe. The original wooden door was destroyed by fire in 1760, and in 1858 it was replaced by bronze doors bearing the text of the theses in Latin. Luther is buried inside the church, as is his friend and colleague Philipp Melanchthon.

The Castle Church and the other Luther memorials in Wittenberg and Eisleben were listed by UNESCO in 1996. They include Luther's house, a former monastery where he lived with his wife Katharina von Bora and their children, now a museum about the Reformation; Melanchthon's house; and the town church of St Mary, where Luther preached and where the first services in German were held. The whole town, officially named Lutherstadt Wittenberg, is a pleasant place to explore, with a long main street lined with old houses, shops and cafes.

The riding around Wittenberg is through the flat, open landscape of the Elbe valley, with fields, forests and small villages. The roads are straight and well surfaced, with little traffic outside the towns, and the riverside roads offer pleasant views over the water meadows. To the west, the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, an eighteenth century landscape of parks, palaces and lakes, is a lovely place to visit, and Dessau is also home to the Bauhaus, the famous school of art and design. To the south, the Dübener Heide is a large area of forest and heath with quiet roads.

Wittenberg, a town of about thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the local speciality is the Lutherbrot, a sweet gingerbread-like pastry. The town gets very busy around Reformation Day on 31 October, and during the festival of Luther's wedding in June, when the streets are filled with people in medieval costume. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters.
t.marienberg mining town@50.7,13.2:
In 1521 Duke Heinrich of Saxony founded a new town in the Ore Mountains to house miners drawn by recent silver strikes, and he had it laid out on a regular grid around a huge square market place, following Renaissance ideas of the ideal city. Marienberg is the result, and its plan is still clearly visible, with straight streets, the town church, the Zschopau gate and a stretch of town wall. The town is part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, the cross-border World Heritage Site inscribed in 2019, which recognises eight hundred years of mining in these mountains.

Mining shaped every aspect of life here, from the landscape, dotted with spoil heaps, shafts and ponds, to the culture. The miners' traditions, with their parades in dark uniforms and the greeting Glück auf, are still kept alive, and the Ore Mountains are famous for their wooden Christmas decorations: nutcrackers, smoking men, candle arches called Schwibbögen, and pyramids turned by the heat of candles, all born from miners' longing for light during the dark winters underground. Nearby Pobershau has a visitor mine and the dramatic rocks of the Black Pockau valley.

For riders, the Ore Mountains offer some of the best roads in eastern Germany, winding through forests and over the ridge between Saxony and Bohemia, with long views and little traffic. The roads around Marienberg are well surfaced and varied, with climbs, descents and curves, and the border crossings into the Czech Republic lead to even quieter roads on the other side. Winters are long and snowy, and the riding season runs from late spring to autumn.

Marienberg is a town of fourteen thousand people, so fuel, a supermarket and a bed are easy to find, and the huge market square, one of the largest in Saxony, has cafés with outdoor tables in summer. Try Buttermilchgetzen, a potato and buttermilk bake, or a plate of Klöße with roast meat. In December the Christmas markets and miners' parades are magical, with brass bands and candlelight, but roads can then be icy. The visitor mine at Pobershau and the Pferdegöpel, a reconstructed horse-powered winding engine, give a vivid sense of the work underground.
t.the red tower of death@50.3,13.0:
The name sounds like a horror film, and the reality was grim enough. In the 1950s, the communist government of Czechoslovakia sent tens of thousands of political prisoners to labour camps in the Jáchymov region to mine uranium for the Soviet nuclear programme. In a red brick building near Ostrov, known as the Red Tower of Death, prisoners crushed and sorted uranium ore by hand, without protection, exposed to dust and radiation. Many died or suffered lasting illness. The building is now a memorial, part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region World Heritage listing, and a powerful reminder of the human cost of the Cold War.

Jáchymov's history goes back much further. In the sixteenth century, silver mines here made the town one of the richest in Europe, and the silver coins minted here, Joachimsthalers, gave their name, through the shortened thaler, to the dollar. Later, the uranium ore pitchblende from Jáchymov supplied Marie Curie with the material from which she isolated radium, and the town became the world's first radon spa, still used for treatments today. Klínovec, the highest peak of the Ore Mountains on the Czech side, rises above the town.

The roads around Jáchymov climb steeply from the Ohře valley into the Ore Mountains, with sharp bends, forest and views, and the road over the border to Oberwiesenthal in Germany, past Klínovec and Fichtelberg, is a fine ride. Surfaces are mixed, and on the ridge it can be sunny in Ostrov and foggy and drizzling at the border. The area is quiet and uncrowded, with little traffic outside the spa town and the ski resorts.

Ostrov, a couple of kilometres down the hill, has petrol stations and supermarkets, and Karlovy Vary, the grand spa town with its colonnades and hot springs, is a short ride south. Jáchymov has a few restaurants and cafés and a faded spa elegance all its own, and the Royal Mint building in the town square now holds a museum on silver mining and the thaler. The memorial at the tower is sobering and deserves quiet attention; the nearby trail of the prison camps, signposted through the forest, adds the stories of individual prisoners.
t.dresden elbe valley@51.0,13.8:
Dresden's Elbe valley once held a World Heritage listing and then lost it. Inscribed in 2004 for its blend of Baroque city, river meadows, palaces and vineyards, it was removed from the list in 2009 after the city built the Waldschlösschen bridge across the meadows, a decision that sparked fierce debate. The landscape itself, however, remains beautiful: the river curves through wide green meadows, with the domes and spires of the old town on one side and the villas and vineyards of the Loschwitz slopes on the other.

The old town, devastated by Allied bombing in February 1945, has been painstakingly rebuilt. The Frauenkirche, a Baroque Lutheran church that collapsed after the raid, was reconstructed from rubble and new stone and reopened in 2005, and the Zwinger palace, the Semperoper opera house and the royal palace with its Green Vault treasury line the river. Upstream, the Blue Wonder, an iron bridge of 1893, crosses the river at Loschwitz, and further on, the Pillnitz palace, with its Chinese-style roofs and gardens, sits on the bank.

For riders, Dresden is a gateway rather than a destination. The city traffic is heavy, but the roads along the Elbe, upstream through Pillnitz and Pirna to Saxon Switzerland, with its sandstone towers and the Bastei bridge, are lovely, and downstream, the vineyards of Radebeul and Meissen, famous for porcelain, offer a pleasant ride. South, the Ore Mountains have great roads, winding through forests and villages. The best seasons are spring and autumn.

Dresden has every service a big city can offer, and its old town is best explored on foot after parking the bike. The Neustadt, across the river, is the lively quarter, full of bars, cafés and street art, while the beer gardens on the Elbe meadows have the best evening view of the skyline. Saxon wine from the slopes around Radebeul is dry and fragrant, and Eierschecke, a layered cake of yeast dough, quark and custard, is the classic afternoon treat. At Christmas, the Striezelmarkt, one of the oldest Christmas markets in Germany, sells the famous Dresden Stollen.
t.naumburg cathedral@51.2,11.8:
The twelve figures in the west choir of Naumburg Cathedral are among the most famous sculptures of the Middle Ages, and once you have seen them, you understand why. Carved around the middle of the thirteenth century by an unknown artist known as the Naumburg Master, they represent the founders and benefactors of the cathedral, noblemen and noblewomen who had died two centuries earlier, but they look like real people, with individual faces, expressions and gestures. The most famous is Uta, the wife of Margrave Ekkehard, standing with her cloak drawn up to her face, cool and enigmatic, who has become an icon of German art. The cathedral, with its Romanesque and Gothic architecture and its rich sculpture, was listed by UNESCO in 2018.

Naumburg is a handsome old town of about thirty thousand people, with a market square surrounded by Renaissance and baroque buildings and the towers of the cathedral rising above the roofs. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche spent much of his youth here, and later his last years in the care of his mother; their house is a museum. Nearby, the school of Schulpforta, founded in a former Cistercian monastery, educated Nietzsche and many other famous Germans.

The surrounding landscape is the Saale-Unstrut wine region, one of the northernmost quality wine regions in Europe, with vineyards on steep terraces above the rivers, castles on the hills and small wine villages. Freyburg on the Unstrut is home to the Rotkäppchen sparkling wine cellars, and the Rudelsburg and Saaleck castles stand above the Saale near Bad Kösen. It is a gentle, beautiful landscape, sometimes called the Tuscany of the North by optimistic locals.

The riding here is relaxed and scenic, on country roads through the river valleys and over the hills, past vineyards, orchards and forests. The roads along the Saale and Unstrut are particularly pretty, with gentle curves and little traffic outside the weekends. Watch for cyclists on the popular cycle routes, and for the occasional rough surface. Naumburg is well stocked with filling stations and wine bars; Bad Kösen, six kilometres upriver, adds a saltworks with a long graduation wall and riverside cafes. Try the local wines, often dry and crisp, and the region's hearty cooking, including Thuringian sausages from just across the state border.
If you have ever drunk a Czech lager, you have tasted Žatec. The town, known in German as Saaz, has been at the centre of a hop-growing region for centuries, and Saaz hops, with their delicate, spicy aroma, are considered among the finest in the world, prized by brewers from Pilsen to Japan. In 2023, Žatec and the landscape of Saaz hops became a World Heritage site, recognised for its hop gardens, drying kilns, packing houses and warehouses, which together tell the story of an industry that shaped the town and its surroundings. In the old town, many of the tall buildings with rows of small ventilation windows in their roofs were used to dry and store the hops.

The town is proud of its heritage. The Temple of Hops and Beer, a museum complex in the centre, explains the history of hop growing and brewing, with a hop lighthouse tower from which you can look out over the roofs, and the local brewery produces beer made, of course, with Saaz hops. The landscape around is open and gently rolling, along the valley of the river Ohře, with fields of hop poles and wires stretching to the horizon, like a vast green maze in summer, when the plants climb several metres high. The harvest takes place in late August and early September, and the town celebrates with a hop festival.

Riding here is easy and pleasant, with quiet roads through fields and villages and wide views. To the north-west, the Ore Mountains, the Krušné hory, rise along the German border, part of the Erzgebirge mining region World Heritage site, with winding roads through forests and old mining towns. In Ostrov, near Jáchymov, the Red Tower of Death recalls the forced labour camps where political prisoners were made to process uranium ore in the 1950s, a sobering reminder of the communist era. Watch out for tractors and farm vehicles on the country roads, especially during the harvest, and remember that Czech motorways require an electronic vignette.

Žatec has fuel, shops, restaurants and a few hotels. Try the local beer in a traditional pub with a plate of Czech food, such as svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with dumplings, or roast pork with sauerkraut and dumplings. In summer, the scent of hops hangs in the air, especially in the evening.
t.frantiskovy lazne@50.1,12.4:
Františkovy Lázně, known in German as Franzensbad, is a small spa town in the far west of the Czech Republic that looks as if it has been painted in a single colour: yellow and white Empire-style buildings, colonnades and pavilions set in spacious parks, all laid out in the early nineteenth century around mineral springs. It was named after Emperor Francis I of Austria, and it became a fashionable resort, especially for women, because its waters and mud baths were believed to help with fertility. The bronze statue of a little boy holding a fish, known as František, is said to bring luck to women who touch it, and you will see that his foot has been polished by countless hands. Since 2021, the town has been part of the Great Spa Towns of Europe World Heritage site, along with its larger neighbours, Karlovy Vary and Mariánské Lázně.

Just outside the town, the Soos nature reserve offers a strange landscape of mineral springs, mud volcanoes and mofettes, where carbon dioxide bubbles up through the wet ground, a reminder of the volcanic activity beneath this region. A boardwalk leads through the reserve, and there is a small museum. Cheb, a few kilometres away, is the main town of the area, with a medieval square of colourful houses, an old castle and a dark episode in history: in 1634, the imperial general Albrecht von Wallenstein was assassinated here by officers loyal to the emperor.

The riding around is relaxed and pleasant. The roads through the countryside of western Bohemia, the old Egerland, wind through fields, forests and villages, with little traffic and good surfaces. To the south-east, the road to Mariánské Lázně crosses wooded hills, and to the north, the Ore Mountains offer more demanding routes. The German border is very close, and the roads into Bavaria and Saxony are easy to reach. Czech motorways require an electronic vignette, and speed limits are enforced.

Františkovy Lázně has fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants, and Cheb has even more choice. Try the spa wafers, large thin wafers filled with sweet cream, and taste the mineral water from the springs, which some like and others find challenging. In the evenings, the parks are quiet and lovely for a walk.
t.parks of worlitz@51.9,12.4:
Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz of Anhalt-Dessau, a ruler of a small German state in the late eighteenth century, came back from travels in England and Italy and decided to turn his whole principality into a garden. The result, the Garden Realm of Dessau-Wörlitz, is now a World Heritage Site, and the parks of Wörlitz are its heart: an English landscape garden laid out around a lake fed by the Elbe, with canals, bridges, temples, a synagogue built as a temple of tolerance, and the palace at Wörlitz, designed by Friedrich Wilhelm von Erdmannsdorff and regarded as one of the first neoclassical buildings in Germany.

The best way to see it is on foot or by one of the small ferries and gondolas that cross the lake, rather than rushing. Paths open onto carefully staged views: a Gothic House with stained glass, a little island called the Stein with a miniature volcano that was once made to erupt with fireworks for guests, and lawns that run down to the water under huge old oaks. It was meant to educate as well as delight, and you can still feel that Enlightenment confidence in the way everything is placed.

Nature does a lot of the work. The parks sit in the Middle Elbe floodplain, part of a biosphere reserve where beavers have their dams, white storks nest on rooftops in the villages and floodplain forest of oak and elm lines the river. Dikes keep the high water out of the gardens, and walking along them gives you long views over meadows. Mosquitoes can be lively on warm evenings.

The riding is flat and gentle, along tree lined avenues and dike roads that link Wörlitz with Oranienbaum, Vockerode and Dessau. Some village streets are cobbled, and the roads can be narrow with soft verges, so this is cruising country. A small cable ferry crosses the Elbe toward Coswig, which is a charming way to arrive or leave; it does not run in high water. Lutherstadt Wittenberg, where the Reformation began, is close enough to combine on the same day.

Coswig, about four kilometres away across the river, is the nearest town of size and has fuel, and Dessau-Rosslau has everything, including the Bauhaus buildings. Wörlitz itself is a small town of under two thousand people with cafés, ice cream and restaurants around the park entrances. Weekdays outside the summer holidays are much quieter.
t.wartburg castle@51.0,10.3:
Martin Luther spent ten months of his life in a small room in the Wartburg, and it changed the German language. In 1521, after he had refused to recant at the Diet of Worms, his protector, the Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony, had him seized on the road and secretly taken to the castle above Eisenach, where he lived in hiding under the name of Junker Jörg, a knight. There, in a few weeks, he translated the New Testament from Greek into German, a version that helped fix the written language and spread Reformation ideas. The room, with its panelled walls and a stove, is the heart of the castle.

The Wartburg is far older than Luther. It was founded in the eleventh century by the Thuringian counts and grew into a major centre of medieval culture. The saint Elisabeth of Hungary lived here in the thirteenth century, famous for her charity to the poor, and the castle is the setting for the legendary singing contest of the minstrels, which inspired Wagner's Tannhäuser. In 1817, student fraternities gathered here for a festival that called for German unity, and the castle became a symbol of national feeling. UNESCO listed it in 1999.

The ride up is short but steep, because the castle sits on a wooded ridge above the town, and the road finishes in a car park from which you walk. The surrounding Thuringian Forest is excellent riding country, with the Rennsteig, the old ridge path, running along the crest, and with roads that climb through spruce and beech, giving long views over the hills. The roads are generally smooth, with plenty of bends, and traffic is light outside summer weekends. Winter brings snow and ice, so the best months are May to October.

Eisenach, two kilometres below, is a town of forty thousand with fuel, cafes and restaurants. It is the birthplace of Johann Sebastian Bach, in 1685, and home to a factory that once built the Wartburg cars, a staple of East German roads. Try a Thuringian bratwurst, grilled over charcoal and served in a roll with mustard. The castle is open daily, but the guided tour is the best way to see the interior, so arrive early, because queues build up in summer.
t.hoher forst mining landscape@50.6,12.6:
The Erzgebirge, the Ore Mountains, got their name for a good reason. In 1168, according to tradition, silver was found near Freiberg, and a rush followed that turned a forested ridge on the border between Saxony and Bohemia into one of the richest mining districts in Europe. For eight centuries, miners dug silver, tin, cobalt and iron from the hills, and later uranium, and the landscape is full of the traces: spoil heaps, pits, water channels, stamp mills and miners' towns. UNESCO listed the Ore Mountain mining region in 2019, in a property that spans Germany and the Czech Republic.

At Schneeberg, not far south, miners found cobalt, and the blue pigment made from it was exported across Europe to colour glass and porcelain. After the Second World War, the Soviet-German company Wismut mined uranium on a huge scale in this district, leaving scars on the land that have been landscaped in recent decades, and the story of the Cold War is part of the mining heritage.

The mountains also gave rise to a craft tradition, because miners used the long winters to carve wooden figures, and the Erzgebirge is the home of the nutcracker, the smoking man, the pyramid and the Schwibbogen, an arched candle-holder with a mining scene that stands in windows at Christmas. The Christmas markets of the region, with their gingerbread, mulled wine and lights, are among the most charming in Germany.

For a rider, the hills are a joy, with a network of quiet roads along ridges and valleys, through small mining towns with slate-clad houses. The Silver Road, the Silberstraße, links many of the historic towns, and the roads around Schwarzenberg and Annaberg offer winding climbs, forest views and mist in the mornings. The surface is mostly good, but winter ice and snow can close high roads, and fog is common.
t.the town church@51.9,12.6:
Wittenberg is a small town on the Elbe, in flat sandy country, and it is the place where the Reformation began. The Town Church of St Mary was the church where Martin Luther preached for decades, and where in 1525 he was married to Katharina von Bora, a former nun. The twin towers rise over the market square, and the interior holds an altarpiece painted by Lucas Cranach the Elder and his workshop, finished in the 1540s, which shows the Lord's Supper, baptism, confession and preaching, illustrating the new Protestant ideas in a way ordinary people could grasp. Luther himself and his friends appear in the paintings.

The famous event is of course the nailing of the Ninety-five Theses to the door of the Castle Church in 1517, although historians disagree about whether he actually used a hammer and nails or simply sent the text to the archbishop. Whichever the case, the Theses set off a storm, and Wittenberg became the centre of the new movement. Luther's house, the former Augustinian monastery, is now a museum, and Philipp Melanchthon, his closest colleague, also lived here. The Luther sites in Wittenberg and Eisleben were listed by UNESCO in 1996.

The countryside around is flat, with pine forest, heath and wide fields, and it is better suited to cycling than to spirited riding. The Elbe cycle path runs along the river, and the roads are smooth and quiet, with long, straight sections and little traffic outside the town. The Fläming hills to the north give a few gentle rises, and the Dübener Heide forest to the south has pleasant tree-lined roads. The wind is the main challenge, and in winter the flat land can be cold and foggy.

Wittenberg has fuel stations, cafes, brewpubs and restaurants, and the old town is compact enough to walk in an hour. Visit the Cranach courtyards, where the painter's workshop and pharmacy once stood, and try a beer in one of the pubs near the market. The church is open daily, though services and events may limit visiting hours.
t.schindlers werk smalt works@50.5,12.7:
In the Erzgebirge, the Ore Mountains of Saxony, a handful of workshops once produced a colour that conquered Europe. Schindlers Werk, at Zschorlau near Aue, was a smalt works, where cobalt ore from the surrounding mines was ground, roasted and fused with sand and potash into a deep blue glass, then milled into pigment. Smalt coloured Dutch tiles, German porcelain and painters' blues, and Saxony held an almost complete monopoly on it for generations. The works was founded in the seventeenth century and has been preserved as a museum.

It belongs to the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, which UNESCO added to the World Heritage List in 2019, a shared German and Czech landscape shaped by silver, tin, cobalt and later uranium mining. That last chapter, the Wismut uranium industry of the Cold War era, left its own scars not far away, around Schlema. The contrast between the small, hand-operated pigment mill and the huge Soviet-run operation is extraordinary.

The nearest town of size is Zschorlau, with almost six thousand people, and Bockau is a smaller neighbour. Aue, a few kilometres off, is bigger and has more services. Fuel and food are easy enough in this part of Saxony, and bakeries serve Eierschecke, a custard cake, and local sausages. In the winter season, shops and markets sell wooden Christmas decorations, such as nutcrackers, candle arches and smokers, which are the Erzgebirge's trademark craft.

For riders the surrounding mountains are excellent: roads climb and twist between spruce forests and small villages, with long, readable bends and good surfaces. Traffic is light on weekdays, though weekends bring day-trippers. Spring and early autumn are best, with clear air and colour in the woods, while winter brings snow and ice, and the higher roads can be treacherous. The museum is small, so check opening times, and allow an hour or two to see the blue pigment workshops.
t.hainich@51.1,10.4:
Hainich is a long, low ridge of beech forest in the middle of Germany, and it has the distinction of being one of the few places in Europe where beech trees have been left to grow old. The national park, established in 1997, covers a large part of the ridge, and its oldest stands are part of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and other Regions of Europe, a UNESCO listing. You notice the difference at once: tall, straight silver trunks, massive fallen logs covered in fungi, and a forest floor that smells of mould and mushrooms.

This is wildcat country. The European wildcat, shy and striped, has found a stronghold here, along with black woodpeckers, bats and a hoard of rare beetles that depend on dead wood. There is a treetop walkway at Thiemsburg, near Bad Langensalza, where a path rises into the canopy and a tower looks out over the woods. In spring the forest floor is carpeted with white wood anemones, then wild garlic, and the whole wood glows green.

Roads along the edges of the ridge are quiet and a delight to ride. They wind between villages like Mihla, Langula and Niederdorla, small places with half-timbered houses, with long, open bends and farmland views. Surfaces are good, traffic is light, and the pace is relaxed. Hills are gentle, never steep, so the ride feels like a flow through the countryside. The weather can change fast, so keep a rain jacket handy.

For supplies, the nearest real town is Eisenach, about thirteen kilometres away, where fuel, restaurants and shops are plentiful. Eisenach is also home to the Wartburg castle, where Martin Luther translated the New Testament into German in 1521 and 1522, and where Johann Sebastian Bach was born in the town below. Thuringian bratwurst grilled over charcoal is the local rider's lunch. Spring for the flowers and October for the colours are the best months, and the beech leaves in autumn glow copper.
t.eibenstock mining landscape@50.5,12.6:
Eibenstock sits high in the western Erzgebirge, at about six hundred metres above the sea, in a country of spruce forests and cold, clear streams. It owes its origins to tin: miners worked the tin deposits here from the Middle Ages, and the mining landscape around the town, with old spoil heaps, shafts and water channels, is part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, which UNESCO recognised in 2019. Today, the traces are quiet, softened by moss and birch.

Later, the town found fame for something very different: machine embroidery. In the nineteenth century, Eibenstock became a centre of Saxon embroidery and lace, supplying fashion houses across Europe, and the tradition lives on in a small museum and a few workshops. To the north, the large Eibenstock reservoir, built on the Zwickauer Mulde in the early 1980s, is the biggest in Saxony and supplies drinking water to a wide region. The lake is dark and long, wrapped in forest, and the dam wall is impressive.

Eibenstock is a town of nearly seven thousand, with fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and a few small hotels. The Erzgebirge generally is well supplied, with villages every few kilometres, and local specialities include wild-game dishes, dumplings, and sweet baked goods during Advent. The Ehrenfriedersdorf tin mine, on a neighbouring ride, is open as a museum and gives a closer look at the underground workings.

The riding around the reservoir and over the plateau is excellent. Roads curve gently through the woods, rise and fall with the land, and open occasionally onto views over the water or the Czech border hills. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays. Winters are long and snowy, with ski runs in nearby villages, and roads may be icy from November to March. Summer is cool and green, ideal for riding, and autumn, with its golden birches and smoky mornings, is the best time of all.
t.historical graveyard dessau@51.8,12.2:
Dessau is best known for the Bauhaus, but the city's older story is one of parks and princes. The Historical Graveyard, laid out in the Enlightenment spirit of the late eighteenth century, was designed as a landscape garden as much as a burial ground, with winding paths, old trees and monuments set among greenery. Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz of Anhalt-Dessau, who created the nearby Garden Realm of Dessau-Wörlitz, believed that gardens could educate and uplift, and the cemetery follows the same idea: a place to walk and reflect.

The Garden Realm is a UNESCO World Heritage Site stretching along the Elbe and Mulde rivers, one of the earliest and finest English-style landscapes on the Continent, with palaces, bridges, temples and even a miniature volcano. The graveyard sits within the city, a quiet green space among the tombs of local families, with mausoleums and ironwork, and moss growing over the stone. It is a sombre but rewarding stop, best visited with respect and a slow pace.

Dessau is a city of about seventy-seven thousand, and one that suffered heavy bombing in 1945, so much of its character is post-war, with wide streets and plain buildings alongside surviving gems such as Walter Gropius's Bauhaus building of 1926. The city was also the home of Hugo Junkers's aircraft factory, and Moses Mendelssohn, the philosopher, was born here in 1729. Fuel, restaurants and shops are plentiful, and the cafés near the Bauhaus are a good place for a pause.

The surrounding countryside is flat, wide and green, with the Elbe floodplain forests and long levee roads that run for kilometres under tall oaks. These are relaxing rides rather than thrilling ones, with straight lines, big skies and plenty of birdlife, including white storks and cranes, and bicycles are everywhere. Spring blossom and autumn mist over the river are the highlights, and summer evenings are warm and long. Elbe floods can close low roads in wet years, so check before you set off.
t.lauenstein administrative centre@50.8,13:
Lauenstein stands on a rock above the Müglitz valley in the eastern Erzgebirge, where the mountains tilt down toward Saxony and the Czech border is only a few kilometres off. The castle, a medieval stronghold that grew into a Renaissance residence, was long the seat of the Bünau family, a powerful Saxon dynasty, and its administrative centre controlled the surrounding district, with its farms, forests and mines. The little town gathered at its feet, with narrow lanes and old houses. Today the castle is a museum, with a dramatic position above the valley.

The surrounding mountains were rich in tin, and the mining landscape is part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří UNESCO World Heritage Site, which links Saxon and Bohemian sites such as Freiberg and Mědník Hill. The Altenberg tin mine, with its vast sinkhole, the Binge, lies close by, and in Zinnwald, on the border, you can visit a historical mine. The power of the lords of Lauenstein rested on that underground wealth.

Bärenstein, a village of about a thousand people, is nearest, and Geising and Altenberg are bigger. Altenberg, with just over five thousand inhabitants, is the sensible place to buy fuel and have a meal, and it is also a winter sports centre, with a bobsleigh track and ski runs. Dippoldiswalde is a larger market town in the valley to the north. Local specialities include game, mushrooms and bilberries, served in sweet or savoury dishes.

For riders, the Müglitz valley road is a classic, with smooth surface, flowing bends and gentle climbs through forest and meadow, while roads up onto the plateau around Geisingberg, a conical hill that stands out on the horizon, offer wide views. Traffic is light on weekdays, but motorcyclists are popular on sunny weekends, so slow down in the villages. Winter brings snow and ice from November, and mist hangs in the valleys for days. Late spring and September are the best seasons for clear air and colour.
t.go siedlung siemensstadt@52.5,13.3:
Berlin's Siemensstadt began as a factory town. Werner von Siemens's company moved its electrical works to the edge of Spandau from 1899, and by the 1920s a whole district of workshops and workers' housing was growing there. The Großsiedlung Siemensstadt, built between 1929 and 1931, is one of the great modernist housing estates of that decade, designed by a team that included Hans Scharoun, Walter Gropius, Hugo Häring, Otto Bartning and Fred Forbat. It is part of the UNESCO listing of Berlin Modernism Housing Estates, inscribed in 2008.

What distinguishes the estate is the flood of light and air. Long, white blocks of flats run between rows of trees, with balconies, strip windows and flat roofs, laid out so that every flat gets sun and a view of green. Scharoun's curved block, nicknamed the Panzerkreuzer, the battleship, because of its long, ship-like form, is the best known, and Gropius's straight rows give a strong contrast. It was social housing with ambition: architecture to make everyday life better.

The district is now a quiet residential suburb, with about twelve thousand residents, and the estate is still lived in, so be respectful when you walk or park. Berlin traffic is manageable by bike, with plenty of fuel stations, and cafés and bakeries are common along the main streets. The Jungfernheide park, a large green space nearby, is a good place for a break.

For a ride, you are in the northwest of the city, where roads head out toward Spandau's old town and the Havel lakes. The surfaces vary, with some cobbles and tram tracks to watch, and traffic can be dense. Escape to the Brandenburg countryside on weekends, where lanes through pine forests and beech woods are far calmer, including the ancient Grumsin beech forest, another UNESCO site, to the north. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and a clear morning gives the white facades their sharpest edge.
t.the house am horn@51.0,11.3:
Weimar has a way of making people feel they have walked into a library. Goethe and Schiller lived and worked here, Bach and Liszt played here, and in 1919 the German National Assembly met in the town to write the constitution of the Weimar Republic. That same year Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar, merging the old art school and the school of applied arts into something new. The Haus Am Horn, built in 1923 for the school's first big exhibition, is the only Bauhaus building that was actually erected in Weimar itself.

The house is small and cubic, designed mainly by the painter Georg Muche, with a square plan, a taller central room lit from above and the other rooms arranged around it. It was a model home, with a fitted kitchen and built-in furniture, intended to show how modern living could be efficient and bright. The Bauhaus sites in Weimar and Dessau are listed by UNESCO, and the house is a short walk from the park along the Ilm river, where Goethe's garden house stands among meadows.

The town is a place of about sixty-five thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and cafés, and a compact historic centre where parking is tight but possible. The Thuringian bratwurst and a glass of Weimar's local beer are the customary lunch. A few kilometres north, on the Ettersberg hill, lies the Buchenwald memorial, a sober reminder of the darkest chapter of German history, and a visit adds important context to the cultural brightness of the town.

Roads out of Weimar lead into rolling Thuringian farmland, with long gentle bends, wide views and little traffic, and the Thuringian Forest to the southwest offers more demanding hills. On weekdays the countryside is peaceful, and the summer evenings are long. Spring and early autumn are comfortable, and winter is cold with some snow. Morning light on the white walls of the Haus Am Horn is lovely, and the small garden around it is pleasant for a rest.
t.altenberg zinnwald mining landscape@50.8:
Altenberg lives with a hole in the ground, and is proud of it. The Pinge, a huge funnel of collapsed workings beside the town, opened up in 1620 when old tin mine tunnels caved in, and later collapses widened it into the crater you can look into today. Tin was the reason for everything here: the town grew around the mines in the fifteenth century, and the Zinnwald workings a few kilometres up the ridge, right on the Czech border, kept digging into modern times. The whole district is part of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region, a UNESCO listing shared between Saxony and Bohemia.

Down in the valley at Dippoldiswalde there is a second chapter, older and stranger. Medieval silver mines were found under the town streets, thirteenth-century galleries with tool marks still fresh in the rock, which were explored and studied after a surprise collapse in 2008. Together the two places show how mining here ran from the Middle Ages to the twentieth century, silver first, then tin, later even lithium prospecting at Zinnwald.

Altenberg is a town of about five thousand people at around seven hundred metres, so it is cold, windy and often foggy, and it has the proper services of a winter-sports place: fuel, bakeries, guesthouses, and a bobsleigh track that has hosted world championships. The old mine buildings, including a stamp mill, are open to visitors, and the museum explains how ore became metal. Nothing here is dainty, which is part of its charm.

Riding up from Dresden through the Müglitz or Weißeritz valleys, you climb steadily through spruce forest and clearings, and the corners get a little tighter the higher you go. Surfaces are generally good, though frost heave leaves a few ripples in spring. At the top, the plateau opens into pasture and heath with long views toward the Czech Teplice basin, and the border crossing at Zinnwald leads straight down toward Teplice and the Bohemian Central Uplands. Autumn is bright and crisp, while winter snow can close the high roads, so check before you leave.
t.herrnhut@51.0,14.7:
Herrnhut is a small town in Upper Lusatia, in the far east of Saxony, with a name that means roughly "under the Lord's watch". It began in 1722, when Moravian Protestant refugees were given land on the estate of Count Zinzendorf and built a settlement here. From that settlement grew the Moravian Church, which sent missionaries to the Caribbean, Greenland and Africa within a decade and still has communities across the world. The town today feels calm and slightly austere in a way that suits the story, with straight streets, plain Baroque houses and a church hall whose big white room is simply there to hold people.

Look up as you ride in and you will notice the stars. The Herrnhut star, a many-pointed paper or plastic lantern, was first made in a boys' school here in the nineteenth century and now hangs in windows across Germany at Advent. A small manufactory still builds them, and there is a good chance to see the process. The Moravians also keep up a tradition of the Losungen, a daily Bible text drawn by lot, which has been published every year since 1731 and is read in dozens of languages. Both give the town a quiet, specific identity that has little to do with tourism.

The riding around is a gentle pleasure. Upper Lusatia is gently hilly country of timber-framed Umgebinde houses, a style of half-wood, half-stone farmhouse that you see in nearby villages, and low volcanic hills topped with forest. The Zittau Mountains rise to the south, and the Czech border is close enough that a day can swing across it and back. Roads are quiet and well surfaced by the standards of the east, with small towns offering bakeries and cake. Expect few real hairpins but plenty of rhythm, and watch for tractors and the occasional cyclist.

Herrnhut itself has a few cafés and a bakery, but for fuel, the nearest big station is at Eibau, about seven kilometres away, which is large enough to offer supermarkets and a proper choice of food. Spring brings blossom in the orchards, autumn brings mist in the valleys, and winter is the time for stars: the town, lit from inside every window, is at its most memorable in December.
t.pohlberg mining landscape@50.6,13.0:
The Pöhlberg is a basalt cone that stands up from the high Ore Mountains like a bump on a bedspread, and Annaberg-Buchholz lies at its feet. Both belong to the Erzgebirge mining region, which UNESCO listed in 2019 after eight centuries of digging for silver, tin, cobalt and later uranium. Annaberg was founded in the 1490s after a silver strike, and for a few decades it was among the richest places in Saxony. The money is still visible in the town's great late-Gothic hall church, St Anne's, whose tall, ribbed interior feels more like a cathedral than a parish church, and whose altar carvings were paid for by miners and mine owners hoping for luck underground.

Annaberg is also where the mathematician Adam Ries lived and worked, and Germans still say "nach Adam Riese" when something adds up properly. The craft traditions of the region are equally well known: carved nutcrackers, smoking men, candle arches called Schwibbögen, and wooden pyramids that turn with the heat of candles. At Advent the whole range goes into a trance of lights. A ride in December can be magical or miserable depending on ice, so choose with care, and in any case the main season for riding is late spring to early autumn.

The mountain itself is a modest climb, around eight hundred metres, and from the top there is a wide view over the plateau and across the border to the Czech side. The roads that wind through the Erzgebirge are a good mix of gentle climbs and open ridges, with villages strung along them in long lines, each house a little different from its neighbour. Expect patchy tarmac after winter, plenty of tractors and a few steep descents that want a firm hand on the front brake.

Annaberg-Buchholz, under three kilometres away, has petrol, supermarkets, good bakeries and a number of cafés on the market square, and Mildenau and Königswalde offer smaller stops. Weather in the mountains turns quickly: even in summer, a cold front can bring fog and rain that remove the view entirely. If it does, drop down to the town and spend an hour in the church, and let the mine owners' ambitions keep you company until the sky clears.
t.uranium mining landscape@50.6,12.7:
Look at this landscape and you would never guess what was under it. The land south of Lößnitz and around Bad Schlema is green, pretty and slightly hilly, a foothill of the Ore Mountains with small towns, orchards and the Zwickauer Mulde river slipping through. But between 1946 and 1990 this was the heart of the Wismut mining company, a Soviet-German enterprise that dug uranium on a huge scale for the Soviet atomic programme. East Germany became one of the world's largest uranium producers, and the work left deep shafts, tall spoil heaps and a population who knew what their work was for and rarely spoke about it.

The irony is that the same rock had made Schlema famous decades earlier as a radon spa. Before the Second World War, visitors came to Oberschlema to take the radioactive waters, and the spa was briefly the richest radium resort anywhere. After the war the Soviets mined the town itself, and entire streets disappeared into subsidence. Today Bad Schlema has been rebuilt with a landscaped park laid over the old workings, and the spa has returned, with radon baths and a good thermal pool. You can take the cure, if you like, in a place that was once the most polluted in the region.

The Wismut clean-up, finished largely by the 2010s, is among the biggest environmental recovery projects Europe has carried out, and the old spoil heaps now sit under grass and young woods. Information boards and walking routes explain the story honestly. Visitors who want to understand more can visit the mining museum in Bad Schlema or take a guided tour underground at certain locations.

On the bike, the roads between Lößnitz, Hartenstein and Bad Schlema are quiet country lanes with gentle bends, and the Mulde valley is a pleasure in autumn. Lößnitz has petrol and supermarkets, with Hartenstein and its castle, Stein, a short ride away. Plan the visit for a clear day, because the heaps look best against sky, and take time to read the signs. They explain what the land has been through, which is more than most places will tell you.
t.mosquee moghzel@33.7,11.0:
Djerba is a flat, low island off the south coast of Tunisia, joined to the mainland by a Roman causeway and a ferry, and its landscape of olive groves, palms and whitewashed farmhouses is dotted with small mosques that look more like fortresses than places of prayer. The Moghzel mosque is one of them. Djerba has a long Ibadi tradition, a branch of Islam that is neither Sunni nor Shia, and many of the island's villages are Berber speaking, with architecture suited to hard times: thick walls, buttresses, small domes, and a plain whitewashed look that fits the sun and the sea.

The island's history is one of defence and trade. Pirates, Spanish raiders and Ottoman fleets all appeared at one time or another, and the Ibadi communities built strong mosques that also served as places of refuge, teaching and meetings. UNESCO listed Djerba in 2023 as a testimony to a settlement pattern in an island territory, recognising the way the houses, wells, mosques and fields fit together in a landscape of scattered farmsteads called menzels. According to old legend, Djerba is the island of the lotus eaters described by Homer, where Ulysses' crew forgot their homes.

On a bike, Djerba is an easy, relaxed place. The roads are flat, the surface is generally good and the distances are small, so you can see most of the island in a day. The wind is the main feature, blowing steadily from the sea, and in the middle of summer the heat is fierce, so the best seasons are spring and autumn, when the days are warm and the evenings gentle. Take care on the sandy verges, and watch for scooters, donkeys and children. Tourist traffic is heavy around the resort strip on the north-east coast, but this part of the island is quieter.

Midoun, about seven kilometres off, serves as the main town on this side, with a lively market and fuel stations, and Houmt Souk, the capital, is farther west with its fort, souks and fish restaurants. Erriadh is home to the famous El Ghriba synagogue, one of the oldest in Africa, and the village of Guellala is known for its pottery. Try a brik, a crisp pastry filled with egg and tuna, or grilled fish with harissa, and drink the strong mint tea.
t.mosquee sidi zekri@33.9,11.0:
Sidi Zekri is one of the many small religious buildings of Djerba, an island where it sometimes seems that every field has a whitewashed dome in it. The name suggests a local holy man, the sort of marabout who is buried under a domed tomb and whose tomb draws believers seeking help with illness or family troubles. Many such places are small and quiet, and are looked after by neighbours rather than by any big institution.

The land is flat and sandy, and the farms are scattered widely, each with its own well, cistern, olive trees and a walled garden. Palms rise above the walls, and old stone windmills and water-lifting wheels remain here and there. In spring the fields are green and the almond and pomegranate blossom is bright against the white walls. The sea is never far away, glimpsed between the palms and bright blue under the sun, and the air smells of salt, dust and woodsmoke.

Djerba has a mixed community with a long history. Muslims, Jews and Christians have lived on the island for centuries, and a Catholic church in Houmt Souk, dedicated to Saint Nicholas, is one of the places on the same ride. The island's craft of weaving, silverwork and pottery is old, and the souks in Houmt Souk are a good place to see it. The small fort there, the Borj el Kebir, stands over the harbour, and the fishermen still bring in octopus, which is a speciality of Djerba and is served in many ways, usually with lemon and a good deal of oil.

Riding around the island means taking small roads between farmhouses. The surface can be sandy or patchy, and the junctions are not always signed, but you cannot get lost for long on an island this size. In the heat of the afternoon the roads empty and the island sleeps, so take a break in the shade with a coffee like the locals. Midoun, five kilometres off, has fuel and food, and Houmt Souk has more, with a good choice of restaurants along the harbour. Evening light on the whitewashed walls is the best time to take photographs, when the shadows lengthen and the dust glows gold.
t.saaz hop landscape@50.3,13.6:
Smell comes first here. Late in summer the air around Žatec turns green and faintly bitter, because this is the heart of the Saaz hop country and the harvest fills the lanes with the scent of cones being picked and dried. The hops grown on these slopes and flats along the Ohře river are the ones that give Czech lager, and Pilsner above all, its clean, spicy bite. The cultural landscape of the town and its fields earned UNESCO status in 2023, and the old hop-drying houses and brewery buildings in Žatec are the reason.

The setting is gentle and a little open. The Ohře runs through a broad basin, with the Ore Mountains hanging on the northern horizon and the Doupov hills to the south. Between them lie fields of tall poles and wires, pale in winter and a dense wall of green by July. The roads are mostly modest and quiet, small asphalt strips linking villages, with the occasional tractor and, in harvest season, lorries full of cones. It is not twisty riding; it is slow, scenic looping through farmland, best on a bright morning with the poles throwing long shadows.

Žatec itself is a proper town of about twenty thousand people, so fuel, food and a bank machine are straightforward. Postoloprty, a few kilometres away, is smaller but has services too. In town the place to look for is the huge brick warehouse district where hops were once stored, graded and sealed for export. This was an international trade, and the old storehouses carried the stamps that told Hamburg and Vienna buyers the cones were genuine. There is a hop museum, and it is worth the time if you have even a passing interest in beer.

Ride through in late August or September if you can bear a slightly slower pace, since that is when the scent and the activity peak. In winter the place is stark and quiet, with bare wires against grey sky, and it has a different kind of beauty. Whichever season you choose, bring a hat for the sun on the flat sections, because there is little shade between the poles and the villages.
t.krupka mining landscape@50.7,13.9:
Krupka is a hillside mining town stuck to the foot of the Ore Mountains, and it wears its history quietly. The town sits a short climb above the plain near Teplice and Ústí nad Labem in the north of Bohemia, with the ridge of the Krušné hory rising behind. Tin was dug here for a very long time, and the shafts and spoil heaps scattered around the slopes are what UNESCO recognised in 2019 when it listed the Ore Mountains mining region, a landscape shared with Saxony on the German side. Marienberg, on the far side of the border, belongs to the same story.

For a rider, the pleasure lies in the climb. From Krupka the road works up into the hills in a series of steady curves, past old spoil heaps now grown with birch and pine, towards the border ridge and the high plateau where Cínovec sits. The surface varies, as it does in much of the Czech north, with patched asphalt and the occasional rough section, so it rewards a measured pace rather than a hard one. In summer the forests are green and cool; in autumn the birches turn yellow and the views back to the plain are long and clear. Winter can bring snow and ice up on the ridge, and the weather above can be very different from the weather in the valley.

With a population above thirteen thousand, Krupka has fuel and food of its own, so there is no need to worry before the climb. It is a working town rather than a showpiece, which suits the history. Mining here was hard, cold and dangerous, and the surviving remains, from old adits to the lines of the shaft heaps, are an honest reminder of what the Ore Mountains cost the people who lived by them.

Keep an eye on the weather as you gain height, because the border plateau can turn windy and wet quickly. If the sky is clear, the descent back toward Teplice gives a good view across the basin and its industrial chimneys, a landscape that has changed a great deal in a single lifetime.
t.buchholz mining landscape@50.6,13.0:
The twin towns of Annaberg and Buchholz grew from silver. In the late fifteenth century a strike in the Ore Mountains set off a rush, and Annaberg was founded as a mining town with remarkable speed, while neighbouring Buchholz joined it later to form the double-barrelled name you see on the signs. The wealth shows in the St Annen church, a vast late-Gothic hall with a soaring vault, which stands over the market square like a promise made by men who suddenly had money. The wider mining landscape was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, with its counterpart across the border in Jáchymov, where silver coins were once minted that gave the world the word thaler, and eventually the dollar.

The ride up here is a good one. The Erzgebirge on the Saxon side is a hilly, wooded plateau of small towns and steep valleys, with roads that climb and fall in honest, medium-speed curves. The Fichtelberg, the highest point in Saxony at about 1,215 metres, is a short ride away, and the Pöhlberg rises just by the town. Weather is more severe than the lowlands, so winter brings snow and ice, while summer is cool and pleasant. Autumn mist can fill the valleys, and the forest turns copper.

Annaberg-Buchholz is a town of twenty-odd thousand people, so you will find fuel, restaurants and shops without difficulty. This is also Christmas country, famous for wooden carvings, candle arches and pyramids that spin above the table. If you pass through in December the market is very good, though a motorbike is a poor choice that month. In other seasons the shops are open year-round for wooden crafts.

Adam Ries, a sixteenth-century calculating master who taught Germans to use Arabic numerals, lived in Annaberg and gave German the phrase nach Adam Riese, roughly meaning according to the correct arithmetic. It is a nice touch that a town built on silver is also tied to the idea of doing the sums properly.
t.synagogue la ghriba@33.8,10.9:
La Ghriba stands on the island of Djerba, just outside the village of Erriadh, and it is among the oldest Jewish places of worship in North Africa. The name means the Stranger, or the Marvellous, and the stories about its beginning stretch back to a priest who fled Jerusalem after the destruction of the First Temple, bringing a door or a stone. Whatever the truth of that, the building you see today is much later, a nineteenth-century structure with a whitewashed exterior and an interior of blue, turquoise and gold tiles, carved wood and low lamps that give the prayer hall an underwater glow.

Each spring the synagogue hosts a pilgrimage, around Lag BaOmer, when Jews from Tunisia, France, Israel and elsewhere gather for several days of prayer, songs and feasting, and the lanes around the building become busy with stalls and buses. Security is serious here, with checkpoints and bag searches, after an attack in 2002 and further incidents since. Expect to show ID and to cover your head, and to be asked politely to dress with respect. The community in Djerba is small but long established, and the island has a history of Jews and Muslims living near each other in the same villages.

For a rider the island is a fine change of rhythm. Djerba is flat, dry and warm, with olive groves, palms, whitewashed houses with domed roofs, and fields divided by low walls. Roads are narrow and ordinary, with roundabouts at every junction, scooters weaving about, and sand blown across the asphalt on windy days. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because midsummer is hot and busy, and winter can be grey and breezy.

Houmt El Souk, the main town about seven kilometres away, has fuel, a fish market, a fort built by the Spanish and later rebuilt by the Ottomans, and plenty of cafés for strong coffee and a sweet pastry. Erriadh itself has a street full of painted murals, made by international artists over the last decade, and is easy to wander. Midoun, to the east, also has fuel and services. Take cash, since smaller shops and cafés do not always take cards, and allow time for the security checks at the gate.
t.historic centre of prague@50.1,14.4:
Prague is one of the few big European capitals that came through the twentieth century with its medieval and baroque centre mostly intact, and the result is a city of spires, bridges and cobbled lanes on either side of the Vltava. The castle, on its hill on the left bank, is the largest ancient castle complex in the world by area, with St Vitus Cathedral at its heart, and across the river the Old Town spreads in a maze of squares and passages. Charles Bridge, begun by Charles IV in 1357, links the two banks, lined with baroque statues of saints and busy at every hour. In the Old Town Square, the astronomical clock, from the fifteenth century, strikes the hour with a parade of apostles, to the delight of the crowd.

Prague has a layered, sometimes strange history. Charles IV made it the capital of the Holy Roman Empire, Jan Hus was burned at Constance in 1415 and became a national hero, the Defenestrations of 1419 and 1618 set off wars, and the Habsburgs, the Nazis and the Communists each left their mark. The Velvet Revolution of 1989 began here, in peaceful demonstrations, and Václav Havel, the playwright, went from prison to the castle as president. It is also the city of Kafka, Dvořák and Mucha, and of pubs where a half litre of excellent lager costs less than a bottle of water in other capitals.

For a motorcyclist, Prague is a place to arrive at and leave alone. The old centre is a labyrinth of one-way lanes, tram lines, cobbles, and restricted zones, all slick when wet, with parking at a premium, so leave the bike in a hotel garage or a guarded car park and use trams and metro, or your feet. Outside, the roads of Bohemia are excellent, with the Vltava valley south of the city, the castles of Křivoklát and Karlštejn, and the Bohemian Paradise within easy reach. Spring and early autumn have the best weather. Summer is crowded, and winter has a quiet charm, with frost on the rooftops.

The city has every service, with fuel on the ring roads, workshops, hotels and endless restaurants. Try svíčková, beef with cream sauce and dumplings, or a fried cheese sandwich, and the local beer, Pilsner or Budvar. The Czech Republic requires a motorway vignette, bought online or at a station, and speed limits are enforced with cameras. Be careful with taxis and currency exchange offices around the centre, and use official ones, with prices shown clearly.
t.wismar@53.9,11.5:
Wismar is a red brick town on the Baltic, on a sheltered bay in Mecklenburg, and its story is that of the Hanseatic League, the medieval trading network of North German cities that dominated commerce in the Baltic and the North Sea. The town grew rich on beer, grain and the herring trade, and put its wealth into huge Gothic churches in dark brick, with towers that serve as landmarks at sea. Together with Stralsund it was listed by UNESCO in 2002 for the quality of its Hanseatic architecture, and the market square, one of the largest in northern Germany, is the heart of the place, with gabled houses of many centuries and a curious twelve-sided fountain house, the Wasserkunst, built in the Dutch Renaissance style in the early seventeenth century.

Between 1648 and 1803 Wismar belonged to Sweden, a chapter that left its mark in the Swedish heads, two stone busts that stand by the harbour. The Nikolaikirche, with its tall nave, is one of the highest brick Gothic churches anywhere, and the damaged remains of the Marienkirche, whose tower still stands, are a reminder of the bombing in the Second World War. The silent film Nosferatu, from 1922, used Wismar for some exterior shots, and the town lives with the legend.

The Baltic coast road here is a gentle, easy ride, with fields of rape, avenues of lime trees, small harbours and long beaches. It is not a twisty route. The pleasures are open skies, a fresh wind from the sea, and brick villages with thatched roofs, and the Baltic light, which is soft and pale. Summer, from June to September, is the season, with weekend traffic on the coast roads. The wind can be strong, and in winter the cold is raw. Watch for deer at dusk and for cyclists on the coastal trail.

Wismar is a town of forty-five thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and workshops, so you are well served. At the harbour, stalls sell Fischbrötchen, bread rolls filled with smoked or pickled fish, and the little restaurants serve Baltic herring and smoked eel. Schwerin, with its fairy-tale castle on a lake, is about thirty kilometres to the south, and the island of Poel lies just north. Parking in the old town is limited, so use the car parks at the harbour or the edge of the centre, and carry some coins for the machines.
t.palace mosigkau@51.8,12.1:
Palace Mosigkau is a small Rococo palace on the edge of Dessau, in Saxony-Anhalt, and its story is that of a princess who wanted a house of her own. It was built in the middle of the eighteenth century for Anna Wilhelmine, a daughter of the Prince Leopold I of Anhalt-Dessau, known as the Old Dessauer, a military commander of the Prussian army. She did not marry, and after she died the palace became a noble ladies' foundation, a Damenstift, where unmarried women of good family could live in comfort. Its name sits within the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, a landscape of palaces and parks created in the age of the Enlightenment, which UNESCO has listed.

The palace is low, yellow and cream, with a central pavilion and long wings, and inside the main hall is a delicate affair of mirrors, stucco and paintings. The gallery holds a famous collection of Flemish and Dutch pictures, with works by Rubens, Van Dyck and Jordaens among them, which Anna Wilhelmine's family collected, and which stayed in place when the building became a foundation. The Rococo garden has a maze of hedges and a small orangery, which is very pleasant in the summer evenings, and it is a calm place beside the more famous parks at Wörlitz.

The landscape is the flat, fertile plain of the Elbe and the Mulde, with fields, poplar avenues, small oak woods and the broad river. Roads are quiet and straight, and the ride between Dessau and Wörlitz, going east along the Elbe, passes through the floodplain forests of the Middle Elbe Biosphere Reserve, which are home to beavers and white-tailed eagles. It is more a ride for contemplation than for bends. The best seasons are late spring and autumn, with mist over the meadows, and floods can close some riverside roads after heavy rain. Dessau is also the home of the Bauhaus, with the famous school building by Walter Gropius, a short ride away.

Dessau, about seven kilometres from here, is a city of seventy-seven thousand, with fuel, bakeries, supermarkets and restaurants, and the nearby village of Quellendorf is much smaller. Try a plate of local freshwater fish, or one of the Bauhaus-inspired cafés in town. The palace is open in season and on weekends in winter, so check times, and tickets can include guided tours. The gardens are pleasant for a walk, and you will find shaded benches among the lime trees.
t.serrahn@53.3,13.2:
Between the lakes of Mecklenburg, north of Berlin, a pocket of old beech forest has been left to grow for the better part of a century, and it is now one of the most unusual places in Germany. Serrahn is a part of the Müritz National Park, a few kilometres from Carpin, and its beeches were once part of a ducal hunting reserve that was protected from logging, so some trees are two hundred years old and more. The Serrahn woods are part of the UNESCO listing of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a serial site that protects the finest remaining beech forests, from Ukraine and Slovakia to Germany, Spain and Italy.

The effect is like a green cathedral. The trunks rise smooth and grey as pillars, the canopy closes overhead, and the light on the floor is soft and green. Fallen trees are left where they lie, and the dead wood is full of fungi, beetles and woodpeckers, since the rule here is that the forest should look after itself. Black woodpeckers hammer on the trunks, and cranes call from the marshes and lakes nearby, with the occasional sea eagle gliding over the tree tops. In late April the woods are carpeted with white wood anemones and yellow lesser celandine, and in autumn the floor turns copper.

This is walking country, and the national park keeps motorised traffic to the public roads. A ride in the area follows quiet lanes through alleys of old trees, past small lakes, marshes and meadows, with pretty brick villages and thatched barns. The roads are flat and straight, with surface variations, and cobbled stretches in some villages. The best seasons are spring and early autumn, when the light is soft and the mosquitoes are fewer, and it is wise to carry a repellent in summer.

Carpin, three kilometres away, is a village with about a thousand people, so for fuel and a full meal plan on Neustrelitz, a baroque town laid out on a star-shaped plan around its market square, about nine kilometres off. Waren on the Müritz lake has a harbour and many fish restaurants, a short ride to the north. Try smoked fish, such as eel or whitefish, and a plate of Mecklenburg pork with red cabbage. Marked trails start from the car parks, and the park centres provide maps, guided walks and seasonal information.
t.bad kissingen@50.2,10.1:
Bad Kissingen is a spa town in the northern corner of Bavaria, in the valley of the Franconian Saale, between the Rhön hills and the Spessart. People have taken the waters here since the Middle Ages, and in the nineteenth century the town became one of the great resorts of Europe, visited by Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, by tsars and kings, and by Bismarck, who drafted his famous Kissinger Diktat in 1877. In 2021 UNESCO added the town to its list of the Great Spa Towns of Europe, alongside Baden-Baden, Bath, Karlsbad and others.

The centre is a pleasure to walk. A long spa park with a rose garden runs along the Saale, and the Wandelhalle, a long colonnade, and the Regentenbau, a building with a concert hall, show the confidence of the age, in pale stone and ornate halls. Mineral springs bubble up in pavilions, including the Rakoczy spring, and the water has a salty, iron taste, and is thought to be good for the digestion. Patients in dressing gowns and day trippers mingle on the promenades, and an orchestra often plays in the park in summer.

For riders, the town is a rewarding start for the Rhön, the so-called land of open distances. A few kilometres east, the Bavarian Rhön is a high plateau of rounded hills, meadows and beech woods, with roads that run along the ridges in smooth curves and offer long views. The Wasserkuppe, the highest summit in Hesse, at 950 metres, is a famous gliding site. Surfaces are good, the traffic moderate, and the weather can turn rough on the heights with fog and cold wind. In summer weekends, motorcyclists and cyclists are numerous, and the police patrol for speed.

Bad Kissingen is a town of twenty-one thousand with every service, including fuel, workshops, supermarkets and a good choice of hotels and restaurants. Local food is Franconian, with bratwurst, sauerkraut and trout, and the wine of the nearby Main valley, in the typical flat bottle called Bocksbeutel. Parking near the spa gardens is limited, so use the car parks on the outskirts, and bear in mind that the park has restrictions on vehicles. If you want a taste of the waters, bring a cup, and pay a small fee at the pump rooms.
t.mosquee el bessi@33.8,10.9:
Djerba is an island that Odysseus is supposed to have visited. Homer's lotus-eaters, who fed him and his men a fruit that made them forget home, are traditionally placed here, and it is easy to see how a visitor might think so, with its white houses, palms, olive groves and slow warm air. The island lies off the south-eastern coast of Tunisia in the Gulf of Gabès, flat, sandy and joined to the mainland by a Roman causeway, and it has long been home to a mix of peoples: Berber-speaking Ibadi Muslims, Jews and Arabs. UNESCO listed the island's pattern of settlement in 2023.

That pattern is unusual. Instead of a single town, Djerba's people live in scattered farmsteads, and the mosques, many of them Ibadi, a branch of Islam distinct from the Sunni majority, stand in the countryside as small, white, buttressed buildings that look partly like fortresses. They had to be defended against pirates, and some are fitted with a refuge underneath. The whitewash, which gets renewed each year, makes them glow against the blue sky.

Houmt Souk, the island capital, has a fine market and a sea fort, the Borj el Kebir, rebuilt in the sixteenth century.

Riding on Djerba is easy, flat and slow. The roads are generally good, with long straight stretches between olive and date palms, and side lanes of sand and gravel leading to farms. Speed limits are low, and police checks are common. The sea wind blows constantly, and in summer the heat is strong. April to June and September to October are the best months. Be careful with sand on the corners and with stray dogs and scooters at dusk.
