Fuel is available at Houmt Souk, a town of over sixty thousand, and in Erriadh and Midoun, and there is no shortage of stations on the island. Arrive by the Roman causeway at El Kantara or by the Ajim ferry, depending on direction, and look for brik, a crisp fried pastry with egg and tuna, as a snack, and a glass of mint tea. Come in the late afternoon, when the light is soft, the whitewash turns pink and the farmers are heading home.
t.mosquee fadhloun@33.8,11.0:
On Djerba, the mosques look like fortresses, and for good reason. The island off the south-east coast of Tunisia was a place of pirates, raiders and rival fleets, and its Ibadi Muslim community, a small branch of Islam distinct from the Sunni and Shia majorities, built its places of prayer as strongholds: thick whitewashed walls, stubby buttresses, few windows and flat roofs with small domes, so low and plain that they seem to grow out of the earth. The Fadhloun Mosque near Midoun is one of the best known, with a courtyard, prayer hall and, as in the others, an underground cistern to store rainwater, since the island has no rivers. Louta, the other mosque on this ride, belongs to the same family.

Djerba as a whole was recognised as a World Heritage site in 2023, for a pattern of settlement that includes these mosques, the farmsteads called menzel, the villages and the careful use of scarce water. It is a flat, sunny island of olive trees and date palms, whitewashed houses with blue doors and low stone walls, and since antiquity it has been connected to the mainland by a causeway. In Homer's Odyssey, it is sometimes identified with the land of the lotus-eaters, where sailors forgot their homes, and visitors still talk of the island's slow pace.

Riding on Djerba is straightforward. The island is only about twenty-five kilometres across, with a network of small, flat roads, mostly well surfaced, that wander between olive groves and villages. Traffic is thick near the main town, Houmt Souk, and around the hotels on the east coast, with scooters, taxis and lorries, and drivers can be unpredictable at roundabouts. Out in the countryside, the roads are quiet, with dogs, goats and the occasional donkey cart. Sand blows across the tarmac after windy days, so take care on bends. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with mild, sunny weather, while July and August are very hot, and winter can be breezy and wet.

Midoun, a town of some thirty thousand people four kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and cafes, and everything you need for a day on the island. In the market, look for the local pottery from Guellala and for woven baskets, and try fresh grilled fish, brik, the thin fried pastry with an egg inside, and mint tea with pine nuts. Dress modestly and ask before entering the mosques, and remember that these are working places of worship, with times of prayer that visitors should respect.
t.hamburg east@53.6,10.3:
This one is a boundary rather than a destination: the place where Hamburg stops being a city and the roads become something a rider might enjoy. The east side of the metropolis frays out through Stormarn district, with Stapelfeld just a few kilometres away, and the motorway and the main roads funnel in toward the centre. For a returning rider, it is a moment to take stock, check the fuel and slow down after a long day of countryside.

The land to the east is gentle, a mixture of Holstein farmland, small woods and commuter villages with brick houses. A few kilometres to the north-east is Ahrensburg, whose Renaissance moated palace, built in the later sixteenth century, is the most notable building in the area, a neat white and red brick pile with a water-filled moat and a long avenue of trees. To the south-east lies the Sachsenwald, a large forest that once belonged to Bismarck, who lived at Friedrichsruh. Its roads are quiet, shaded and good for an hour of relaxed riding.

Practical matters are simple. The towns around here have all the fuel you need, with stations at the main junctions and along the roads into the city, and supermarkets and bakeries open early. Hamburg's rush hour, which can last from about half past six to nearly ten in the morning and from three to seven in the evening, is the thing to avoid, as the arterial roads clog and the motorway can crawl. If you are coming from Mecklenburg, as this ride does, a Sunday evening return can be very slow, so consider stopping for a coffee and letting the traffic pass.

For comfort, this is a good place to put on or take off layers. Northern Germany is flat, wide open and windy, and the temperature drops quickly after sunset, even in summer. The light in the evening over the fields is often beautiful, and a short pause at the edge of town is worth it.
t.lutjenburg@54.3,10.6:
Lütjenburg is a small, tidy market town on the Baltic side of Schleswig-Holstein, a few kilometres from the sea in a rolling country of fields, lakes and low hills. People here call the region Holstein Switzerland, a joke that is half serious, because by the flat standards of northern Germany the landscape counts as dramatic, with hills of a hundred metres or so and lakes in the hollows. About five and a half thousand people live in the town, and it has the feel of a place that has been a local centre for a long time.

The market square, with its church and its stepped gables, is the heart of town, and on market days it fills with stalls selling vegetables, fish, flowers and cheese. A hill above the town, the Hohe Lütjenburg, offers a view over the roofs and the bay, and a short drive takes you to the beaches at Hohwacht, where the Baltic is shallow, grey-blue and quiet. The coast here is gentle, with dunes, reed beds and long beaches, and in summer it fills with holidaymakers from Hamburg and Kiel.

The surrounding country is manor-house land, with big estates, brick farm buildings and long avenues of beech and lime trees, a legacy of the Danish and German nobility who owned most of the land until the twentieth century. Several of these estates, with their moats and parks, can be seen from the road.

The riding is easy and relaxed. Narrow lanes follow ridges and valleys, bend through villages and cross low rises, with wide views over the fields, and traffic is light outside the summer weekends. The wind from the sea is the main hazard, and on exposed stretches, it can push a bike around. Fuel is available in town, along with bakeries, cafes and fish shops, where you can get a smoked fish roll, a local favourite. At about thirty-five metres above sea level, the town is not high, but the surroundings roll gently. Spring and early summer are lovely, with yellow rapeseed fields, and autumn brings misty mornings and golden light.
t.celle@52.6,10.1:
Celle is a town that looks like it has been preserved in a jar. More than four hundred half-timbered houses, with carved beams, painted inscriptions and crooked upper storeys, line the streets of the old centre, and the whole place has survived with very little damage because it escaped bombing in the Second World War. About seventy-one thousand people live here, on the banks of the Aller, at the southern edge of the Luneburg Heath.

At the centre stands the Schloss, the castle of the dukes of Brunswick-Luneburg, a large building with a baroque theatre inside, said to be the oldest in Germany still in use. It has a sad link with Danish history, because Queen Caroline Matilda of Denmark, banished after a scandal at the court of Copenhagen, spent her last years here and died in 1775 at the age of only twenty-three. A small memorial stands in the castle garden.

The Heath, a broad area of heather, juniper, birch and sandy soil, begins just north of the town. In late August and September, the heather blooms purple, and the whole country glows. Flocks of Heidschnucken, a hardy local breed of sheep with curling horns, graze the heath to keep it open. The landscape has been shaped by centuries of grazing and burning, and it is a rare habitat, protected as a nature reserve.

For riders, Celle is a place to fill the tank and have a coffee. Fuel stations are on the roads into town, the old town is closed to most traffic and parking is easy near the edge. A walk past the half-timbered houses and a cake in a cafe makes a good break. From here, the roads north and south run straight and smooth, with long views over farmland, forest and heath, and traffic is moderate. Wind can be strong over open ground, and on summer weekends, the heath roads fill with day-trippers. Early morning light on the heather is the finest, and a thermos of coffee helps on cool days.
Boží Dar claims to be the highest town in the Czech Republic, at about a thousand metres on the ridge of the Ore Mountains, and it has the climate to prove it: long winters, deep snow, and a cool, damp feel even in summer. The name means God's Gift, and the settlement was founded in the sixteenth century by miners who came after silver was found on the slopes. Abertamy, Horní Blatná and Mining Landscape are all part of the same story, a string of hill villages that grew up around the mines.

The Ore Mountains, called Krušné hory in Czech and Erzgebirge in German, have been mined for silver, tin, cobalt and later uranium for eight centuries, and in 2019 UNESCO recognised the mining landscape on both sides of the border. Jáchymov, a few kilometres away, is where the silver coin called the thaler, the ancestor of the word dollar, was first minted. Later, Marie Curie obtained her uranium ore from here, and in the twentieth century, Jáchymov was a place of forced labour in the uranium mines under the communist regime, a dark chapter that is remembered in local museums.

The landscape is a plateau of spruce forest, peat bog and open meadows, with old spoil heaps, adits and mine buildings among the trees. Wooden houses with steep roofs and shingled walls give the villages a Central European mountain look. In summer, it is green and cool, and in autumn, the forest is golden. In winter, cross-country skiers fill the trails, and the roads can be icy.

Riding here is pleasant on well-surfaced roads that climb through forest, with long bends and open ridge views, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. Fuel is not always available in the villages, so fill up in Jáchymov, Karlovy Vary or on the German side, and carry a little spare. Fog is common, and temperatures can be much lower than in the valley, so bring a warm layer. In the villages, you will find small cafes and guesthouses serving hearty Czech food, including dumplings and goulash. The nearby Klínovec, at 1,244 metres, is the highest peak of the range.
t.hanseatic city of lubeck@53.9,10.7:
Lubeck was once the queen of the Hanseatic League, the medieval trading network that dominated the Baltic and North Sea. From the twelfth century, merchants here shipped salt from Luneburg, fish from Scandinavia, grain and furs from the east, and the wealth they made went into brick: huge churches, tall gabled houses, warehouses and a city gate that still leans slightly under its own weight. The Holstentor, built in 1478, with its two round towers and sagging central block, has been the symbol of the city ever since.

The old town sits on an island formed by the Trave river, and the skyline of seven church spires is one of the most distinctive in northern Europe. UNESCO listed the old town in 1987, one of the first German old towns to be recognised. On the night of 28 March 1942, British bombers hit the city, and much of the centre burned, but enough survived to make the survivors' effort to rebuild worthwhile.

Lubeck is also the home of marzipan, and the confectioner Niederegger has been selling it here since the early nineteenth century, so a small box of marzipan loaves makes a sweet souvenir. Thomas Mann, born here in 1875, put the city into his novel Buddenbrooks, and the Buddenbrookhaus is a museum about the family and the author. Brick Gothic is the architectural style that defines the place, and you see it everywhere in the red walls and pointed arches.

For riders, Lubeck is a pleasant city with a manageable centre, though parking near the island can be tight, and many streets in the old town are cobbled. From here, the road to Travemunde, on the Baltic coast, is short and flat, with a beach promenade. Fuel is available at stations on the outskirts, and food ranges from fish rolls to elegant restaurants with local specialities. About two hundred thousand people live here, so every service is available. Visit in spring or early autumn, when the light is clear and the crowds are smaller, and leave time for a walk along the canal and through the gabled streets.
t.zone 2 petrikirche dom zu lubeck@53.9,10:
Lubeck's old town is a compact island, and Zone 2 is where its religious and civic heart lies. The Petrikirche, the church of St Peter, is a brick Gothic hall church that now serves as an exhibition space, and its tower has a lift that takes you up to a viewing platform with a view over the red roofs, the Trave river and the silhouettes of the other churches. It is the best way to understand the shape of the city, an oval island ringed by water.

A few streets away, the cathedral, the Dom, was founded in 1173 by Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, and it is the oldest large brick building in the city. The two west towers rise above the surrounding roofs, and inside is a famous triumphal cross by the artist Bernt Notke, a huge carved crucifix from the late fifteenth century. The cathedral was badly damaged in the bombing of 1942 and restored over decades, with the dark, soaring nave giving a sense of the wealth and ambition of the medieval merchants.

Between the two churches runs a quiet part of the city, with cobbled lanes, courtyards, and tiny houses called Gange and Hofe, built by merchants and guilds to house the poor, hidden behind the main streets. Some of these still serve as homes, and a few are open to the public, so peer through the gate and walk in if it is permitted. The area near the Dom has a calm, almost village-like feel compared with the busy market square.

Lubeck was a major trading city of the Hanseatic League, and the museums and churches are full of its history. Approaching on a bike, expect cobbles in places, traffic around the island, and limited parking. Leave the machine at the edge, perhaps near the Holsten gate, and walk. Fuel is available on the outer roads, and food is easy to find, including smoked fish, marzipan and fresh bread. Summer is busy, and early morning or late afternoon is calmer. Take a jacket, as the wind from the Baltic can be cold.
t.zone 3 marienkirche@53.9,10.7:
Walk into the Marienkirche in Lubeck and your neck tips back without any instruction. The nave rises to a brick vault nearly forty metres above the floor, among the highest brick vaults in the world, and the whole church is a statement from the merchants who paid for it, built in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries as the main church of a city that considered itself the equal of any bishop. It became the model for brick Gothic churches all round the Baltic, from Stralsund to Tallinn.

The church was hit in the air raid of 28 March 1942 and burned, and the great bells fell from the tower and smashed on the stone floor. They have been left where they landed, a heap of twisted bronze, as a memorial, and it is one of the most powerful sights in Germany. The church itself was rebuilt, with its tall white interior, restored vaults and, high in the north transept, a medieval astronomical clock that shows the date and the phases of the moon.

Music runs deep here. Dieterich Buxtehude was organist at the Marienkirche from 1668 until 1707, and held famous evening concerts, and in 1705 the young Johann Sebastian Bach is said to have walked here from Arnstadt, more than four hundred kilometres, to hear him play. He stayed for months, far longer than his leave allowed, and the story gives the church a special place in the history of baroque music. Organ concerts are still held in the church.

The location is the town hall square, with the market, the old town hall and the stepped gables of merchants' houses, and it is a pleasant place to sit with a coffee. Marzipan shops are close by. Parking is difficult in the centre, so leave your bike at the edge and walk. Fuel and services are available elsewhere in the city. Come on a weekday in spring or autumn, when it is quieter, and take a few moments to sit under the vault and look up.
t.the bauhaus@51.8,12.2:
The Bauhaus building in Dessau is a glass box that changed the way the world builds. Walter Gropius designed it in 1925 and 1926 for the school he had moved here from Weimar, and the structure combines workshops, classrooms, a studio block and a theatre in a plan that looks like a pinwheel from above. The famous feature is the glass curtain wall on the workshop wing, which hangs in front of the structure like a transparent skin, one of the first of its kind in the world. Inside, the stairs, the lamps and the lettering carry the look of the movement.

The school lasted only fourteen years in all, and only seven in Dessau, until the Nazis forced it to close in 1932. In those years, it brought together artists and designers including Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, Josef Albers, Marcel Breuer and Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, who experimented with the idea that good design should be for everyone, and that art, craft and industry could work together. Chairs, lamps, textiles, typefaces and buildings from the school are still copied. UNESCO listed the Bauhaus buildings in Weimar and Dessau in 1996.

The building was damaged in the Second World War, neglected in the East German period, and carefully restored after reunification, and today you can walk through the studios, the canteen and the stage. A visit takes around an hour, and a guided tour explains how the spaces were used. Students still live in the studio block.

Dessau is a medium-sized city of about seventy-seven thousand people, on the Mulde and Elbe rivers in Saxony-Anhalt, and it has fuel, food and rooms. The Garden Realm of Dessau-Worlitz, an eighteenth-century landscape park listed by UNESCO, is close by, and its roads are flat and pleasant on a bike. Parking at the Bauhaus is easy, and the area is quiet outside peak hours. Spring and autumn are the nicest times to go, with soft light on the glass.
t.the masters houses@51.8,12.2:
Walter Gropius did not only design a school, he designed the houses for its teachers, and the Masters' Houses in Dessau are among the most elegant homes of the modern movement. Built in 1925 and 1926 on a quiet street at the edge of a pine wood, they form a row of white, flat-roofed, cubic buildings, each one a variation on the same set of simple geometric forms: three semi-detached pairs for the masters and a larger villa for Gropius himself. Their clean lines, large windows and balanced proportions were a statement of what modern living could look like.

The residents read like a roll call of twentieth-century art. Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee shared one house, each with a separate studio, and other masters, including Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, Lyonel Feininger and Georg Muche, lived in the others. The street was a small community of artists, who held parties, talked late and experimented. The houses were designed with built-in furniture and colour schemes, and the interiors were painted in strong colours chosen by the occupants.

During the Second World War, bombing destroyed Gropius's house and one of the others, and for decades the remaining buildings were altered and neglected. A careful restoration brought the surviving houses back to their original appearance, and the missing ones were rebuilt as new interpretations in a design that suggests their shape without copying it. UNESCO listed the Bauhaus sites in 1996. Inside, you can see the colours and furniture, and learn how the residents lived.

The setting is peaceful, among tall pines, and the street is quiet. Dessau, about a mile and a half away, has fuel, cafes, supermarkets and hotels, and the Bauhaus building is a short ride. The surrounding region of Saxony-Anhalt is flat, with the Elbe and Mulde rivers and the Dessau-Worlitz garden realm, and the roads are good and quiet. Weekdays are calmer, and spring and autumn offer the best light. Book ahead if you want a guided tour, since slots can be limited.
t.pruhonice park@50.0,14.6:
Průhonice is a village on the south-eastern edge of Prague, close enough to the capital that you can hear the city's hum, and yet its park feels like a separate country. The park was shaped from the 1880s by Count Arnošt Emanuel Silva-Tarouca, a passionate plantsman who worked with the landscape designer Adolf Vaněk to create a naturalistic landscape of lakes, meadows and woodland. He collected trees and shrubs from across the temperate world, and the park is especially known for its rhododendrons, which bloom in a riot of colour around May.

The castle at its heart, with its old pond and mirror-like reflection, is a modest and rather pretty building. Today the grounds belong to a botanical research institute, so there is a serious working side to the place as well as the pleasure of the walk. Old oaks stand beside the water, and the paths wind between plantings that were designed to look as though nature had made them. In the early morning, with mist on the pond and birdsong in the trees, it is very hard to remember that the Prague ring road is only a few minutes away.

The riding in this area is easy but not dull. Roads fan out of Prague through small villages and farmland, often with a gentle roll, and you can leave the city traffic behind quite quickly if you start early on a weekday. The surface is generally good, corners are mild, and the main hazard is commuter traffic around the ring road. If you are heading toward Saxony and the Erzgebirge, as the ride to the Pöhlberg mining landscape does, this is a good place to warm up and stretch before the long run north-west.

Průhonice is a small place, about two thousand people, so you will find a petrol station and a few places to eat, but for anything more you should look to Prague or the nearby larger towns. Czech cooking is simple and filling, and a lunch of goulash and dumplings is the sensible choice before a day on the road.

The best time to come is late spring, when the rhododendrons and azaleas are in flower, though autumn colour is also splendid. Winter has its own stark charm, and the park is far less crowded.
t.luneburg@53.2,10.4:
Lüneburg got rich on salt, and you can still see that in the brick. For centuries brine from under the town was boiled into the white salt that was shipped to Lübeck and used to preserve the herring of the Baltic, and the money from this trade paid for the Gothic town hall, the gabled merchant houses and the old crane by the Ilmenau. The Hanseatic League was good to Lüneburg. The streets are lined with stepped brick gables, many of them leaning a little because of subsidence from the salt mines below, which gives the whole old town a gently drunken look.

It makes a very good stop between Hamburg and the Harz. The town is only about fifty kilometres south-east of Hamburg, on the edge of the Lüneburg Heath, and it is large enough, with over seventy thousand people, to have all the fuel, food and bed you could ask for. The old harbour area, with its restored crane and its cafés on the water, is a pleasant place to sit with a coffee, and the pedestrian centre is a short walk. A lot of local restaurants serve dishes made with heath lamb or with the asparagus that comes in spring.

The ride here from Hamburg is easy, a mix of main roads and quiet country lanes. The surface is good, the bends are gentle, and the landscape is flat to gently rolling, with woodland, farms and the occasional heath. It is not a place for adrenaline but it is a place to relax, especially in the late summer when the heather turns the landscape purple, and in the early morning when mist hangs over the fields. On the road south toward the Harz, the terrain starts to lift and the corners get more interesting.

Parking in the old town can be limited, and some streets are cobbled, so take care. Lüneburg is also a university town, which keeps it lively in term time, and its Sunday market and small independent shops are worth a browse.

A sensible plan is to fill the tank on the edge of town, then walk the centre on foot, leave the bike near the harbour and enjoy an hour wandering streets that have hardly changed in character for five hundred years.
t.dresden@51.1,13.7:
Dresden sits in a wide, gentle bend of the Elbe, with the hills of Saxon Switzerland to the south-east and the vineyards of the Elbe valley to the north-west. For two centuries it was the showpiece of the Saxon electors, above all Augustus the Strong, who turned it into a Baroque capital of palaces, galleries and festivals, so that the city was known as Florence on the Elbe. The Zwinger, the Semper Opera and the Frauenkirche were its crown, and the skyline painted by Canaletto in the eighteenth century was among the most celebrated in Europe.

That world was erased in the firebombing of February 1945, which flattened the old centre in a single night. For decades the Frauenkirche lay as a heap of stones, a memorial to the war, and only after reunification was it rebuilt, with the new church consecrated in 2005. Some of the original dark stones are visible in the new walls, patterning the pale sandstone like scars. The Elbe valley was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2004 and removed in 2009 after the construction of the Waldschlösschen Bridge, a dispute that tells you something about the tension between preservation and modern life.

For a rider, Dresden is the gateway to the Saxon Wine Route, which runs north-west along the right bank of the Elbe through Radebeul to Meissen. It is one of the northernmost wine regions in Europe, with steep terraced slopes and small, old-fashioned estates, and the road winds between villas and vineyards with the river below. Traffic can be slow in the city, with trams and many one-way streets, but once you are out, the surface is good and the bends are gentle.

There is no problem with fuel or food in a city of nearly half a million. Try a Saxon speciality such as Eierschecke, a layered cake of curd and custard, and finish with a glass of local white from the valley. The Elbe is a good guide: follow it and you will find the best views.

Spring and early autumn are lovely, when the river is calm and the vines turn yellow. Summer weekends are busy, so start early.
t.lauenburg@53.4,10.6:
Lauenburg is where the Elbe stops being a big river and starts being a working waterway with serious ambitions. The town stretches along a steep bank, with the old town clinging to the hill and the lower town, the Elbstrasse, running along the water's edge, and the river below is wide, brown and busy with barges. For centuries this was a toll town, collecting dues from the traffic that moved between Hamburg and the Baltic, and the Elbe-Lübeck canal begins nearby, which once carried salt from Lüneburg to the sea.

It was the capital of a small duchy, and Bismarck took the title Duke of Lauenburg when he was dismissed from office in 1890, a piece of local trivia that the town has not forgotten. Its riverside houses, many of them half-timbered, were long threatened by the Elbe's floods, and the water has left marks on the walls to show the high-water years. The altitude here is a modest twenty metres, so the river feels close, and on a misty morning the barges drift past like ghosts.

The riding is simple and pleasant, mostly on flat roads through farmland, dikes and woods, with easy curves and good surface. The ride from Hamburg here is an easy hour or so, then on to Mecklenburg, where roads become quieter and the lakes begin. Traffic is lighter than around Hamburg, but trucks are common on the main road, so stay alert.

With about twelve thousand people, Lauenburg has a petrol station and shops, and is a sensible place to refuel before heading into the quieter country of Mecklenburg. There are fish restaurants along the river, and a plate of fried herring or a bowl of eel soup, a north German classic, is good value. Ice cream is also a local passion in summer.

Early morning or evening light is best, when the sun picks out the old roofs and the river turns to metal, and spring is nice when the hedges are in bloom.
t.plon lake road@54.2,10.4:
Plön sits on a ridge between two lakes in the part of eastern Holstein that the locals call the Holstein Switzerland, a name that sounds absurd until you see the rolling, wooded country and the lines of blue water lying between the hills. The Great Plön Lake is the biggest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, with islands, bays and many smaller lakes around it, and the town of Plön, with thirteen thousand people, occupies a narrow strip of land between them. The altitude here is only twenty-eight metres, but the glacial landscape gives it a lot of character.

On the highest point stands the castle, a large white Baroque palace built for a duke of the Holstein-Plön line in the seventeenth century, later used as a school and still imposing today. It looks out over the lake and the town below, and the park around it has views that explain why the dukes chose the site. The old town below is small and attractive, with a street of low houses, a church and a market square that is a good place for a coffee.

The riding here is a pleasure. The roads wind around lakes and through beech woods, with gentle ups and downs, shaded avenues and glimpses of water through the trees. The surface is generally good, bends are easy and the pace is relaxed, so it is a good ride for a warm evening. The lake road is also a swimming spot, and in summer small beaches on the shores are popular with locals, with clear water and sandy bottoms in places. The water warms slowly, so it is refreshing rather than warm.

Plön has fuel, restaurants and cafés, and there are smoked-fish stands near the lake in season. You can also hire a boat or take a lake cruise if you want to see the shore from the water. The region is popular on summer weekends, so arrive early or ride on a weekday.

The best seasons are late spring, when the beech leaves are fresh green, and early autumn, when the colours turn and the lake is calm. This stop sits at the end of a ride that starts along the Elbe dikes and the Altes Land, a very different landscape of fruit orchards and flat marsh.
t.jasmund@54.6,13.7:
White cliffs rise out of a dark beech forest on the north-east corner of Rügen, which is a strange thing to see in Germany. Jasmund is a peninsula of chalk, laid down in the Cretaceous sea some seventy million years ago and then pushed and folded by the ice that covered the Baltic coast. Its best-known point is the Königsstuhl, the King's Chair, where the cliffs reach more than a hundred metres over the water, and the scene was made famous by Caspar David Friedrich's painting of the chalk cliffs, in which small figures peer over the edge in a mixture of awe and fear.

The national park here is the smallest in Germany, but it packs a lot in. The ancient beech woods that run along the cliff tops are part of a World Heritage listing for primeval beech forests in Europe, and the shade under the trees is cool and green, with fallen trunks and moss. Chalk cliffs are unstable, and landslides still happen, sometimes sending a whole section onto the beach, along with flints and fossils that collectors love. Walking the beach below the cliffs is not advised in some conditions, so follow the signs.

Riding on Rügen is gentle and enjoyable. The roads here run through avenues of old trees, past thatched farmhouses and small harbours, with a surface that is mostly good and bends that are relaxed. The island can be crowded in summer, and the roads near Sassnitz and the park entrance fill with cars and buses, so go early. Wind off the Baltic can be strong, and in autumn or winter a grey sea under a low sky has a moody beauty of its own.

Sassnitz, about five kilometres from the cliffs, is a port town of over ten thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and a long harbour where fish sandwiches are a classic lunch. Sagard is a smaller place in the other direction. From Stralsund you cross to the island by the long bridge, and this ride then continues toward Denmark and the chalk cliffs of Møn, which are the same geology on the other side of the sea.

Visit in early morning or evening, when the light on the white face is warmest, and the tour groups have gone.
t.collegiate church@51.8,11.2:
High on a rock above Quedlinburg stands the Collegiate Church of St Servatius, a heavy Romanesque church that is one of the most important of its kind in Germany. The first church on the hill was connected to the Ottonian kings, and Henry the Fowler, the first king of the East Frankish realm in the early tenth century, was buried here. His widow Mathilda founded a convent of noblewomen on the site, which became powerful, with abbesses who were often relatives of the emperors and ran a small state of their own.

What you see today is largely twelfth-century, with a crypt that is among the finest in Germany, its carved capitals of animals and plants still sharp. The church treasury contains medieval manuscripts and reliquaries, and some of its finest pieces were stolen by an American soldier in 1945, though most were eventually recovered. The hill also carries the castle and the view over the town below, with its hundreds of half-timbered houses, most of them restored.

Quedlinburg lies at the northern edge of the Harz, where the mountains meet the Saxony-Anhalt plain, and the town itself is a World Heritage Site. The riding in the area is rewarding, with winding roads that climb from the plain into the hills, through forest and past small villages. The surface is generally good, curves are plentiful, and the Brocken, the highest peak of the Harz, is within easy reach. The ride that includes this stop travels between Luther's death house at Eisleben and the Rammelsberg mines at Goslar, so you cross a lot of German history in a short space.

The town has twenty thousand people, so there are fuel stations, restaurants and plenty of cafés. Try a local sausage or a slice of the cake known as Baumkuchen, which is layered and baked on a spit, a speciality of Saxony-Anhalt. The cobbled lanes near the church are steep and rough, so park below and walk up.

Go in the morning, when the light on the Romanesque walls is warm, and the lanes are empty. Autumn colour in the surrounding hills is particularly pleasing.
t.stone house@51.0,11.0:
In the middle of Erfurt's old town, among tall, narrow houses with steep roofs, stands a stone building that has outlived most of its neighbours. The Steinernes Haus, the Stone House, is a medieval house built in the thirteenth century, and it is one of several buildings that record the life of the town's Jewish community, which was among the most important in medieval Germany. In 2023 the group of sites was added to the World Heritage list, together with the old synagogue and the ritual bath.

The house is called the Stone House because most buildings of the time were timber, and a stone house signalled wealth and security. The Jewish merchants of Erfurt, a town on the trade routes between east and west, were bankers and traders, and they lived and worked in the streets around the Krämerbrücke, the bridge lined with shops. The community was destroyed in the pogrom of 1349, when many were killed during the plague years, and the town took possession of the property. The house passed through many hands and was rebuilt and altered over the centuries, and its long survival is part of what makes it valuable.

Erfurt is a lively place, a university city and the capital of Thuringia, with a compact medieval centre, a cathedral and a church on a hill and a long tradition of gardening and horticulture. Riding in is easy from the autobahn, but the centre is mostly pedestrian and cobbled, so leave the bike in a car park and walk. The surrounding country, with the Thuringian Forest to the south-west and rolling farmland to the north, has good roads and gentle bends.

With over two hundred thousand people, Erfurt has all the fuel, food and beds you could want. Thuringian bratwurst, grilled over charcoal and served in a roll with mustard, is the local classic, and the dumplings known as Klöße are served with roast meats. A coffee near the Fischmarkt is a good break.

The ride combines Erfurt with Bad Kissingen, so you pass through Thuringia and Franconia, with plenty of woodland and small towns between.
t.wei e stadt@52.6,13.4:
The first thing you notice in the Weiße Stadt is how little it shouts. This is a housing estate in Reinickendorf, in the north of Berlin, built between 1929 and 1931 to a design by Otto Rudolf Salvisberg, with Bruno Ahrends and Wilhelm Büning, and its smooth white walls, strip windows and flat roofs were a quiet manifesto for a new way of living. It is called the White City for obvious reasons, and in the late Weimar years it was meant to show that ordinary people could have light, air and a balcony.

The estate belongs to the group of Berlin Modernism housing estates that UNESCO listed in 2008, and it is perhaps the most photogenic of them. A long bridge-like block spans the street at the entrance, with a slight curve to its profile, and the colour accents, in red and blue and ochre, on stair towers and balcony fronts, show that the architects were not austere by nature. Shops and a laundry were part of the plan, and inside the blocks are large courtyards with lawns and trees.

For a rider, Berlin is a city to be taken as it comes. The streets are wide, the traffic heavy but orderly, with tram lines, cyclists and the occasional rough cobbled stretch. Reinickendorf, in the north-west, is a leafy district with plenty of parking and the green belt of the Tegeler Forest and the lake close by, so it is a good place to ease in or out of the city. The roads north toward Brandenburg become quickly rural, with avenues of old trees and quiet villages.

The ride that includes this stop goes on to Dessau, which has its own great modernist legacy at the Bauhaus. Together they make a tour of the architecture that shaped the twentieth century. Fuel and food are no problem in a city of this size: there are petrol stations on the main roads and, in Reinickendorf, bakeries, Turkish snack bars and cafés on every corner.

Go on a calm morning, when the white walls are bright and the streets are quiet. Please remember that people live here, so keep voices and engines low.
t.house with balcony access mittelbreite 6:
Hannes Meyer was a Swiss architect and the second director of the Bauhaus, and in Dessau he designed a row of houses that put his ideas into concrete form. The Laubenganghäuser in Törten, finished around 1930, are blocks of flats reached by external walkways, the balcony access, so that each floor has a long open gallery along the front. It was a cheap, efficient way to give small flats light and ventilation, and it was an experiment in social housing, in an age when a decent flat was a political question.

The houses stand in Dessau-Törten, a district south of the town centre, close to the earlier estate that Walter Gropius had built in the mid-1920s, in which each house was assembled from standardised parts using a kind of production line. Together they show the Bauhaus's practical side, with the focus on ordinary housing, not just on grand design. The Bauhaus buildings in Dessau, including the school itself, are on the World Heritage list.

Dessau lies on the Mulde near its meeting with the Elbe, in a flat, green region of floodplain forests and meadows, part of the Middle Elbe biosphere reserve. The roads here are straight and gentle, lined with old trees and often busy with local traffic, and the surface is mostly good. It is a landscape that suits a relaxed ride, with long views and big skies, and the Wörlitz park, a short ride to the east, is one of the great English-style gardens of Germany.

Dessau has over seventy thousand people, so fuel and food are easy, though the housing estate itself is a residential area where you should park quietly and respect the residents. There is a good selection of cafés near the Bauhaus where you can have lunch and look at the sunlit glass of the famous workshop wing.

The ride pairs this house with another early modern housing estate, creating a small tour of how the twentieth century learned to build homes. Come on a dry day in spring or autumn, when the low light picks out the long balconies and the white walls.
t.old synagogue@51.0,11.0:
For a long time nobody in Erfurt knew that they were living above one of the oldest synagogues in Europe. The Old Synagogue stands in the narrow streets of the medieval centre, and its oldest walls date from the late eleventh century, with later enlargements in the Gothic style. After the pogrom of 1349, when the Jewish community was destroyed, the building passed into other hands and was used as a warehouse, a restaurant and a ballroom. Its original function was largely forgotten, until a restoration in the 1990s revealed the medieval walls under the later alterations.

The building is now a museum, and in it you can see the Erfurt Treasure, a hoard of silver, coins and jewellery that was hidden in a cellar wall in 1349, probably by a Jewish merchant who never came back. It was found in 1998 during building works at a nearby house, and it includes a magnificent gold wedding ring in the form of a tiny Gothic building. The collection is a rare and moving record of medieval Jewish life in a trading town.

The synagogue, along with the Stone House and the ritual bath, was added to the World Heritage list in 2023. Erfurt was a centre of trade at the crossing of two great roads, and the Jewish community was a vital part of it, with scholars, bankers and merchants. The city today is the capital of Thuringia, a lively university town with an old cathedral on a hill, a bridge lined with shops and a good deal of green space.

Riding to Erfurt is simple. The roads from the Thuringian Forest or the Harz run through rolling hills and farmland, with good surface and gentle bends, and the city has a ring road that makes it easy to get close to the centre. The old town is mostly pedestrian, so park the bike outside and walk. With over two hundred thousand people, Erfurt offers all the fuel, food and accommodation you could want, and the local sausage grilled over charcoal and served in a roll is a good lunch.

The ride pairs the synagogue with Naumburg Cathedral, a short trip east along the old trade road. Go early, when the museum is quiet, and take your time with the treasure.
t.berlin motorcycle escapes@52.1,14.1:
The Spree flows through here on its way from the Spreewald to Berlin, and its slow brown water, edged with reeds and willows, shapes everything. Along its banks stand the usual boathouses, jetties and campsites that tell you the river is used for paddling and fishing.

Beeskow has a medieval castle, one of the oldest in the region, and a surviving ring of town walls. The castle houses a cultural centre and, unexpectedly, a large archive of art from East Germany, with thousands of paintings and sculptures made under the socialist state, many of which were once displayed in factories and public buildings. For anyone interested in how art was produced under a dictatorship, it is a fascinating place. The old town has a quiet, slightly faded charm, with a market square and a handful of cafes.

The land around is a mix of pine forest, meadow and farmland, with a scattering of small lakes. Roads are flat to gently rolling, mostly good, and lined with trees in many places. Corners are mild, and traffic is light, with the main hazards being tractors and the occasional deer. Spring brings the smell of blossom and cut grass, and in autumn mist lies over the river valley in the morning.

This is a sensible start and finish point because the area is easy to reach from Berlin by the A12 motorway, and the quiet roads begin almost at once. Fuel and supermarkets are available in Beeskow, and the smaller villages have little. A swim in the river or one of the small lakes is possible, but look for signed bathing places, as banks can be steep and muddy. Late afternoon in summer, with warm light on the water and the smell of hay, is a lovely time to arrive.
t.beelitz@52.2,13.0:
There are stations at the edge of town, supermarkets, and a handful of bakeries, and the A10 motorway is close enough that the town gets its share of passing trade. From here, the roads south and west leave the flat farmland and climb gently into a country of old castles and quiet villages.

The castles are the point of this ride. West of here, on a wooded hill above Bad Belzig, stands Burg Eisenhardt, a medieval fortress with a tall keep that you can climb for a view across the Fläming. A few kilometres away, Burg Rabenstein, a restored hilltop castle, hosts falconry displays and has a forest setting that looks as though it came from a fairy tale. Nearer, at Ziesar, lies a bishop's castle, now a museum. The Fläming never had grand princes, and its castles are modest but atmospheric, standing in woods and old villages, with a sense of having been forgotten.

The Fläming is also a landscape of unusual quiet. It is a glacial ridge, rising to about two hundred metres at its highest point, covered in pine, beech and heath, with long views from the heights. The villages have stone churches, thatched roofs in places and few visitors. The roads are among the best empty ones in the region, with gentle gradients, long curves, and tree-lined stretches.

Before leaving, it is worth taking time to walk around the old centre of Beelitz, which has a Gothic church and a few remaining parts of its walls. Then fill up, buy water, and head out. Services in the Fläming are limited, with small villages offering little more than a bakery or an inn, and some closed on Mondays. The best months are May to October, with golden autumn light making the castles look their best.
t.lubeck return road@53.9,10.7:
Lübeck made its fortune from salt and herring. In the Middle Ages, the city on the Trave was the head of the Hanseatic League, the great trading association of North German towns, and its merchants controlled trade across the Baltic and the North Sea. The Holstentor, the brick gate with two round towers that leans slightly under its own weight, was built in the fifteenth century and is the symbol of the city, and the old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Gothic churches, merchants' houses and narrow lanes.

For a rider, the city is a good place to eat. Lübeck is known for its marzipan, and the confectioners' shops around the centre sell it in every form, from simple loaves to chocolate-covered fruit. The best known is the old marzipan house near the town hall, and the cafe upstairs is a good place for coffee and cake. The city also has the Buddenbrookhaus, the family house of the novelist Thomas Mann, who wrote about the decline of a merchant family in his first great novel.

With over two hundred thousand people, Lübeck has every service, including fuel stations on the edge of the city, bike dealers and plenty of restaurants. Fish is the local speciality, and a plate of fried herring or smoked eel with potato salad is the classic dish of the Baltic coast. The harbour at Travemünde, at the mouth of the river, has a beach and a long promenade, a short ride from the old town.

The riding in the area is flat and easy, with long, straight roads, tree-lined avenues and views of the sea. Wind is a factor, and it can be strong and cold, even in summer. The traffic around the city can be heavy, so avoid the rush hours. Come in spring, when the rapeseed fields are yellow, or in early autumn, when the air is clear and the light is golden.
t.eutin lake@54.1,10.6:
Eutin is a town with a lake, a castle and a composer. The lake, the Großer Eutiner See, is a broad stretch of water at the heart of the Holstein Switzerland region, with wooded shores and a slender island, and the castle stands at its edge, a moated palace of the old prince-bishops of Lübeck, surrounded by a landscape park. The composer is Carl Maria von Weber, who was born in the town in 1786, and the summer opera festival here is held in his honour on an open-air stage by the lake.

The town, with about seventeen thousand people, is known as the rose town, for the flowers that fill the gardens and the market square. It has a pleasant old centre of low brick houses, cafes and shops, and a lakeside promenade. Fuel and groceries are plentiful, and the cafes serve the cake and coffee that are essential to north German life. Malente, with its lakes and spa gardens, is a few kilometres away.

The Holstein Switzerland is a hilly region of glacial landscapes, left by the last ice age, with lakes, beech woods and rolling fields, and it is among the best riding in the north. The roads are smooth, with gentle curves and short climbs, and the lakes appear at every turn. The surface is generally excellent, but the verges are lined with trees, so look out for shadows and patches of damp in the morning. Cyclists are everywhere in summer, so share the road.

The lake is a good place to take a break, with benches and a path along the shore, and boat trips in summer. The light in the evening is soft and golden, and swans glide on the water. Spring and autumn bring colour and quiet, while summer can be busy at weekends. Come on a weekday, and you may have the shore to yourself.
t.northeim@51.7,10.0:
Northeim is a Hanseatic town that gets passed by, which is a pity. It sits on the Leine river, in the broad valley between the Harz mountains to the east and the Solling hills to the west, and it has a long history, with its origins in the early Middle Ages and a time as a member of the Hanseatic League. The medieval counts of Northeim were once powerful in the region, and one of them, Otto, became Duke of Bavaria in the eleventh century.

The old town has some good half-timbered houses, a Gothic church of St Sixti with a high tower, and parts of the old walls, a relaxed place for a short stroll. With about thirty-one thousand people, the town has everything a rider needs: petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries, and a few decent restaurants, and it is a practical place to stop and fill up. The pumps are on the edge of town, easily reached from the main road.

The surrounding country is rolling and green, with farms and woods, and it makes for pleasant easy riding. The roads along the Leine valley are smooth and quiet, with gentle bends and well-kept villages, and the hills on either side offer a bit of climbing. To the east, the Harz rises in a wooded wall, and the roads leading up to it are among the best in northern Germany, with tight bends, steep sections and fast, sweeping corners.

The weather in this area is changeable, with rain showers at any time of year, and the hills can be foggy in autumn. Summer is warm and pleasant, with long days, but weekends can bring many riders heading for the Harz. If you plan to ride the Harz roads, this is a good place to top up the tank and check the forecast, because the mountain weather is rarely the same as the valley's.
t.bad harzburg high road@51.9,10.6:
Bad Harzburg is where the Harz begins. The town sits at the northern edge of the mountains, where the flat land of the North German plain gives way to a steep wooded wall, and it has been a spa since the nineteenth century, with a brine bath, a park and a casino. A cable car climbs the Burgberg above the town, where the ruins of an eleventh-century imperial castle stand, built by Henry IV and destroyed by the Saxons not long after.

The road that climbs from here is the real attraction. The old Harz High Road, which runs south and east through the heart of the mountains, rises through spruce forest in a series of fast, flowing bends, passing the little waterfall of the Radau and the rocky outcrop of the Rabenklippe, where you can look out over the plain. At the top, near Torfhaus, the road reaches about 800 metres, with open moorland, bare spruce trees killed by bark beetles, and the dome of the Brocken, the highest peak in northern Germany, in view.

The Brocken has a long place in German legend, as the mountain where witches meet on Walpurgis Night, 30 April, and Goethe set a scene of Faust here. Tourists come in large numbers on that night, and the villages put on festivals. The weather on the Brocken is notoriously bad, with fog on most days, and the high road can be icy from October to April.

Bad Harzburg has about twenty-three thousand people and has fuel, supermarkets, cafes and a number of hotels. It is the best place to fill up before the climb. Traffic can be heavy at weekends, with riders, cars and tourists on the narrow roads, so aim for a weekday. Take warm clothing, since the temperature can drop by ten degrees from the valley to the top.
t.blankenburg return road@51.8,11.0:
Blankenburg sits under a wall of rock. The town on the northern edge of the Harz is dominated by the Regenstein, a sandstone ridge crowned by the ruins of a fortress, whose rooms are carved from the rock itself, with caves, tunnels and a chapel cut straight into the stone. It is one of the most unusual castles in Germany, and a short walk from the road.

Close by runs the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall, a jagged ridge of Cretaceous sandstone that rises from the fields like the spine of some enormous beast. The legend says the devil and God quarrelled over the land, and the devil built the wall in a rage, and the rocks are a great place for a stroll. The Harz foreland is full of such formations, and the roads here run along them, with views of the ridge from the saddle.

The town of Blankenburg has about sixteen thousand people and a baroque palace on a hill that was once the residence of the dukes of Brunswick. It has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes, and is a practical stop for riders crossing the Harz. The old town has a few half-timbered houses, and the large palace gardens are open to visitors.

The roads in the area are quiet and winding, with plenty of bends and short climbs, and they link the villages of the Harz foreland and the Selke valley. The surface is generally good, though some side roads are patched. In summer, it is warm, and the woods are a deep green. Autumn brings colour, and the rocks are lovely in the low sun. The area was part of East Germany until 1990, and you can still see signs of that past in the architecture. After the ride, a plate of Harzer cheese, a sharp, soft cheese, with onions and bread, is a local speciality worth trying.
t.quedlinburg overnight base@51.8,11.1:
Quedlinburg holds more than a thousand half-timbered houses, and it is hard to take a bad photograph there. The whole old town, with its winding lanes, market square and hilltop castle, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised in 1994, and it has survived largely intact through centuries of wars, partly because it was neglected in East German times and escaped the demolition of the old quarters that happened elsewhere.

The town is also one of the places where German history began. Henry I, called the Fowler, who became king of the East Frankish realm in 919, was buried at Quedlinburg, and his son Otto the Great made the town one of the centres of the empire. The Stiftskirche of St Servatius, a Romanesque church on the castle hill, holds his tomb, and the treasury has a collection of medieval manuscripts and relics. A women's abbey ruled the town for centuries.

With about twenty-three thousand people, Quedlinburg is the right size for an overnight stay, with a range of hotels and guesthouses, good restaurants and cafes, and fuel in the outskirts. The cobbled streets can be tricky on a loaded bike, so park at your hotel or a public car park and walk. Evening is the best time, when the tour groups have gone, the light is low and the half-timbered houses glow. Breakfast in a bakery on the market square, with a view of the town hall and a statue of Roland, the symbol of civic freedom, is a pleasant way to begin the next day.

The ride in from the Harz or the foreland is gentle, with smooth roads and light traffic, and the town appears over the fields with its castle and church towers on the hill. In winter, the town has a Christmas market that is among the prettiest in the region, and in spring the gardens and orchards are in bloom. Be careful of cobbles and tram-like lines in the streets, which can be slippery when wet.
t.bad malente@54.2,10.6:
Malente is a spa town that sits between two lakes, and it has the quiet manners of a place that has been taking care of visitors since the nineteenth century. The Dieksee lies to the west and the Kellersee to the east, and between them runs a canal and a path, lined with chestnut trees and villas, with boat landings and cafes. The old spa quarter, Gremsmühlen, has a park, a spa house and a fine collection of wooden villas with turrets and balconies.

The big attraction is the Five Lakes Tour, a boat trip that links the lakes of the Holstein Switzerland by canals and short channels, with a launch that runs in summer between Malente and Plön or Eutin. The trip lasts a couple of hours, and passes through reeds, beech woods and small hills, with swans and herons. It is slow and peaceful, a good way to spend an afternoon when the road is damp.

For riders, the town offers an easy coffee stop. There are bakeries and cafes along the main street, with cakes and coffee, and fuel stations on the road to Eutin. The town has about ten thousand people, and everything you need is within a short walk or ride. Eutin, a few kilometres away, is bigger and has more services.

The roads around Malente are among the most pleasant in the north, with smooth surfaces, gentle bends and a succession of lakes and woods. The hills are small, but they give a surprising sense of variety after the flat coast. The weather is mild, but showers can arrive quickly. In summer, the lakes are warm enough for swimming, and the beaches are busy at weekends. Come in the morning, when the water is still, and the first light picks out the reeds. A slice of plum cake and a pot of coffee at one of the lakeside cafes costs little and takes the edge off any amount of damp.
t.wernigerode@51.8,10.8:
Wernigerode likes to call itself the colourful town of the Harz, and it earns the title. The old town, at the foot of the mountains, has half-timbered houses in every shade of red, yellow, blue and green, carved with figures and inscriptions, and a Gothic town hall with two slim towers that looks like a toy. One of the houses is among the smallest in Germany, squeezed into a gap between two larger buildings, and visitors queue to look at it.

Above the town stands the castle, a Romantic fantasy of towers and turrets, rebuilt in the nineteenth century by the counts of Stolberg-Wernigerode, with rooms furnished in the style of the period. The castle looks out over the roofs of the old town and the forested hills beyond. Wernigerode is also the terminus of the narrow-gauge Harz railway, whose steam locomotives climb to the summit of the Brocken, the highest mountain in northern Germany at 1,141 metres, and run on regular schedules.

With about thirty-four thousand people, the town has fuel, supermarkets, cafes and hotels, and is a good base for riding in the Harz. The mountain roads from here are tight and enjoyable, climbing through spruce forest, with long views from the ridges. The old border between East and West Germany ran through the Harz, and you can find traces of it on the hills. The Brocken, once a restricted military zone, is now a place of walks and views.

The weather in the Harz is variable, with fog and rain common, and snow from October to April. Summer is the best time, but the roads are busy at weekends. Autumn brings colour, with golden beech woods, and the first snow dusts the peaks in November. For a meal, try the Harz specialities, such as the hearty stews, game dishes and local sausage, with a glass of beer, and the cafes in the old town are good for coffee and cake.
t.undeloh heath road@53.2,10.0:
Ask a German about Undeloh and he will tell you about the heather. The village lies in the middle of the Lüneburg Heath, one of the largest areas of heathland left in central Europe, and it is the quiet gate to the nature reserve that surrounds the hill of Wilsede. Thatched farmhouses sit under old oaks, there is a small church with a wooden tower, and in the main street horse-drawn carriages wait for tourists, which gives the place the look of a postcard from about 1925. Part of the track beyond the village is closed to motor traffic, so the last kilometres to Wilsede are for walkers, cyclists and the carriages. The bike stays where you leave it.

The heath itself is not wild nature but a landscape made by people. For centuries farmers cut turf, burnt the ground and let sheep graze, and the result was open, poor sandy land that only heather could live on. Heidschnucken, the grey, horned heath sheep, still keep the shrubs in check, along with juniper bushes that look like dark green candles standing in the sand. The heather turns purple from August into the first weeks of September, and on a sunny weekend then you will share the lanes with half of Hamburg. On a weekday morning in early autumn, with mist in the hollows and the heather gone brown and rust, it is a lot more private and, to my taste, better.

The riding in and out is gentle. These are narrow country roads through birch, pine and meadow, with low gradients and slow curves, and the main thing to watch is the other traffic: cyclists in pairs, tractors, and drivers looking at the view rather than at you. Surfaces are generally good but can have sand drifted on the corners after rain. It is a road for being slow, and that suits a finish. Hanstedt is the nearest place of any size with fuel, and Egestorf and the small inns around the heath serve coffee and cake in the German manner, with the heather honey and buckwheat pancakes you see on local menus.
t.hildesheim@52.2,10.0:
Hildesheim looks, from the ring road, like any prosperous middle-sized German city, with chain stores, car dealers and a ring of fuel stations, and that is exactly why it is a useful gate. Over a hundred thousand people live here, the fuel is plentiful, and the town sits in the open farmland of the Hildesheimer Börde, where black soil grows sugar beet and wheat. Filling up here before the Harz means you can take the hills without watching the needle, because once you climb towards Bad Harzburg and the Okertal the villages get small and stations get scarce.

The reason to stay a little longer is the old centre, and the story that goes with it. In March 1945 a bombing raid destroyed most of the historic town, which had been one of the finest collections of half-timbered houses in northern Germany. The market square was rebuilt in the decades after, as a careful copy of what had been there, including the tall Knochenhauer-Amtshaus, a butchers' guildhall with its carved upper floors. It looks old but it is young, and the locals will tell you so with pride. Hildesheim also has two churches, the cathedral and St Michael's, that are both on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Behind the cathedral a wild rose grows against the apse wall, and according to the legend it has been there since the ninth century, when Emperor Louis the Pious founded the bishopric. It was bombed to nothing in 1945, and sent up fresh shoots from the roots afterwards. Whatever you believe about the date, it is a nice story.

For a rider, the pleasure of the place is mostly the way it connects. To the south the Innerste valley and the green wooded ridges of the Harz foothills begin within half an hour, and the roads there turn from straight and fast to tight and shaded. In the morning the sun is behind you as you ride east, and in summer it is warm enough that you want a coffee in the old market before you start. Parking for bikes is easy in the pedestrian zone fringe, but watch the cobbles and the tram-free streets around the centre where one-way systems can confuse a satnav.
t.torfhaus high road@51.8,10.5:
Torfhaus is where the Harz stops pretending to be a gentle hill country. The settlement is little more than a cluster of buildings strung along the B4 at somewhere around 800 metres, between Bad Harzburg on the northern edge and Braunlage to the south, and it stands on open moorland where the spruce forest gives way to bog and wind. On a clear day the Brocken, at 1,141 metres the highest summit in northern Germany, stands over the horizon as a bald, slightly sinister dome, and it is the reason most people stop here. On a bad day you will see nothing at all, because this is one of the foggiest and wettest corners of the country.

The climb from Bad Harzburg is the part a rider remembers. The B4 leaves the town in a series of long, well-built bends through beech and then spruce forest, and the temperature falls with every few hundred metres. In early spring there can still be snow beside the road when it is dry and warm in the lowlands, so check the weather and carry a layer. Surfaces are good, but this is a popular road for cars, camper vans and other bikes, and a Saturday afternoon in summer can mean a slow convoy behind a lorry. A weekday morning, or early evening when the day-trippers have left, is when you get the road for yourself.

Torfhaus has a National Park information centre and a few places for coffee and sausage, and a short marked walk across the moor to a lookout point. Goethe walked up to the Brocken from here in the winter of 1777, which is why the main path to the summit is still called the Goetheweg. The Brocken has a long literary reputation: in the old stories it is where witches gather on Walpurgis Night at the end of April, and you can still buy witch dolls at every kiosk in the Harz. The nearest proper fuel is down in Bad Harzburg or in Braunlage, so do not count on filling a tank on the hill, and bring a warm drink. The wind up here finds every gap in your jacket.
t.uelzen hundertwasser station@53.0,10.6:
A railway station is not what you would expect on a list of highlights, but Uelzen is not an ordinary case. The town's main station was rebuilt in the late 1990s to a design by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, the Austrian artist who hated straight lines, and it opened in 2000, the year of his death. The result is a joyful mess: coloured columns, tiles in shining patterns, golden onion domes on the roof, trees growing out of windows and a floor that undulates beneath your feet. It looks as if a child had been allowed to design a station and had been given a big budget. Inside there is a normal functioning railway. Outside there is a line of motorcyclists taking photos, because this has become a kind of pilgrimage for people on two wheels.

Uelzen itself is a calm town of about thirty-five thousand people on the Ilmenau, at the eastern edge of the Lüneburg Heath. It was a Hanseatic member in the Middle Ages and it has some good brick churches and old timber houses, and in the surrounding countryside there are sugar beet fields, potatoes and the straight, flat roads of the north German plain. The Elbe Side Canal runs by the town and has a large ship lift, which is a minor attraction for people who like engineering. Fuel, groceries and cafés are easy to find in the centre, so it is a very good place for a reset.

The riding here is mostly about the connections. The roads to the north and south are straight, with long views across open fields, and the main risk is wind rather than curves. If the wind is from the west, it can be a long day on a light bike. There are quiet lanes through forest and farmland on both sides, and in spring the verges are full of wild flowers and, in a good year, the fields of rape that turn the landscape bright yellow. The old trading route between Lüneburg and Magdeburg ran through this region.

Take your photo from the forecourt, and if the sun is behind you the colours are strongest. A weekday morning is calmer. The staff are used to people who come to look and not to travel, and the cafés in the station building are a pleasant place for a coffee.
t.cooke city@45.0,-109.9:
Cooke City is a one-street mining town in the corner of Montana, perched at roughly 2,300 metres in a valley that feels cut off from everything else. It is the last settlement on the eastern end of the Beartooth Highway, only a few kilometres from the northeast entrance to Yellowstone National Park, and it sits so deep in the mountains that its main road is the only one in Yellowstone's neighbourhood that stays open to cars all winter. Snow here is serious. The town, along with its tiny neighbour Silver Gate, spends half the year under drifts and the other half welcoming motorcyclists who have come over the pass.

The reason for the town's existence is metal. Prospectors found silver, lead, copper and gold in these mountains in the 1860s and 1870s, and the settlement took its name from a financier who backed some of the early mining. The boom never quite became the bonanza people hoped for, partly because of the sheer difficulty of getting ore out through such rugged country, and in the 1990s a proposed new mine just outside Yellowstone's boundary became a national fight that ended with the federal government buying out the company. Old cabins, mine buildings and a few historic false-front shops give Cooke City a frontier look that is mostly genuine.

For riders, the town is the reward at the end of one of America's great mountain roads. Coming down from the Beartooth plateau, the highway drops through switchbacks and alpine meadows into the valley, and you roll into town with the peaks of the Absaroka range around you. The road from the east is only open from late spring to early autumn, and snow can still shut it in June or September, so check conditions before committing. From Cooke City you can continue west through the Lamar Valley, a road that rewards slow riding with bison, elk and, if you are lucky, wolves.

Fuel is available in town, which matters, because services are thin on both sides. There are a few places to eat, a handful of motels and lodges, and a general store, and in summer they fill quickly, so book a bed if you plan to stay the night. The nights are cold even in August, and the thin air makes the stars very sharp. The Chief Joseph Scenic Byway, which also arrives here, follows the route the Nez Perce took in 1877 when they fled the US Army across these mountains, and it adds a layer of history to a corner that already feels like the edge of the map.
t.decin cliffs@50.8,14.2:
Děčín stands where the Elbe leaves the Czech Republic, and the river here is dramatic. The town sits in a gorge in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains, with steep cliffs of pale rock rising straight from the water, topped with trees. The castle on the rock above the old town has stood guard on this spot for a thousand years, and from its terraces you look down onto the roofs, the river and the bridge. It is one of the more theatrical settings in Bohemia.

The photograph here is the cliffs themselves. A viewpoint called the Shepherd's Wall, on the left bank of the river, looks across the river toward the castle and the town, and it is a favourite for sunrise and sunset, when the stone glows. A path leads up through the forest, and the view over the loops of the river and the stacked ridges beyond is memorable. Another viewpoint, on the high rock called Sněžník, lies not far away, with a lookout tower from which the sandstone landscape stretches out in all directions.

The sandstone is the heart of the area. These rocks were laid down as sand in a Cretaceous sea, and erosion has carved them into pillars, gorges and rock towers, a landscape that has drawn painters since the nineteenth century. Downriver, the Elbe crosses into Germany and runs to Dresden, through the Saxon part of the same formation. The river was once the main trade route for coal, timber and grain, and old boat sheds and harbours speak of the days of steamers.

Děčín is a town of more than fifty thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, so supplies are never an issue. The riding around it is varied: the road along the river is flat and fast, while the roads up into the hills are narrow and twisty, with steep sections and sometimes rough pavement. Summer weekends are busy with tourists heading for the national park, so an early start helps. In autumn, mist rises from the river and the woods turn gold, and the town takes on a moody beauty.
t.litomerice food@50.5,14.1:
Litoměřice is the old wine town of northern Bohemia, and it feels like a smaller cousin of Prague with fewer crowds. It lies on the Elbe in the fertile basin beneath the Central Uplands, in a region called the garden of Bohemia, where orchards, vineyards and market gardens fill the plain. The main square is spacious and lined with arcaded houses, and the town has a cathedral on a hill and a number of baroque churches, giving it a quiet dignity.

Litoměřice has been a bishopric since the seventeenth century, and the cathedral of Saint Stephen, standing on its hill, is a landmark visible from far off. The town was fortified in the Middle Ages, and part of the old walls survive. Vineyards on the slopes of the nearby hills, such as Radobýl, a cone-shaped volcanic hill with its own nature reserve, produce wines that have been drunk here since the days of Charles IV, who is said to have encouraged the planting of vines in the region.

Just a few kilometres away lies Terezín, a fortress town built by Emperor Joseph II in the 1780s. In the Second World War the town was used by the Nazis as a ghetto and transit camp for Jews, and the Small Fortress was a Gestapo prison. A memorial and museum tell this history with dignity, and a visit is sobering and worthwhile, though it needs time.

As a food stop the town is excellent. The main square has restaurants serving Czech classics, as well as lighter dishes and cakes, and local wine is on the menu in most places. Fuel is available in the town, which has about twenty-four thousand inhabitants, with stations on the main road, and parking for bikes is easy near the square.

The roads around the town are calm, flat along the river and gently rolling in the hills, with the volcanic cones of the Central Uplands rising in the distance. A ride in the late afternoon, with the low sun on the vineyards, makes a lovely end to a day. Spring brings blossom, and autumn the grape harvest.
t.salzgitter@52.2,10.3:
Salzgitter is not a town for postcards, and that is exactly why it makes a good fuel gate. It was built around steel. In 1937 the Nazi government founded a huge ironworks here to exploit local iron ore, and the city that grew around it was a collection of villages merged into one, with a sprawling industrial landscape. Today the steelworks still operates, and the skyline is a mix of chimneys, rail yards and housing estates, softened by green belts and lakes.

With over a hundred thousand people, the city is large enough that fuel is never an issue. Stations line the main roads, supermarkets are open late, and there are cafes and restaurants of all kinds. It is a place to fill the tank, check the bike, and eat something sensible before heading into the hills of the Harz or the quiet countryside to the south. Riders arriving from the north across the flat plain of Brunswick find it a useful marker.

There is more to the area than industry. Salzgitter-Bad, the old spa and salt-springs district of the city, has a pretty historic centre with half-timbered houses, and a church, and the name of the city comes from the brine springs that were worked here for centuries. The surrounding countryside has low hills, the Salzgitter Heights, covered in forest, with a few quiet roads that give a good ride for those with time.

The roads in the area are a mix of fast main roads, good for covering distance, and minor lanes through villages and fields. The surface is generally good, the traffic is heavy around the works at shift times, and the weather can be changeable, with the wind sweeping over the flat land from the north. In winter fog is common.

The best choice is to treat Salzgitter as a base and a service stop rather than a destination, and to enjoy the contrast with the forest roads that wait to the south. A hearty meal here costs less than in the tourist towns of the Harz, which is a welcome bonus.
t.goslar old road@51.9,10.4:
Goslar is one of those towns that makes you stop the engine and simply look. It sits on the northern edge of the Harz mountains in Lower Saxony, and it was for centuries an imperial city, with a palace where German emperors held court in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The Kaiserpfalz, a huge Romanesque hall restored in the nineteenth century, still stands on the hill, with murals showing scenes of imperial history. Around it the old town is a maze of cobbled lanes, crooked half-timbered houses and slate-roofed gables, so well preserved that UNESCO listed it in 1992.

The wealth that built it came from the Rammelsberg, the hill just above town, where silver, lead, copper and zinc were mined for roughly a thousand years, until the mine closed in 1988. The mine is now a museum, and visitors can go underground and see the old galleries and waterwheels. The market square has a clock whose figures emerge to perform scenes of mining life, and the Kaiserworth, a tall guild house, stands on the corner. There is a real sense here of a city that was built on rock and ore.

The way in is part of the experience: you leave the plain, climb through woods and then drop into the town, with the old walls and towers coming into view. Cobbles in the old centre are rough and wet-slippery, so go slowly and park outside the pedestrian area. The roads out toward Bad Harzburg and the Oker valley are the real riding, with long bends through forest.

Goslar has more than forty thousand people, so fuel, food and everything else are easy to find, and the old town has cafes and restaurants of every kind, with game, hearty stews and a good deal of beer. In summer the market square is full of tables and the atmosphere is cheerful, and in December the Christmas market makes the town a magnet.

The weather in the Harz is changeable, with fog and rain in autumn and snow in winter. A clear spring morning, with the sun on the slate roofs and the smell of woodsmoke, is hard to beat.
t.oker valley bends@51.9,10.5:
The Oker is the river that cuts the Harz in two, and the road that follows it from Goslar toward Altenau is among the best in northern Germany. The valley is narrow and steep, with dark spruce forest on the slopes and bare granite cliffs breaking through, and the road keeps close company with the water, bending with every meander. The corners come one after another, tight enough to keep you busy and open enough to enjoy, and the surface is generally good.

The valley holds the Okertalsperre, a dam built in the 1950s to supply drinking water and control floods, which forms a long lake behind a massive wall of masonry.
