The lake is a deep green and the shore is quiet, and the walk along the dam is a pleasant way to stretch after the bends. Further down the valley, a short footpath leads to the Romkerhall waterfall, a small cascade in a rocky gorge, and above it the cliffs known as the Adlerklippen, where eagles were once said to nest, offer a view over the forest.

The Harz is one of Germany's oldest mountain regions, a block of ancient rock that was pushed up long ago and then worn down, and its highest point, the Brocken, is famous in German literature as the place where witches gather on Walpurgis Night. The mists that gather on these slopes make the legend easy to believe, and the forest has a haunting quality in cloud. The bark beetle has hit the spruce woods hard in recent years, and the dead trees on some slopes are a sad sight.

The road is popular with riders, and it pays to keep to the posted limits. Weekends are busy, and mid-week mornings are best. Fuel is not on the valley road itself: Goslar, six kilometres away, is the big town with everything, and Bad Harzburg, nearly eight kilometres, is a good alternative. Altenau, at the top, is a small resort with cafes. Late spring, when the forest is fresh, and autumn, when the beeches turn, are the best times to ride.
Clausthal-Zellerfeld sits on a plateau at around six hundred metres in the Upper Harz, and the town has a surprise at its centre: the Marktkirche, a huge church built entirely of wood, said to be the largest wooden church in Germany. It was built in the seventeenth century by a mining community that was rich enough to afford it and short of stone, and it is a fine sight, with its dark timber walls and a roof of slate. Inside it is painted and carved with a quiet grandeur.

Silver is the reason the town exists. Mining began here in the Middle Ages and flourished for centuries, and the Upper Harz became one of the most important mining regions in Europe. To power the pumps that kept the mines dry, the miners built an extraordinary network of artificial ponds, ditches and tunnels that collected rainwater from the high plateau, known as the Upper Harz Water Regale, and it is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. Walking around the forest ponds, you see how thoroughly the people of the Harz shaped their landscape.

The town is also home to a technical university, founded as a mining academy in the eighteenth century, which gives the place a lively student population and a good supply of cafes. The university's mineral collection is well regarded. With over fifteen thousand people, the town has fuel, shops and restaurants, and it is the best place to fill up before riding into the high Harz.

The photograph here is of the plateau itself, a high, open landscape of spruce, moor and ponds, where the road runs through long, gentle bends with wide views. The weather can be raw, with cloud and drizzle blowing over the heights, and winter comes early. The roads in the area are well surfaced, though frost can damage them, and traffic is moderate.

In summer the plateau is cool compared with the lowlands, and a light jacket is welcome. Autumn mists lend the ponds an eerie beauty, and spring brings fresh green.
t.seesen@51.9,10.2:
Seesen sits at the western edge of the Harz, where the hills begin to rise out of the plain, and it is a handy town for a stop with a little history tucked inside. In the early nineteenth century it was the home of the Jacobson School, founded by a Jewish banker and reformer named Israel Jacobson, one of the first schools to bring Jewish and Christian pupils together and to push for the reform of Jewish worship, and a temple he built beside it became a model for the first Reform synagogues. The temple was destroyed in 1938, and a memorial now marks the site.

Another famous figure is linked to the area. The writer and illustrator Wilhelm Busch, the creator of Max and Moritz, spent his last years in nearby Mechtshausen and is buried there, and his memory is kept alive there. His rhymes, with their sharp sketches and black humour, are known to every German child, and a copy of one in a local bookshop makes a nice souvenir.

The town itself has an old centre with half-timbered houses and a market square, and the remains of a castle on a hill, and it is easy to wander. With nearly twenty-two thousand people it has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat, including bakeries where you can pick up a Harz speciality. Sandwiches, cake, sausages and a strong coffee are all easy to find, and the prices are fair.

The roads leading out of Seesen go in several directions, but the most interesting lead into the hills, toward Bad Grund, Wildemann and Clausthal, climbing through forest in a series of bends. The surface is generally good, the gradients moderate, and the traffic is lighter than on the more famous roads to the east. The foothills are also a good place for a gentle warm-up before the harder riding of the Oker valley.

Weather is changeable, with fog in the lowlands in autumn and winter and cool, damp air in the hills. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, when the light is clear and the forest is fresh.
t.bosau road@54.1,10.4:
The Bosau road runs out onto a narrow peninsula in the Great Plön Lake, the largest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, and it is the sort of road where the surface of the water appears on both sides at once. This is the Holstein Switzerland, a name that exaggerates the hills but not the beauty: a landscape left behind by the glaciers of the last ice age, with rounded hills, hollows filled by lakes, and woods of beech that come down to the shore. The lake has islands, reedy bays and swans.

Bosau itself is a village with an old church, Saint Peter's, standing on a rise by the water. It is one of the oldest in the region, built in the twelfth century on the site of an earlier mission church, and it was the home of the priest and chronicler Helmold of Bosau, who wrote a history of the Slavs and of the Christianisation of the lands east of the Elbe. His chronicle is one of the main sources for the period. The church, with its plain brick walls and simple interior, is a quiet, atmospheric place.

The riding is relaxed and gentle, with long straight sections, mild bends and plenty of glimpses of water through the trees. The surface is mostly good, traffic is light in the morning and busier on fine weekends, when families head to the lake. Cyclists are frequent. The lanes in the area, lined with old trees, are among the nicest in the north, and the combination of lake, wood and farm creates a pastoral, unhurried feel.

The town of Plön, about seven kilometres away, has a castle on a hill overlooking the lake and is the nearest place with a full range of services, including fuel. Bosau has a few thousand people and cafes by the water, where you can eat smoked fish and cake while watching the boats. In summer there is swimming, sailing and kayaking, and ferries run on the lake.

Early morning on the water is the best time, with mist and a golden light. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and the evening air is quiet.
t.kuhlungsborn sea road@54.2,11.8:
Kühlungsborn is the largest seaside resort on the German Baltic coast, and from the top of the sea road you see why. A promenade runs for several kilometres along the beach, backed by rows of white villas in the old seaside style, with turrets, balconies and carved woodwork, many of them built in the decades before the First World War, when this was a fashionable resort for the Mecklenburg court and for visitors from Berlin. The beach is wide, pale and fine-grained, and the sea beyond is calm and shallow.

The word Kühlung in the name comes from the hills behind the town, a forested ridge that rises a little above the coast and catches the sea breeze. They are not high by Alpine standards, but in this flat land they give shelter and views, and the road that runs along the foot of the hills is a pleasant ride, with beech woods, small valleys and glimpses of the sea. The town has a long pier and a yacht harbour, as well as a tradition of spa treatments.

A narrow-gauge steam railway known as Molli, a railway that has run for well over a century, links Kühlungsborn with Bad Doberan and Heiligendamm. The little train puffs along the street and through the fields, with a whistle and a plume of smoke, and the sight is a delight for children and adults alike. Nearby Heiligendamm is Germany's oldest seaside resort, founded in the late eighteenth century, with a row of white classical buildings along the shore.

Swimming is a pleasure in summer. The Baltic is less salty than the North Sea and is shallow and gentle, though it stays cool until July, and lifeguards patrol the main beaches in season. A bathing break after a ride in leathers is a treat. The town has about seven and a half thousand people, with fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants serving smoked fish and cake.

Summer weekends bring heavy traffic and full car parks, so go early or visit in late spring or autumn, when the promenade is quiet and the air is clear.
t.rerik coast view@54.1,11.6:
Rerik lies on the Salzhaff, a sheltered lagoon on the Mecklenburg Baltic coast, separated from the open sea by a long narrow peninsula called Wustrow, and the viewpoint looks across a landscape of water, reeds and low hills. It is a place of birds: in spring and autumn migrating geese, cranes and waders fill the lagoon, and the quiet shore draws birdwatchers with binoculars. The air smells of salt, seaweed and grass, and the light is wide and pale.

The town is a small seaside place with a harbour, a promenade and a number of old fishermen's houses, now mixed with holiday villas. It has a fine church tower that can be seen from far out on the water. Local lore holds that a Slavic trading place called Reric stood somewhere on this coast over a thousand years ago, and while scholars debate the exact site, the claim gives the town a pleasant air of antiquity. The coast here was long a border zone between Slavic and German peoples, and the layers of that history are everywhere in the village names.

The riding is the usual Mecklenburg pleasure: flat or gently rolling, with avenues of old trees, fields of rapeseed and barley, and distant glimpses of the sea. The road along the coast offers long views, and the surface is mostly good, with patches of repair. Wind is the main factor. Gusts from the sea can be strong, and a headwind on the open stretches can slow progress, so a relaxed pace is the way.

Neubukow, a few kilometres inland, is the nearest town with a few services, though fuel is best taken at Kühlungsborn, about eleven kilometres to the east, where the stations and supermarkets are plentiful. Rerik has small shops and cafes, serving fish, cake and coffee at tables facing the water.

Summer evenings are lovely, with the light lingering long over the lagoon, and the sunsets across the water are among the best on this coast. Spring and autumn are quieter and have their own charm.
t.ahrenshoop coast art@54.4,12.4:
Ahrenshoop is a village where artists came first and tourists followed. In the 1890s painters from Berlin, Munich and elsewhere found this thin strip of land between the Baltic and the Saaler Bodden, drawn by the light, the sea, the reed-thatched cottages and the wide sky, and they founded an artists' colony that still defines the place. The landscape painter Paul Müller-Kaempff was among the first to settle, and the village has been a haven for creative people ever since.

Galleries and studios line the main street, and many of the thatched cottages that once belonged to fishermen and sailors now hold shops and cafes. A small art museum, built in the style of the local houses with a glossy dark exterior, displays works from the colony, and a stroll between the galleries is a pleasant way to spend an hour. The village has an unhurried, creative feel, and the coastline is just beyond the dunes.

The Fischland-Darß peninsula, of which Ahrenshoop is a part, is a thin spit of land with the open sea on one side and a chain of shallow lagoons, the Bodden, on the other. The beach is on the sea side, a long strip of sand with a steep, crumbling cliff known as the Hohes Ufer, where the bluffs are eaten away by storms and slowly retreat. The beaches are wide and clean, and the light at sunset is magnificent.

The road through the village is narrow and often busy with visitors in summer, so patience is needed. Speed limits are low, and cyclists and pedestrians are everywhere. Outside the main season the road is calmer and a pleasure, with long views of reeds and water. The surface is generally good, with some bumps.

Cafes in Ahrenshoop serve coffee, cake and smoked fish, with outdoor tables in the sun. The best times to visit are late spring and early autumn, when the light is soft and the crowds are smaller, and the sea in September is still warm enough for a quick plunge.
t.dar forest road edge@54.4,12.5:
The Darß forest is the wildest piece of woodland on the German Baltic coast, and the road that skirts its edge between Born and Prerow runs along the border of a landscape that has been left largely to itself. The Darß Urwald, as it is called, is a mix of beech, alder, pine and birch growing on old dune ridges and wet hollows, where fallen trunks are left to rot and the undergrowth is thick with fern. It belongs to the Western Pomerania Lagoon Area National Park, and walkers follow marked paths among trees draped in moss.

Near the sea the trees take a strange shape. On the western beach, wind and salt have bent the trees into low, windswept forms called Windflüchter, a fleeing-from-the-wind effect that gives the shore its look, and the forest edge appears to lean away from the water as if in flight. At the northern tip, Darßer Ort, a lighthouse and a nature centre mark the end of the peninsula, a place of drifting sand and sea birds.

In autumn the whole area becomes a stage for one of the great sights of northern Europe. Thousands of common cranes gather in the shallow lagoons of the Bodden during their migration south, and their calls carry across the water at dawn and dusk. Zingst, at the eastern end of the peninsula, holds a crane festival every October, and the sight of long lines of grey birds against a red sunset is unforgettable.

The road itself is narrow, lined by trees, with a surface that is generally good but bumpy in places from tree roots. Speed limits are low, wildlife crossing is a real concern, especially deer at dusk, and the traffic in summer can be dense, with cyclists and families heading for the beaches. A calm, careful ride is the way to enjoy it, and the shade of the forest is welcome on a hot day.

Prerow, a short distance away, is a small seaside village with a lovely sailors' church hung with model ships, and a few cafes. Fuel is scarce on the peninsula, and Barth, the nearest town of any size, is about fifteen kilometres away, so fill the tank before you come. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the crowds are thin and the light is clear.
t.gettorf return road@54.4,10.0:
Gettorf is a small town in the rolling country between Kiel and Eckernförde Bay, and the road that leads from it back toward Kiel is a pleasant, easy way to end a day. The landscape is the classic hummocky farmland of eastern Schleswig-Holstein, shaped by glaciers: low hills, hollows filled with ponds, hedgerows and patches of beech wood. It is a gentle country, rich in birds, and the lanes follow the curves of the land.

The town is old, with a church and a number of brick houses, and it grew as a market centre for the surrounding farms. Today it is mostly a commuter town for Kiel, with a pleasant centre and a few cafes. The Gettorf area belongs to a region known as Dänischer Wohld, the Danish Forest, a name that recalls the long centuries when this land was part of the Danish realm, and the district is still dotted with old manor houses with parks and farm shops.

The ride toward the city is calm. The road runs through villages and fields, with moderate bends and a good surface, and the traffic is light on weekends and heavier at commuting hours. As you approach Kiel the view opens toward the fjord, with ferries and ships in the distance, and the sense of arrival is satisfying. The coast of the Baltic is only a few kilometres away on either side, and on a clear day you can smell the sea.

For fuel and food the town has what a rider needs, with stations, a supermarket, bakeries and a few restaurants. Gettorf has about six thousand people, so it is large enough to be self-sufficient, and it makes a sensible last stop before the city. Farm shops along the road sell eggs, honey and apples in season.

The best light comes in the late afternoon, when the sun is low and the fields are golden. In May the rapeseed turns the landscape yellow, and in August the grain is ripe. A slow ride with the visor up is the way to finish.
t.lauenburg elbe@53.4,10.6:
Lauenburg is the gate of the Elbe, the last town in Schleswig-Holstein before the river runs on into Lower Saxony and Hamburg, and it clings to a steep bank above the water in a way that gives its old town an unusual shape. The main street, the Elbstraße, runs along the shore below the cliff, lined with old half-timbered houses, and the upper town sits on the ridge above, linked by steps and winding lanes. A castle tower still rises over the roofs.

The river has made the town and, more than once, flooded it. The Elbe was for centuries the great trade road of northern Germany, carrying salt from Lüneburg and timber and grain downstream, and Lauenburg grew up as a customs and shipping point. A museum on the quay tells the story of the river boats, including the old sailing barges and steamers, and the quay itself is a fine place for a stroll. The floods of 2013 reached extraordinary heights, and marks on the buildings show how high the water rose.

The river runs through a broad green valley here, with meadows, reeds and old willows, and across the water the land of Lower Saxony stretches away. The Elbe cycle route follows the bank, so cyclists are a common sight, and the road along the river is calm, with a good surface and light traffic. Birds are plentiful: storks nest in the villages, and cranes and geese pass through in autumn.

Lauenburg has nearly twelve thousand people, so fuel is easy to find, with stations on the main road, and supermarkets and cafes in the centre. As the start of a ride it is a practical place to fill up and eat, with Hamburg about forty-five kilometres to the west and the Wendland country to the south-east, a region of quiet forests and round villages.

Spring, when the river is high with meltwater and the meadows are bright, and early autumn, when the light is soft and the birds are moving, are the best seasons. A morning start gives mist on the river and quiet roads.
t.hitzacker river balcony@53.2,11.0:
Hitzacker is a small town on an island in the Elbe, and it looks like a model of itself. The old centre is a tight cluster of half-timbered houses with carved beams and painted panels, grouped around a church and a handful of narrow streets, surrounded on all sides by water and meadow. The town sits in the Wendland, the far north-eastern corner of Lower Saxony, a region of quiet villages, forests and wide river plains.

The balcony of the title is the river terrace above the town, where you look out over the Elbe floodplain, a broad sweep of green meadows, with the river wandering through and the far bank low and blue. On a clear morning the mist lies in the hollows and the sun rises over the water, and it is a place to stop and breathe. The Elbe floods here from time to time, and the old houses are marked with the high-water lines from past years, some of them well above head height.

The Wendland has its own character, shaped by the Slavic people who lived here in the Middle Ages and left behind the round villages, called Rundlinge, in which the houses are arranged in a ring around a central green with a single entrance. Several survive near Hitzacker and Dannenberg, and the pattern is easy to see from the air. The area has also been a centre of protest and independent thinking, and the town hosts a well-known summer music festival.

The roads here are quiet, with long views, gentle bends, a good surface and almost no traffic outside the summer holidays. Riding along the dike, with the river on one side and fields on the other, is a pleasure. The sun can be strong, and wind from the west can blow across the open land.

With just over five thousand people, Hitzacker has a few cafes, a bakery and small shops, though fuel is not guaranteed in a town this small, and Dannenberg, seven kilometres away, is a larger town with more choice. Local fish and a plate of Wendland sausage are good for lunch. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the light is soft and the river is full of birds.
t.dannenberg food town@53.1,11.1:
Dannenberg sits on the Jeetzel, a slow, brown little river that wanders through the Wendland, the odd bulge of Lower Saxony that pokes east across the Elbe almost to Brandenburg. For years the East German border ran a few kilometres away, and the region still has the faintly forgotten feel of a place that was a dead end. Riders from Hamburg tend to find that rather pleasant. The traffic is thin, the villages are low and tidy, and nobody is in a hurry.

The town itself is small enough to walk end to end in a quarter of an hour. There is a stump of old castle, the Waldemarturm, standing above the lower town, and a market square with the kind of brick and half-timber that survived because nothing important ever happened to it. That is a joke, but only half of one: Dannenberg is better known to Germans for the protests around the nuclear waste store at nearby Gorleben, which for decades brought tractors, sit-downs and yellow crosses to these fields. You still see the crosses in some gardens. It is worth knowing that history when you notice how many cafés and bakeries here cater to a politically opinionated, slightly bohemian crowd.

As a stop it does the job well. With more than eight thousand people it has several fuel stations, supermarkets and a handful of places to sit down with a proper lunch, and parking a bike on the square is no trouble. A regional habit worth trying is the baked goods and the sausage from local butchers, plain and good, with nothing that needs explaining.

What I like most is what lies around the town. The Wendland is famous for its Rundlinge, villages laid out in a ring around a central green with all the farm gables facing inward, an arrangement that goes back to Slavic settlers. Ride a few kilometres in almost any direction and you can find one, usually on a road where you meet more cyclists than cars. The surface is mostly good, the corners are gentle, and the landscape is soft: wet meadows, alder carrs, the occasional stork nest on a chimney. Add the Elbe dikes just to the north and you have a day of easy, unpressured riding. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the light is low and the fields smell of cut grass or wood smoke.
t.gohrde forest sweep@53.1,10.9:
The Göhrde is one of the biggest continuous woods in northern Lower Saxony, a patch of oak, beech and pine that stretches for kilometres between Lüneburg, Dahlenburg and Dannenberg. Ride into it from any direction and the temperature drops by a couple of degrees, the light turns green, and the noise of the open country just stops. After the flat, windy farmland of the Elbe plain it feels like a different country.

The wood has a past worth knowing. It was a hunting ground of the Hanoverian rulers, who kept a lodge here, and the forest was managed for deer and boar long before anyone thought of it as a place for recreation. In September 1813 a small but notable battle was fought in these trees, when allied troops fought a French and Danish force in the last stages of the Napoleonic wars. Locals still remember it and there is a memorial for it. Today the forestry is gentler, and the Göhrde is a nature-heavy place where red deer, wild boar and the occasional cranes pass through, and where you might see a buzzard from the saddle if you ride early.

The riding itself is quiet and rhythmic. The roads are narrow and straight at first and then bend lazily around clearings and old tree lines, with patchy shade that makes the surface alternate between dry and damp. There are root heaves and fallen needles in places, so treat the dark stretches with respect, particularly in autumn when leaves hide patches of moisture. In summer the tunnel of trees is a relief on a hot day. In winter it can hold ice in the shade long after the open fields have cleared.

Nothing here is a fuel stop. Zernien and Nahrendorf are villages without much to offer a hungry rider, and the closest decent options are Dannenberg to the east and Hitzacker on the Elbe, about twelve kilometres away, which has a pretty old centre of timbered houses and cafés. Fill the tank before you commit to the forest and carry a bottle of water. The point of the Göhrde is not to arrive anywhere but to spend half an hour in a long green corridor with the visor up and the engine ticking quietly.
t.luneburg old town meal@53.2,10.4:
Lüneburg got rich on salt, and the evidence is on every street corner. For a thousand years brine was pumped up from under the town and boiled down into what the Hanseatic merchants called white gold, then carted along the old Salt Road to Lübeck and shipped across the Baltic to preserve herring. The money built brick gables of tremendous height and swagger, a town hall with rooms that are still painted and carved to dazzle, and a harbour on the little Ilmenau river with a wooden crane that hauled barrels onto barges. The old crane is still there and worth a look.

The odd part is that the old houses lean. Centuries of salt extraction made the ground sink unevenly, and whole rows of buildings tilt as if they were listening to each other. Streets in the Sülze quarter bend and dip in ways that are not charming by design. The saltworks closed in 1980, but the old town was left largely intact, and the university and the students now fill the cafés that the merchants once filled with hogsheads of herring.

For a rider, Lüneburg is a straightforward and satisfying meal stop. It is big enough, more than seventy thousand people, to have fuel on the edges, supermarkets and a wide choice of places to eat, from fast bakeries to proper restaurants with heath lamb, local potatoes and the regional dish called Labskaus, a mash of corned beef, beetroot and potato that looks worse than it tastes. Parking a bike near the old town is usually easy, though the cobbles around the Am Sande square are rough, and the lanes inside the core are narrow. Go on foot from the first sensible place you find.

Coming in from the heath side the approach is calm, long and pretty open, and from the Elbe side it is flat and fast. Weekends in summer fill the centre, so earlier in the day, or a weekday, suits better. Allow yourself an hour to walk down to the river and back before you gear up again. You will see why people stay.
t.elbe marsh@53.4,10.2:
South of Hamburg the Elbe loosens into marsh, flat and open to the sky, with the river kept in place by a long dike that you can ride along or beside. The land behind it sits below the level of the high tide, and the old farms stand on little mounds, their fruit trees and thatch looking oddly protective. This is the Elbmarsch, close to the Vier- und Marschlande, and the horizon is made of sky.

The dike road is the place to be. It is narrow and straight, with the grass slope on one side and the fields on the other, and the surface changes from newly laid to patched. Sheep graze on the slope and move aside with some reluctance. Ride slowly and look at the river: container ships and bulk carriers come past silently, and from the level of the dike they seem to glide across the fields. The wind is the main character. On a clear, cold day it comes at you from the west with real force, and a heavy bike will feel it in the shoulders for the next hour.

The Elbe has shaped this area for centuries, and not always kindly. Great floods, including the storm surge of 1962 which hit Hamburg so hard, led to the raising and strengthening of dikes along the whole river. The soil behind them is rich silt, which is why the marsh is full of vegetable growers and orchards. In late spring you can smell blossom, and in autumn the roadside stalls sell apples and pumpkins on an honesty basis.

Nothing practical sits right at the dike. Drage is a village with a handful of services, but the sensible place for fuel, a proper meal and a rest is Winsen on the Luhe river, about four kilometres away, which has pumps, supermarkets and a pleasant old centre with a moated castle. The dike works best as the last scene of a day, with the light turning gold over the water and the long road back toward Hamburg ahead. Bring a windproof layer and be ready to be a little slower than you planned.
t.braunlage@51.7,10.6:
Braunlage is the Harz mountains' main winter town, a place of hotels and guesthouses sitting in a high bowl at around five hundred and sixty metres, ringed by spruce forest. Above it rises the Wurmberg, at 971 metres the highest summit in Lower Saxony, with a cable car, a ski area and, on a clear day, a good view of the Brocken, the Harz's bald and brooding top, which sits across the old inner-German border in Saxony-Anhalt. The Brocken is where Goethe sent Faust and his witches to dance on Walpurgis Night, and the whole region leans happily into the witch theme.

The town has been a mining and forestry place, then a spa and holiday resort, and it still feels like a place built for visitors, with a long main street of cafés, bakeries and shops selling Harz sausage, honey and wooden carvings. It is a comfortable place for a long lunch or an overnight, especially if the weather turns, which it often does at this height. Fog, drizzle and sudden snow flurries can arrive in any month except high summer, and the temperature can be ten degrees lower than down in the valley.

Riding here is a different business from the plains to the north. The roads climb through dense spruce, with wide, flowing corners and long straights on the plateau, and the surface is generally good, though frost heaves appear after winter. The Harz roads are popular with riders and drivers alike, so on a dry summer weekend expect crowds, plus the occasional speed check. The B4 and B27 meet here, and the roads toward Torfhaus and Sankt Andreasberg are among the best in the region. A lot of the forest around has suffered from bark beetle in recent years, and the bare grey trunks on some slopes are a sobering sight.

Braunlage has just over five thousand people, but it has fuel, shops and a good choice of restaurants, so it is a sound base. Carry warm layers even in summer, and check the weather before taking the higher roads. The best times are early autumn, with clear light and quiet roads, and midweek in June.
t.malente cafe@54.2,10.6:
The lakes of Holstein Switzerland form a loose chain around Malente, and the town's main street is the place where the lake atmosphere turns into something you can sit in with a cup of coffee. The name Holstein Switzerland is a nineteenth-century tourist invention, given by visitors who thought the rolling hills and blue water looked like Swiss scenery. It is not a bad comparison if you squint, and the area has a gentle, glacial beauty of its own, shaped by ice that left behind hills, hollows and a string of lakes.

Malente itself is a spa and holiday town, with a long tradition as a Kneipp resort, a water-cure centre where people came to take cold footbaths and walk in the woods. It has a calm, slightly old-fashioned air, with villas along the lakes and a good number of bakeries and cafés. Sit down at one of them and order a slice of cake, since the north Germans' attachment to afternoon coffee and cake is serious. On the lakes, small passenger boats run a circuit connecting several of them, called the Five Lakes tour, and it is a pleasant thing to do on a warm day.

The riding to and from Malente is modest but engaging. Roads run through low hills, past fields, lakes and beech woods, with plenty of gentle bends and the occasional small climb. The hills are not high, and the highest point in Schleswig-Holstein, the Bungsberg at about 168 metres, lies not far away to the northeast, which tells you how much altitude you can expect. Tarmac is mostly fine. On summer weekends the lake roads can be busy with cyclists and cars, and the lanes around Eutin are popular, so go early.

Services are easy. Malente has more than ten thousand people, so you will find fuel, supermarkets and several choices for lunch, while neighbouring Eutin has a bigger range. Parking a motorbike on the main street is not a problem. A small piece of advice: you will be tempted to stay longer than planned, particularly if the sun is out and a table by the water is free. Allow for that in the day's plan.
t.molln@53.6,10.7:
Mölln is a small town in the Lauenburg Lakes, southeast of Lübeck, and it carries one very odd claim to fame. According to local tradition it is where the famous prankster Till Eulenspiegel died of plague in the fourteenth century, and his gravestone is built into the wall of the church of St Nicolai. The stone shows an owl and a mirror, which is what his name means in German. A fountain on the market square shows him as a cheerful figure, and the town's tourist trade is lightly sprinkled with jokes about it.

The town itself is a pretty, compact place on a hill between lakes, with a medieval core of narrow streets and old brick and half-timbered houses. In the Middle Ages Mölln was a staging point on the Old Salt Road that ran from Lüneburg to Lübeck, and in the fourteenth century the city of Lübeck even took over the town for a time to protect the route. A canal known as the Stecknitz canal was built nearby to carry salt by barge, and traces of it remain. It is a good place to walk and wander before you ride again.

For riders, Mölln is a sensible refuelling point, with eighteen thousand people and fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets and restaurants. Parking near the centre is easy, but the old streets have cobbles that are rough and slippery after rain, so be careful in the lanes. The lakes around town, the Schulsee, Stadtsee and several others, give pleasant views, and a stroll along their edges is a good way to stretch your back after a long morning in the saddle.

The roads in and out of Mölln are among the better ones in the region. They run through the Lauenburg Lakes Nature Park, a country of low hills, beech forest and still water left behind by the last ice age, with smooth tarmac and gentle curves. Traffic is moderate on weekdays and busy on warm weekends, when day-trippers from Hamburg arrive. Early morning gives you the best of the lakes, with mist on the water and the roads nearly empty.
t.ratzeburg lake road@53.7,10.8:
Ratzeburg's lakes are long, narrow and clean, the leftovers of ice that gouged out troughs across this part of Schleswig-Holstein, and the road along them is one of the nicest pieces of easy riding between Hamburg and the Baltic. It follows the shore, rising and falling over small bluffs, and gives glimpses of water through the trees, with sailing boats and rowing eights moving in the distance. In the calm hours of the morning, the surface of the lake looks like polished metal.

The rowing is not an accident. Ratzeburg has been one of Germany's centres of the sport since the middle of the twentieth century, and the long, straight lake is ideal for it. A famous coach worked here and trained crews that won Olympic gold, and you will often see slim boats gliding on the water with a trainer cycling or motoring alongside. On weekends there are regattas, and the shore comes alive with spectators.

Behind the lakeshore, the country is gentle and rural: rolling fields, woods and neat villages with brick churches. This area was once on the edge of the Iron Curtain, since the border with East Germany lay just a few kilometres to the east, and the quiet that fell on the region after 1945 has left it undeveloped and peaceful. The road is smooth for most of its length, with a mix of long, easy bends and short, sharp corners where the road dips to cross a stream. In summer there are cyclists and families heading for the lake beaches, and the speed limits through the villages are enforced.

If you want to swim, there are public beaches along the lake in warm weather, and the water is clear enough for it, though you should check local signs and stay near the lifeguarded areas. Ratzeburg itself has about fourteen thousand people and plenty of places for fuel, food and coffee, so you do not need to plan around services. The town's old centre on its island is a short walk away, and it is worth a visit. Come on a weekday in June or September if you can, when the water is warm enough for a dip and the roads have room on them.
t.schaalsee biosphere@53.6,10.9:
The Schaalsee is the deepest lake in northern Germany, a long, dark, cold trough more than seventy metres down in its deepest part, gouged by a glacier and then filled with meltwater. The area around it is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and it is one of the least spoiled landscapes in the north: lakes, reedbeds, meadows, beech forest and small villages with brick farmhouses and church towers.

The reason it is so undisturbed is political. For forty years the inner German border ran through the middle of the lake, with the western shore in the Federal Republic and the eastern in the GDR, and a strip of land on either side was off limits. Fences, watchtowers and patrols kept people out and nature in. When the border opened in 1989, the strip had become an accidental wildlife refuge, and it now forms part of the Green Belt, the chain of protected land that runs along the former frontier from the Baltic to Bohemia. White-tailed eagles nest here, cranes gather on the fields in autumn, and the reedbeds hold bitterns and otters.

On a bike the biosphere is a landscape for slow, curving riding. Roads run between hedges and fields, through villages and along the lake in places, with a rolling pattern that keeps things interesting. The tarmac is generally good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends, when the lake beaches fill up. Be alert for cyclists and farm vehicles, and for deer at dawn and dusk. Autumn is a spectacular time, with mist on the water, migrating geese and the beeches in colour.

There is not much in the way of services right at the water. Zarrentin, a few kilometres away, is a small town with a lake beach and a ruined monastery and has shops and cafés, and Wittenburg, about thirteen kilometres off, is the nearest place with a good range, including fuel. Plan fuel in advance. A visitor centre in the area explains the reserve and the history of the border, and it is worth a short stop if you have time. Bring a layer, because the wind off the lake can be cool even in July.
t.zarrentin water edge@53.6,10.9:
Zarrentin sits at the southern end of the Schaalsee, and the town's whole personality is turned toward the water. A path runs along the shore past a small beach, a boat landing and a row of cafés, and on a warm day it is as close to a seaside promenade as you can get in the middle of the country. Reeds fringe the edge of the lake, ducks and swans patrol the shallows, and the water is clear and cold, a reminder of how deep this lake is.

Zarrentin has a long past that is easy to miss. In the thirteenth century Cistercian monks founded a monastery here, and its ruins and some of its buildings still stand beside the church, with a gentle, grassy character. The brick church, with its high roof, can be seen from some distance across the water. After the Reformation the monastery was turned into a ducal residence, and later the area fell under Mecklenburg, which is why the place has a different feel from the Schleswig-Holstein towns just across the former border.

That border is the dominant fact of the recent past. Until 1989 the lake was split between East and West, and Zarrentin was on the eastern side, so people here could not freely travel to the western shore a few hundred metres away. Today you can wander freely along the lake, and information boards tell the story of the divided shore. It is a quiet, moving thing, set against the cheerful sound of children splashing in the water.

For a swim, the lake beach in town is the straightforward option, though in cooler months it is for looking at rather than entering. The roads to Zarrentin are good, and the approach from the west runs through rolling country with the lake glinting between trees. The town is small, around three thousand people, so there is food and a shop or two but not much more, and the nearest place with proper fuel and supermarkets is Wittenburg, about twelve kilometres away. Gudow, in the opposite direction, is a smaller village. A drink on a terrace by the water in the late afternoon is the best use of an hour you could think of.
t.eutin@54.1,10.6:
Eutin calls itself the Rose Town, and in summer you can see why, with rose beds in the market square, the park and the front gardens, but its better claim is a small, pale baroque palace on an island in a lake. The palace was the residence of the prince-bishops of Lübeck for several centuries, and it is surrounded by a moat and a landscape park that slopes down to the water of the Great Eutin Lake. In summer an open-air opera festival is staged in the palace gardens, with the lake as a backdrop, and it has done so for decades.

Eutin has a distinguished cultural connection too. The composer Carl Maria von Weber, whose Freischütz is one of the great German romantic operas, was born here in 1786, and the town remembers him with a monument and a festival. The poet and translator Johann Heinrich Voss, who gave German readers a famous version of Homer, taught at the local school, and the town became known as the Weimar of the North for its circle of writers and thinkers in the late eighteenth century. It is a lot of history for a small place with seventeen thousand people.

The market square is small and cobbled, and the streets around it have half-timbered houses, bakeries and cafés with outdoor tables. It is a place to walk slowly. As a gate to Holstein Switzerland, it also serves as the starting point for lake roads that run toward Malente, Plön and the Baltic coast. The riding nearby is gentle but constant, with smooth bends, short climbs and views through trees to the lakes. The roads are well kept and, on a weekday, mostly empty. On summer weekends the lake shores are busy with cyclists and families.

For practical needs, Eutin has plenty: fuel stations at the edge of town, supermarkets and a large choice of cafés. Parking a bike in the centre is simple, though the cobbles around the market need a cautious hand when wet. If you have an hour, walk down to the lake and look back at the palace from the water's edge. In the evening, when the opera audience arrives, the light on the water is soft and gold.
t.bergen@52.8,10.0:
Bergen is a small town on the southern edge of the Lüneburg Heath, close to the sandy plain that the army has used for training for more than a century. It has little to show by way of fame, but it is a useful, friendly, ordinary place with a sensible set of services, and for riders crossing the heath it makes a natural break. The town's surroundings are pine woods, heather and sandy fields, laced with quiet lanes.

Bergen's name is known to many people for another reason. A few kilometres to the northwest lies the site of Bergen-Belsen, the concentration camp where tens of thousands of people died in the last years of the Second World War, among them Anne Frank and her sister Margot. The camp itself was burned after liberation to stop disease from spreading, and the memorial today is a landscape of heath and birch with mass graves marked by grassy mounds, along with a documentation centre. It is a place of great quiet and weight, and it is open to visitors. If you go, allow time and go on foot, and leave the bike's noise behind.

The roads around Bergen are straight and smooth, running through pine plantations and open heath, with few bends and plenty of long views. Because the area is part military zone, you will sometimes see signs and barriers, and on some days there are convoys of army vehicles on the road, so keep your eyes open. The landscape has the dry, sandy smell of the heath, and in late summer the heather turns the ground purple. Wind on the open stretches can be fierce.

For food, Bergen has bakeries, snack bars and a few restaurants, and regional dishes such as Heidschnucken lamb and buckwheat pancakes are on the menus. The town is big enough, about fourteen thousand people, for fuel stations and supermarkets, so it is an easy place to fill the tank and have a sandwich. Traffic is moderate. If you find yourself in the area on a weekday in spring or autumn, you will have the roads almost to yourself, and the heath will be quiet.
t.muden ortze photo@52.9,10.1:
Müden is one of those villages that photographers find without being told. It sits where the little Örtze river winds through the southern Lüneburg Heath, a clear, sandy-bottomed stream running between alders and meadows, and it is surrounded by thatched half-timbered farmhouses, old oaks and a small church. Several of the buildings have the typical heath style, with low eaves, brick infill and a big roof of reed or straw, and the whole thing looks as though it has been waiting for a painter. Many painters did indeed come, and the village has attracted artists for generations.

The river is the heart of the picture. In the morning mist rises off the water, and the light slants through the trees and picks out the edges of the roofs. There are old mills and bridges along the stream, and the clear water is a good place to see small fish, ducks and, with luck, a kingfisher flashing past. A footpath along the bank gives a quiet walk, and a canoe trip along the Örtze is a popular summer activity.

The riding here is leisurely. The roads in and out of the village are narrow and gently winding, lined with birch and pine, with some stretches of cobble or patched tarmac. In heather season, late summer, the clearings turn purple and the whole region is busy with visitors, so choose a weekday if you can. Nearby Faßberg has a place in history as one of the air bases used during the Berlin Airlift in 1948 and 1949, when planes brought food and coal to the besieged city, and a small museum recalls the event.

Müden itself has little more than a few inns, a café or two and an occasional farm shop, so it is a place to stop for a coffee and a walk rather than for provisions. The nearest larger town is Hermannsburg, about five kilometres away, which has fuel, supermarkets and several restaurants. Bring a camera, and give yourself half an hour at the bridge. Locals are used to photographers, but it is polite to keep clear of private farmyards and gardens.
t.hermannsburg heath road@52.8,10.1:
Hermannsburg is a surprise in the middle of the heath, a village with a missionary history that stretches all the way to southern Africa. In the middle of the nineteenth century a local pastor named Ludwig Harms founded a mission here that trained and sent out farmer-missionaries, and over the following decades the Hermannsburg Mission sent hundreds of workers to Africa and India. Places in South Africa were named after the village, and a few of them still carry it, which is a strange thing to come across in a quiet corner of Lower Saxony. A museum and a large church recall the story.

The heath around the village is in the Südheide Nature Park, a landscape of pine, heather, juniper and birch, with sandy soil and slow rivers. It is less visited than the more famous northern heath around Wilsede, and for that reason it is a quieter place. Roads here run mostly straight, but they bend a little around old farms and woodland, and they have a smooth, easy character that suits a relaxed ride. Traffic is light on weekdays, and the main risks are farm vehicles, deer and the occasional patch of sand blown across the tarmac.

The Örtze river flows through the village, clear and shallow, and a stroll along it is pleasant after a spell in the saddle. In late summer, the heath blooms and the air smells of honey. Sheep graze in the open areas, helping to keep the heather from being overtaken by trees, and you may see a shepherd with a dog moving a flock along a lane. The timber houses, with their thatched or tiled roofs and old oak beams, are often decorated with carved horse heads on the gable.

For services, Hermannsburg has about eight thousand people, which means fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a few restaurants, so it is a good stop. Try the heath lamb or the buckwheat cakes at a local inn. The roads toward Müden and Bergen are among the nicest in the area, and you can combine the three places in a loop of an hour or two. Early morning or late afternoon, when the low sun sets the heather glowing, is the time to be out.
t.neumunster fuel escape@54.1,10.0:
Neumünster is not a town people ride to, but it is a very good town to ride out of. It lies in the middle of Schleswig-Holstein, where the motorways from Hamburg, Kiel and the north meet, and it has the practical, working feel of a place built by industry. For centuries it was a centre of cloth and leather, and the textile mills lined the little Schwale river, though most of them closed in the twentieth century. The town grew from a monastery, founded in the early twelfth century by the missionary Vicelin, and his name is still borne by the main church.

This is a place for filling tanks and starting days. With more than seventy-eight thousand people, Neumünster has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries open early, and it is easy to find a quick breakfast. There is nothing here you would call romantic, but the practicality is a relief, and it saves you worrying about whether the village ahead has a pump. Riders heading north to the Baltic coast, or the Danish border beyond, often gather here before the long run into the quiet country of Angeln.

The roads leaving town to the north and east are the part worth noting. They quickly turn into small country roads through low, rolling farmland, with Knicks, hedged fields and red-brick villages, and the traffic thins within a few kilometres. The land is gently hilly, a leftover from the ice age, with patches of woodland and some small lakes. The surface is mostly good, and the corners are open and easy, so the first hour of the day is a good chance to warm up the tyres and settle into the rhythm.

Weather in Schleswig-Holstein changes fast, with bright sun, a squall and sun again within an hour, and the wind is a constant companion. Take a waterproof layer. If the day is long, tank up properly before leaving, since the countryside to the north has plenty of villages but fewer petrol stations than you might expect. In the early morning, with mist lying in the hollows and the first light coming across the fields, this plain stretch of Holstein is surprisingly pleasant.
t.schonberg coast@54.4,10.4:
East of Kiel the coast flattens into the Probstei, a farming district whose name recalls the provost of the convent at Preetz, who once held the land. The fields are open and treeless, the villages built along old dike lines, and the Baltic sits low behind a grass bank with a long, wide beach in front. Schönberger Strand is the main resort, a sprawl of holiday flats, campsites and ice-cream stands that fills up in July, and it has some odd local names, since nearby hamlets are called Kalifornien and Brasilien, a joke by holiday-makers of earlier generations.

The sea is the thing to come for. The Baltic is nearly tideless and brackish, so the water is calm and gentle, and it warms up quickly in the shallows. Families paddle and play, and further out sails dot the horizon, with the big ferries and cargo ships of Kiel passing in the distance. The beach is sandy with scattered stones, and amber turns up on this coast after storms, though you would need good eyes and some luck. On clear days the light is wide and pale, and the horizon is a long, clean line.

The road along the coast is flat, direct and relaxed, with the sea hidden behind the dike for most of the way and revealed in gaps by the beach car parks. It is not a road for corners, but it is a good road for letting the mind wander, and the wind off the Baltic can be brisk. On summer weekends the traffic is dense and slow, with cyclists at the sides, so aim for an early start or a weekday. In spring the rape fields flare yellow behind the dike, and in autumn the wind blows the beach clean.

Services are numerous in season, with kiosks, cafés and fish stalls along the beach, but fuel is a different matter. The nearest town of any size is Laboe, about ten kilometres off, which is a small harbour town with a huge naval memorial tower, and Kiel is not far beyond. Fill the tank in town before heading out to the coast, and take a windproof jacket. The best moment is an evening in June, when the beaches are quiet and the sunset spreads across the water.
t.lutjenburg food@54.3,10.6:
Lütjenburg is a small town in Holstein with a market square, a church on a rise and a calm, unhurried air that makes it good for lunch. It lies a few kilometres inland from the Baltic bay of Hohwacht, in rolling farmland that was once held by great landowning families. The name carries the Low German word for little, and the place lives up to it.

The estates around it are the interesting bit. At nearby Panker, the manor house and park belong to the family of the princes of Hesse, and the estate is known for its stud of Trakehner horses, a breed that was saved after the Second World War when refugees brought surviving animals west from East Prussia. A hill near Panker called the Hessenstein, about 128 metres high, carries a lookout tower with a wide view over the countryside and the Baltic, and it counts among the higher points in this flat part of Schleswig-Holstein. On clear days it is a short climb to a view that stretches from the Bay of Kiel to Fehmarn.

The riding around Lütjenburg is some of the nicest in the area, a pattern of small hills and Knick-lined lanes where the road rises and falls and bends through fields of wheat, barley and rape. Surfaces are generally good, but farm traffic and sections of patched tarmac mean that you cannot go too fast, and there are blind brows where a tractor may be waiting. The light in the evening, slanting across the fields, is very fine. Spring brings yellow rape and a smell like honey, and autumn brings harvest dust and low sun.

For services, the town has about six thousand people, which means a couple of fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and a handful of places to eat in the centre. Parking on the market is easy, and the cobbles around it are short. Order something from the baker and sit on a bench in the square, and watch the town go about its morning. A café meal, a drink and a quiet half hour are all you need before taking the lanes toward the coast at Hohwacht or inland to Plön and the lakes.
t.plon lakes@54.2,10.4:
The Great Plön Lake is the largest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, a broad sheet of water of some thirty square kilometres, dotted with islands and fringed with reed and woods. It lies in the middle of the Holstein Switzerland lake district, where the retreat of the ice sheet some fifteen thousand years ago left a landscape of hollows, ridges and dozens of lakes, large and small. The town of Plön sits on a narrow neck of land between the big lake and the smaller ones, and as a result you rarely lose sight of water anywhere in it.

The lake is an important site for wildlife. Reed beds hold great crested grebes, herons and warblers, white-tailed eagles hunt over the water, and in winter large flocks of ducks and geese gather on the open areas. A research institute for evolutionary biology, run by the Max Planck Society, has been based in the town for decades, and it studies the plants and animals of the lakes, among other things. There is something pleasing about a place where scientists spend their days measuring sticklebacks and mice within sight of a castle.

On a bike, the lake roads here are some of the best in the north. They curl around bays and headlands, climb the low moraine hills and drop through beech woods, with glimpses of water and sky at every turn. The bends are smooth and open, the surface mostly good, and the traffic light enough that you can settle into a rhythm. On a still, bright morning, with mist on the water and the sun low, it is a lovely way to spend an hour. Summer weekends bring cyclists, caravans and lakeside crowds, so avoid peak afternoons if you can.

Plön is a town of about thirteen thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, so there is no need to plan anything special. The lakeside promenade is a nice place for a stroll and a coffee, with views over the water and the ducks to keep you company. If you want to see more of the lake, small passenger boats run in the season, and you can rent rowing boats at several places. Be careful of the wind on the open water, which can get up quickly. Autumn, when the beeches turn gold and the reeds are tawny, may be the best season of all.
t.segeberg fuel and@53.9,10.3:
Bad Segeberg is known to every German of a certain age for one reason: Karl May. Every summer since the early 1950s, an open-air theatre cut into the side of a hill in the town stages dramas based on the adventure novels of the Saxon writer, with real horses, stunt riders, gunfights and a cast of cowboys and Native American characters in a mock Wild West setting. Hundreds of thousands of people come for it. The setting is an unusual hill, the Kalkberg, a block of gypsum and limestone that rises about ninety metres above the flat land around, and that is itself a rarity in this part of the country.

Inside the hill is a cave, one of the biggest bat roosts in Europe, where thousands of bats gather to hibernate in winter. The cave system is closed to visitors during that time, but a visitor centre explains the animals, and in late summer there are guided evenings for watching the bats emerge. The hill once carried a castle, which was destroyed in the Middle Ages, and a nearby lake adds to the scenery.

For riders the town is a gate. It lies at the northern edge of the Hamburg area, on roads that lead out toward Lübeck, Kiel and the lakes of Holstein, and it makes a practical place to start a day or to take a last chance at fuel. With about sixteen thousand people, Bad Segeberg has several fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, and it is simple to find a cup of coffee and a roll at an early hour. The old town has a pleasant square and some old houses, though nothing grand.

The roads to the north and east are the attraction. Within a few kilometres of the town, you reach the quiet lanes of the Holstein country, with soft hills, Knick hedges and small lakes. The surface is generally good, the traffic is thin outside the commuter hours, and the corners are easy. In the summer weeks of the Karl May festival, traffic around the town on show days can be heavy, so allow time. Take a windproof layer, and note that the weather can change quickly. Early morning, with the sun low and mist in the fields, is a gentle start.
t.plon lake balcony@54.2,10.4:
Plön has a castle on a hill, and the hill is what makes the town. The big, white, many-windowed building stands on a rise between two lakes, and from its terrace the view runs over the water, the islands and the wooded shore. The castle was built in the seventeenth century as a residence for the dukes of Holstein-Plön, and later served as a Prussian military school, where sons of the Kaiser were among the pupils, and then as a boarding school. It is not open in all parts, but the grounds and the terrace give a fine look at the lake.

The lake balcony is one of those places where the whole region becomes legible. You can see the way the glacier shaped the land: the long troughs of water, the rounded hills, the islands that are hills drowned to the neck. A small island called the Prinzeninsel lies in the lake, once the retreat of princes and now a quiet park with a bathing place. The town has a public beach on the lake, and swimming there is pleasant in summer, with the water clean and mild. A lifeguard is on duty in the high season, and the shallow, sandy entry is good for children.

Getting up to the castle is a short but pleasing climb on a cobbled road that is steep for a few hundred metres. Take it slowly, since the cobbles are uneven, and park at the foot if there is no space at the top. The road around the lake from there is among the best in Schleswig-Holstein, a smooth, curving ribbon with views of water between the trees, and it rewards a slow, unhurried pace. Evenings in summer are the best, when the lake takes on the colours of the sky.

Plön itself has about thirteen thousand people, with fuel stations at the edge of town, supermarkets and many cafés. A drink at a terrace on the lakefront is a fine way to end the afternoon. Be aware that the wind can pick up quickly on the open water, and sudden showers are common, so keep a jacket nearby. If you have time, take one of the little passenger boats that cross the lake, since from the water you can see the castle's full outline above the trees.
t.malente forest lanes@54.2,10.6:
Away from the cafés and promenades, Malente has another face, and it is made of beech trees. The forests around the town, between the Dieksee and the Kellersee, are among the finest broadleaf woods in Schleswig-Holstein, tall and grey-barked, with a high canopy that turns the light green in summer and copper in autumn. The ground beneath is soft with leaf litter, and the quiet is broken only by woodpeckers, jays and the sound of wind in the crowns.

A small lake called the Ukleisee lies hidden in the woods, a dark, still sheet of water surrounded by steep banks, which is reached by paths from the road and is a favourite with walkers. The highest ground in the whole state, the Bungsberg, rises only a short way to the northeast, and though at less than 170 metres it sounds modest, it gives the forest lanes a tilt and a pattern, with small climbs and descents that keep the riding interesting.

The lanes themselves are narrow, winding and quiet, often with a low tunnel of branches over the road. Corners come quickly, often blind, with soft verges and occasional patches of moss or leaf where the sun does not reach, so take them with respect. In autumn the road surface can be treacherous with wet leaves, and in winter, shaded sections hold ice long after the open roads have cleared. In summer the forest provides a cool refuge on a hot day, and the scent of damp earth and beech mast is unmistakable.

Wildlife is plentiful. Roe deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, and foxes and badgers live in the forest, while red kites and buzzards circle over the clearings. The woods are managed with care, and you may see signs of selective felling and the green markers that foresters use. Ride quietly and you are likely to see something.

For services, Malente is close, with about ten thousand people, fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and Eutin is a few kilometres farther with a larger range. The forest itself has nothing, apart from the occasional forest inn or lake kiosk, so carry water. An early morning ride on a weekday in May, when the beeches are in fresh leaf and the forest floor is carpeted with wood anemones, is a pleasure hard to match.
t.zarrentin@53.6,10.9:
Zarrentin is the kind of lake town where you finish a ride sooner than planned because a bench by the water makes a better argument than the map does. It sits at the southern tip of the Schaalsee, on the Mecklenburg side of a line that for four decades was the most heavily guarded boundary in Europe. Riders coming from Hamburg cross it without noticing, apart from a subtle shift in the roads, which are a little rougher, a little emptier and lined with the tall avenue trees that Mecklenburg does so well.

The swimming spot is the town's own beach and landing stage, on a lake that is clean, cold and extremely deep by northern standards. You walk in over firm sand and within a few strides the bottom drops away, so it suits a quick dip better than a long paddle. Locals bring their children in July and August, and the water, helped by a protected lake status that keeps motorboats away, stays clear. Out of season the water is for looking at, and the reed margins fill with coots and great crested grebes.

What to eat is simple. Fish from the lake, usually smoked whitefish, is sold by small producers in the area, and a bread roll with it, eaten on the shore, is the right lunch. Cake and coffee are never hard to find in the village, and an ice-cream window does a roaring trade on warm days. Do not expect a big choice, but do not expect to go hungry either.

The ride in from the west threads through the Lauenburg lakes and past the old Elbe-Lübeck canal, on gently undulating lanes with good tarmac and the occasional wet leaf-fall patch under the trees. Farm tractors are the main obstacles. In the late afternoon the low sun comes through the avenue trunks in flickering bars, which can be disorienting at speed, so ease off.

Zarrentin is small, with around three thousand people. It has a baker, a shop or two and a few places to sit, but if you need a proper fuel station and supermarkets, Wittenburg is the answer, twelve kilometres away, with just over five thousand inhabitants. Fill up before you come, and keep a dry towel in the pannier. It is easy to forget one, and the sun does not always last.
t.schaalsee biosphere edge@53.6,11.0:
The edge of a biosphere reserve is not a line on the ground, it is a change in mood. Somewhere around here the farmland of western Mecklenburg stops being merely quiet and starts being protected, and you notice it in small ways: hedgerows left wild, meadows cut late, ponds with frogs in them, and the sight of cranes stalking across a stubble field as if they owned it. Which, for part of the year, they do.

The land was shaped by the last ice age, which dropped a ridge of rubble, the terminal moraine, across the region and left behind a basin that became the Schaalsee. The soil around it is a rich mix of clay and gravel, and the pattern of low, rounded hills and hollows runs for kilometres. The lake lies just out of sight to the west, and the road traces a looping course around the farmland to the east, dipping into villages with brick churches and thatched barns, then out again into wide fields.

The road itself is one of the pleasures of this part of Mecklenburg. Many of the country roads here are lined with old avenue trees, mostly lime, oak and maple, planted generations ago, and riding down one on a bright day is like riding down a long green corridor with the sun strobing through. The tarmac is patchy, some of it narrow and with broken edges, so it rewards a measured pace, and in damp weather the shade holds moisture on the bends. In autumn, when leaves lie on the road, extra care pays off.

Birdwatching is the main reason people linger. In October and November cranes gather in the evening in large numbers before roosting, and the sound of their calling carries over the fields. White-tailed eagles hunt over the lake, and on a clear winter morning with frost on the grass a rider might see two or three in the sky. Bring binoculars if you have room in the luggage.

There is nothing in the way of fuel or shops at the road edge itself. Zarrentin, six kilometres off, has a few small shops and a place for a coffee, and Wittenburg, about eleven kilometres, has the proper supermarkets and petrol stations. Carry water, and keep to the roads that look as though people use them.
t.peine@52.3,10.2:
Peine is a steel town, and it has never pretended otherwise. A rolling mill has stood on the edge of the town since the nineteenth century, and the smoke, the chimneys and the sound of trains hauling girders still shape the skyline. The people who work in it live in tidy brick streets, and the main square has the honest, unshowy look of a place that makes things rather than sells postcards. As a fuel stop, it fits the mood perfectly: efficient, plain, with all you need and nothing you do not.

The town sits on the flat, rich farmland of the Hildesheim Börde, a landscape of loess soil that is among the most fertile in Germany. Fields of sugar beet, wheat and rape run to the horizon, and the roads across them are straight and fast. The Mittelland Canal, the great east-west waterway, cuts through the town, and watching a long barge slide past between the houses is an unexpected pleasure. In the Middle Ages the bishops of Hildesheim fortified Peine as a border outpost against the dukes of Brunswick, and the two were at war over it more than once, which explains why a flat farm town ever needed walls.

With nearly fifty thousand people, Peine has everything you could ask of a refuelling gate. Petrol stations sit along the main roads, and supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars are easy to find. It is a good moment to check tyre pressure, stow the jacket liner and buy a sandwich for later. Parking is easy, and the old market with its church is a few minutes' walk if you want to see something that is not a pump.

The riding from here is the business. Heading south and east you leave the flat Börde and begin to climb gently toward the low ridges of the Elm and the Harz foothills, and the roads change from long straights to rolling, curving lanes through half-timbered villages. Wind is a factor on the open plain, so expect gusts from the west and a feeling of being pushed. Morning is the best time, with the sun low behind you and the traffic still thin. Take a minute to enjoy the practical charm of a town that has decided to be itself.
t.konigslutter elm road@52.3,10.8:
Königslutter has a cathedral that looks as if it belongs in Lombardy, and the reason is that the men who built it had been to Italy. The Kaiserdom, a great Romanesque church of pale stone begun in the 1130s, was founded by Emperor Lothar the Third, who is buried inside, and the craftsmen who carved its apse brought with them a style from the south. Round the outside runs a frieze of hunters chasing a stag, with hounds, a boar and an unlikely fox, and by the entrance sit a pair of lions with columns on their backs, one of them with a little man in its paws. They are some of the best medieval sculptures in northern Germany, set in a small Lower Saxon town that gets few crowds.

Behind the town rises the Elm, a long, low ridge of limestone covered in old beech forest. It is a geological curiosity, a fold of ancient seabed lifted above the plain and worn into hollows and caves, and it forms a nature park with an unusual amount of fossil-bearing rock. The beeches, some of them very large, hold deep shade in summer and glow copper in autumn.

The road climbing the Elm is a gentle surprise after the flat farmland to the north. It rises through woods in a series of easy bends, with clear sightlines and a fairly smooth surface, though leaf litter and the odd root-lifted patch call for attention. You will meet walkers and cyclists on sunny weekends, and the forestry trucks that take timber out use some of the roads. At the top you can find clearings with views over fields toward the Harz on a clear day, and the air feels a degree or two cooler than in the town.

The town has about sixteen thousand people, which means fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and there are a few restaurants near the cathedral. Park near the church and walk. Allow time for the carvings in particular, because it is easy to ride past and not realise what you have missed. Early in the day, before the coach tours, the stone is warm in the low sun and the lions look almost alive.
t.schoningen ridge@52.1,11.0:
Schöningen has a reputation that has nothing to do with riding, and it is a startling one. In the 1990s, archaeologists working ahead of the lignite diggers found wooden spears here that were about three hundred thousand years old, the oldest known hunting weapons in the world, along with the bones of horses butchered by the people who threw them. The finds changed what scientists thought early humans could do, since the spears were balanced like modern javelins and made with real skill. A modern museum beside the old mine, shaped like a lump of glass and steel, tells the story and shows a reconstruction of the shore where the hunters worked.

The ridge that carries the road lies on the eastern side of the Elm and Lappwald hills, the low upland that runs near the old border with Saxony-Anhalt. For forty years this was a frontier zone, and the quiet, thinly populated feeling of the villages still carries some of that. The ridge is not high, just a couple of hundred metres, but after the flat farmland it gives long views across fields and wind turbines, and on a clear day you see the outline of the Harz far to the south.

Riding here is open and easy. The road follows the crest and rolls over a number of gentle rises, with wide, forgiving bends and patchy but generally acceptable tarmac. The traffic is light, apart from the occasional coal or farm truck, and the wind is the main thing you notice. It is a country of big skies, harvested fields and church spires, and the light at the end of the day turns the stubble gold. Spring brings the bright yellow of rape and a sharp, green smell.

Schöningen town, a few hundred metres away, has about thirteen thousand people, a handsome old castle and some half-timbered streets, and services are not a problem: fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries along the main roads, plus a few cafés near the market. Park near the centre and spend ten minutes at the castle. If the museum interests you, allow an hour or two, since it is well done and worth more than a quick glance. Bring a windproof layer, because the ridge is exposed and the weather can change.
t.wolfenbuttel@52.2,10.5:
Wolfenbüttel is a town of books and timber. For nearly three centuries the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel ruled from the castle here, and one of them, Duke August the Younger, built up a library in the seventeenth century that became one of the largest in Europe. The Herzog August Library still stands, and the philosopher and playwright Gotthold Ephraim Lessing worked in it as librarian in the eighteenth century and wrote part of his drama Nathan the Wise in the town. Its old reading rooms and the remarkable collection of illuminated manuscripts make it one of the few libraries in the world worth visiting for the building alone.

Around the library lies one of the best half-timbered old towns in Germany. More than six hundred timber-framed houses, carved with scrolls, beams and inscriptions, line the streets and canals, and they survived the war largely untouched because the town had no major industry. The Oker river splits into channels around the old centre, giving the place a gentle waterside air, and the lanes between the houses are narrow, cobbled and quiet in the morning. The castle, in the red brick and pale stone of the Renaissance, sits on its own moated island at the edge of the centre.

Wolfenbüttel is also home to one of Germany's best known herbal liqueurs, the Jägermeister, which is made in the town, and the smell of its ingredients can sometimes hang over the east side of the centre. It is a bit of local humour that the dukes' famous library and a stag-labelled digestif share a postcode.

As a food stop the town is easy and generous. It has more than fifty thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and a wide range of cafés, bakeries and restaurants are all close, with tables out in the squares in summer. Local menus lean toward hearty Lower Saxon dishes, with sausage, asparagus in season and plenty of cake. Parking a motorbike near the centre is simple, though the cobbles are slippery after rain and the traffic in the old streets is slow. Give yourself an hour on foot, and aim to be there before the lunchtime crowds. The roads in and out run through flat fields, and the real riding begins after the town, as the land lifts toward the Harz.
t.okertal bends@51.9,10.5:
The Oker comes out of the high Harz in a hurry, and the road through its valley follows the river's rush from the dam above down to the plain at Goslar. The valley is narrow, steep and wooded, with granite crags poking through the spruce above the road, and for a few kilometres it feels like a small Alpine gorge dropped into northern Germany. It is one of the best known bike roads in the Harz, and on a fine weekend you will see that the riders know it.

The bends are the point. The road follows the river in a long series of tight curves, some of them blind, with the water on one side and rock on the other, and the gradient is gentle but constant. The surface is mostly good, though the shaded sections hold damp and can have gravel washed down from the slopes after rain. A speed limit and enforcement are not unknown here, and the road has seen its share of accidents, so a measured pace pays off. Because the valley is narrow, the road is not wide, and you will meet coaches, cyclists and walkers at some of the pull-offs.

Geology is the story. The granite of the Brocken massif, a large mass of molten rock that cooled underground some three hundred million years ago, has been exposed by the river and carved into crags and boulders. A reservoir, built in the 1950s, fills the upper valley with dark green water and holds back the floods that once raced down the Oker, and there is a waterfall at Romkerhall, said to be the highest in the Harz, which drops in a long, thin stream over a rock lip. The spruce forest here has suffered from bark beetle in recent years, and the bare grey slopes are a reminder of how much the climate has shifted.

Services on the valley road are limited to a couple of small inns and kiosks near the reservoir and the waterfall. Goslar, about six kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a fine old centre that is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Altenau and Bad Harzburg are close too. Fill up before the valley, and bring a warm layer. Early on a weekday, when the mist lingers in the trees, it is a very good road.
t.bad harzburg@51.9,10.6:
Bad Harzburg is a spa town at the northern gate of the Harz, a place of grand villas, a Kurpark, a casino and, on the hill behind it, a cable car that carries visitors to the ruins of a medieval castle. The castle, called the Harzburg, was built in the eleventh century by Emperor Henry the Fourth as part of his campaign to control the Saxon lands, and when the Saxon nobles rebelled in 1074 they destroyed it. The ruin is mostly a few walls and a tower stump now, but the place has a dramatic position, and a viewing area gives a wide look over the plain to the north.
