On the same hill stands the Canossa Column, a granite pillar put up in 1877 by order of Bismarck, who wanted to remind everyone of the moment when his chancellorship refused to bend to Rome. It carries a line from his speech, famous in German politics: we will not go to Canossa. You do not have to share his views to enjoy the quiet woods around it, and the walk up is short and easy.

The town's other claim is its water. Brine springs have been used here since the nineteenth century, and the spa buildings, pump rooms and promenades speak of the age when doctors prescribed walks and mineral water for almost everything. The centre today is lively and a bit old-fashioned in a pleasant way, with cafés serving cake, restaurants with Harz specialities such as game and trout, and shops selling local sausages. A little waterfall called the Radau falls in a ravine near the edge of town and is an easy walk.

As a food stop it is a good one, with about twenty-three thousand people, fuel stations, supermarkets and many places to sit down. Parking a motorbike near the pedestrian zone is straightforward, and the cobbles in the centre are short. Weekends in good weather are busy, as riders from Hanover, Brunswick and Hamburg arrive in numbers, and the town can be filled with the sound of engines, so a weekday gives more room to breathe. After a meal, the climb into the hills begins at once, and the road toward Torfhaus and the high Harz gets steep and bendy within minutes.
t.schonberg coast road@54.4,10.4:
East of the Kiel Fjord the shore settles into the long, open sweep of the Probstei, and the coast road gives you the Baltic in small glimpses between dike and field. The most famous landmark of the area stands at the fjord's mouth: the naval memorial at Laboe, a tall, narrow brick tower, around eighty-five metres high, shaped like the stern of a ship, that can be seen from far across the water. It was built in the 1930s as a monument to German sailors and was reopened after the war as a memorial to seafarers of all nations, and a lift takes visitors to the top for a view over the fjord and the sea. Beside it lies a Second World War submarine, which can be visited.

From Laboe the road runs east along the coast through Stein, Wendtorf and Schönberg, between the sea dike and the open fields of the Probstei. The farmland is among the flattest in the region, and there are long, straight sections where you can see the church tower of the next village a long way before you reach it. The sea often appears as a thin silver strip beyond the dike, with ferries and cargo ships gliding across the horizon toward Kiel.

The riding is gentle and open. The surface is mostly good and the bends, when they come, are broad, though the wind off the Baltic can push a light bike sideways on exposed sections, and sand blown from the beach car parks sometimes gathers on the tarmac. On summer weekends the road is crowded with cars and cyclists, and the villages fill with holidaymakers, so an early morning ride is a big improvement. Out of season, on a bright day in spring or autumn, the whole coast belongs to you.

The beaches are the reason for the traffic. Long stretches of sand and shingle front the sea at Wendtorf and Schönberger Strand, with grass-covered dunes and kiosks selling fish rolls and ice cream. Swimming is pleasant in summer, with calm, shallow water, though jellyfish are common in late summer. For services, Laboe has about five thousand people, with fuel, shops and cafés, and Kiel offers everything else. Fill the tank before heading out along the coast, and keep a windproof layer ready for when the sun goes down.
t.lutjenburg old road@54.3,10.6:
The land around Lütjenburg is what geologists call young moraine, which means the last ice sheet only left about fifteen thousand years ago, and the ground still looks freshly rumpled. Instead of the flat plains of the west or the old, rounded hills of the south, this corner of Holstein is a patchwork of small hills, hollows and ponds, with farmland cut into fields by hedges and lines of trees. The old roads here follow the grain of the land, dipping into valleys, crossing little streams and climbing again, with none of the dead-straight grid of the modern bypasses.

That is why the older road is worth taking. It runs through hamlets with names ending in dorf and hagen, past brick farms, tall barns and the occasional red-roofed manor house, and the bends are tight enough to keep you awake without being a worry. The surface varies from smooth tarmac to patched, sandy sections, and there are blind crests where tractors loom suddenly out of sight. Slow down at the crests, watch for gravel at field entrances, and keep an eye on the wind, which blows steadily from the west and brings sudden showers.

Lütjenburg, on its low rise, is the natural place for a reset. The market square has a small fountain, a few cafés and a bakery or two, and the church stands over it with a solid, plain tower. It is a town of about six thousand people, large enough for fuel stations, supermarkets and a pharmacy, and small enough that you can see all of the centre in ten minutes. Park on or near the square and take your time over a coffee and cake. Franzbrötchen, a cinnamon pastry pressed flat, is a northern German snack that deserves more fame than it gets.

The Baltic is a few kilometres north, and in summer many riders head there for a swim, so the road toward Hohwacht can be busy with cars and bicycles on weekends. Inland, the roads toward Plön and the lakes are quieter, with fewer cars and more trees, and the light on a clear evening there is a joy. Spring is the best time, when the rape flowers and the beeches are in new leaf, and September is a close second.
t.plon lake sweep@54.2,10.4:
A circuit of the Great Plön Lake is one of the nicest easy rides in Schleswig-Holstein, and the best part of it is that the lake never really leaves you. At times the water is a bright sheet ahead through the trees, at others a dark gleam behind a field, and now and then the road comes down to the shore itself, at a harbour, a landing stage or a beach. The lake is the largest in the state, wide and island-dotted, and the glacial hills around it give the road a pleasant rise and fall.

On the south side, near Ascheberg, the road runs close to the water through beech woods and lakeside meadows, and the bends are smooth and open, with good tarmac. Farther round, near Bosau, lies a small, ancient church on a spit of land that juts into the lake, and it is easily one of the most beautiful spots on the shore. A medieval priest named Helmold of Bosau wrote a chronicle here in the twelfth century about the Slavic peoples of the region and the German conquest of their lands, and it is still the best source of information about that period. Bosau's brick church dates from around the same time as his writing, and the setting beside the water is serene.

The wind is the main factor on the open sections, and on warm, still days the lake smells of reeds and sun-warmed mud. Cyclists use the lakeside paths in large numbers, so keep your speed down and pass with care. On summer weekends the road fills with cars, and parking at the beaches and landings can be difficult, so an early start is wise. In autumn the beech woods turn gold and the water is cold and clear, and the roads are quiet.

The villages along the way are small, with a bakery or a shop at best, and you may find a café at one of the harbours in season. Plön, with about thirteen thousand people, is the main town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and many places to eat, and Ascheberg and Bösdorf are smaller. Plan fuel in Plön before you set off round the lake, and carry a drink. Plan at least two hours for the circuit, with stops, and more if you want to swim.
t.hohwacht bay view@54.3,10.7:
Hohwacht Bay is a wide, shallow curve of the Baltic between the Bay of Kiel and the Fehmarn Belt, and the view from the shore on a clear day opens a long, gentle arc of pale sand and low green land. The beach at Hohwacht is a broad one, backed by low dunes and a wooded cliff, and the water in front of it is so shallow that you can wade out a long way before it reaches your waist. That makes it good for families, and for anyone who wants a cool dip without the effort of swimming.

The place began as a small fishing village, and the fishermen's cottages and the little harbour are still there, now surrounded by holiday flats and hotels. The harbour is a pleasant place to wander, with fishing cutters and yachts lined along the quay and a smokehouse nearby. The sea changes by the hour, from a flat blue to a choppy grey, and the sky is nearly always large and full of moving cloud. Gulls and terns wheel over the water, and in autumn flocks of geese pass overhead in long lines.

Behind the beach lies a lagoon, the Sehlendorfer Binnensee, a protected area where many birds breed and rest, and it is a good place for a short walk. The land between the sea and the lagoon is low and open, with reeds, meadows and grazing cattle, and the road along the shore passes through it. Riding here is a matter of flat, open tarmac with the wind off the sea, and the main hazards are tourist cars, cyclists and the occasional drift of sand.

If you want to swim, the main beach is lifeguarded in summer, and the water warms up quickly in a hot spell. The Baltic is nearly tideless and brackish, so it has no strong currents, but wind can raise a chop and you should watch the flags. Services are not on the beach itself beyond kiosks and cafés. For fuel and shops, Lütjenburg, about six kilometres inland, is the nearest town of any size, with petrol stations and supermarkets. Take sun cream, a towel and a layer for the evening. Sunset over the bay on a clear evening, with the water the colour of a peach, is a very good reason to linger.
t.heiligenhafen harbour@54.4,11.0:
The first thing you notice in Heiligenhafen is the smell, a mix of diesel, salt and smoked fish that tells you the harbour is still working. A small fleet of cutters ties up along the quay, and in the morning you may see men sorting the catch of herring, cod and flatfish before it goes to the fish shops and the stalls. The harbour sits at the end of a peninsula that pushes out into the Baltic, and the town spreads around it, with a seafront promenade, a long pier and a marina full of sailing boats.

Fish is what to eat here, and it is simple. A smoked mackerel or herring from a stand, a Fischbrötchen with pickled herring or fried fish, or a plate of fresh plaice with fried potatoes in a harbourside restaurant are all fine choices, and the prices are fair. In the right season, the local speciality is smoked eel, though it divides opinion. Ice cream is available on every corner, and a coffee on a terrace by the water is a pleasure, though gulls will do their best to steal your lunch.

Just outside town is a nature reserve of real value, the Graswarder, a long, low spit of sand, shingle and grass that curves out into the sea. It is a breeding and resting place for terns, avocets and other seabirds, and the lagoon behind it holds waders in migration. Access is limited during the breeding season in spring and summer, and it is worth keeping to the signed paths. In the distance, to the east, the great arch of the Fehmarn Sound Bridge rises over the water, linking the mainland to the island of Fehmarn.

The roads in are flat and relaxed, crossing farmland with wide skies and the sea glinting at the edge of view. In summer the town is very busy, and traffic along the coast road can be slow, so a weekday or an early start makes the day easier. Heiligenhafen has about nine thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafés and restaurants are all on hand. Parking a bike near the harbour is usually possible, though the quay cobbles are slippery with spray. Wind can make a cool day cold, so a windproof layer is wise.
t.eutin return lake@54.1,10.6:
The ride back toward Eutin at the end of the day has its own light. The sun is low, the colours deepen, and the lakes of Holstein Switzerland turn from blue to a deep pewter or a burnished gold, depending on the sky. The road comes in from the north through beech and farmland, past Kasseedorf and the small lakes, and the town appears with its church tower and palace roofs above the trees. On a still evening the water is like glass, and the only sound is the tick of the engine cooling.

The lakes here were made by ice. The glaciers of the last ice age scoured out deep basins and left behind a jumble of hills, and the meltwater filled the hollows, creating the chain that now stretches from Eutin to Plön. The Great Eutin Lake is the biggest in the immediate neighbourhood, and the smaller lakes around it are linked by streams and channels. Reed beds line the banks and hold warblers and rails, while on the open water swans, coots and great crested grebes are easy to see. Late in the day, fishermen in small boats sit motionless, and rowers practise off the shore.

For the riding, the return road is one of the gentlest in the state. The bends are open and smooth, the surface mostly good, and the gradients are no more than a long slope up from a lake or a short rise through a wood. The lanes around Eutin are popular with cyclists in the evening, so keep to a measured pace and give plenty of room. Deer come out of the woods at dusk, and a collision with one is a real risk, so scan the verges and ease off when the light fails.

For services the town offers everything a tired rider needs: fuel stations at the edge, supermarkets, bakeries, and a variety of cafés and restaurants in the centre, with outdoor tables around the market in summer. With about seventeen thousand people, it is easy to find a bed if you decide to stay. A short walk down to the lake gives a view of the palace across the water, with its reflection in the evening light. Allow time for a drink at the water's edge before the last leg of the day.
t.lutjenburg snack@54.3,10.6:
A snack stop in a town like Lütjenburg is an education in how small-town northern Germany eats between meals. Every bakery has a counter of rolls, filled with ham, cheese, egg, smoked fish or a slab of Leberwurst, and most of them also sell cake by the slice and coffee in paper cups. You pay at the till, take your bag and sit on a bench in the square, and nobody minds. A fish roll from a stall, with pickled herring, onions and a dill pickle, is the more adventurous choice, and a sweet pastry from the baker the safer one.

The town sits a few kilometres inland from the Baltic on a low hill, and its modest size, about six thousand people, makes it easy to read at a glance. A brick church stands on the rise above the market, and the streets run down from it in a loose fan. It is a place that sees few tourists in comparison with the beach resorts just north, and as a result the shopkeepers and the people in the queue have time to chat. If you speak any German, a question about the best local cake will usually bring a firm opinion.

The surroundings are the draw. Nearby Panker has a manor estate with a famous stud of Trakehner horses and a hill called the Hessenstein, topped with a viewing tower from which you can look out over the Baltic on a clear day. The lanes around it are lined with old trees and dotted with farm shops, and in autumn you can buy apples and pumpkins by the roadside. The countryside is rolling, with gentle climbs and drops, and the riding is relaxed and rhythmic.

Traffic is generally light, though summer weekends bring cars headed for the coast, and harvest brings tractors. Look out for wet leaves and mud on the corners, especially after rain. Lütjenburg has fuel stations and supermarkets, so a refill and a bite can be done in one stop. Parking is easy near the market, and the cobbles are brief. A quick stop is all this place needs, but it rewards a slower one, and the best moment is the middle of a weekday morning, when the square is quiet and the bakery smells of fresh bread.
t.hohwacht@54.3,10.7:
Not every water stop has to involve getting wet. Hohwacht works for riders because it offers a place to refill a bottle, sit near the sea and let the engine cool, and because the little harbour has a calm, working character that is a relief after the busier resorts to the east. The marina holds a mix of small fishing boats and sailing yachts, and a few smokehouses and kiosks do a quiet trade. In the early morning, before the day-trippers arrive, you can hear the halyards tapping against the masts and the cry of gulls.

The place started as a fishermen's settlement on a sheltered bay, and the old name was little more than a fishing station. It grew into a resort in the twentieth century, and today it is a small and comparatively unspoiled seaside village, with a promenade, a sandy beach and a line of low houses behind the dunes. A short walk along the shore brings you to a wooded cliff on one side and a protected lagoon on the other, the Sehlendorfer Binnensee, an important place for waterbirds. The land between the sea and the lagoon is flat and open, with grazing cattle and reeds.

The roads to and from Hohwacht run through rolling farmland, with views of the sea appearing through gaps in the hedges. They are quiet in the morning and busy in the afternoon on fine summer days, and the surface is generally good. Wind off the Baltic is a constant, and a cool breeze can feel pleasant at midday and bitter by evening. If you are carrying a passenger, a spare layer is a kindness.

Facilities are mostly seasonal, with cafés, kiosks and a few restaurants open in summer and many closed in winter. Drinking water is easy to find in cafés if you buy something, and public taps are not widespread, so carry a bottle. For fuel and a proper supermarket, Lütjenburg, about six kilometres inland, is the nearest. A late afternoon here, with a coffee and a fish roll and a bench facing the sea, is a very good way to let the miles settle. The light turns golden around seven in midsummer, and the bay is at its best then.
t.malente@54.2,10.6:
The thing about Malente is that it is really two villages that grew into one, Malente proper and Gremsmühlen, with a short stretch of the Schwentine river between them. The Schwentine rises in the hills near the Bungsberg, flows through the chain of lakes here, and eventually reaches the Kiel Fjord some sixty kilometres to the north, and in Malente it takes on the character of a lazy canal, moving slowly under bridges and between villas with gardens that run down to the water. You can sit at a café by the bridge and watch small boats pass, with the quiet noise of oars and the occasional quack of a duck.

The town makes a good coffee stop because it is geared to people who are not in a hurry. For more than a century it has been a health resort, with a spa park, a promenade and a handful of grand old hotels from the age when doctors prescribed fresh air, lakes and good walking. Cafés cluster around the station and along the water, with tables out in summer, and the cake is generous. The Kurpark has paths and benches by the Dieksee and the Kellersee, and on sunny days walkers and cyclists drift through it at a snail's pace.

Riding into Malente from the surrounding country is a pleasure of small things. The roads run through rolling farmland and beech woods, past lakes that flash blue between the trees, and there are many gentle bends and short hills. The tarmac is generally good, though some of the lanes are narrow, and in autumn the leaves collect on the corners. Eutin, a few kilometres to the east, has the palace and the opera festival, and Plön, to the south, has its castle on the great lake, so the area suits a loop of an afternoon.

For practical matters, the place has about eleven thousand people, which means fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and a station with trains to Kiel and Lübeck if the weather turns. Parking a motorbike by the station or the Kurpark is easy. Go in the morning for the best light on the water, or in the late afternoon, when the day-trippers have left and the lakes turn to copper. Order the cake of the day and ask nothing more of the afternoon.
t.ratzeburg return road@53.7,10.8:
The old town of Ratzeburg sits on an island in the middle of a lake, joined to the land by three causeways, and the best way to photograph it is from the road that heads back out. As you leave the town and climb the gentle slope toward the east shore, the island appears across the water: the red-brick cathedral with its twin towers, the roofs of the old houses, the line of trees along the shore, and the long, calm surface of the lake in front. It is a view that has not changed greatly in centuries, and it is at its best in the low light of late afternoon.

The lake is the other half of the story. Ratzeburg's water is long, narrow and clean, left behind by the ice, and in the early morning it can be flat enough to double the cathedral perfectly upside down. The town became the capital of a small duchy, Saxe-Lauenburg, and later a quiet country seat, and that long, peaceful history is part of why the island looks so well preserved from the shore. For forty years the inner German border lay only a few kilometres east, which kept development low and the surroundings calm.

The road itself runs along the lake shore and into farmland, with a gentle series of bends and glimpses of water. It is pleasantly empty on weekday evenings, and the tarmac is mostly good. A few stretches under trees stay damp, and in autumn the leaves can be slippery. Cyclists use the road heavily in summer. There are laybys and small car parks where you can stop for a photograph, and a few benches look out across the lake. The water is calm in the evening, and rowers sometimes pass in slim boats.

Ratzeburg has about fourteen thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés are easy to find in the modern part of town on the mainland shore. The road back toward Hamburg is a straightforward run through farmland and small towns, with some traffic at rush hour. If you have time before leaving, buy a cake or an ice cream and eat it on the bank. The lake has a way of keeping you there a little longer than planned.
t.travemunde ferry view@54.0,10.9:
Travemünde is where the Trave river reaches the sea, and the ferry view is the best way to take in that moment. A small passenger and vehicle ferry crosses the river mouth to the Priwall peninsula, and from the quay on the town side you can watch it go back and forth, with the lighthouse, the harbour mouth and the open Baltic framing the scene. Across the water lies the Priwall, a long spit of dunes, holiday homes and a small marina, and moored there is the Passat, a steel four-masted barque built in 1911 that once carried grain from Australia and now serves as a museum ship.

The river mouth is a busy place. Large ferries from Scandinavia and the Baltic states dock at the terminal just upstream, and their huge white shapes slide past the beach with surprising quiet. Cargo ships and tankers make their way to Lübeck's port, and sailing yachts dodge between them. In July the town hosts Travemünde Week, one of the great sailing regattas of the Baltic, when hundreds of boats fill the bay and the quays are packed with visitors.

Travemünde belonged to the Hanseatic city of Lübeck for centuries and still does administratively, which explains the Lübeck-style brick buildings and the sense of a town that has always looked outward. The lighthouse, dating from the sixteenth century, is claimed to be the oldest in Germany, and it still stands on the waterfront. The seafront promenade, with its hotels, casino and old pavilion, has the slightly faded air of a nineteenth century resort, and a stroll along it before dinner is a good way to unwind.

Riding in, you come off the long, flat roads of Ostholstein into a town that is often busy, with tourist traffic and ferry queues. The cobbles near the harbour are slippery in the wet, and parking near the ferry can be tight in summer. Travemünde has about fourteen thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets, and cafés are all available, and fish rolls and ice cream stands crowd the quay. The ferry itself is short and cheap, and carrying a motorbike across is simple, though queues can build on summer weekends. Bring a windproof layer, since the breeze at the river mouth is brisk even on a warm day.
t.timmendorfer beach road@54.0,10.8:
The coast of the Bay of Lübeck is the closest thing northern Germany has to a riviera, and the road that links Travemünde, Niendorf, Timmendorfer Strand, Scharbeutz and Haffkrug is its promenade. It runs a little inland from the sea, through a string of resort towns that merge into one another, with villas, hotels and shops on either side, and gaps between them that show the beach, the sea and the long wooden piers. This is a landscape of holiday, and it has been since the late nineteenth century, when the first bathing guests arrived by train from Lübeck and Hamburg.

The beaches are the draw. Long, wide stretches of fine pale sand slope gently into shallow water, backed by dunes, and in summer they are packed with striped wicker beach chairs, which are a local institution. The Baltic is calm and brackish, and warms quickly, and families come for weeks at a time. Timmendorfer Strand has the broadest promenade, with a pier and a smart, slightly showy air, while Niendorf has a small fishing harbour and a more relaxed character. A walk along the shore at the end of the day, with the sun going down behind the sand, is one of the pleasures of the coast.

For riders the road is not about corners. It is a series of stop-and-go stretches through resort traffic, with speed limits and crossings, and in July and August it can be slow and crowded. The best way to enjoy it is to come outside peak season, in May, June or September, when the beaches are still warm enough for a paddle and the roads are manageable. Early morning is the quiet hour, with the light soft and the first walkers on the sand. Watch for pedestrians stepping out between parked cars.

Services are everywhere. Timmendorfer Strand has about nine thousand people, which in season swells to many times that, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a hundred places to eat and drink. Fish rolls, ice cream, coffee and cake are all on offer along the promenade. Parking a motorbike near the beach is easy in the off-season and a struggle in July, and some car parks charge a fee. If you want to swim, lifeguarded stretches are marked, and the flags give the conditions. Take a towel, sun cream and a spare layer, because the sea breeze cools quickly after sunset.
t.ahrensburg clean@53.7,10.2:
Ahrensburg is where Hamburg lets go of you. Northeast of the city, on the edge of the Stormarn district, the urban sprawl thins out into villas and fields, and the town acts as a final pocket of services before the roads open into proper countryside. It is a prosperous commuter town of about thirty thousand people, with tidy streets, a good supply of fuel stations and a station on the S-Bahn line, and for riders leaving the city, it is a clean, simple place to top up and get your bearings.

It has a surprise at its heart. The palace of Ahrensburg, a Renaissance building from the late sixteenth century, stands on a moated island, white and red with stepped gables and corner towers, and looks as though it belongs in the Netherlands or Denmark. It was built by the Rantzau family, one of the powerful noble houses of Holstein, and it is among the best preserved of its kind in northern Germany. The interior is open to visitors as a museum, and the grounds, with their avenue and canal, are free to walk. A short stroll in the park is a pleasant way to stretch after the city traffic.

The name also belongs to archaeology. Ahrensburg gave its name to the Ahrensburg culture, a group of reindeer hunters who lived in the region at the end of the last ice age, about twelve thousand years ago, and whose flint tools and arrow shafts were first found in the tunnel valley nearby. It is a reminder that the plain north of Hamburg has been hunted over and lived in since the glaciers retreated.

The riding is the main thing. From Ahrensburg, a number of country roads run north and east into Schleswig-Holstein, through farmland, woods and little villages. The surface is generally good, the traffic thins quickly after the town, and the landscape grows softer with every kilometre. The morning rush hour is the main hazard, and it makes sense to leave before seven or after nine. Fill up here, since the first stretch of the countryside has fewer petrol stations than you might think. Take a moment in the quiet streets of the old town before you go, and enjoy the feeling of the city falling away.
t.travemunde bay@54.0,10.9:
At the mouth of the Trave, where the river gives up and the Baltic begins, the beach at Travemünde runs in a long, pale curve beneath the promenade. It is a proper town beach, with striped wicker beach chairs, a pier, a casino and a long row of hotels, and in summer it is very busy. The water is shallow and gentle, warming quickly, and the beach slopes so gradually that small children can paddle a long way out. A small lighthouse on the waterfront is claimed to be the oldest in Germany, dating from the sixteenth century, and it is a pleasant landmark to meet at.

The resort has a long history. Travemünde has been a bathing place since the early nineteenth century, when the first visitors came by coach from Lübeck for the sea air, and by the end of the century it was a fashionable resort with a Kurhaus and a casino. The town's connection to Lübeck is old, and for centuries it was the city's port, guarding the river mouth. The brick buildings along the front and the weight of the old ships in the harbour speak of that long maritime history.

Out on the water, the Baltic is busy. Ferries to Sweden, Finland and the Baltic states leave from the terminal on the other side of the river mouth, and their enormous white hulls move past with a slow, stately tread. Sailing yachts and fishing boats weave between them, and on summer evenings the sky above the bay is full of colour. Swimming is pleasant on calm days, though jellyfish can appear in late summer and the lifeguards raise warning flags when the wind is up.

For riders the stop is straightforward. The approach from Lübeck is a fast road across flat farmland, with traffic that builds on summer weekends, and the final stretch through the town is slow and often congested. Parking close to the beach is possible, especially on weekdays, though some car parks charge a fee and the cobbles near the harbour are slippery. Fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés are plentiful, since the town has about fourteen thousand people, and an ice cream on the promenade is practically obligatory. The best moment is the early evening, when the day-trippers have gone and the sea is calm.
t.plon water view@54.2,10.4:
There is a particular bend of the path at the water's edge in Plön where the whole lake seems to open at once. The castle stands on its hill to one side, white against the trees, the great lake spreads out in front with its islands and reed beds, and the sky sits large over it all. In the morning, with a light mist on the surface and swans moving slowly along the margin, it is a picture that needs very little help from a camera.

The town is hemmed in by water on several sides, and that is the point of its geography. Plön lies on a neck of land between the Great Plön Lake and a string of smaller lakes, and every street seems to end in a glimpse of blue. The lakes are the legacy of the last ice age, when the ice left behind a landscape of hollows that filled with meltwater, and the largest of them is the biggest lake in Schleswig-Holstein. The depth varies and the water is clear in places, and in winter hard frosts sometimes allow skating.

A walk along the promenade is the best way to see it. The path is flat and well kept, with benches and small jetties, and it runs along the shore past boathouses, reed beds and a small beach. You can hire rowing boats in season, and passenger boats run tours of the lake, stopping at several landings. Birds are easy to see, with coots, grebes and cormorants on the water and herons standing in the reeds, and in winter a surprising number of ducks gather on the open surface.

Riding to the water is simple. The approach roads run through gentle farmland and beech woods, with smooth bends and light traffic outside the weekends. Plön has about thirteen thousand people, and fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés are close to the centre. Parking near the lakefront is easy on weekdays, and the cobbles are short. Bring a camera, and give yourself half an hour for the light. Sunset over the lake in late summer is a good time, when the sky turns pink and the water takes on the colour.
t.molln lake@53.6,10.7:
Mölln is a town built between lakes, and the one to head for is the Stadtsee, the town lake, which laps right up to the old centre and has a small public beach, a lawn and a landing stage for pedal boats. The water is clear, gently sloping and mild by midsummer, and the park behind the beach is shaded by old trees. You change on the grass, nobody minds, and an hour in and out of the water is worth more than any amount of roadside coffee. Smaller lakes lie around the town, the Schulsee, the Hellbachsee and others, each with its own bathing place and its own reed margin.

The lakes are the legacy of the ice age, and they sit along the line of an old glacial meltwater valley. Around them the land is gently hilly, wooded with beech and oak, and the surrounding nature park, the Lauenburg Lakes, is full of paths, boat landings and quiet corners. In the Middle Ages the lakes were part of a trade route, since the salt barges from Lüneburg reached Lübeck by a chain of waterways and canals that passed through here. The old Stecknitz canal, one of the oldest artificial waterways in Europe, was dug in the fourteenth century, and the Hanseatic city of Lübeck held Mölln as a pawn for nearly three centuries, to protect the salt road.

The ride in is one of the nicer approaches to the Baltic from Hamburg. Roads run through beech woods and across farmland, with views of lakes flashing between trees and a lot of gentle bends. The tarmac is mostly good, and the traffic is light on weekdays. On hot weekends it fills with bathers and cyclists, and parking near the town lake can be hard to find, so an early start helps. In autumn the woods turn gold and the lakes are quiet.

Water safety is simple common sense. The bathing places are marked, and lifeguards are on duty at the main beach in high season. Do not dive into unknown water, and keep clear of the paddle boats. With about eighteen thousand people, Mölln has fuel stations, supermarkets and many cafés and restaurants, and the old centre, with its crooked streets and brick church, is a short walk from the lake. Bring a towel, because it is easy to forget it, and a dry layer for the ride afterward.
t.ratzeburg island@53.7,10.8:
Coffee in Ratzeburg is a small expedition, because the old town is an island. You cross one of three causeways, park near the cathedral and walk the cobbled lanes, with the lake glinting at the end of every street. The island is only a few hundred metres across, and it takes less than half an hour to walk around, but it is packed with history and has a number of cafés where you can sit with a pot of coffee and a slice of cake.

The cathedral dominates the island. Begun in the 1160s by Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, it is among the oldest large brick churches in northern Germany, a plain and sturdy building of dark red brick with a tall nave and heavy towers. Inside, the stone is austere, and the light is soft. The duke built it as a statement of Christian rule over the Slavic lands he had just conquered, and when you stand in front of it you can feel the intention.

Another figure is tied to the town. The sculptor and writer Ernst Barlach spent part of his youth here, and the town has a museum dedicated to his work, in a pair of buildings on the island, with his brooding wooden and bronze figures, including a number of drawings and plays. Barlach is best known for the floating angel in Güstrow and for his war memorials, which the Nazis later removed as degenerate. Even if sculpture is not your thing, the museum is quiet and compact and well worth half an hour.

For riders the island is easy to reach. The approach from Hamburg is a straightforward run through farmland and lakes, and the roads near the town are scenic and gentle. Cobbles on the island are rough and slippery after rain, so park at the edge and walk. The town has about fourteen thousand people, with fuel stations and supermarkets on the mainland side, and plenty of cafés on the island. Weekends in summer are busy, with tourists and rowers, so the best time is a weekday morning, when the light on the water is silver and the cathedral bell rings the hour. Take your coffee outside, if you can, and look at the water.
t.zollenspieker dike@53.4,10.2:
Zollenspieker is a place where a river crossing has been important for a very long time. The name comes from the old customs post, the Zoll, that stood here to tax traffic crossing the Elbe, and the little ferry that carries cars, bikes and walkers across to Hoopte on the south bank still runs, a short, unhurried journey of a few minutes. A half-timbered inn stands beside the landing stage, one of the oldest in the region, with a thatched roof, low beams and a terrace facing the river. It is a place where Hamburgers come for coffee and cake on fine Sundays.

The dike is the best place from which to view the scene. The grass bank rises several metres above the fields, with a path along the top, and from it you look out across the broad, brown river with its sandbanks, its reed beds and its slow procession of barges. On the landward side lie the Vierlande, a country of market gardens and nurseries, where flowers, vegetables and strawberries grow in the rich silt, and brick farmhouses with thatched roofs stand among orchards. In spring and summer the colours are bright, and roadside stalls sell what the gardens produce.

The Elbe is a tidal river here, and the water rises and falls by a metre or more, which shows in the mud flats and the wet lines on the pilings. Storm floods have swept over the dikes in the past, notably in 1962, and the river is carefully watched. A walk along the dike at dusk, with the lights coming on across the water and the sound of gulls, is a quiet pleasure.

Riding here is flat, open and slow. The dike road is narrow and often one-way for cars, with speed limits and a lot of cyclists, and the tarmac is rough in places. Wind is the main factor, and on a cool day it will find every gap in your clothing. Weekends in summer see heavy traffic and queues for the ferry, so go on a weekday if you can. Stelle, about four kilometres away, has fuel stations and supermarkets, and Winsen a few kilometres farther has more. Bring a camera for the light on the water, particularly at the end of the day, when the sun drops behind the far bank.
t.creel@27.8,-107.6:
Creel stands at about 2,300 metres in the Sierra Tarahumara, in the state of Chihuahua, and it feels like a frontier town that never quite finished growing. Wooden-fronted shops, pickup trucks and a plaza with a church make up the centre, and the surrounding hills are covered in pine and oak, with the smell of woodsmoke in the cold evenings. The town was named after Enrique Creel, a governor of Chihuahua, and it grew up around the railway, the Chihuahua-Pacific line, one of the great engineering feats of Mexico, completed in 1961 after decades of work.

The area belongs to the Raramuri, or Tarahumara, the indigenous people famed for their running endurance, who live in scattered homesteads and caves throughout the sierra. Women in bright skirts sell woven baskets, wooden dolls and carved violins on the plaza, and men in sandals run long distances over the rocky trails. The Raramuri have kept their language and customs, and they are the key to the region's culture. Please ask before taking photographs, and buy their crafts directly, if you can.

Near the town, the landscape is a strange and beautiful one. The Valley of the Monks is a field of tall rock pillars, and Lake Arareko is a pretty pine-fringed lake a short ride away. Beyond lies the vast network of canyons known as the Copper Canyon, larger than the Grand Canyon in total area, a maze of gorges that fall to subtropical depths. The road from Creel to Batopilas drops into the canyon in a series of steep descents, with unsurfaced sections, and it requires care, particularly in the rainy season.

Creel has about five thousand people, and fuel stations, supermarkets and basic hotels. It is the last reliable place for fuel before the canyon roads, so fill the tank and bring spare fuel if you can. Nights are cold at this altitude, often below freezing in winter, and days can be hot in summer, so bring layers. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the weather is dry and the light is clear, and the roads are safest. Ask locally about road conditions before setting out, since landslides and washouts are not uncommon after heavy rain, and check that your bike is in good shape.
t.divisadero@27.5,-107.8:
Divisadero means lookout, and the name is accurate. At the edge of the Sierra Tarahumara, the plateau ends abruptly, and the ground falls away into the Copper Canyon, a maze of gorges more than a mile deep, with pine-covered rims, red cliffs and, far below, the green of the subtropical river valleys. From the viewpoint, the canyons meet from three directions, and the view stretches to the horizon, with clouds drifting below. It is one of the great sights of Mexico, and it never fails to stop people mid-sentence.

The Chepe train, which runs from Chihuahua to the Pacific coast, stops here for fifteen minutes so that passengers can step out and see the view, and the platform fills with tourists, vendors and Raramuri women selling baskets and food. Artisans in traditional dress sell weavings, woven pine-needle baskets and small violins, and the smell of grilled corn and tortillas drifts across. If you ride here outside the train time, the place is much quieter.

There is more to do than look. A cable car runs across a side canyon, there are zip lines for the brave and a walk along the rim gives different views, with trails leading down into the gorge. The canyon floor is very different, with orange trees and warm air, while at the top, pines and cold wind prevail. The temperature difference can be many degrees, and the Raramuri, who live in both zones, move between them with the seasons. In the rainy months, from July to September, the canyon turns bright green.

There are no big supplies of fuel here, and Creel, thirty-one kilometres away, is the main source, so make sure you fill up before riding out. San Rafael, nearer, has only a small supply. Food stalls near the viewpoint sell tacos, quesadillas and coffee, and a few simple hotels offer rooms. The road from Creel is paved, winding through pine forest with views opening between the trees, and it is a fine ride, although animals and trucks require care. Mornings are clear and cold, and by afternoon clouds often build. Sunrise and sunset are the best times to see the canyon, when the light turns the cliffs orange and purple, and the silence is deep.
t.uelzen@53.0,10.6:
Uelzen sits on the edge of the Lüneburg Heath, a mid-sized town in a landscape of sand, pine and sugar beet, and its station is the strangest sight in Lower Saxony. The Hundertwasser railway station, rebuilt in 2000 as a project connected with Expo in Hanover, is a riot of colour, with tilting columns, golden onion domes, tiled mosaics and trees growing from the roof. The Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser had planned the redesign before his death, and the result is a cheerful, slightly mad entrance to an otherwise orderly town.

Uelzen is also where the Elbe Lateral Canal runs through, built to link the Elbe with the Mittelland Canal, and the double lock here lifts boats by about twenty-three metres, among the larger ones on the German waterways. Watching a barge rise in the chamber is oddly hypnotic. The town was a Hanseatic trading place, and has an old church, the St. Marien, with a tall brick tower, and a market square. Beyond the town lies the Heath, famous for the purple bloom of heather in late summer, and for sheep, the horned Heidschnucken, that keep it open.

As a fuel gate, Uelzen is convenient and practical. The main roads cross here, the stations are large and open late, and there is a good choice of cafés and bakeries near the station. The ride south runs through flat country of farms and forests, with straight, quiet roads, long avenues of oak and birch, and little traffic on weekdays. Winds can be strong on the open land, and rain in autumn comes in grey, steady sheets.

For a longer day toward the Harz mountains, this is the place to top up. Fill the tank, get a coffee and a Franzbrötchen if you can, and head south. Late August and September are best for the heather, and spring brings fresh green.
t.burgdorf@52.4,10.0:
Burgdorf is a town of around thirty thousand people in the flat country northeast of Hanover, on the sandy plain between Hanover and the Aller valley, and it serves as a useful gate for riders heading north into the Lüneburg and Südheide country. The landscape is open and agricultural, with fields of wheat, rape and sugar beet, and long, straight roads lined with trees. This is not mountain land, and the pleasures of the ride lie in rhythm, light and the quiet, unpressured miles.

The Aller itself is a slow, meandering river, running northwest to join the Weser, with marshy meadows and wooded banks that make good habitat for storks and herons. To the north lies Celle, an hour or so's ride, one of the best-preserved old towns in Germany, with more than four hundred half-timbered houses, a ducal castle and a handsome market square. The Südheide Nature Park beyond has heath, pine forest and sandy lanes, and in August and September the heather blooms purple. Near Wietze, a small German Oil Museum recalls that Germany's first oil boom happened here in the late nineteenth century, when wells in the heath produced a large share of the country's supply.

For a rider, the Aller valley and the Südheide give easy, gentle roads, with long sightlines, smooth surfaces and some rural bends. Hazards include tractors, farm traffic and deer at dawn and dusk. In spring and early summer the asparagus season brings farm stalls to every roadside, and local restaurants serve it with new potatoes, ham and butter. Crosswinds on the open stretches can be strong.

Burgdorf has all the services you would expect, with several fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets and bakeries, and a pleasant old town centre. Fill up before you leave, since the countryside beyond has fewer stations and many close early on Sundays. Grab a coffee, enjoy the town and settle into the long, easy rhythm of the north German plain.
t.radebeul@51.1,13.7:
Radebeul is where Dresden's suburbs turn into vineyards. The town spreads along the right bank of the Elbe, northwest of the Saxon capital, and its hillsides are terraced with vines running up from villas and cottages to little summerhouses on the ridge. It is one of the northernmost wine regions in Germany, and Saxony's vintners are fiercely proud of their small production, most of which never leaves the state. Dry Riesling, Müller-Thurgau and Weissburgunder are the usual suspects, and a glass of Federweisser in autumn is almost a local duty.

The town's cultural fame comes from an unexpected direction. Karl May, the author who wrote hugely popular adventure novels about Winnetou and Old Shatterhand long before he had seen the American West, spent his later years in Radebeul, in a villa he named Villa Shatterhand. It is now a museum, and a pilgrimage point for German fans, with Native American artefacts and the writer's own fantasies on display. Nearby, Schloss Wackerbarth is a baroque estate that produces sparkling wine, with tours and tastings, and the Hoflössnitz, an old royal wine estate, holds a small wine museum in a painted pavilion.

For riding, the Saxon Wine Route is a gentle, rolling affair. The road follows the Elbe between Pillnitz and Meissen, sometimes right beside the river, sometimes up in the hills among the vines, with views over the water and the meadows. It is not a road for speed, because it passes through villages and has plenty of traffic, especially on weekends, but the scenery is lovely and the stops are easy. Look out for the narrow-gauge steam railway, the Lössnitzgrundbahn, that runs from Radebeul up a side valley to Radeburg and can be heard puffing in the distance.

Radebeul is a proper town of more than thirty thousand people, so it has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants of every kind, plus a tram link with Dresden. It is an excellent place for a coffee and cake in one of the old villas, or for a glass of wine on a vineyard terrace at sunset, preferably when someone else is riding home.

The valley is mild, with a long growing season, and the best months are September and October, when the vines turn gold and the harvest brings festivals up and down the slopes.
t.meissen@51.2,13.5:
Meissen is where Saxony began. The Albrechtsburg castle, a late Gothic masterpiece, stands on a rock above the Elbe, next to the cathedral with its tall spires, and together they form a skyline that looks straight out of a medieval manuscript. In the tenth century, a fortress was founded here by German kings to guard against the Slavs to the east, and from it grew the margraviate that eventually became Saxony. Walking up the cobbled alleys from the market square to the castle gate is one of the better ways to spend an hour in Germany.

The town is also the home of European porcelain. In 1710, Augustus the Strong, the Elector of Saxony, set up a factory in the Albrechtsburg after the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, forced to find a way to make gold, instead worked out how to make hard-paste porcelain. For years the process was a state secret, and workers were practically held prisoners. The factory moved to a purpose-built site in the nineteenth century and still produces the famous blue crossed swords on its pieces. A museum shows how it is done and displays some astonishing work. Even the bells in one of the church towers are made of porcelain, and their sound is surprisingly soft.

For riders, Meissen is the northern anchor of the Saxon Wine Route. The road from Radebeul follows the Elbe through small wine villages and vineyards on steep slopes, and arrives in the town beneath the castle. The streets in the old town are steep and cobbled, so take care with the bike, especially in the wet, and park below the old centre rather than trying to climb to the top. The surrounding hills are low but pretty, and the Elbe is wide and slow, with riverside paths busy with cyclists.

With nearly thirty thousand people, Meissen has petrol stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, and it is easy to find a table. Look for the local wines, light, dry whites with a bright acidity, and for the Meissner Fummel, a large, crisp pastry traditionally shaped like a large knot or twist, which is eaten with a cup of coffee.

Autumn is excellent here, with the vines turning colour and the river mist hanging below the castle in the morning.
t.torfhaus@51.8,10.5:
There is a point on the B4 where the forest stops pretending and the Harz shows its real face: open moor, stunted spruce, grey sky and, on a clear day, the bald dome of the Brocken on the horizon. Torfhaus is a cluster of buildings on that high plateau, at about eight hundred metres, built around a car park, a few cafés and a visitor centre for the Harz National Park. It has the feel of a place on the edge of something, which is accurate, because until 1990 the inner German border ran only a short distance east, and the Brocken beyond it was a closed military zone with listening posts on the summit.

The Brocken, at 1,141 metres, is the highest peak in northern Germany and the great stage of German witch lore. According to tradition, witches gather on its summit on the night of 30 April, Walpurgisnacht, and Goethe set a famous scene of Faust there. The mountain is famous for its weather, with fog on most days and snow into May, and from Torfhaus you can see why. In winter the plateau becomes a cross-country ski area, and the road can be slick with ice or closed by snow, so check conditions. Fog and wind are the standard setting; on a bad day you can lose sight of the road edge.

The ride from Bad Harzburg is the part that matters. The B4 climbs from the lowland town through beech and spruce in a series of confident, well-surfaced curves, then levels out on the moor. It is a road for a steady, relaxed pace, with a view of the sky and the odd stag. There is a lot of traffic on dry weekends, including lorries and cyclists. On the other side, the road descends toward Braunlage, a larger resort with more places to eat. The Harz is the northernmost of the German uplands, so the weather arrives from the North Sea with little to stop it, and you should treat even a summer ride with some respect.

Cafés in the village serve sausage and hot drinks. A short walk onto the moor shows how the peat bog holds the water, with cotton grass in early summer and a dark, slightly sinister stillness around the pools.

In winter the whole area goes quiet and white, and you will see more snowshoes than motorcycles.
t.putbus@54.4,13.5:
Putbus is the odd one out on Rügen. It was not a fishing village that grew into a resort, but a deliberate planned town, laid out from 1810 by Prince Malte of Putbus, who wanted a classical residence that could compete with the grand capitals of Europe. Everything is white. The houses along the circular green known as the Circus are white, the theatre is white, the villas are white, and the town has long been called the White Town. After the grey of the East German years, it is a little startling to find such a polished set of buildings in a corner of the Baltic that is mostly reed and sand.

The prince's palace was demolished in the 1960s, which is a sad piece of history, but the park that surrounded it survives, with ancient trees, an orangery and winding paths, and it is worth an hour. The theatre has been restored, and in summer its stage hosts concerts and plays. You can also pick up the Rasender Roland, the narrow-gauge steam railway that has run from Putbus to the seaside resorts of Binz, Sellin and Göhren since the late nineteenth century, still puffing along on tracks that cross the road at several points. Listen for the whistle as you ride.

The riding on Rügen is flat and soft. The island has long straight roads lined with old trees, usually limes or maples, which meet overhead in places and create a green tunnel with dappled light. Traffic is thick in summer and the speed limits are low, but the scenery is lovely, with fields and reed beds and sudden glimpses of the sea. The surface varies, with the occasional stretch of old cobbles near small villages, and in July and August it is better to ride early, before the beach traffic begins.

Putbus has a few thousand residents and plenty of services, including fuel, supermarkets and a handful of cafés and restaurants. Bergen auf Rügen, the island's main town, is about eight kilometres away if you need a bigger shop. Local cooking leans on fish, with smoked herring and fried Baltic flounder in most places, and a sea buckthorn drink or ice cream that you will see in every shop and that tastes tart and slightly medicinal.

Late afternoon is lovely, with white walls catching the light and long shadows on the green.
t.sellin@54.4,13.7:
Sellin is Rügen's showpiece for the kind of seaside holiday that Germans were taking before the First World War: long white villas with wooden balconies and turrets, set on a bluff above a beach of fine pale sand. The architecture is called Bäderarchitektur, spa architecture, and Sellin has some of the best surviving examples on the Baltic. The grand hotels and villas run in a line along the cliff top, painted white and decorated with fretwork like icing, and the whole thing looks like a film set, only with real tourists in real deckchairs.

The most famous feature is the pier. The Seebrücke, a long wooden jetty that stretches out into the Baltic, has a restaurant at the end and a design that recalls the earlier pier, which was burned down in the twentieth century and rebuilt. A long flight of steps and a lift connect the beach and the promenade, because the bluff is steep. In the surrounding forest, the Jagdschloss Granitz, a hunting lodge built for the Prince of Putbus in the nineteenth century, stands on a hill with a central tower that you climb by an iron spiral staircase. The views from the top, over the forest and the sea, are worth the climb.

For riders, the roads around Sellin are quiet and leafy. The route from Putbus through the Granitz forest has a handful of gentle bends beneath tall beech trees, and the surface is good. The Baltic is never far, and between villages you find fields of rape in spring, bright yellow against a pale sky. Traffic can be thick in high summer, particularly on the coastal road toward Binz, but the island is flat, so you can pick your moment. On some days the sea wind makes the bike feel lively, and a crosswind on an open stretch deserves respect.

Sellin has enough shops and cafés for a lunch stop but is small, so for fuel it is better to go to Binz, about six kilometres to the north, which has a bigger range of services. The beach is a short walk from the centre. There is a smoked fish stand or two, and in the evening the restaurants serve fresh catch.

A visit out of season is quieter and more atmospheric, with grey waves, empty promenades and a mood close to melancholy.
t.sassnitz@54.5,13.6:
Sassnitz is the harbour town for Rügen's chalk cliffs, and it looks like it has been practising for the role. Built into a steep hillside above a working port, it has a long stone pier with a lighthouse at its tip, a fishing fleet that still goes out, and a ferry connection to Sweden that runs from the nearby terminal at Mukran. The town grew up in the nineteenth century, when the railway reached the island, and the ferry link to Sweden dates back to the early twentieth century.

The real attraction is north of the town, in Jasmund National Park, where the chalk comes out of the forest in white cliffs that drop vertically to the sea. The most famous point is the Königsstuhl, the King's Chair, a cliff more than a hundred metres high, a landscape that Caspar David Friedrich painted in the early nineteenth century in one of the most recognisable images of German Romanticism. The cliffs are made of Cretaceous chalk, full of flint nodules and fossils of sea creatures, and they erode constantly, so there are occasional landslips and the viewing platforms have to be moved back. Inland, the beech woods of Jasmund are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site that protects ancient beech forests across Europe, and a walk through them in spring, with wild garlic underfoot, is a pleasure.

For riders, the road from Sassnitz toward the national park is a gentle curl through forest, with a few bends and a well-maintained surface. Access to the Königsstuhl itself is on foot from a visitor centre car park, and there is a fee. The road around the coast is pleasant, but traffic is heavy in summer, and the island's speed limits are strictly enforced. The weather is changeable, with sea mist rolling in off the Baltic and the light changing quickly.

Sassnitz is a town of about eleven thousand, so it has fuel, supermarkets and places to eat, with fish sandwiches by the harbour that are almost obligatory. Smoked herring, Matjes and fried flounder appear on every menu. The harbour is a pleasant place for a coffee, with the boats creaking and the gulls screaming.

White cliffs and green trees look best in clear afternoon light, after rain has washed the air.
t.cape arkona@54.7,13.4:
Cape Arkona is the northernmost point of Rügen and, for a thousand years, it was where the western Slavs kept their holiest place. On this chalk headland, about forty-five metres above the sea, the Rani tribe built a temple fortress dedicated to Svantevit, a god of war and fertility with four heads, and the whole Baltic knew it. In 1168, the Danish king Valdemar the Great, with Bishop Absalon, sailed up, stormed the fortress, cut down the idol and converted the island by force. The earth ramparts of that stronghold, the Jaromarsburg, still curve across the headland, and half of it has been eaten by the sea over the centuries.

Two lighthouses stand on the cape. The older was built in 1827 to a design by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, the great Prussian architect, as a square brick tower of simple dignity, and it is now a museum with a view from the top. Beside it, a newer lighthouse dating from the early twentieth century has taken over the job, and a concrete bunker and radar tower left by the military sit close by, a strange modern addition to the headland. A few hundred metres away, the small fishing village of Vitt has thatched cottages in a hollow near the sea, with a tiny chapel and a few boats pulled up on the stones.

Cars are not allowed to the tip. You park at Putgarten and walk the last kilometre, or ride in a small tourist train, a rule that keeps the headland quiet. The ride from the south, via Altenkirchen, is flat and easy, with long avenues and wide fields, and the road is generally good but busy on summer weekends. The wind can be fierce on the open cape, so plan for it. This is the Baltic, where the weather comes straight from the sea, and the temperature on the cliff can be several degrees colder than in town.

Altenkirchen and Wiek are small, and the safest approach is to start with a full tank from Sassnitz, which is about twenty kilometres away, or Bergen. There are cafés and fish stands in Putgarten, and the fried herring sandwich is a good way to warm up.

Stand at the cliff edge on a clear day and the horizon is a perfectly flat line of water, with nothing between you and Scandinavia.
t.timmendorfer strand@54.0,10.8:
Lübeck Bay curves round in a long, shallow arc, and Timmendorfer Strand sits halfway along it, which is why the whole stretch from Travemünde to Neustadt in Holstein feels like one continuous holiday. The beach is wide and pale, the water is shallow enough that children paddle out a long way, and in July the sand is dotted with Strandkörbe, those hooded wicker beach chairs that Germans treat as portable living rooms. Behind the dunes, the promenade is lined with big hotels, ice cream stalls and a pier, and in the evening it fills with people in sandals pretending not to look at their phones.

The town has been a seaside resort since the late nineteenth century, when the railway and the Baltic bathing fashion arrived together. It grew past the shingled fishing cottages that were here before, and the sense of two layers lives on in Niendorf, the harbour district at the eastern end, where a few fishing cutters still go out and sell smoked herring and fresh flounder from the quay. It is worth a stop just to see that the Baltic fishing trade has not entirely gone.

For riders, the coast is not about corners. The road from Travemünde, past Haffkrug and Scharbeutz, runs close behind the dunes through resort towns, and the speed limits are low and enforced. The pleasure is in the long views of the sea and in the strip of green between towns, and in the fact that the Baltic is a calm companion rather than a wild one. If you want bends, turn inland and cross the low hills of Holstein, where beech woods and small lakes give the road a lively roll, and where the traffic thins out almost at once. A few kilometres south is Lübeck, the old Hanseatic city, with its brick Gothic towers and marzipan shops, and it is an easy side trip.

With over nine thousand year-round residents, Timmendorfer Strand has proper fuel stops and supermarkets, though in high summer everything gets crowded. Parking by the beach costs money and fills early. A fish sandwich with pickled herring and onions is the local fuel, and a bag of Lübeck marzipan lasts exactly as long as the next red light.

On a fine day in May, before the main crowds arrive, the sea is a pale grey-green and the whole coast is yours.
t.kuhlungsborn@54.2,11.8:
Kühlungsborn is long and thin because it was three villages that grew together. Brunshaupten, Arendsee and Fulgen were joined in 1938 and given a single name, and the result is a seaside resort that stretches for several kilometres along the Mecklenburg coast, with a continuous promenade backed by white villas and grand hotels from the Bäderarchitektur period. Behind the town the land rises into the Kühlung, a low wooded ridge that gives the place its name and protects it from the worst of the wind, an unusual luxury on this coast.

The best way to arrive is on the Molli, the narrow-gauge steam train that has puffed from Bad Doberan through fields and along the beach road since the late nineteenth century, hooting at pedestrians and leaving a smell of coal in the sea air. It is the sort of railway that attracts photographers and children in equal numbers. Bad Doberan, at the other end, has a magnificent brick Gothic minster, one of the finest on the Baltic, and the line also stops at Heiligendamm, Germany's first seaside resort, founded in 1793 by the Duke of Mecklenburg. Its row of white classical buildings along the shore, known as the White Town by the Sea, hosted the G8 summit in 2007.

The road along the coast from Heiligendamm to Kühlungsborn is a pleasant one for a relaxed ride. It runs through beech woods and fields, with glimpses of the sea, in gentle bends that make a satisfying change from the flat country farther east. The surface is mostly good, though local traffic and cyclists are plentiful in summer, and you will often be stuck behind a tractor or a coach. A quieter alternative is to leave the main road and follow the lanes through Bastorf, where the lighthouse stands among fields, and along the cliffs.

Kühlungsborn has about seven and a half thousand residents, which is enough for fuel, supermarkets and a wide choice of cafés. Restaurants serve plenty of fish, and the specialty is smoked eel, which tastes better than it sounds. The pier is a good place to watch the sun go down and to see how the weather moves over the sea.

Come in September, when the beaches are quiet, the water is still mild and the light is slanting and warm.
t.warnemunde@54.2,12.1:
Warnemünde is where Rostock goes to the sea. The old fishing village at the mouth of the Warnow river was swallowed by the city long ago, but it keeps a stubborn independence, with a narrow canal called the Alter Strom lined with low fishermen's houses, rows of small fishing boats tied up at the quay, and stalls selling fish sandwiches straight off the cutters. The smell of smoked fish and diesel is the first thing you notice, and the second is the wind.

The lighthouse, built in 1898, is the centre of the postcard, standing at the head of the promenade next to the Teepott, a shell-shaped concrete roof from the East German era that now holds shops and restaurants. Opposite, the beach is huge, wide and white, one of the broadest on the German Baltic, and in summer it is filled with Strandkörbe, a Mecklenburg invention. The first one was built in Rostock in 1882 by a basket maker, who made it for a woman with rheumatism who wanted shelter from the wind. That is the legend, and everyone in the town agrees on it.

Warnemünde is also a ship-watching place. Ferries leave for Denmark, cargo ships slide through the channel, and in summer huge cruise liners turn in the river mouth and tower over the fishing boats like an optical illusion. The East Mole, a long stone pier, lets you walk out into the traffic and wave. In July, the town holds a sailing regatta and a week-long festival, and the whole place feels as if it has been taken over by sailors.

As for riding, the road from Kühlungsborn along the coast, past Heiligendamm and Bad Doberan, ends here at the tip of the Rostock agglomeration. It is a gentle, flat run through woods and fields, and the surface is good, but the nearer you get to Rostock, the busier the roads become. Do not expect to ride fast. Instead, park near the station, which is the main transport hub, and walk the old streets. A ferry across the river reaches the other bank.

Warnemünde has a proper town's worth of services, including fuel and supermarkets, though in high season the car parks fill by mid-morning. The local speciality is a Fischbrötchen with herring, and the best ones come from the stalls along the Alter Strom. Eat one with a view of the water and a gull watching your hand. Early morning or late evening, when the cruise passengers have gone, is the right time to see the village as it really is.
t.matmata@33.5,10.0:
Matmata is a village you have to look down into. The houses of this Berber settlement in southern Tunisia are dug into the earth, around deep circular pits with rooms cut into the walls around them, so that from the road you see only a scatter of craters in the stony ground and a few chimneys. The people built them like this to escape the extreme heat and cold, and the clay and limestone keep temperatures steady through the year. Walking into one, down a ramp or tunnel, you pass from glaring sunlight into a cool, whitewashed courtyard where goats and chickens wander.

Many of the families have moved up to modern houses nearby, and some of the old pit homes now serve visitors, with rooms or a café in the courtyard. One of them was used as the home of Luke Skywalker's family in the first Star Wars film, and it is still a popular visit. The film crews came back later to nearby places, and the area is dotted with sets and relics that give it an odd mix of ancient and modern.

The landscape is part of the Jebel Dahar, a range of hills and plateaux that rise out of the desert plain, and it is dry, rocky and stripped, with olives and palms in the oasis pockets. The ride from Gabès, about forty kilometres to the east, climbs through low barren hills on a road that is mostly good but narrow in places, with trucks, goats and occasional gravel on the bends. Wind can be strong on the exposed ridges and dust can blow across the road. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride; summer afternoons are scorching, and you should start early and carry plenty of water.

In the village you can find simple restaurants serving brik, a fried pastry parcel with egg, couscous with lamb and sweet mint tea. Bargaining is part of daily life, so stay friendly and good humoured. Fuel is best taken in Gabès before you climb, since only small supplies are available in the village, and mechanics are scarce out here.

Take time to wander through a courtyard and look up at the sky from the bottom of a pit. It is a rare way to see the desert.
t.chenini@32.9,10.3:
Chenini clings to a ridge in the Ksour hills south of Tataouine, a Berber village of stone and plaster whose houses seem to grow out of the hillside. Rooms are carved into the rock, some of them below ground, with whitewashed walls and vaulted ceilings, and above them stands a small mosque with a white dome. From a distance, the village is the same colour as the hill and almost vanishes in the afternoon haze, and only a few pale domes give it away.

Its history is long. The Berbers who settled here built hilltop villages for defence, and fortified granaries called ksour, which gave the region its name, served as storehouses for grain, olives and dates. The troglodyte homes kept cool in summer and warm in winter. Local legend also links the mosque to the Seven Sleepers, the youths who, in Christian and Muslim tradition, slept for centuries in a cave, and a row of long graves is said to hold them. It is a sweet, strange story, told by the villagers with a straight face.

This is also Star Wars country. George Lucas took the name Tatooine from nearby Tataouine, and the film crews used landscapes and buildings around here, which has brought a trickle of visitors. The result is a mixture of authentic village life and small souvenir stalls, but the heart of Chenini remains quiet. You will see women in bright wraps, children playing in the lanes, and goats picking along the stony paths.

The road from Tataouine winds across a dry plateau of pale rock and scrub, and it is a pleasant ride, with long views and few other vehicles. Surfaces are mostly tarmac but patchy, with sand and gravel on the bends, and wind sometimes carries dust. Spring and autumn are the best times, with warm days and cool evenings, while midsummer heat is fierce. Start early, carry water, and wear sun protection.

Tataouine, about eighteen kilometres away, has petrol stations, shops and restaurants, and it is the place to fill the tank. In the village there are small cafés and stalls selling tea, bread, and sometimes simple lunches. Bargaining is expected for souvenirs, and a friendly greeting makes everything easier.

Climb through the village to the top and look out across the plain. The silence and the scale give you a sense of how old this country is.
t.top of the world@45.0,-109.4:
Somewhere on the Beartooth Highway the trees give up, and at the place called Top of the World you are standing in a landscape that belongs to the sky. The plateau is a rolling tundra of grass, sedge and tiny flowers, with granite boulders, snowfields and small lakes, and the horizon is mountains in every direction. At more than ten thousand feet it feels like a different planet from the Montana prairie far below, and the wind carries a sharpness that makes you reach for another layer.

This is the Beartooth Plateau, the largest high-altitude plateau in the contiguous United States, a block of ancient granite that was scoured by glaciers and holds some of the oldest exposed rock in North America. Hundreds of small lakes sit in the hollows, and in July the tundra bursts into colour with alpine forget-me-nots, moss campion and paintbrush. Mountain goats can be seen on the slopes, marmots whistle from the rocks, and pikas squeak from piles of stones. The air is thin and cold, and clouds can form and dissolve within minutes.

The highway that crosses it, US 212, was opened in the 1930s and has been called the most beautiful drive in America by a famous television journalist. It climbs from Red Lodge in Montana in a spectacular series of switchbacks and crosses the plateau before dropping toward Wyoming. It is a seasonal road, usually open from late spring to mid-autumn, and snow can fall on any day of the year, so check conditions before you go. The surface is generally good, but frost heaves, gravel and sudden fog or sleet can catch riders out. Start early, dress for winter in July, and watch for wildlife and tourists stopping suddenly.

A small store and lodge sometimes operate at the Top of the World stop in summer, but you cannot count on them. Red Lodge, about twenty-seven kilometres below, is a lively little town with petrol stations, restaurants and shops, and it is the place to fill the tank and eat well before the climb. On the other side, Cooke City has limited services. Carry water, snacks and a rain jacket.

Stay a moment in the quiet and watch the clouds move across the tundra. It is one of the great places to feel small.
t.beartooth pass@45.0,-109.5:
At 10,947 feet, Beartooth Pass is the highest point on the Beartooth Highway, and the top of the road in every sense. The summit is a broad saddle of bare rock and tundra, with a pull-off, a plaque and a view over the Absaroka and Beartooth ranges that goes on until the air gets hazy. The peaks that give the range its name stand to the north, their jagged granite spires said to resemble bears' teeth, and snowfields cling to the shaded slopes well into summer.

The road to the pass is one of the best mountain rides in the United States. From Red Lodge the highway climbs in a series of long switchbacks to the plateau, with steep drops and no guard rail in places, and the views over the valley widen with every hairpin. Over the top, it winds along open ridges to the Wyoming border and down toward Cooke City and the northeast entrance of Yellowstone. It took years of work to build, and it opened in 1936. The surface is generally good, though frost damage and patches of gravel are common, and sudden hailstorms can turn the road greasy. Traffic is light early in the morning, heavier by midday, with plenty of motorcyclists and campers.

The seasons rule everything. The road is typically open from around Memorial Day to mid-October, but snow can close it at almost any time, and even in July you may find ice on the road. Weather changes fast, so a clear morning may turn to freezing rain by afternoon, and lightning is a real danger on the open tundra. The thin air can make newcomers breathless, so take it easy and drink water.

Wildlife is part of the scene. Mountain goats and bighorn sheep appear on the rocks, and grizzly bears roam the surrounding country, so never leave food out. Small lakes dot the plateau, and the wildflowers in July are spectacular.

Red Lodge, about thirty kilometres below, is the place to fill up, and Cooke City on the far side has limited supplies. Carry layers, gloves and a rain jacket, and give yourself time. The pass is not a place to hurry.
t.rappbode dam photo@51.7,10.9:
From the road, the Rappbode Dam is a surprise. You ride through the quiet Harz forest, on gentle roads with spruce on either side, and then the trees open and a vast curved wall of concrete and stone appears across the valley, with a long lake behind it and a long drop below. It is the highest dam wall in Germany, rising a little over a hundred metres, and the scale is the thing: it makes the cars on the road below look like toys.

The dam was built in the 1950s as part of a chain of reservoirs in the Harz mountains to supply drinking water and control floods, and the lake it holds is the largest in the Harz, the Rappbode Reservoir, a long, branching body of water that winds through steep wooded hills. The water is cold and clean, and it supplies a large part of the drinking water of the region around Halle and Magdeburg. In recent years, the dam has added a more daring attraction, a pedestrian suspension bridge of nearly five hundred metres across the valley, among the longest of its kind in Europe, and a zip line, if you are in the mood.

The roads that lead to the dam are a joy. The Harz is the northernmost range in Germany, and its roads climb through spruce forest in gentle, flowing bends, often with the sound of streams. Near Rübeland, there are limestone caves, among the best in the country, with huge halls of stalactites. The forest here has suffered badly from drought and bark beetle in recent years, and large patches of dead spruce stand on the slopes, a sad sight but a reminder of climate change. Fog and low cloud are common, and the weather is often cooler than in the lowlands.
