Fuel is available in Blankenburg, about seven kilometres to the north-east, where the stations, shops, and restaurants are, and the villages of Hüttenrode and Rübeland have only small shops and cafes. A parking area near the dam provides the best views, and a footpath leads out onto the wall. Best seasons are late spring and autumn, when the light is clear and the crowds thin. In winter, snow and ice can make the Harz roads tricky, and a good set of gloves is not a luxury.
t.goslar old town base@51.9,10.4:
Goslar is one of those towns where history is not a museum but the architecture itself. It sits on the northern edge of the Harz mountains, with a perfectly preserved old town of half-timbered houses, slate roofs, and cobbled lanes, and in 1992 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, together with the old Rammelsberg mine above it. Silver, copper, and lead were mined at the Rammelsberg for roughly a thousand years, until the mine closed in 1988, and that wealth built the town.

The riches also attracted emperors. In the eleventh century, the German kings made Goslar a favourite residence, and the Imperial Palace, or Kaiserpfalz, a huge restored hall of the Salian dynasty, still stands above the old town, with large paintings of imperial history inside. In the market square, a clock with figures that come out to perform several times a day draws a small crowd, and the Kaiserworth, a guildhall that is now a hotel, shows a row of statues of emperors above its door. The streets are narrow, and cobbles can be slippery when wet, so take care walking in motorcycle boots.

Goslar makes a good base for the Harz. From here, roads lead up into the mountains, toward Clausthal-Zellerfeld, Torfhaus, and the Brocken, a high peak that was once behind the Iron Curtain. The roads are good, with long curves, spruce forests, and good views, and in summer they are popular with riders, so weekends can be busy. In winter, snow comes early to the high Harz. The surrounding hills are heavily forested, though the forest has suffered badly in recent dry years.

Fuel is straightforward, with several stations around the edges of town, and Langelsheim, about seven kilometres to the north-west, is a smaller place for supplies. The town has a wide range of cafes and restaurants, serving everything from Harz sausage and mushrooms to cake and strong coffee. Park on the edge and walk in, because the old town is largely pedestrianised. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the crowds are thinner, and a stop in the late afternoon, when the slate roofs glow, is a pleasant way to end a day.
t.gifhorn@52.5,10.5:
Gifhorn is a town of mills, and it has an unexpected claim to fame: the International Mill Museum, which has one of the largest collections of windmills and watermills in the world, with full-sized examples from Germany, the Netherlands, Greece, Russia, and as far away as China. They stand in a park on the edge of town, some turning in the breeze, and a small Russian Orthodox chapel and a Japanese pavilion add to the mix. It is an odd, delightful place, and children and adults alike seem to enjoy it.

The town sits on the Aller river and the Ise, at the edge of the Lüneburg Heath and the Wendland, and it has a pleasant, small-town centre with a Renaissance castle at its heart. The castle was built in the sixteenth century as a residence for Duke Franz of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and it is still the town's most impressive building. The area around is flat and sandy, with pine forests and farmland, and the lakes and gravel pits provide a number of spots for a swim in warm weather.

The roads around Gifhorn are flat and easy, with long straights, gentle bends, and tree-lined avenues. They are not thrilling, but they are pleasant and quiet, and on a warm summer afternoon the sandy lanes through the pine woods have a charm of their own. Traffic is moderate, and Wolfsburg, with its huge car factory, is about twenty-five kilometres to the east. Watch for sand on the road after wind, and for tractors and deer at dawn and dusk.

Fuel, supermarkets, and cafes are all available in town, and Ribbesbüttel, a smaller village about six kilometres away, has limited services. The water stop here is a simple one: the lakes around town, flooded gravel pits among them, have beaches and shady shores, and the Aller offers quiet places to sit. In summer, it can be warm, and a break by the water is a welcome relief. Mornings are best for quiet, and evenings for light. In winter, the area is damp and grey, with frost and fog, and the roads can be icy early on.
t.peine food@52.3,10.2:
Peine is an industrial town between Hanover and Braunschweig, and it does not pretend to be anything else, which is its charm. For more than a century, steel was its business: the Ilseder Hütte steelworks, founded in 1858, shaped the town and the surrounding villages, and the Peiner Träger, steel beams made here, were exported across Europe. The heavy industry has declined, but it left behind a working-class town with a strong sense of identity, brick housing, and honest, unfussy places to eat.

The old centre, rebuilt after wartime damage, has a market square with a town hall and a church, and a few half-timbered buildings survive. The Mittelland Canal, one of Germany's major waterways, passes close by, and barges and cargo ships pass the town day and night. Beyond the canal, the land is flat and open, with farmland and sugar beet fields, and the horizon is dominated by wind turbines and the occasional chimney.

For a rider, Peine is a convenient stop for food and fuel on the way between Hanover and Braunschweig or on the return leg of a day out. The town has a good range of bakeries, cafes, and restaurants, and the prices are reasonable. It is a place to have a plain, filling lunch, such as a schnitzel with fried potatoes or a bowl of soup, and to sit for a while. The roads around are flat and straight, with farm traffic and a few trucks, and the surface is generally decent. It is not scenic, but it is practical.

There are fuel stations around the edges of town and on the main roads, and supermarkets and bakeries in the centre. Meerdorf, a smaller village about six kilometres away, has few services. The best time to stop is late morning or early afternoon, when the lunch places are open, and the weather is usually mild in spring and autumn. In winter, the open farmland can be cold and windy, with fog and ice on the roads. If you are heading back to Hanover at the end of the day, a coffee and a slice of cake here is a good way to prepare for the traffic.
t.celle river road@52.6,10.1:
Celle is among the best-preserved old towns in Germany, and a stop here is rarely wasted. More than four hundred half-timbered houses stand in the old centre, many of them with carved beams and painted inscriptions, and the streets, unlike in many German towns, escaped the wartime bombing. On a sunny afternoon, the market square, the ducal castle, and the cobbled lanes make a very pleasant place to wander.

The castle was the seat of the Welf dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg for centuries, and it has a Baroque theatre, one of the oldest in Europe still in use. It was also the place of exile for Caroline Matilda, Queen of Denmark, banished here in 1772 after a scandal at the Copenhagen court, who died in Celle three years later at the age of twenty-three. The town also has a famous stud, where Hanoverian horses are bred, and its stallion parade each autumn draws large crowds. The Aller river flows through the town, and canals and boat trips on the water add to the charm.

For a rider, the river roads along the Aller are a gentle pleasure. Flat, quiet, and tree-lined, they follow the river past meadows, small villages, and farm stalls. The surface is generally good, with the occasional bump, and the bends are open and easy. A swim in the river is possible in summer at certain spots, though the current can be strong, and signs should be read carefully. Traffic in the old town is heavy at weekends, with one-way streets and busy car parks, so use the parking on the edge and walk in.

Celle is a town of seventy thousand, so fuel, food, and anything else you need are close at hand. Adelheidsdorf, a smaller village about seven kilometres away, has limited services. The cafes on the squares are a good place for a long lunch, and the asparagus season in spring, with local white asparagus served with ham and potatoes, is a regional treat. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild weather and fewer crowds, and winter brings frost and a quiet beauty.
t.bergen heath edge@52.8,10.0:
Bergen sits on the edge of the Lüneburg Heath, where the sandy, open heather country meets the pine forests and the farmland of the Aller valley, and it is a quiet town with a heavy history on its doorstep. A few kilometres to the north-west lies the memorial at Bergen-Belsen, where a Nazi concentration camp stood, and where tens of thousands of people died, among them Anne Frank and her sister Margot, in early 1945. The site is a place of remembrance, with a documentation centre and a large cemetery, and many visitors come to pay their respects. It is a sobering place and deserves time and quiet.

The country around the town is also home to a large military training area, one of the biggest in Germany, which has had the unintended effect of preserving large areas of heath from development. Access to the training grounds is restricted, but the roads and tracks around the edges pass through some beautiful scenery: heather, juniper, birch, and pine, with wide skies and few houses. Hermannsburg, a village a few kilometres to the south-west, was the seat of a Lutheran mission society, founded in the nineteenth century, that sent missionaries to Africa and elsewhere.

The riding is calm and pleasant. The roads are mostly flat, with long straights and open bends, running between pine plantations and fields, and the surface is generally good. The heath is best in late summer, when the heather blooms, and in autumn, when the birch leaves turn gold. Traffic is light, though weekends in August can bring cyclists, walkers, and tourists. Watch for military vehicles on some roads, and for deer and wild boar at dusk. Sand can drift across the surface after dry, windy days.

Fuel, supermarkets, and cafes are available in Bergen, and Hermannsburg is a smaller place, about nine kilometres away, with a few places to eat. If you have time, visit the memorial first, and then take a break at a cafe in town. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with fresh air and soft light, and winters are cold and grey, with frost and sometimes snow. Bring a rain layer, since the weather can change quickly in the flat country, and take care on sandy side roads.
t.damp coast road@54.6,10.0:
Damp sits on the northern shore of Eckernförde Bay, on the Schwansen peninsula, where Schleswig-Holstein stops pretending to be anything other than flat, open and wet around the edges. The Baltic here is not the dramatic kind. It is shallow, low in salt, and in July it warms up faster than almost any sea a Central European rider is likely to meet, which is exactly why people come and why this stop is listed for a swim.

The village itself is odd and worth a look. In the 1970s a whole holiday resort was built on the shore, with high-rise blocks and a spa district, and it still stands there like a piece of ambitious planning that landed in a field of rapeseed. Behind it the old manor estate and the farmland carry on as before. That contrast is typical of this coast: modest brick villages, long hedgerows planted on low earth banks that locals call Knicks, and every few kilometres a gap in the fields with a view of grey-blue water.

The riding is relaxed. From Eckernförde the minor roads run north along the bay through Schwansen, narrow in places, with tight little jogs where the road dodges a farmyard or a drainage ditch. Nothing climbs worth mentioning, so the pleasure is rhythm and light. Go in the evening when the low sun pushes long shadows across the fields, and watch for tractors and the occasional slug of mud after harvest. Wind is the real variable. A westerly off the land is easy, but a northeaster straight off the Baltic can lean on a loaded bike for an hour.

For practicalities, Damp is small, with around seventeen hundred people, so do not count on fuel in the village. Kappeln, about ten kilometres to the north on the Schlei inlet, is the sensible place to fill up, and it is also a pleasant town for a coffee, with its harbour and the old herring-smoking tradition on the quay. Waabs, closer by, is a quieter beach village.

Park by the beach and walk down. The water is shallow enough that you can wade a good way out, and the sand and pebbles are clean. Bring a towel in the pannier because the wind dries you off but also chills you quickly once the sun drops behind the hedges. Late in the day the light over the bay turns the colour of weak tea, and that is when you should leave.
t.gettorf@54.4,10.0:
Gettorf is the kind of town that makes a ride feel like a normal day. It sits on the Danish Wohld, the green peninsula between Kiel and Eckernförde Bay, roughly six thousand people around a church, a main street and a handful of cafés and bakeries. The name Danish Wohld goes back to a time when this was borderland between Danish and German influence, and the land was forested and thinly settled. Today it is farmland, hedgerow and quiet manor estates, with the sea close but rarely in view.

That is the appeal of the evening ride that stops here. You leave Kiel, cross a few kilometres of suburban sprawl, and within twenty minutes the road narrows and starts to follow the lie of the land. The corners are small, the surface is mostly good, and every so often a gap in the hedge opens onto a field of barley or rapeseed with the Baltic as a pale strip behind it. Because the roads are used mainly by locals and farm vehicles, you can usually hold a steady pace, but slow down for the blind farm entries and watch for tractors with wide trailers, especially in harvest weeks.

Gettorf works well as a coffee and a snack. There is no tourist spectacle, and that is a relief. Sit outside if the weather allows, watch people carry their shopping, and ask the person behind the counter where the good back road to Eckernförde goes. Local advice usually beats a map here. The larger road through town carries commuter traffic between Kiel and Eckernförde, so pick your timing if you want calm.

Fuel is easy. A town this size has petrol stations, and so does Kiel on the way in. Rest-wise, there are benches and small greens near the centre, and the villages of Tüttendorf and Neudorf-Bornstein, a few kilometres off, offer quieter stops if the main street is busy.

The best time is the early evening in late spring or summer, when the light slants across the fields and the air smells of cut grass and diesel and, if the wind is right, of salt from the bay. By the time you head back to Kiel, the sky behind you is usually doing something worth turning around for.
t.top of the world store@45.0,-109.5:
The Beartooth Highway climbs out of the plains of Montana into a world of rock, snow and alpine lakes, and it has a reputation to match. The journalist Charles Kuralt called it the most beautiful drive in America, and plenty of riders agree. US 212 crosses the Beartooth Plateau at nearly 3,340 metres, one of the highest highways in the northern Rockies, and its twists and switchbacks carry you from pine forest to bare tundra in the space of a few kilometres. The road was finished in 1936 after years of difficult work through steep terrain.

The Top of the World store is a small, seasonal outpost near the high point of the road on the Wyoming side, and its position, surrounded by lakes and peaks, gives it the feel of a mountain hut. Services here are basic. Expect a few supplies, snacks and drinks when it is open, which depends on the season and the snow, and do not plan on anything more. In this country, the road itself is open only for part of the year, usually from late spring to mid-autumn, and sudden snowstorms can close it even in summer, so check conditions before you ride.

The scenery is hard to overstate. Granite peaks rise on every side, including Granite Peak, the highest point in Montana at over 3,900 metres, and glacial lakes lie in the hollows like dropped coins. Wildflowers bloom in the alpine meadows in July, and mountain goats and marmots live among the rocks. The air is thin and clear, and the light has a hard, bright quality that makes colours sharper. Weather can change in minutes, and temperatures at the top can be near freezing in any month, so bring warm layers, gloves and a waterproof jacket.

Riding here is exhilarating. The road has tight switchbacks on the Montana side, with steep drops and big views, and it eases into long, high curves across the plateau. The surface is generally good, but frost heaves and patches appear, and gravel can collect on corners. Traffic is moderate, with campers and sightseers, so be ready to follow slower vehicles.

Fuel is not guaranteed at the store. Red Lodge, about thirty kilometres away on the Montana side, and Cooke City on the other are the places to fill up, and the distance between them is considerable. Carry water and snacks, and make sure your tank is full before the climb.
t.ahrenshoop coast@54.4,12.4:
Ahrenshoop sits on the narrow neck of land where the Fischland meets the Darß, a thin strip of dune, forest and reed between the Baltic Sea and the Bodden lagoons. It was a fishing village until the 1890s, when painters arrived, drawn by the light and the quiet, and settled to form an artists' colony that has lasted more than a century. The reed-thatched cottages, the small galleries and the Kunstkaten, little art studios in old houses, are the legacy, and the village still has an easy, creative feel. On a grey day the sea and sky merge into silver, and on a clear one the horizon is a hard, bright line.

The coast here is dynamic. The sea eats at the cliff, called the Hohes Ufer, a bluff of sand and clay several metres high, and every winter storm takes a little more. Behind the beach, the land narrows so much that you can see both the Baltic and the lagoon from one spot. On the lagoon side, the Bodden are shallow and sheltered, with reed beds that hold cranes, herons and sea eagles, and in autumn thousands of cranes gather in the area to rest on their way south, one of the great bird spectacles of northern Germany.

On the road, Ahrenshoop is the point where the long ride through the Fischland and Darß finds its rhythm. The road is a single main route, flat and gently curving through pine woods and fields, and there are few alternatives, so traffic can build up on summer weekends. A steady pace and patience are the keys. Surface quality is good, and bends are mild, so this is a ride for scenery rather than speed. Wind off the sea can be strong, and crosswinds on the exposed stretches need attention. Early morning and evening are the best times.

Parking near the beach is limited and charged, so look for the official lots and leave valuables with you. Fuel is not abundant in the village itself, and the nearest town of real size is Ribnitz-Damgarten, about fifteen kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and a good amber museum. Born and Wustrow, smaller villages nearby, have cafés and fish stalls.

Try smoked fish from a stand, particularly herring or eel, with fresh bread, and eat it on the dune or the harbour wall. The air tastes of salt and pine, and the gulls watch you closely.
t.prerow forest edge@54.4,12.6:
At Prerow the road meets the Darß forest, and the sense of being at the end of something sets in. The village is a former seafarers' settlement, with long, low houses with reed roofs and a church that holds model ships hanging from the ceiling, a custom that tells you how many men from this coast went to sea. Beyond the village a protected national park begins, a wide wilderness of forest, dune and bog that is among the wildest stretches of the German Baltic. The old forest has trees bent by wind into strange shapes, and the ground is carpeted in moss and fern.

The beach at Prerow is one of the broadest and finest on the coast, a long band of white sand stretching away on both sides, backed by dunes and pine, and the water is clean and shallow for a long way out. In summer, families fill the beach, and the Baltic warms to a pleasant temperature in July and August, though it is still cool compared with the Mediterranean. Strandkörbe, the wicker beach chairs with hoods, line the sand and are the traditional shelter against wind. In autumn, the beach empties and the light turns steely, and a walk along the tideline in a jacket is an honest pleasure.

The road into the forest is narrow and quiet. East of Prerow, cars are restricted, and the track toward the Darßer Ort lighthouse is open only to walkers and cyclists, so the bike stays behind. That keeps the forest peaceful and means you can wander without traffic. Deer and wild boar live here, and in autumn the red deer rut can be heard from far off. On the ride in, watch for deer at dusk and slow down on the forest road, where the surface can be damp and covered in needles.

Barth, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services, and Zingst, a bit closer, has shops and fuel. Prerow has cafés, bakeries and fish stands, so you can eat well without leaving the village, but fuel should be topped up before you arrive.

Be prepared for wind and sudden showers, and keep a dry layer in the pannier. After a swim, the warm sand and the smell of resin from the pines make a good place to sit and watch the sea.
t.barth bodden roads@54.4,12.7:
Barth is a harbour town on the Bodden, the shallow lagoons that lie behind the Darß peninsula, and it has the unhurried quality of a place that has been a port for centuries. Its centre is a pleasant mix of brick buildings, a church with a tall tower and a waterfront lined with boats, and from the quay you can look across the water to flat green shores and reed beds. The town's nickname, Vinetastadt, refers to a legend of a lost city called Vineta that was swallowed by the sea, and the story has become part of the town's charm.

Barth has a more serious past too. In the sixteenth century, the dukes of Pomerania had a printing press here that produced the Barther Bibel, an early Low German Bible printed in 1588. In the Second World War, the town housed a large camp for captured Allied airmen, Stalag Luft I, which held many American and British prisoners until it was liberated by Soviet troops in 1945. A museum now remembers the camp and the people who passed through it.

The roads around Barth are some of the best leisurely riding on the coast. Avenues of old trees, mostly lime, chestnut and maple, line the narrow back roads, and the tunnel of branches filters the light into green and gold. The surface is generally fair, though some of the old roads have patched asphalt and the occasional bump, and the bends are gentle. Farmland, reed and water alternate, and in the evening the Bodden turns pink and silver. Cranes pass overhead in spring and autumn, and the sound of their calls carries a long way.

Barth, with about nine thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and fish restaurants along the harbour, so it is a natural place to refuel and eat. Smoked fish, zander and herring are on most menus, often served with potatoes and a cold beer. Parking for motorcycles is easy near the harbour, though it gets busy in summer.

Wind is the main factor. The land is flat, and gusts can build over the open water, so a crosswind on an exposed stretch needs steady hands. In summer, midges and gnats can be bothersome near the reeds in the evening, and a bit of repellent helps.

Take the avenue roads rather than the main highway when you can. They are slower and quieter, and they give a better sense of the land. The best light is in the late afternoon, when the sun slants through the trees.
t.schwaan river road@53.9,12.1:
Schwaan lies on the Warnow river a short ride south of Rostock, and it is one of those small Mecklenburg towns that surprise you with a bit of art. In the late nineteenth century, painters were drawn to the Warnow valley for its meadows, light and quiet, and Schwaan became known as a colony of artists, a bit like Ahrenshoop on the coast. A small museum shows work from the period, and the old town still has a gentle, creative atmosphere. The Gothic brick church, built in the typical north German style of red brick, stands above the river and gives the place its character.

The Warnow is a slow, wide river that winds through wet meadows and reed beds on its way to the Baltic at Rostock. Along its banks, the land is flat and open, with willows and alders and the occasional heron standing in the shallows. The river was once a trade route, carrying grain and timber, and old mills and bridges still mark the water. In spring, the fields are bright yellow with rapeseed, and in summer they turn gold with wheat.

The riding here is soft and relaxed. The river road follows the valley with gentle bends, avenues of old trees and a surface that is mostly good, though some stretches of old tarmac are patched. Traffic is light, apart from farm vehicles, and the whole ride has an easy rhythm that suits a slow afternoon. Early morning, when mist lies over the water, is lovely, and evening gives a long, soft light across the fields. Wind can be a problem on exposed sections, and the road can be slick with leaves in autumn.

Schwaan has about five thousand people, so it has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries and a couple of cafés, and it is a sensible place to stop before moving on into the more rural country. The small cafés near the church serve cake and coffee, and the local bakeries sell fresh bread and pastries. Rostock, the large city nearby, offers everything else, with a historic centre, a harbour and a long Hanseatic history.

Take a moment on the bridge to look at the river. In summer, canoeists drift past, and in the evening the water reflects the sky in a long band of colour. If you have time, a short detour along the river to a mill or a ferry crossing gives a good sense of how the valley has worked for centuries.
t.malchin lake view@53.7,12.8:
Malchin is a lake town in the heart of what is called Mecklenburg Switzerland, a name that makes visitors from the Alps smile, because the highest hills here are not much more than a hundred metres. But the name has a point. After the flat plains of northern Germany, this area of rolling moraine, deep lakes and beech woods does feel like a small world of its own, shaped by the last ice sheet that left behind a landscape of ridges, hollows and scattered boulders.

The town sits between two lakes, the Malchiner See and the larger Kummerower See, with the Peene river flowing out through meadows toward the Baltic. Two big brick churches, St. Maria and St. Johannis, stand over the old town, and their towers can be seen from far across the water. The streets are quiet and the buildings a mix of Gothic, baroque and plain functional, reflecting centuries of trade in grain and cattle. The region also produced the Low German writer Fritz Reuter, born in nearby Stavenhagen, whose humorous stories of country life are still loved here, and a museum in his birthplace tells his story.

The lake view is the point of the stop. From the shore, the water spreads out in a broad sheet, with reeds along the edge and fields rising gently on the far side. In summer, sailing boats and canoes dot the surface, and in autumn mist lies over the lake in the morning. Birds are plentiful, with swans, grebes, herons and, if you are lucky, a white-tailed eagle circling high above the water.

For riders, the roads here are among the most pleasant in the north. Narrow tree-lined lanes wind between lakes and manor houses, with gentle gradients and good views, and the surface is generally decent. Many of the villages have a manor, a church and a few cottages, and the estates, once the seat of local nobility, give the landscape a faded grandeur. Traffic is light, and a relaxed pace is the right one. Watch for farm vehicles, and for deer on the roads at dusk.

Malchin has about eight thousand people, with fuel, shops and cafés, so it is easy to stop here. Neukalen, a smaller town nearby, has a quiet harbour and a few places for food. Smoked fish and local cake are the usual snacks, and you can eat them on a bench by the water.

A mild afternoon in late spring or early autumn is the time to come, when the light is soft and the lake is calm.
t.teterow food window@53.8,12.6:
Teterow is a small town beside a lake, and among motorcycle people it has a bigger reputation than its size suggests. The Bergring, a hilly circuit just outside the town, has hosted motorcycle racing since the 1920s and 1930s, and it was one of the best-known tracks in East Germany, drawing crowds to watch grass track and speedway on the steep slopes. It is a place where riders from across the region come to watch, and the local pride in it is real. If you ride through when a meeting is on, the roads fill with bikes and the air smells of two-stroke.

The old town is pleasant. Two medieval gates, the Rostocker Tor and the Malchiner Tor, survive from the town walls, and the market square has a mix of brick and half-timbered houses. The Teterower See, a lake beside the town, has an island and a path around it, and in summer people swim and fish from its shores. Locals have a nickname, the pike, and the fish appears on coats of arms and in stories, a bit of humour the town wears with pride.

For a rider, Teterow works well as a food window, a place to pause between the lakes and manors of Mecklenburg Switzerland. The roads to the town are tree-lined and gentle, with pleasant curves, moderate surfaces and little traffic. The land is rolling farmland and forest, and the manor houses that appear along the way are reminders of the great estates that dominated this part of Germany for centuries. Early summer, when the rapeseed blooms and the beeches are bright green, is the best season.

Teterow has about nine and a half thousand people, so fuel is available at stations along the main roads, and there are supermarkets, bakeries and a few restaurants. The market square has cafés with outdoor seating, and the local menus feature fish, game and potatoes, with regional beer. Many places close in the afternoon, so aim for lunch before two, and expect modest prices.

Parking for motorcycles is easy near the centre, and you can walk to the lake in a few minutes. If you have time, take a short ride up to the Bergring and look at the slopes, even when there is no racing.

In the evening, the lake is quiet and the sky turns pink, and the road home through the fields is gentle.
t.kuhlungsborn beach road@54.2,11.8:
Kühlungsborn is really three villages that were married in 1938 and given a name that sounds like a spa. Brunshaupten, Arendsee and Fulgen had all been fishing hamlets and then bathing resorts, and today the merged town runs along the Baltic for some three kilometres, with a long promenade, a sea bridge that reaches out over the water, and a line of white villas in the old resort style with carved balconies and little towers.

That style has a reason. The grand duke of Mecklenburg made the coast fashionable in the nineteenth century, starting a few kilometres east at Heiligendamm, the so-called white town, and the lesser seaside towns followed. Between Kühlungsborn and Bad Doberan runs the narrow-gauge steam railway everyone calls Molli, which has puffed along since the 1880s and still arrives with a whistle and plenty of coal smoke. If you hear a whistle while you are parked, that is the explanation.

The beach road is a gentle affair, not a challenge. You come down off the low Kühlung hills, which are only about a hundred and thirty metres high but feel substantial against the flat coast, and run along the waterfront at promenade speed with the Baltic on one side. The sand is fine and pale, the water is shallow and brisk, and even in August you will want a moment before going in. The sea here is almost tideless and only mildly salty, one of the reasons the brackish water feels softer than the North Sea. On a clear evening the sun slips into the water to the north-west, which is fair compensation for the cold.

Practical things are easy because the place lives for visitors. There are petrol stations and shops near the main roads, ice cream and fish rolls along the front, and plenty of cafés where you can sit with a coffee and watch cyclists. Weekends in July and August are packed, parking is tight and the promenade is a place for strolling, not riding, so pick a weekday morning if you can. Spring and autumn, when the beech woods behind the town turn green or copper, are the best times for the road.
t.rerik cliffs photo@54.1,11.6:
The coast between Kühlungsborn and Rerik is the one stretch of this part of Mecklenburg that has any drama. The land here rises into a low cliff of clay and sand, a metre-by-metre record of the ice age, and the Baltic keeps chewing at it so that trees lean out over the edge and every storm drops a slice onto the beach. Stand back from the lip when you take a photo. The ground is softer than it looks, and the sea does not care about a view.

Rerik itself, a small resort on the Salzhaff lagoon, sits just beyond. The Salzhaff is a shallow, brackish inlet separated from the open sea by a narrow peninsula, popular with kitesurfers and with birdwatchers, since waders and geese gather in large numbers outside the summer season. A Slavic trading place called Reric is mentioned in medieval sources, and historians still argue about whether it stood here or somewhere nearer Wismar, so you can pick your side of the argument over a fish sandwich.

Near Bastorf, a few minutes away, a small lighthouse from the late nineteenth century stands on a wooded rise, a quiet corner that few visitors reach. The roads that lead to it are narrow country lanes, often lined with old trees, and much of this coastal belt is reached by two-lane roads with no hurry in them. The best light for pictures comes either in the early morning, when mist hangs over the fields, or in the evening, when the sky over the water goes pink and the cliff catches the last sun.

Fuel is not available in Bastorf, which is a tiny village. The nearest proper stop is Kühlungsborn, about eleven kilometres back, where you will find petrol stations and shops, and Rerik also has basic supplies. Weather matters on this coast. A cold wind from the north-east can strip the warmth out of a day even in June, and gusts across open fields make a loaded bike twitchy. Dress for the sea rather than for the road, and carry a waterproof layer, because a clear sky here can change in half an hour.
t.neukloster inland sweep@53.9,11.7:
Neukloster is a small town of just over four thousand people, tucked between woods and a lake south of the Baltic coast, and it is named for the thing that made it. In the early thirteenth century a Cistercian nunnery was founded here, and its brick church still stands at the centre, a good example of the Gothic building style that spread along this part of the Baltic. Brick instead of stone because there is no stone here: the glaciers left clay, so the whole region learned to bake its own building material and became very good at it.

After the Reformation the nuns' estate passed to the dukes and later to a school, and the former convent buildings and church still shape the heart of town. Inside, the church is plain and tall, with a long nave and some late medieval furnishings, and it is worth a short visit if the door is open. Outside, Neuklosterer See lies a short walk away, with a small beach that locals use and no hotels to speak of, which is a quiet kind of pleasure on a hot afternoon.

The inland sweep is what gives this stretch its charm. After the busy, polished coast with its seaside villas, the road turns inland to farmland and forest, with avenues of lime and oak, long straights over rolling fields and sudden dips through villages built of red brick. It is not a technical road. The bends are mild, the asphalt is mostly fine, and the speed is dictated by tractors and the occasional cyclist. In early summer the rapeseed turns whole slopes yellow, and in September the harvest dust hangs in the low light.

Neukloster is big enough for a petrol station, a bakery and a couple of simple places for lunch, though you should not count on long opening hours on Sundays. Wismar lies sixteen kilometres away to the north, a Hanseatic port with a UNESCO old town, and it is the place to go for anything bigger, including a full tank or a proper meal. Keep an eye out for deer on the edges of woodland, especially at dusk, and for farm vehicles pulling out of side tracks without much warning.
t.yataki jo site@35.1,132.4:
The name Yataki-jo sounds like a puzzle until you realise it just means Yataki castle, and the castle is a ridge in the forested hills behind the old silver town of Omori, in Shimane on the Sea of Japan side. There is no keep, no white walls. What survives is earthworks, terraces cut into the hillside, and the kind of lookout position that makes sense once you stand there and see how many routes it watches. The reason anyone fought over this ground is under it. Iwami Ginzan was among the largest silver mines in the world in the sixteenth century, and the lords of the region, the Ouchi, the Amago and the Mori among them, spent decades taking it from one another.

The riding in these hills is a quiet one. Prefectural roads narrow into one-and-a-half lanes, climb through cedar plantations and cut across steep valleys with a few rice terraces left in the folds. The surface is usually decent but often damp and sprinkled with pine needles, leaves or the odd fallen branch, so stay modest after rain. Moss grows on every north-facing wall, and you will meet more farm trucks than other motorcycles. The nearest proper town is Odachō-oda, about fourteen kilometres away, which has fuel stations, convenience stores and a few places to eat. Higher up, nothing of the sort.

The silver mines and the old street at Omori carry UNESCO listing, and what makes the landscape special is how little scarring there is. Miners worked tunnels rather than open pits and replanted behind them, so the forest has largely taken the area back. Walking up to a castle site you pass over stone steps that are older than most of the villages near them. The trail is rough enough that boots beat riding gear.

Bring a little patience with the weather. The Sea of Japan coast is wet in winter, with heavy snow in the hills some years, and rainy season in June can mean a grey week. Autumn is the best time, when the maples turn and the light slants through the cedars late in the afternoon. Let the day finish on the coast: the harbours along this stretch have good fish at modest prices and are never in a rush.
t.okidomari@35.1,132.3:
Okidomari is a small fishing harbour on the Shimane coast, wedged into a cove with steep green hills at its back, and today it looks like nothing much at all. Boats are pulled up, nets are drying, an old man is doing something patient to an engine. In the sixteenth century the same cove was one of the ports through which Iwami silver left for the world. Ore from the mines at Omori was carried down to the coast on foot along a mountain track, the Iwami Ginzan Kaido, and shipped from places like this to the markets of Japan and abroad. Silver from this stretch of coast helped shape trade across East Asia, and it is a startling thought when you are looking at a tiny slipway.

The coast road is the reason to ride here. Route 9 and the smaller roads around Yunotsu run in and out of headlands, with short climbs, blind bends and little villages of dark tile roofs and stacked stone walls. The Sea of Japan is often rough and grey, and the wind off it can push a bike around on exposed stretches. After rain the slopes shed mud and leaves onto the tarmac, so take the bends gently. Fishermen park half on the road, which is just part of the charm. In summer there is a smell of seaweed and warm tar, in winter salt and diesel.

Yunotsu, the next harbour town, is an old hot-spring village with a street of narrow houses and a tradition of bathing in mineral water. It is also on the UNESCO listing with the silver mines. Gotsu, about fourteen kilometres away, is the bigger place for fuel and a proper meal, and it has a good port of its own. Smaller stations along the coast tend to close early in the evening, so do not run the tank too low.

Eat fish here without hesitation. The catch is landed in the morning and cooked simply, with plenty of rice and pickles. If you want a quiet evening, the coast around sunset, when the sea goes pewter and orange, is worth waiting for. Spring and autumn are the kindest seasons; summer is humid and the winter sea is dramatic but cold.
t.yahazu jo site@35.1,132.4:
Yahazu-jo is another mountain castle site in the hills behind Omori, among the ridges that guarded the Iwami silver mines, and it adds up to the same story as its neighbour Yataki-jo, but with its own angle. Where one site is about watching a valley, this one is about the chain: a series of small fortresses linked by ridgeline paths, so that smoke or a signal fire could pass a warning along the hills. Silver paid for armies in the sixteenth century, and whoever held the mountains held the mines. The castles were mostly built of earth and timber, and what remains are ditches, flat platforms and the shape of old gateways, now overgrown with cedar, oak and bamboo grass.

Reaching it is a country ride more than a destination. The roads climb out of the Omori and Odachō valleys in short steep runs, and in places the surface turns patchy, with moss on the shady side and fallen leaves in autumn. There are few guardrails and no real shoulders. A single narrow lane may serve three farmhouses and a shrine. Timber trucks use some of the routes, so listen on blind corners. Traffic is sparse, but whatever comes is large.

The nearest sizeable town is Odachō-oda, fourteen kilometres away, where you will find fuel, a supermarket and a handful of eateries. Gotsu on the coast is the other option, a bit further. If you have time, the old town of Omori is worth walking through, a single long street of tiled merchant houses, small cafes and shrines, with a gentle slope and almost no traffic. The silver mine tunnel at Ryugenji Mabu is open to walkers, and the cool air inside is welcome in summer.

Nature here is deep Chugoku mountain forest. Macaques are sometimes seen, boar leave their rooting in the damp soil, and the dawn chorus in May and June is loud. Snakes sun themselves on warm tarmac in summer. If you stop to look around, give the ground a glance before you step. Autumn is lovely, with red maple and golden ginkgo, but the light goes quickly, so plan to be down from the hills by late afternoon.
t.mosquee berdaoui@33.8,10.8:
The mosques of Djerba are like nothing else in the Muslim world. They are low, white and plain, with thick buttressed walls, small windows and flat or domed roofs, and from a distance they look like fortresses, which is more or less what they were. Djerba is an island off the south of Tunisia, flat and hot, and over the centuries it was raided by pirates and attacked by the Spanish, so its mosques were built to protect worshippers and store supplies. Most belong to the Ibadi school of Islam, a small branch distinct from the Sunni and Shia, which has survived on Djerba and in a few other places in North Africa for over a thousand years.

Berdaoui is typical of the island's mosques, set among palms and olive trees on the flat farmland between Houmt Souk and the villages of the interior. Its whitewashed walls are thick and sloped, and a small minaret rises from one corner. Inside, there is a prayer hall with plain columns and a niche facing Mecca, with space for studying, and often a well or cistern for water. The whitewash is renewed regularly, and the buttresses give the mosque a gently sculpted look, like a carved piece of soap.

As a visitor, treat these as active places of worship. Non-Muslims are generally not admitted, and it is best to observe from outside, quietly and without intruding. A respectful photograph from the road is usually fine, but do not walk into the courtyard during prayer.

The ride across the island is flat and easy, along straight roads lined with olive trees, date palms and low white houses with domed roofs. Traffic is moderate, with scooters, vans and horse carts, and the occasional donkey. Roads can be sandy at the edges. Sirocco winds from the south bring heat and dust, while summer temperatures are very high. The best seasons are spring and autumn.

Houmt Souk, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and a lively market with fine pottery, and the fort, Borj el Kebir, stands at the harbour. Erriadh, closer, is home to El Ghriba, one of the oldest synagogues in North Africa, and a village where artists have painted street murals. Eat brik, a thin pastry filled with egg and tuna, and fresh grilled fish.
t.mosquee sidi jmour@33.8,10.7:
Sidi Jmour is a mosque near the north coast of Djerba, in an area of dunes, olive groves and sandy tracks, and it is named, as many Tunisian shrines are, for a holy man. The mosque has the family look of the island's buildings: thick white walls, strong buttresses and a small dome, and it stands in open country, so you see it from a distance, bright against the dark green of the olives. Most mosques on Djerba have a sacred feeling of austere simplicity, and the whitewashed walls reflect the sun in a way that is almost dazzling at midday.

The area is known as a place of quiet. Zone Temlel, the area the route pairs with it, is part of the quieter, less built-up side of the island, and some stretches of the coast are lined with beaches of fine pale sand. The Mediterranean here is warm and shallow, with water that turns turquoise on calm days. Flamingos sometimes feed in the island's lagoons, and the whole place has a sleepy, sun-baked air.

The riding is gentle. Roads here are narrow and may have sand drifting across the tarmac, so take care in bends. Farmers use the roads with carts, tractors and animals, and the right of way is often claimed by the larger vehicle. Distances are short, and it is hard to get lost, since the island is only about twenty-five kilometres across. The usual hazards are heat, dust and the occasional dog.

Erriadh and Houmt Souk are the nearest towns, about ten and eleven kilometres away. Houmt Souk has fuel, food and a pleasant harbour where fishermen unload the catch each afternoon. Djerba is famous for its octopus, which is cooked in stews and salads, and for couscous with fish. Dates and olives are everywhere, and a glass of mint tea with pine nuts is the usual conclusion to a meal.

Visit in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the heat gentler. Be respectful at religious buildings. A scarf over the shoulders is sensible near mosques.
t.mosquee abou messouer@33.9,10.8:
Abou Messouer sits closer to Houmt Souk than most of the island's mosques, in a landscape of small farms and walled gardens, and it is a handy place to understand what makes a Djerban mosque different. The building is a compact block of white plaster, with the typical heavy buttresses, a small dome over the prayer hall and an outdoor space where people gather. The old Ibadi mosques were not only places of prayer but community centres, courts and schools, and some still hold a small Koranic school for children.

The island has hundreds of mosques, a figure often quoted as more than three hundred, and almost none is big. Villagers built them in neighbourhoods called houma, each with its own mosque, and in the past a family or tribe would pay for it. The effect is a landscape dotted with white domes, like salt crystals on a green cloth. The proportion, the plain geometry and the way the buildings seem to grow from the land are what visitors remember.

For the rider, Djerba is a pleasant place to unwind after the mainland. The causeway from the mainland at El Kantara, an ancient Roman crossing, carries a road, and a car ferry runs from Jorf to Ajim. The island is flat, and the roads are mostly straight, with traffic that gets dense near Houmt Souk. Watch for pedestrians and mopeds, and drive right-handed. The Tunisian police carry out frequent checks, and speed limits are enforced.

Houmt Souk is the island's capital, a lively town of white buildings with blue shutters, with a covered market, a fort on the harbour and a clutch of cafes. The market sells ceramics from Guellala, a village in the south famous for its potters, and leather, spices and woven goods. Fuel is available at stations around the town. Try the local seafood, such as grilled sea bream, or brik, a crisp pastry.

Summer is very hot, and many visitors come in spring and autumn. In April the island is green and flowering, and the air is soft.
t.mosquee el fguira@33.7,10.8:
El Fguira stands in the south of Djerba, a long way from the bustle of Houmt Souk, in a part of the island where the farms are bigger and the roads quiet. The label puts it among the more remote of the mosques that make up the Djerba listing, and the journey is a pleasure in itself. The mosque is a small, whitewashed building with strong buttresses and a rounded roof, standing among olive trees and palms, and its shape is as simple as a child's drawing of a house. Like the others, it is still used for prayer, so it should be seen from outside and with respect.

The south of the island has a different feel. Flat, sandy land stretches toward the sea, and the coast has lagoons where birds gather, including flamingos in winter. Ajim, the old ferry port on the southwest corner, looks across to the mainland, and in Guellala, where potters have dug clay for centuries, workshops sell large red jars and plates, and a museum tells the story of the island's heritage.

Oil and water are central to life here. Olive trees, some many centuries old, cover wide parts of Djerba, and the oil is pressed in village mills. Wells and cisterns collect rainwater, which is precious on an island with no rivers. The traditional Djerban house, the menzel, is a walled farm compound with a dome-roofed living quarters, and it is designed to keep cool. Many are decorated with blue and white paint. They are scattered among the fields, with a mosque for each neighbourhood.

The roads are good for relaxed riding, but long stretches lack shade, so take water. Distances are modest, though signposting is sparse, and a map is useful. Erriadh, fourteen kilometres off, has basic services, and Houmt Souk, almost twenty kilometres, has fuel and everything else. Fill up in town before exploring the south, since stations are fewer.

Wind is frequent, and when the sirocco blows the sky turns a milky yellow. The best time is April or October, when the days are warm and the evenings cool. At sunset, the white domes turn pink and gold.
t.former hacienda of the limpia concepcion:
Out on the high desert of northern Durango, where the land is pale, flat and ringed by distant ranges, a hacienda is still the most natural sort of landmark. These great estates grew along the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the silver road that ran from Mexico City all the way north to Santa Fe in New Mexico, and the stretch near Villa Ocampo is part of the route that UNESCO listed in 2010. Wagons, mule trains, soldiers, friars and miners all passed this way, and the haciendas fed them, watered them and sometimes cheated them.

The country here is huge and quiet. Roads are straight for long stretches and then bend briefly around a dry arroyo or a low hill, with mesquite, huizache and cactus lining the verge and cattle wandering where they like. Tarmac in this region can be patchy, with broken edges and potholes that appear without warning, so keep your speed sensible and your eyes ahead. Distances are large, towns are small, and cell coverage is not something to count on. The best months are October to April, when the sun is bearable. Summer is fiercely hot, and brief thunderstorms in July and August can flood the washes in minutes.

Look at an old hacienda and you read the whole logic of the colonial north. There is usually a big courtyard, a chapel, thick adobe or stone walls, store rooms, stables, and a main house where the owner lived in relative comfort while the workers lived outside the gate. Many are now ruins, softly collapsing back into the earth, with arches still standing against the sky and swallows nesting where the chapel bell once hung. The quiet is remarkable, broken only by wind and the odd dog.

On the practical side, plan carefully. Villa Ocampo is a small town of about a thousand people, and while it may have a small shop and a simple fuel supply, you should not count on it. Fill your tank in a larger place before you come, carry water and some food, and tell somebody your route. Ask permission before walking onto land, since many of these sites sit on private ranches. If you get the pace right, the reward is a feeling of space and unhurried history, a silver road that is now a quiet one.
t.temple of san miguel of the town of vill:
The little church of San Miguel is the quiet heart of Villa Ocampo, which sits in the dry north of Durango, close to where the state meets Chihuahua. The settlement belongs to the long chain of towns strung along the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the old road that carried silver south and supplies, settlers and missionaries north, and it still has the layout you would expect: a plaza, a church at its edge, low houses of adobe and brick, and a feeling that nobody is in a hurry.

Churches along this road were usually built with whatever the land gave, which here means earth, lime and timber. They tend to be simple, with a plain facade, a bell tower, and an interior that surprises you with its colour, a painted altar, candles, saints wearing real fabric. San Miguel, the archangel, is a popular patron of frontier towns, protector of those who live at the edge.

The riding that leads to the town is quiet desert road, broad and open, with long straights that give way to occasional curves around dry watercourses. The surface can be rough in places, with the edges eaten away and cattle drifting across, so it rewards patience. Light is the thing to savour. In the early morning and again before sunset, the hills turn gold and rose, the shadows grow long, and the sky seems far bigger than elsewhere. Winter nights can be cold at this altitude, while summer afternoons are hot and sometimes broken by sudden storms.

Practicalities are limited, and it is better to be honest about that. Villa Ocampo has only about a thousand inhabitants, and the next town of any size, Matamoros, is a good distance away, so fuel is not something to gamble on. Arrive with a full tank, water, and a little cash, since small shops may not take cards. Ask politely before going inside the church, and be quiet if a service is going on. A simple meal of tacos, beans or machaca, the dried and shredded beef of the north, is the sort of thing you may find, if the day is kind.
t.oderbruch@52.4,13.9:
East of Berlin, the land flattens and the lakes begin, and this start and finish lies near Grünheide and Spreenhagen, in Brandenburg, at the edge of the forested lake country around Erkner and the Müggelsee. The area has a long literary link, since the playwright Gerhart Hauptmann lived in Erkner and set some of his early plays here, and today it is known more for the large Tesla factory in Grünheide, which opened in 2022. Pine forest, sandy tracks and small lakes surround it, and in summer the roads are busy with cyclists and swimmers.

The Oderbruch, the destination, lies about sixty kilometres to the northeast, along the Polish border, and it is a strange and beautiful place, a wide, flat plain of former marsh that was drained in the eighteenth century by order of Frederick the Great. His engineers cut a new channel for the Oder river and built dikes, creating fertile farmland where there had been floods and fever, and settlers from across Europe moved in. The villages lie along the dikes, with brick churches and low houses, and the horizon is wide and empty. Storks nest on the roofs and cranes gather in the fields in autumn.

The Oderbruch has a darker history too. In April 1945, the Seelow Heights, at its western edge, saw one of the last big battles of the Second World War, when the Red Army broke through German defences on its way to Berlin. A museum at Seelow tells the story. The plain has also flooded several times, most recently in 1997, when the dikes were tested.

The ride across the plain is gentle and open. The roads run straight along the dikes and between fields, with the wind an almost constant companion, and views stretching for miles. The surface is mostly good, with some old cobbles in the villages. Sunsets are huge here, and the flat light in late autumn has a special quality, with mist rising from the fields. Winter is cold and the roads can ice up.

Fuel is available in Grünheide, Fürstenwalde and the larger towns, but the villages on the plain have few services, so fill the tank before heading out. Roadside stalls sell seasonal produce, from asparagus to apples, and village inns serve game and fish.
t.speicherstadt and kontorhaus district wi:
There is nowhere in Europe quite like the Speicherstadt, a whole district of warehouses built of dark red brick, rising straight out of the canals as if the water were a street. The buildings date from the 1880s, when Hamburg joined the German customs union and needed a place to store goods outside the customs zone, and they stand on thousands of oak piles driven into the soft mud. Their neo-Gothic gables, turrets and copper roofs make them look like a row of castles, and the streets between them are so narrow that you can touch both sides with outstretched hands. UNESCO recognised the district in 2015, together with the neighbouring Kontorhaus quarter.

The warehouses were built to hold coffee, tea, spices and carpets, and some of these goods are still stored here today, so the smell of roasting coffee sometimes drifts along the canals. At high tide the canals rise almost to the street, and in a storm surge the lower floors flood, which is why the ground levels are designed with removable barriers. Across the road, the Kontorhaus district is another style entirely: tall brick office buildings from the 1920s, of which the Chilehaus, built for a merchant who made his fortune in Chilean saltpetre, is the best known, shaped like the prow of a ship with sharp corners.

For a motorcyclist, this is a place for walking and looking rather than riding. The streets are cobbled and tight, and traffic is dense around the HafenCity and the Elbphilharmonie, the concert hall built on an old warehouse that opened in 2017 and has a public viewing terrace. Park at the edge, because access to some of the lanes is restricted, and wander through the quiet courtyards. A railway crosses the district on a viaduct, adding to the industrial feel. The model railway museum in the old warehouses is one of the busiest attractions in Germany.

The practical side is simple. This is the middle of a city of nearly two million, with fuel on the ring roads and cafes in every street. Early morning is the best time, when the light is soft and the tourist groups are still asleep, and the canals are quiet and reflect the brick. In autumn, when the mist rises from the water, the Speicherstadt looks like something out of a detective film.
t.zone houmt souk@33.9,10.9:
Houmt Souk is the main town of Djerba, the low flat island off the south-east coast of Tunisia that Greek legend identified as the land of the lotus-eaters, where Odysseus's men forgot their homeward journey after eating a sweet fruit. The island is only a short ferry hop or a Roman causeway from the mainland, and its main town sits on the north coast, a sprawl of whitewashed houses, arcaded squares and market lanes around a small harbour. The name means market quarter, and its alleys still hold stalls of spices, leather slippers, silver and pottery, with a daily fish market down by the quay.

A squat sea fortress, Borj el Kebir, built by the Spanish in the fifteenth century and later rebuilt by the Ottomans, guards the harbour. It has a gruesome history, since in 1560 an Ottoman fleet crushed a Christian expedition here, and the bones of the dead were piled into a tower that stood for three centuries. Today the fort is a museum, and the view from the ramparts over the boats and the flat blue gulf is pleasant. The town has several old caravanserais, called fondouks, and mosques of the local Ibadi tradition, in which whitewashed domes and buttressed walls give an almost fortified look.

Djerba is a gentle island to ride around, with roads that are mostly straight and level, lined with olive groves, date palms and whitewashed farm compounds. The speed limits are low and enforced, and the traffic includes scooters, tourist buses, donkey carts and the occasional camel, so do not expect speed. Strong winds can blow in from the sea, bringing sand across the road, and in summer the heat is intense by midday. Spring and autumn are the pleasantest times to ride. At junctions and roundabouts, local driving can be improvised, so take care.

Houmt Souk has about sixty thousand people and plenty of fuel, restaurants and workshops. Grilled fish, brik pastries filled with egg and tuna, and strong sweet mint tea are the usual orders. The streets are busy in the morning and quiet after the midday meal, and evenings in the main square are lively. A visit to the nearby potters' village of Guellala, in the south of the island, shows how the craft has survived.
t.mosquee e cheikh@33.8,10.9:
Djerba has hundreds of small mosques, and a first-time visitor may wonder how a flat island of olive trees and palms could carry so many. The reason is partly history and partly faith. Most islanders belong to the Ibadi school, a very old branch of Islam that is neither Sunni nor Shia, introduced by Berber converts in the early centuries and kept alive here through isolation. Ibadi communities built mosques for each neighbourhood or family, and they are often small and plain, with thick white walls, a low dome, a few steps and a sheltered prayer space, designed to be defended and to stay cool.

Erriadh, the old Hara Sghira, is the place most visitors know for its street art, since in 2014 artists from around the world painted murals on the walls of the village, and the project, called Djerbahood, turned the lanes into an open gallery. It also lies close to El Ghriba, one of the oldest synagogues in Africa, a place of pilgrimage for Jews from Tunisia and abroad.

In this landscape the farms are walled compounds called menzels, each with its cistern, olive trees, palms and a house with a white dome, and between them narrow lanes run on a grid so regular that it seems planned. The riding is gentle and slow, on flat tarmac with low speed limits and the occasional pothole, and the main hazards are scooters, dogs and children who dart across. On a clear morning the air smells of salt and wood smoke, and the light is soft over the white walls. A stiff wind in spring can blow sand.

Fuel and food are within a few kilometres in Houmt Souk, which is only about five kilometres away, or in Erriadh, and nothing needs advance planning. Non-Muslim visitors should not enter active mosques unless invited, and should respect prayer times and dress modestly near religious buildings.
t.mosquee esselaouti@33.8,11.0:
The east side of Djerba is the tourist side, with beaches, hotels and golf, but the road to this mosque runs a little inland from the sand, among farms and small villages, and it shows the older island that the resorts mostly hide. The nearest real town is Midoun, about five kilometres away, the second market centre of the island, with a lively weekly market where farmers sell fruit, spices, textiles and handmade pottery. Houmt Souk, the capital, is more than ten kilometres to the north-west.

Many of the Ibadi mosques in Djerba were designed in part as strongpoints, because the island was raided for centuries by Spanish, Maltese and Sicilian forces, and local people took refuge in the buildings when pirates came. The island's Ibadi cultural landscape of villages, mosques, farms and fields has been recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage property.

Further along the coast the beach of Sidi Mahrez is a long white strip of fine sand, and the lighthouse at Ras Tourgueness at the north-east corner looks over a lagoon where flamingos gather in winter. A visit in January or February can bring thousands of birds, standing pink against the blue. Riding here is simple, along flat coast and inland roads with palms and olive trees, and the roads are mostly good, but traffic can be thick near the resorts in summer, with taxis, minibuses and quad bikes on the shoulder. Take care at roundabouts, which are used loosely.

Midoun has fuel, cafes, a bank and a market, and so you never need to plan ahead for supplies. The sea air is warm until late in the autumn, and the best months for riding are March to May and October to November, when the wind is moderate and the heat is not oppressive. In midsummer, ride in the early morning or evening. A glass of mint tea with pine nuts in a cafe in Midoun is the local way to sit out the afternoon.
t.mosquee tajdit@33.9,10.9:
Tajdit is an Arabic word meaning renewal, and a mosque with that name usually means one that was rebuilt or enlarged at some point, which suits an island where buildings are whitewashed every year and constantly mended. It is not a place with a famous monument, but a pleasant piece of country that rewards a slow ride.

Water is the thing to notice here. Djerba has almost no rivers and little rain, and for centuries families have collected the winter rain in underground cisterns, called majel, dug into the limestone and sealed with lime plaster. The catchment areas are the whitewashed roofs and yards of the houses, which slope down toward a channel. Each farm compound, or menzel, has its cistern, its olive and date trees and a few animals, and the mosque often has its own cistern too, with a basin outside for ablutions. The lanes between the compounds are lined with prickly pear hedges, and in spring the fields are bright with wildflowers.

Riding in this part of Djerba is quiet and unhurried, with fairly little traffic once you leave the main road. Surfaces vary from smooth tarmac to rough patches, with sand on the edges, and dogs, chickens and the occasional donkey cart share the lanes. There are many unmarked junctions, so a map or phone is useful, and a spot on one of the straight lanes is a good place to stop and look at the white domes against the olive trees. The light in the late afternoon is warm, and the sea is never more than a few kilometres away, bringing a salty breeze. Summer can be very hot, and spring and autumn are better.

Houmt Souk is about four kilometres away, and has everything you may want, from fuel and food to repairs. The fish restaurants near the harbour serve grilled bream and sea bass at modest prices, and the ferry at Ajim, in the south-west, connects the island to the mainland in ten minutes if you want to continue the trip toward Zarzis or Matmata.
t.zone mejmej@33.8,10.8:
Mejmej is a rural district in the south-west of Djerba, a little way from Erriadh, and it feels like the island's countryside as it was before tourism: small fields of barley and vegetables between lines of olive trees, palm groves, and low white farmhouses behind hedges of prickly pear. The ground is flat and the horizon wide, and the sky looks bigger than it does on the mainland. A few kilometres to the south, the sea is shallow and warm, and the tide leaves long flats where people gather shellfish.

Djerba's olives are a staple. Some of the trees are very old, with trunks as thick as barrels, and olive oil has been pressed here for centuries, in old stone mills turned by camels or donkeys. The island also produces dates, figs, pomegranates and a famous variety of apple, and in the markets you can buy jars of harissa, bunches of dried herbs and honey. Women in the villages weave wool into striped blankets and shawls, and a traditional trade in pottery, linked to the clay of Guellala, continues in the south. Local people speak Arabic, and some in the villages speak Berber, a legacy of the early Ibadi communities.

The riding is slow and absorbing. Tracks cross the district in a lattice, some paved and some sandy, and the main roads that skirt it carry heavier traffic, including lorries and tourist coaches. Because the land is so flat, a headwind can make a ride hard, and a sandy gust can blow across the road, particularly in spring. Few of the lanes have signs, so stop and ask if you lose your way, as locals are usually friendly and curious. At dusk, take care of animals and of unlit scooters.

Erriadh, about four kilometres away, has shops and cafes, and Houmt Souk to the north has fuel stations and a good selection of places to eat and sleep, while Midoun lies on the opposite side of the island. A good way to finish the day is to head to the coast at Aghir or Sidi Mahrez for the sunset, and to try fresh fish at a simple restaurant. Remember that the sun here is strong, even in winter, and carry water.
t.mosquee sidi salem@33.9,10.8:
Sidi is the title given to a local holy man, and many Djerban mosques and small domed tombs carry a saint's name, with a whitewashed cube or dome standing beside a tree at the edge of a field. Sidi Salem sits in the north-west of the island, between Houmt Souk and the sea, in an area of olive groves and market gardens where the land is so flat that you can see every dome for miles. On the coast not far away, the Borj Ghazi Mustapha, a square sixteenth-century fort that the Spanish built and the Ottomans took, stands over the shallow water at the old harbour entrance.

The saints' tombs are part of the island's daily life. Women leave small offerings, candles are lit on Thursdays, and families stop to say a prayer when they pass. Local festivals mark the birthdays of saints, with food, music and processions, and the holiness of the places is felt by Muslims and, in some cases, by Jews, who share some traditions with their neighbours in a way that is typical of Tunisia's past. The Jewish community of Djerba is among the oldest in the Mediterranean, with villages that have been inhabited for many centuries.

The riding from Houmt Souk is flat and easy, with low speed limits and a good surface, and the road that follows the northern coast gives views over mudflats and shallow water, where herons and flamingos feed in winter. In summer, the heat shimmers over the road, and there is little shade. Take care at the island's roundabouts, where local drivers use their own rules, and watch for pedestrians and animals. Dust and sand can blow across the road in a strong wind, so a visor and goggles help.

Houmt Souk is only about four kilometres away, with fuel, banks, restaurants and workshops, so there is no need to plan supplies. The fish in the harbour restaurants is usually grilled whole, with a plate of salad and bread, and mint tea afterward. The old part of the town is good for a stroll in the early evening when the shops reopen after the midday break, and the lanes are cool in the shade.
t.mosquee ben biene@33.8,10.8:
In the south-west of Djerba, between Erriadh and the pottery village of Guellala, the island's farmland is at its most traditional, and the mosque of Ben Biene sits among it. This is the part of the island where the compounds stand furthest apart, each one an island of white wall and green trees in the middle of a field, and where the lanes are quiet enough for a rider to hear the pigeons and the wind in the palms.

The Ibadi mosques of the island belong to a tradition that stresses simplicity and community, and many of them were built in a style quite unlike the minaret-and-courtyard mosques of the Arab world. Instead they look like fortified houses, with thick, sloping buttresses, a flat roof of domes and vaults, and an interior that is cool, dim and quiet. Some are partially underground, designed to be safe from raiders, and a few have small schools attached, where children once learned the Koran. Their whitewash is renewed each year, so the shapes look soft and clean even when the walls are many centuries old.

Guellala, a few kilometres south, is where the island's pottery is made. The potters dig clay from nearby pits, shape it by hand and fire it in kilns, and the village is lined with workshops selling amphorae, jars and plates, most of them in plain terracotta. A small museum shows how islanders lived, with scenes of weddings and trades. Not far away is the ferry at Ajim, which connects Djerba to the mainland over a narrow channel, and the old Roman causeway at El Kantara lies at the south-east corner.

Riding in the area is relaxed, with straight roads and rough patches on the lanes, and a strong wind can blow in from the coast. The mid-afternoon sun in summer is harsh, so ride early or late. The nearest town of any size on the map is Erriadh, about three and a half kilometres away, with Houmt Souk to the north offering fuel and the fullest range of services. A stop at one of the potters' shops, where you can watch clay being thrown, is a good way to spend an hour.
t.karlstejn and@50.2,14.7:
The dot sits east of Prague, in the broad valley of the Elbe at Brandýs nad Labem and Stará Boleslav, two towns that run into each other across the river. It is a long way from Karlštejn, on the other side of the capital, and the ride is on its way home, crossing the flat farmland of the Polabí, the Elbe lowland, where the land is wide, the roads are straight and the sky is huge.

Stará Boleslav is a place of deep significance for the Czechs. According to tradition, Prince Wenceslas, the good king of the Christmas carol, was murdered here by his brother Boleslav around 935, after being invited to a feast, and the spot is marked by a Romanesque church. Pilgrims come each September on the saint's day, and the town is also home to a famous Marian shrine, a small image of the Virgin that was carried into battle by Habsburg armies. Brandýs nad Labem, across the river, has a Renaissance castle, once a hunting lodge for the emperors, and a quiet old centre.

The earlier part of the ride lies in the valley of the Berounka, west of Prague, and Karlštejn castle is the highlight. Charles IV had it built in the 1340s to protect the imperial crown jewels and holy relics, and its great tower, with a Chapel of the Holy Cross decorated with precious stones and painted panels, stands above the village on a steep limestone crag. The road from Karlštejn through the Berounka valley is narrow and winding, with high rock walls and pretty villages.

By comparison, the final stretch is plain riding. The roads around Brandýs are busy with traffic bound for Prague, and the Elbe is crossed by bridges that can be congested at rush hour. Speed limits are enforced, and in towns, the cobbled centres can be slippery. At a quiet moment, though, the river bank has trees, benches and a calm, wide view.

Fuel is easy in both towns, with supermarkets and cafes near the main square, and there are a number of traditional pubs serving beer and hearty food. Kostelec nad Labem, a smaller town nearby, is pleasant and has an old castle. In spring the orchards are in blossom, and in autumn the fields are brown and mist hangs over the river.
t.sumava forest@50.1,14.9:
The dot lies in the Elbe lowland east of Prague, between the small villages of Přerov nad Labem and Poříčany, about two hundred kilometres from the forests of the Šumava where the ride began. This is flat, open, intensively farmed land, with big fields of cereal and rapeseed, small villages with a pond and a chapel, and a horizon that stretches in every direction. It is the quiet exhale at the end of a weekend.

The Šumava, or Bohemian Forest, is the great wooded range along the border with Bavaria and Austria, a landscape of spruce, peat bogs, glacial lakes and old farmsteads that is protected as a national park. For decades, during the Cold War, the border zone was closed and fenced, and nature recovered in the empty space, which is why lynx, otter and capercaillie are found there today. The Boubín primeval forest, with its huge old beeches and firs, is among the last such places in central Europe, and Lipno, a vast reservoir, offers sailing and swimming in summer.

In Přerov nad Labem, there is an open-air museum, the Polabí skanzen, which preserves rural houses, barns and a small church from the Elbe region, and gives a good idea of how people lived on the plain before collectivisation. It is a gentle stop, especially with children, and it shows the practical, thatched architecture of the lowlands. Nymburk, the nearest bigger town, was the home of the writer Bohumil Hrabal, and its walls and brewery are well preserved.

The riding here is straightforward. The roads are straight and well surfaced, though busy at commuter hours, and farm vehicles are common. Wind is a factor across the open fields, and the best time is early evening in summer, when the long light turns the grain gold. Fog is common in autumn. Speed cameras guard the main roads and village entrances.

Fuel is available in Nymburk, Český Brod and Kolín, and every village has some kind of pub or snack bar. Czech lunch menus are cheap and generous, with soup, a main dish and often a drink for a modest price. After a day in the mountains and forests, the flatness is a relief, and the long sky is its own reward.
t.wernigerode old town@51.8,10.8:
Wernigerode calls itself the colourful town of the Harz, and it earns the name: the market square is lined with half-timbered houses painted in warm reds, yellows and greens, with carved beams and crooked upper storeys that lean slightly toward each other. The town hall, built in the fifteenth century, has two slim towers like a fairy-tale building, and the whole place feels as though it had been arranged for a picture book. With about thirty-four thousand inhabitants, it is a lively town with a real life of its own, not simply a museum.

Above it all stands the castle, a Romantic fantasy of turrets and pinnacles on a hillside that was rebuilt in the nineteenth century by the Counts of Stolberg-Wernigerode as a residence in the neo-Gothic style. It is reached by a steep path or a little tourist train, and the view from its terrace over the red roofs and wooded hills is wide. Down in the lanes, a famous curiosity is the Smallest House, a narrow building less than three metres wide, which was squeezed between two larger neighbours in the eighteenth century.

For railway lovers, the narrow-gauge Harz railways start here. Old steam locomotives pull trains through the forest to the Brocken, the Harz's highest mountain, in a slow climb of about an hour and a half, and the sight and sound of a steam engine in the spruce forest is hard to resist.
