A ride on the train, rather than the bike, is a pleasant way to see the mountain.

The riding in the area is a pleasure. Roads wind up through spruce forest toward the high Harz, past the Drei Annen Hohne station and the open moors, and in autumn, mist fills the valleys. The old town is cobbled, and the lanes are narrow, so it is best to park outside and walk in. In summer, the market square is full of people eating ice cream under umbrellas.

Fuel and food are easy, with several stations on the ring road and a wide choice of cafes and restaurants in the centre. Try a slice of Harzer cheese or a plate of venison with dumplings in one of the old inns.
t.hamburg@53.4,10.0:
Harburg, on the south bank of the Elbe, is the part of Hamburg that visitors rarely see. It was a separate town until 1937, and it still has its own centre, its own inner harbour with old warehouses, and a slightly rough, working feel that contrasts with the polished facades of the city across the river. Behind it lies Seevetal, a green commuter district at the northern edge of the Lüneburg Heath, and the land begins to open into woods and sand. The dot sits at this seam between city and country.

To get here from the north, you cross the Elbe, which at Hamburg is wide, tidal and busy with container ships, tugs and ferries. The bridges and tunnels that carry traffic are among the busiest in Germany, and the long, curving Köhlbrand Bridge, opened in 1974, is a sight in itself, rising high over the harbour with cranes on either side. The Elbe tunnel, a Hamburg landmark since 1911, can be walked or ridden through.

The day's loop has taken in the Wendland, a remote, thinly populated district in the far east of Lower Saxony, where the villages are built in a circle, known as Rundlingsdörfer, with the houses facing a central green. It is an unusual landscape of half-timbered farmsteads, quiet roads and wide meadows along the Elbe, with a gentle, almost forgotten feeling. The Elbe forest and the Harz edge give contrast, with winding roads and woodland.

Riding in the south of Hamburg demands patience. The roads are busy with lorries going to and from the port, the Autobahn A7 is often jammed, and the tunnels have strict speed limits. The best option is to travel in the middle of the day or on a Sunday. Cobbled streets and tram rails are slippery in the wet.

Fuel and food are easy in Harburg and Seevetal, with a wide choice of stations, supermarkets and restaurants. Harburg's inner harbour has cafes in converted warehouses, and a coffee with a view of the water is a good end to the ride. In the evenings, the harbour lights come on, and the cranes glow against the sky.
t.lauenburg old town@53.4,10.6:
Lauenburg is built on a steep bank above the Elbe, and its old town is a strip of narrow, cobbled lanes squeezed between the cliff and the river. It is the most southerly town in Schleswig-Holstein, a small place of about twelve thousand, and its position as a crossing point of an important river explains everything about it. Ships have passed here for centuries, and a museum devoted to Elbe river shipping, housed in an old building on the waterfront, tells the story of the barges and steamers that once carried salt, timber and grain between Hamburg and Magdeburg.

The old town stands at about twenty metres above sea level, only a little higher than the river, and the Elbe has often claimed it. Marks on the walls of houses in the lower town record the heights of floods, including the great flood of 2013, when the water rose to levels not seen for centuries. The buildings are narrow and often half-timbered, with steep stairs leading up to the upper town, and walking along the riverside, you can watch the barges pass close enough to count the cargo.

The ride has crossed Schleswig-Holstein by way of the Wingst forest, a low wooded hill on the other side of the Elbe, and the Elbe ferry crossings. It also visits Schaalsee, a deep, clear lake that lies right on the former border between East and West Germany, and the Ratzeburg lakes, a chain of waters where the cathedral stands on an island in the middle of the town. The roads in this area are narrow and winding, with oak avenues, farm fields and frequent views of the water.

In Lauenburg itself, the cobbles can be slippery, and the street layout is awkward for a large bike. Parking at the riverside is easy and the walk is short. At the Elbe, the Elbe-Lübeck Canal begins, a historic waterway that was dug in the Middle Ages to carry salt from Lüneburg to the Baltic, and it is a pleasure to ride along its towpath roads.

Fuel and food are easy, with stations on the main road and a few cafes and fish restaurants by the river. Try a plate of smoked eel or a bowl of fish soup if you want to eat in the local way.
t.harz edge@52.1,13.5:
Baruth/Mark lies in a landscape that is flatter than most people picture when they think of Germany, a sandy basin south of Berlin in which glaciers and meltwater carved wide shallow valleys at the end of the last ice age. The valley is called the Baruther Urstromtal, and it is filled with pine woods, heath and slow ponds, with the low ridge of the Fläming rising to the south-west.

The area has an odd twentieth-century history. At Wünsdorf, a short drive north, the German army and then, after 1945, the Soviet army had a vast military headquarters, hidden in the woods, and when the Soviets left in 1994 the site was abandoned. Part of it has become a town of books, with antiquarian shops in old barracks, which is as unlikely as it sounds. Baruth itself has a modest castle and a glassworks tradition, and its villages have long street layouts typical of the Brandenburg countryside.

For riding, this is quiet, open country. Roads run straight through pine forests, with long views over fields, and occasional bends where they cross streams. The surface is generally good but can be rough on minor roads, with sand on the edges, and avenues of old trees line some stretches. Wild boar and deer cross at dusk, and in summer the heat shimmers on the tarmac. In autumn, mist lies in the hollows. The area is not dramatic, but it is a calm place to spend a long day.

Practically, fuel stations and supermarkets are in Baruth and in larger towns like Zossen and Luckenwalde, and village bakeries open early. Gasthäuser serve hearty food, such as schnitzel and potato dishes, and asparagus appears in spring. Distances between services can be long, so keep the tank topped. A short stop at the lake in Teupitz is pleasant on a hot day. The Harz mountains lie far to the west, and on a long day this is a quiet place to wind down before the return to Berlin.
t.saxon switzerland@52.4,13.3:
It owes its modest fame to a battle. In August 1813, during the Napoleonic Wars, a Prussian and Swedish army under Bülow defeated a French force marching on Berlin, which saved the Prussian capital from occupation. A monument in the town marks the spot, and the battle is remembered each year with a local commemoration.

The town has another claim to local pride, the Teltower Rübchen, a small, sweet turnip grown in the sandy soil of this district since the Middle Ages. It was prized by gourmets, and Goethe is said to have been a fan, although the story is better as a legend than as fact. Today the fields are interspersed with a huge freight distribution centre, which supplies the capital, and the roar of lorries on the nearby motorway ring is the dominant sound. Teltow, Stahnsdorf and Kleinmachnow, nearby, form a prosperous belt of commuter suburbs.

For a rider, the area is a mixture of ring road and quiet lanes. The A10 motorway ring and the A115 carry heavy traffic, and the junctions can be tricky, but small roads between Großbeeren and the neighbouring villages run straight through fields of grain and rapeseed. The surface is good, and there are few bends, so the main hazards are crosswinds on open stretches and farm vehicles. Sunsets on the flat horizon are striking. The best time to ride is early on a weekday, before the commuter traffic builds. Wild boar and deer appear on forest edges.

Practically, fuel is easy to find at stations along the main road and in the logistics area, and there are supermarkets and bakeries in Großbeeren and nearby Teltow. Gasthäuser serve German classics, and in season you might find asparagus and strawberries sold from roadside stalls. The S-Bahn at Teltow Stadt connects to central Berlin, so you could leave the bike and travel in. For anyone finishing a long day on the Saxon Switzerland route, this is a quiet last stretch.
t.dahme heideseen@53.0,13.4:
Zehdenick is a small town on the Havel in the north of Brandenburg, and it is tied to a thing most people would not think about, bricks. In the nineteenth century, the clay pits around the town fed hundreds of brickworks that shipped their product by barge down the Havel to build Berlin, and much of the capital's tenement-blocks came from here. When the pits were abandoned they flooded, turning the district into a landscape of small lakes and channels. The Ziegeleipark at Mildenberg, a few kilometres south, preserves a ring kiln and machinery, and gives an honest picture of the industry.

The town itself has about fifteen thousand people across its wider area, with a Cistercian nunnery foundation from the thirteenth century that left a handful of buildings by the river. The Havel here is slow and winding, lined with reeds and willows, and boats in summer drift between locks. The land around is flat, forested and sparsely populated, a mix of pine, birch and wet meadows that merges northward into the Schorfheide and the lakes of the Uckermark. Cranes breed in the wet places, and in autumn they gather in numbers.

Riding in this region is quiet and unhurried. The roads are mostly straight and smooth, with avenues of old oak, lime and chestnut trees, and the bends come when the road meets a river or a lake. You may share the tarmac with farm vehicles and cyclists, and the surface turns rough on minor roads where the old concrete slabs of the GDR days peek through. Wildlife is common, with deer in the forest edges and boar in the fields at dusk. Summer weekends bring bathers to the lakes, and in winter, snow lingers under the trees.

Practically, Zehdenick has a couple of fuel stations, a supermarket, bakeries and a few restaurants by the water, and Gransee and Liebenwalde, a little further off, offer more of the same. The Dahme-Heideseen park, named in this stop's label, is a long way to the south-east, so treat this as a separate landscape. A stop at the Mildenberg brickworks museum, with its tall chimney, is a good way to spend an hour, and the cafe there serves cake and coffee. Carry some cash, because small places still prefer it.
t.bad saarow@52.4,13.3:
Stahnsdorf has a cemetery that people cross the city to see. The Südwestkirchhof, opened in 1909 to relieve Berlin's overcrowded graveyards, spreads through pine woods like a park, and its Jugendstil chapels and carved family tombs hold a roll-call of Berlin's cultural life, including the illustrator Heinrich Zille and the painter Lovis Corinth. It feels more like a forest than a burial ground, quiet and shadowy, with moss on the stone and light filtering through the trees.

The setting is the Teltow plateau, the sandy upland just south-west of Berlin, cut by the Teltow Canal, which was dug in the early twentieth century to take shipping around the city. At Kleinmachnow, the canal has a lock and a small harbour, and the area carried a particular weight in the Cold War, when the Wall ran along its edge and separated the towns from West Berlin. Wealthy suburbs now fill the villages, and the old Prussian estates are surrounded by new development.

For riders, the area is a patchwork of suburban roads and green corridors. The Königsweg, a forest road, and the lanes along the canal give some relief from the traffic, with trees overhead and cyclists everywhere. The surface is mostly good, but cobbles and tram tracks in older centres call for care. Traffic around the Autobahn junctions is heavy, and local police check speed on the main roads. In late autumn, leaves cover the road and make the surface slick. In summer, the forest is cool and shady, which makes it a pleasure at midday.

The real Bad Saarow lies about fifty kilometres to the south-east, on the Scharmützelsee, and has a spa tradition that goes back to the 1900s. Here, though, services are easy and close. Fuel stations are on the main roads, and the three towns have supermarkets, bakeries and cafes. A small bar or restaurant in the old village centre of Stahnsdorf serves local food. The cemetery is open during daylight and is free to enter, though respectful behaviour is expected. It is a good place for a quiet end to a ride, and perhaps a walk.
t.bohemian@50.2,14.5:
North of Prague the land flattens out and opens, and this point lies in the middle of that wide plain, right beside Neratovice on the river Elbe, which Czechs call the Labe. The Vltava joins the Elbe a few kilometres to the north at Mělník, so by the time you reach this spot you are riding through the heart of the Elbe lowlands, a broad, fertile basin where the soil is sandy and the fields are given over to vegetables and grain. It is a long way from the sandstone gorges of Bohemian Switzerland that the name suggests.

Neratovice is a town of sixteen thousand, known for its chemical works, which dominate the skyline with pipes and chimneys. During the great floods of August 2002 the river swamped the plant and the town, causing a chlorine leak that became one of the more dramatic episodes of that disaster. The river has been calm since, but the memory lingers, and the levees you ride along now are newer and higher.

The riding here is flat and fast, with long straights, gentle bends and few surprises. It is not a place for corners, but it is a good place to cover distance, especially on a clear morning when the light is clean. A headwind can wear you down, so pick your direction accordingly, and watch for slow farm machinery and cyclists on the many riverside routes. The villages around, Libiš and Tišice among them, are small and straightforward, and the old road bridges across the water are worth a look.

Fuel is no problem, since Neratovice is big enough to have several filling stations and supermarkets, and there is the usual run of cafés and bakeries in the centre. If you want a break, the riverbank is an easy place to pull off and watch the barges and the herons. This is a plain, honest, working landscape, and it pays off more with each visit, once you have stopped expecting drama.
t.hrensko gorge@50.9,14.2:
The Elbe, which the Czechs call the Labe, does something dramatic here: it cuts its way out of Bohemia through a deep sandstone gorge, and the village of Hřensko sits right in the neck of it, on the Czech side of the border with Germany. This is the lowest point in the Czech Republic, around 115 metres above the sea, and the river leaves the country here to run on through Saxony towards Dresden and the North Sea. The data labels it a German point, but you are right on the line, with the cliffs towering above.

The sandstone is the star. Over millions of years the rock has been carved into towers, chimneys and narrow canyons, and the best known of them lie a short walk from here. The Pravčice Gate, the largest natural sandstone arch in Europe, stands on a ridge above the village, and the gorges of the Kamenice river, where flat boats are poled through narrow cliffs, are open in the warmer months. This is Bohemian Switzerland, a national park, and a magnet for hikers.

The road along the river from Děčín is narrow and winding, with the cliffs on one side and the water on the other, and in summer it fills with coaches and cars. The best time to ride is early, before the first tourist buses, or on a weekday in spring or autumn. The border town of Hřensko itself is a bit of a tourist trap, with rows of souvenir stalls and cheap goods, but the setting is spectacular, and a coffee by the river is good value.

Děčín, with about fifty thousand people, is the nearest large town for fuel and shops, while Bad Schandau, on the German side, is smaller but has a pleasant riverfront. The surrounding forests are home to deer, wild boar, and, quietly returned in recent decades, lynx. Take your time; parking is limited, and the gorge is worth walking. It is a short, steep detour that stays in the memory longer than most.
t.plon lake view@54.2,10.4:
The Great Lake of Plön is the biggest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, and from this spot at the edge of the town you can see how much water the last Ice Age left behind. The glaciers that retreated from here some twelve thousand years ago scraped out hollows, dumped hills of gravel and clay, and left behind a landscape of lakes and rolling ridges that locals call Holstein Switzerland. It is a bit of a joke to anyone who has seen the Alps, since the highest hills are barely above a hundred metres, but the name stuck, and the landscape has a gentle charm of its own.

The town of Plön, with some thirteen thousand people, sits on a narrow neck of land between two lakes, so its streets run up and down and every turn opens a view over the water. The point itself lies at twenty-eight metres above the sea, just above the shore, with the castle on the hill above you. Early morning, with mist rising off the lake and the first swans moving across it, is the time to be here.

The roads around the lake are some of the best in the district, with long, easy bends through beech woods and past fields of rape, which flowers a startling yellow in May. Surfaces are mostly good, though some of the lanes are narrow and patched, and cyclists and families make them busy on summer weekends. Tractor mud and the occasional rain shower will keep you honest. Autumn brings low golden light and quieter roads.

For fuel and food you are in luck, since Plön is large enough for stations, supermarkets and several cafés, and the lakeside has places to sit with a coffee and a smoked fish roll. Ascheberg and Bösdorf are smaller villages on the lake, with their own swimming spots and marinas. Be aware that swimming is popular and the water is clean, though shallow shores can be muddy, so bring flip-flops. It is a gentle, easy place to ride, and a good one to linger in.
t.satow inland bends@54.0,11.9:
Satow is a village on the long, low plateau behind the Mecklenburg Baltic coast, a few kilometres inland from the sea and well off the usual tourist track. The town of Satow-Oberhagen has about six thousand people, and the countryside around it is a mix of cornfields, small woods and the avenues of old lime and chestnut trees that line so many roads in Mecklenburg. Following them is half the pleasure of riding here.

The ground lifts gently towards the Kühlung, a range of low wooded hills along the coast, whose highest point is only about 130 metres but which feels much bigger because everything around it is so flat. Beech forest covers the slopes, and the roads wind through it with a bend or two and a short climb or descent. After a day of flat roads it is a welcome change, and the sea breeze that comes over the ridge cools you on warm days.

The area has a lot of history. Bad Doberan, a few kilometres east, has a great brick Gothic minster, consecrated in the fourteenth century, which was once a Cistercian monastery church and is among the best of its kind in northern Europe. A narrow-gauge steam railway, nicknamed Molli, still runs from Bad Doberan to the seaside resort of Kühlungsborn, puffing through the streets and across the fields, and it is a wonderful thing to see from the road. East Germany's socialist era left its mark here, but the old villages and churches have outlasted it.

Satow has shops and fuel, and Jürgenshagen and Retschow are smaller. There are bakeries in every village, and a coffee and a slice of plum cake at a village bakery is a sensible reward. The bends here are gentle and the surface mostly smooth, with some cobbled village stretches. Come in late summer, when the fields are gold and the sky is huge, and leave time to follow the lanes you did not plan on.
t.stralsund old town@54.3,13.1:
Stralsund sits on a strip of land between the Baltic and a chain of shallow lagoons, facing the island of Rügen across a narrow sound, and its old town is one of the finest assemblies of brick Gothic in Europe. UNESCO listed it in 2002 together with Wismar, and the reason is plain as soon as you walk onto the Old Market: the great town hall with its ornate, almost theatrical gabled facade, and across the square the enormous church of St Nicholas, built when the town was a rich member of the Hanseatic League and wanted everyone to know it.

The city is surrounded on three sides by water and was long a fortress. In 1628 Wallenstein, the imperial general, besieged it in the Thirty Years' War and failed to take it, helped by Swedish reinforcements, and Stralsund remained Swedish until the early nineteenth century. Sail-training ship Gorch Fock, a famous German vessel, lies in the harbour as a museum, and the Ozeaneum, a modern aquarium, has a bold, white seaside shape that shows how the city has changed.

Riding into the old town is a matter of care, because the streets are cobbled, narrow and full of pedestrians, and parking is limited. Leave the bike somewhere sensible and walk. The ride to get here is a different matter, with the road from Rostock running along the coast through flat, open farmland with wide skies, and the bridge across to Rügen visible in the distance. The wind off the Baltic can be strong, so expect to lean into it.

Fuel is no problem in a city of fifty-nine thousand, where stations and supermarkets are plentiful. For lunch, try a fish roll from a harbour stall, which is the local fast food and tastes better in the wind. If you are riding on towards the Darß, make sure you fill up first, since the peninsula has fewer options. Come in the evening, when the brick glows red in the low sun and the day-trippers have gone home.
t.plon castle lake@54.2,10.4:
Plön castle stands on a hill above the lake and the town, a pale, solid, rather formal building that looks as though it was designed to impress someone, which it was. Duke Joachim Ernst of Schleswig-Holstein-Plön had it built in the early seventeenth century, and the dukes of Plön lived here until their line ran out in the eighteenth century, when the Danish crown took over. Later it became a Prussian military school, and today it is a private boarding school, so you can look at the exterior and the terraced gardens but not walk through the rooms.

What matters most to a rider is the setting. The castle sits on a ridge between two lakes, the Great Lake of Plön and the smaller Lake of Plön, and the view from its edge covers islands, reed beds and forested shores. The town's streets slope down towards the water, and the old centre has some good half-timbered houses and a pleasant market square. Plön is a town of about thirteen thousand, which means it has fuel, supermarkets and several cafés.

The roads around here are some of the best in Holstein, with long, curving lanes that follow the lake shores and climb the low glacial hills. The hills, left by the Ice Age, are gentle but numerous, so the riding has a rolling, rhythmic quality, with the occasional sharp bend at the bottom of a dip. In summer, the lakes fill with sailboats and swimmers, and the roads fill with cyclists and day-trippers, so the early morning and the evening are best. Spring brings fields of rape and blossoming orchards.

Ascheberg and Bösdorf, both just five kilometres away, are small lakeside villages with swimming spots and small restaurants serving fresh fish. Try the local smoked fish if you see it. Pull in at the car park by the lake for a few minutes, and the view will explain why people have been building castles here for four hundred years. Stay for the sunset if you can, because the lake turns copper.
t.selent waterline@54.3,10.4:
Selent is a village of barely thirteen hundred people at the northern tip of its lake, and the lake is the reason to come. The Selenter See is the second largest in Schleswig-Holstein after the Great Lake of Plön, a long, clear, slightly wild sheet of water fringed with reeds and woods, and the road runs along its shore for much of the way. The place sits at thirty metres above sea level, on a low glacial ridge, and the lake lies just below it.

The village has a manor house and a church, and the old estate shaped the surrounding landscape as a patchwork of fields, hedgerows and carefully managed woods. Many such manors, owned by the Holstein nobility, still dominate the villages and farmland of this part of the country, and a few have been turned into hotels or cultural centres. The ground beneath it all is the work of the Ice Age, rolling and lumpy, with hollows that hold lakes and ponds like loose change.

The riding here is gentle and enjoyable. Lanes wind between hedges and fields, dip into hollows, and rise again over low moraine ridges, with views of the water opening and closing between the trees. Surfaces are generally good, though farm traffic leaves dirt on the road, and in summer the lake draws swimmers and cyclists. Come on a weekday morning, when the water is still and the light slants over the reeds.

For fuel, Selent is too small to count on a station, and the nearest larger town is Lütjenburg, about ten kilometres to the north, which also has supermarkets, bakeries and cafés. If you are heading to the Baltic coast, it lies just beyond. Selent itself has a bakery or two and perhaps an ice-cream shop in summer. Pull in at the lakeside and have a sandwich, because the water is better company than most roadside tables. A quiet corner of Holstein, quietly good.
t.teterow market@53.8,12.6:
Teterow is a market town in the lake country of Mecklenburg, with a population of just over nine thousand, and it comes with a curiosity that every motorcyclist ought to know: the Bergring. This old natural-terrain track just outside the town has hosted motorcycle races since the early 1930s, and its steep, bowl-shaped hillside, with the crowd packed on the slopes, makes it a place of real atmosphere. Speedway and grass-track meetings are still held there, and the Teterow race weekends draw riders from across the region.

The town itself is an old one, with medieval gates still standing, the Rostock and Malchin gates, and a long market square lined with low brick and timber buildings. Teterow sits beside a lake, the Teterower See, which is a pleasant spot for a rest, with a lakeside path and a small bathing place in summer. It's a town you pass through, not a destination, but the market square is a decent place to get some fuel, buy a roll and watch the locals.

The landscape around is called Mecklenburg Switzerland, a humorous name for rolling, glacial hills, lakes and beech woods, a long way from the Alps but pleasant to ride. The roads are quiet, with long curves through avenues of old trees and low rises over the moraines, and the traffic is light, with only the occasional tractor. Surfaces vary, from smooth tarmac to patched and cobbled village streets, and you should be ready for the odd bumpy stretch.

For fuel, Teterow has stations on the main roads, which is why it is a natural stop, and Pampow and Groß Wokern are smaller villages without much beyond a bakery. The wind sweeps across the open farmland, and in autumn the cranes gather on the fields, a wonderful sight and sound. Try to time your visit to one of the quieter days, and you will have the place to yourself. Keep an eye on the clock, because daylight goes quickly in winter.
t.hamburg north east edge@53.6,10.2:
On the north-eastern edge of Hamburg the city thins into a green ring of woods, meadows and villages, and the point here sits close to the boundary with Schleswig-Holstein. Stapelfeld, a small village in the Stormarn district, is just across the line, while the big residential districts of Farmsen-Berne and Sasel lie on the Hamburg side. The ground is gently rolling, and the landscape is a mix of fields, small woods, and the quiet backwaters of the Bille and the Alster.

This is where the ride begins, and it is a good start. In ten minutes you are out of the city's grip and into lanes lined with oaks and beeches, past thatched farms and stables, with the traffic lights of Hamburg already forgotten. Horse riders are common here, and the lanes are shared with cyclists and joggers, so keep your speed down in the villages. The surfaces are generally good, with the occasional patch of broken tarmac after winter.

The countryside north and east of here is the beginning of the Holstein lake district, where the glaciers of the last Ice Age left behind their moraines and hollows, and the day is meant to carry you towards the lakes and low hills around Eutin and Plön. It takes a while to get there, so use the quiet lanes in the first hour to settle in. Early on a clear morning the light is low and the fields are damp, a good time for a quiet start.

Fuel is easy in Hamburg's suburbs, with stations on the main roads, and it is sensible to fill up here before leaving the city, since the lakes have fewer pumps. Farmsen-Berne and Sasel have supermarkets and bakeries, and Stapelfeld has a handful of small places for a coffee. Check the weather, because North German days can change from sunshine to showers in the time it takes to put on a jacket. Pack a waterproof, and leave without hurry.
t.eutin castle sight@54.1,10.6:
Eutin is called the city of roses, and it deserves it, but it was a bishop's town first. The castle stands on an island-like spot at the edge of the old centre, a moated, baroque building of pale brick and green copper roofs, set in a landscaped park that slopes down to the Great Eutin Lake. For centuries it was the residence of the prince-bishops of Lübeck, and later of the Dukes of Oldenburg, who gave the town a refined, slightly provincial court air that you can still feel in its elegant streets.

The composer Carl Maria von Weber was born in Eutin in 1786, and a summer opera festival named in his honour is staged in the castle gardens, on a floating stage by the lake. The town has a market square lined with old houses and a cluster of small shops and cafés, and a friendly, unhurried atmosphere. Eutin has about seventeen thousand people, and has everything a rider needs, from fuel to bakeries and places to eat.

The countryside around Eutin is part of Holstein Switzerland, the glacial hill and lake country of eastern Schleswig-Holstein. The roads wind between lakes and beech woods, rise over small hills and drop into hollows, offering short stretches of real enjoyment, with gentle bends and long views. Spring brings fields of yellow rape and fruit blossom, summer fills the lakes with sailors and swimmers, and autumn gives you low gold light and quiet roads. Winter can be damp and grey, but the castle looks fine in the frost.

Malente, a bigger village on the neighbouring lake, is a spa town with a pleasant lakeside walk, five kilometres away. Park the bike, walk across the bridge to the castle gardens, and sit on a bench with a coffee. The lake is calm and full of birds, and you may see swans and herons. If the weather is fine, stay for the evening, when the lake turns to silver and the swifts wheel overhead.
t.hamburg@53.6,10.2:
Wandsbek is the neighbourhood that most people never think of as a place, but it was once a town of its own, and a Danish one at that. Until the middle of the nineteenth century it belonged to the Danish crown, and a poet named Matthias Claudius lived here in the late eighteenth century, editing a newspaper called the Wandsbecker Bote and writing the evening song Der Mond ist aufgegangen, which every German schoolchild knows. Now the district is an anonymous sprawl of housing blocks and shopping streets, but the story is worth remembering as you ride in.

The point here lies at the north-eastern fringe, in the quiet housing estates between Farmsen-Berne and Sasel, where the city meets the fields. It is a landing strip for the end of a ride, a moment of calm after the lakes and hills of Holstein. The roads in these suburbs are quiet in the evening, lined with lime trees and detached houses, and the traffic is easy compared to the centre.

Coming home at the end of a day is a time to think about the road you rode. Holstein Switzerland is not high or wild, but it is full of small pleasures: a lake shining between the trees, a baroque castle, a village with a good bakery. The ride back often runs on straight roads through farmland with big skies, and the evening light, in late summer, is long and honey-coloured. Watch for deer at dusk, particularly where the road crosses woods or hedges.

Fuel is plentiful, because the suburbs are packed with stations and supermarkets, and the nearby districts have everything. A short ride south brings you to the centre of Hamburg, with its harbour and the big ships. If you have time left, head for the Alster, the lake in the middle of the city, and walk along its shore as the lights come on. The evening air smells of water and linden, and the city quiets down. A good place to end the day, whatever the weather.
t.burgdorf return road@52.4,10.0:
Burgdorf is a solid, practical town of thirty thousand people on the eastern edge of the Hannover region, where the farmland begins to turn into heath and pine. The name means castle village, and the place grew around a medieval fortress that has since vanished. Today it is a commuter town, with a brick-built centre, a pedestrian precinct and a good supply of shops, bakeries and filling stations, and it is the sort of place you stop at when you need to take care of practical things.

The return road here comes in from the east, from the Lüneburg Heath side, and the landscape changes as you ride. The Südheide, the southern heath, is a country of sandy soils, birch and pine woods, open fields and tiny villages, with long straight roads and gentle curves. Sandy ground and cool air make for a distinctive smell, a mixture of resin and dry grass, and in late summer the heather blooms purple in the nature reserves further north.

Burgdorf marks the point where the heath yields to the Hannover plain, and the traffic increases accordingly. On the final stretch to the city the roads are wider and busier, and speed limits are strictly enforced, so keep an eye on the signs. Rush hour can be slow, so a coffee stop here is a good way to let the traffic die down. The town has a few cafés on the main street and a weekly market, which is a good place for fresh bread and local cheese.

Lehrte, a larger town eight kilometres south-west, has more shops, and Hänigsen is a smaller village to the north. Fuel is easy, with several stations on the main road, and it is wise to fill up here at the end of a long ride. If you have time, take a short detour into the woods and let the bike cool down. The pine smell, the quiet and the soft sand under the trees are a world away from the city, and a good way to end the day.
t.neumunster@54.1,10.0:
Neumünster is a town of seventy-eight thousand, the biggest between Hamburg and Kiel, and it earns its keep as a place where roads, railways and fortunes cross. It grew rich on cloth, and for much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries its mills and tanneries made it one of the great textile and leather towns of northern Germany. A museum of cloth and technology tells that story, and the old industrial buildings still stand in the quarters near the river.

It is not a pretty town, and does not pretend to be, but it is honest. The centre is built of brick and concrete, with a pedestrian zone, a covered market and the usual high-street shops, and the people are friendly in the dry, no-nonsense way of the north. Neumünster also has a lake on its edge, the Einfelder See, where families come at the weekend to swim, walk and sail, and a few green corners among the housing estates.

For a rider, it is a practical finish, and a useful one. The roads in from the west, from the Schlei and the Angeln countryside, pass through flat farmland and woods, with the odd bend and a lot of straight, and the final miles are on busy roads that lead through suburbs and shopping centres. Traffic can be thick at rush hour, with the nearby motorways feeding in lorries and commuters, so give yourself time and keep your lane discipline.

Fuel is not an issue, since the town has stations all around its ring roads, and bakeries, cafés and supermarkets on every main street. Padenstedt and Bönebüttel, smaller villages near the town, offer quieter places for a stop, though they have little to offer beyond the basics. If you have time to spare, park near the central square and take a short walk. After the water and wide horizons of the north, the town feels solid, and welcome.
t.eutin castle roads@54.1,10.6:
Eutin had its literary moment long before it had a reputation for roses. In the late eighteenth century the little residence town of the prince-bishops of Lübeck became a quiet meeting place for poets and painters, and people spoke of it as the Weimar of the north. Johann Heinrich Voss, who gave Germany its beloved translation of Homer's Odyssey, taught at the Latin school here, and the painter Wilhelm Tischbein, famous for his portrait of Goethe in the Roman countryside, spent his last years in the town and died here in 1829.

The roads that lead out from the castle quarter do so with an easy, rolling grace. They run east through a landscape the glaciers shaped, a quilt of lakes, low ridges, beech woods and rape fields, and then drift towards the old Hanseatic city of Lübeck and the long, thin lakes of the Lauenburg country. The surfaces are mostly good, the junctions are sparse, and the bends are the kind that let you lean without a worry. In May the fields are a shock of yellow, and in October the beech woods burn copper, so the ride rewards the calendar twice.

The goal of this stretch is the edge of the Schaalsee, a clear, deep lake on the old border with East Germany that is now part of a biosphere reserve. For forty years the line of the inner-German frontier ran through the water, which meant the shores stayed undisturbed, and today they are rich with cranes, sea eagles and rare orchids. That strange gift of history makes this one of the quietest landscapes in northern Germany.

Eutin itself is a town of seventeen thousand and offers all the practical comforts: stations on the edges, supermarkets, bakeries, and a pleasant market square where you can sit and watch the town go about its morning. Malente, five kilometres away, is the neighbouring spa town on the next lake. Start with a full tank and a decent breakfast, because once you leave the lakeland and drop into the farming country further east the services thin out, and the cafés will not open until ten.
t.segeberg@53.9,10.3:
Bad Segeberg is the town with a limestone hill in the middle of a flat plain, and everything about it follows from that odd fact. The Kalkberg, a lump of gypsum and limestone pushed up by an ancient salt dome, rises sharply from the surrounding fields, and for a thousand years it has been the natural place for a fortress. Dukes and kings built castles on it and fought over it, and the stones of the last one are still scattered about its flanks. Today the hill's chief purpose is theatre: since 1952 the open-air stage at its foot has staged the Karl May Festival every summer, with galloping horses, gunfights and Winnetou, drawing hundreds of thousands of spectators from across Germany.

Under the hill is a cave system, and it holds one of the largest winter roosts of bats in Europe, which is why the cave is closed to visitors for part of the year. The town around it, some sixteen thousand people strong, has a spa heritage built on salt springs, a pleasant lake, the Great Segeberg Lake, and a long main street of shops and cafés. It is a handy place to arrive, because everything is close together.

For a rider, Segeberg is the final stop after a long day coming out of the Holstein lake country and the Mecklenburg border region. The last stretch of road is gentle and often straight, over low fields with long views to the horizon. The land is only slightly rolling here, so the Kalkberg stands out from far away, a landmark that tells you the end is near. Weekdays are quiet. On a summer evening when the festival is playing, the town fills up, and finding a parking spot near the hill takes patience.

There are several filling stations around the ring roads and supermarkets in the centre, and Klein Rönnau and Fahrenkrug, the nearby villages, have little more than a bakery. Finish the day with a plate of something hearty and a stroll along the lakeside, and watch the sky darken over the hill.
t.ratzeburg island photo@53.7,10.8:
Ratzeburg sits on an island, and you notice it only when you ride onto it. The old town lies on a long, narrow strip of land in the middle of the Ratzeburg Lake, joined to the shores by three causeways, and as you come in along one of them the water opens out on both sides, with the cathedral rising ahead like a ship's bridge. Photographers love it, with good reason: from the western shore the whole town hangs on the water, brick and green copper, with the reflection doubling it.

The cathedral is one of the oldest brick buildings in northern Germany. Henry the Lion, the powerful Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, founded it in the twelfth century, and its Romanesque austerity still feels commanding today, with thick walls and a restrained, almost severe beauty. The sculptor Ernst Barlach spent part of his childhood in Ratzeburg, and there is a museum to him in the town. Rowing has a serious history here too, since the lake became a training ground for German rowers, and on a fine morning you may see eights gliding past, with a coach cycling along the bank.

A less cheerful piece of history is the line of the former inner-German border, which ran through the lake. For decades the east shore lay in a restricted zone, and the dead zone left behind a strip of wild shoreline that is now a nature reserve. The Lauenburg Lakes region around it is wooded, hilly and full of water, with quiet, winding roads that suit a relaxed pace, though tractors and cyclists are common.

Ratzeburg has about fourteen thousand people and has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafés, many with a view across the lake. A good approach is to arrive in the morning, park on the island, and walk the causeway for the classic view. The old town streets are cobbled and narrow, so leave the bike on the edge. Schlagsdorf, five kilometres away, is a small village on the old border, with a museum about the frontier. If the day is fine, take the long way round the lake before you leave.
t.helmstedt old town@52.2,11.0:
Helmstedt is a town that has lived through several lives. In the sixteenth century it was a university town: the Academia Julia, founded in 1576 by Duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, drew scholars from across Europe, and its handsome building, the Juleum, still stands in the old quarter. The university closed in 1810, but the streets kept their half-timbered charm, with lovely house fronts and a little market square that is a pleasure to sit in.

Then came the Cold War. Just a few kilometres east of town at Marienborn was the biggest border crossing between West and East Germany, where the motorway from Hanover to Berlin passed through checkpoints, watchtowers and long queues of trucks. Helmstedt itself was the last West German town on the transit route, a place where drivers filled their tanks and bought their last coffee before the long, tense journey across the other side. The border installations at Marienborn are now a memorial and museum.

Lignite shaped the area too. Open-pit mines ate into the countryside for decades, and the diggings gave up something astonishing: near Schöningen, archaeologists found wooden throwing spears about three hundred thousand years old, some of the oldest hunting weapons ever found, and a museum there tells the story. To the south, just outside town, stand the Lübbensteine, a pair of Stone Age megalithic tombs, huge slabs of rock lying quietly in the woods.

As a rider's stop, Helmstedt is easy. There are filling stations on the roads in, bakeries and cafés around the market, and plenty of parking. The roads in from the west cross the low ridge of the Elm, a wooded upland of beech, with a mix of straight and curving sections, and they carry little traffic outside commuter hours. Park by the old university, and have a slow walk around the old streets. You will see how small a town can hold a great deal of history.
t.goslar old town edge@51.9,10.4:
Goslar has been a town of silver and emperors for a thousand years, and its old centre feels like the set of a very long play. The Rammelsberg mine, just south of the town, produced copper, lead, zinc and silver from the early Middle Ages until 1988, making it one of the longest-working mines in history, and the wealth from it paid for the town's splendid half-timbered houses, its guildhalls and its churches. UNESCO has listed both the mine and the old town as World Heritage.

In the eleventh century German emperors made Goslar a favoured residence, building a great imperial palace, the Kaiserpfalz, which was heavily restored in the nineteenth century and now stands in a green park at the foot of the town. In front of it sits a pair of equestrian statues of emperors in bronze and gilt. The market square is the heart of the old town, dominated by the town hall and the Glockenspiel, which plays a tune and shows figures of miners several times a day.

The road in from the north skirts the edge of the Harz mountains, the highest range in northern Germany. The Harz is a low but rugged upland of spruce forest, granite outcrops and deep valleys, and the roads that climb into it are a motorcyclist's dream, with long sweeping bends and tight hairpins, and good tarmac on the main routes. Weekends and holidays bring plenty of riders and tourists, and the best time is a weekday morning in spring or autumn. Weather in the hills changes fast, and fog and drizzle can arrive in minutes, so carry a waterproof layer.

Goslar is a town of nearly forty-four thousand and has fuel stations, supermarkets and many cafés, so you can top up before you go up. Langelsheim and Bad Harzburg, both within ten kilometres, have more. Park outside the pedestrian core, where the streets are cobbled and narrow, and walk in to the square. Try a plate of the regional speciality, Harzer cheese, a pungent small round cheese, if you are brave. Then leave time for the climb. The hills are waiting just beyond the last roofs.
t.laboe memorial view@54.4,10.2:
The Laboe naval memorial is the tallest thing on this coast by a long way, a slim brick tower, seventy-two metres high, that rises from a bluff at the mouth of Kiel Fjord and can be seen from far out at sea. It was built between 1927 and 1936 to commemorate German sailors who died in the First World War, and later its meaning was widened to remember seafarers of all nations who lost their lives at sea, a gesture that still stirs debate. You can climb the tower, or take a lift, for a view over the whole fjord, where ferries, warships and sailing yachts cross the water in a constant parade.

Beside the memorial, on dry land, lies a Second World War submarine, U-995, now a museum. It is cramped, cold and surprisingly small inside, and walking through it gives you a very direct feel for what the crews endured. Both attractions sit on a bluff above the beach, and the walk down to the water takes a few minutes.

Laboe itself is a small seaside town of about five thousand, with a harbour, a promenade, and shops selling smoked fish and ice cream. The beach is a pleasant stretch of sand, popular with families in summer, and the air smells of salt and seaweed. In the evening the sun sets over the fjord, and the lights of Kiel glimmer in the distance.

The ride to get here from Kiel runs along the eastern shore of the fjord, through quiet villages such as Heikendorf, with views of the water through the trees. The road is gentle and winding, with the odd short rise, and in summer weekend traffic can be heavy, with cyclists and families heading for the beach. An early morning start gives you the best light, and a quiet road. Fuel is available in Laboe and Heikendorf, and Kiel has everything. If you start here, take a slow breakfast in the harbour first, and leave the climb until you are warm.
t.laboe@54.4,10.2:
By the time the road brings you back to Laboe, the day has usually done its work, and the town greets you with the particular tiredness of a seaside place at dusk. Fishing boats bump gently in the harbour, the promenade lights flicker on, and somewhere a ship's horn sounds out on the fjord. It is a pleasant place to end a ride, small enough that you can see everything in a few minutes.

Kiel Fjord has a long sailing tradition. The city hosts Kiel Week every June, which is the largest sailing event in the world, with thousands of boats and a huge festival on the shore, and the Olympic sailing competitions of 1936 and 1972 were held at Schilksee, on the western side of the fjord. Laboe, on the opposite shore, has always had a front-row seat. In summer the water is full of white sails, and the ferries run to Kiel across the fjord, a short, cheap and pleasant crossing if you leave the bike behind.

The smell of the place is a mixture of tar, seaweed and smoked fish, and you can buy the last at a stall by the harbour. Try a smoked herring or a sprat, eaten with your fingers from paper, and wash it down with a coffee or a beer. The restaurants along the front serve the usual north German fare of fried fish with potatoes, and portions are generous.

Fuel is on hand in Laboe itself and in Heikendorf, five kilometres away, a bigger place with supermarkets. After a day on the road, a short walk along the beach is the best way to unwind. The tide barely moves in the Baltic, so there is no need to time anything, and the water is calm in the evening. If the weather is clear, stay to see the last of the light fade over the fjord, and watch the ships pass. It is a modest and peaceful finish.
t.fehmarn bridge view@54.4,11.1:
Fehmarn is joined to the mainland by one of the most recognisable bridges in Germany, a steel arch about a kilometre long that spans the Fehmarnsund and carries both road and rail. Opened in 1963, it has an elegant, slightly improbable shape, and locals call it the coat hanger. The bridge was built as part of the so-called Bird Flight Line, a transport route linking Hamburg with Copenhagen via the island and a ferry to Denmark, and it has been the main way on and off Fehmarn ever since.

A far bigger project is now taking shape just to the east. A road and rail tunnel is being built under the Fehmarn Belt to link Germany and Denmark directly, a project that has been discussed for decades and has already changed the look of the island's northern shore with construction sites and new roads. When it opens, the ferries that have crossed here for generations will lose most of their traffic.

Riding across the bridge is a small thrill, though a windy one, since the crossing is exposed and gusts can be strong. Once on the island, you ride through a flat, open landscape of big fields, wind turbines, sheep grazing on the dikes and small brick villages, with the sea showing in glimpses on every side. The roads are straight and gently curved, and traffic is light except on summer weekends, when holidaymakers fill the beaches and the roads to them.

Fehmarn is a cyclists' paradise, and you will share the road with many of them, so give them room. The island's main town, Burg, has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and the whole island is just over a dozen thousand people. Wind is the dominant feature, so check the forecast and pick your direction carefully, as riding into a strong headwind on a flat road can be tiring. Keep your fuel stops simple: Burg is the best option, and the island is small enough that you will never be far from it.
t.preetz return line@54.2,10.3:
Preetz sits on the Schwentine river between two lakes, and its old convent is the reason to slow down. The Benedictine nunnery of Preetz, founded in the early thirteenth century, survived the Reformation by turning into a Protestant convent for unmarried daughters of the Holstein nobility, a role it still plays today, and its Gothic brick church and cloister stand on a peaceful spit of land beside the Kellersee. The nuns, or rather the ladies, are not in view, but the buildings are lovely, and a short walk around the grounds is a quiet pleasure.

Preetz is a town of nearly sixteen thousand, and it has a straightforward market square and a handful of cafés. It also marks a gateway: from here the hills and lakes of Holstein Switzerland begin to the east, and the road toward Kiel starts to fill with traffic to the west. That makes it a convenient spot to regroup before the last leg of a ride.

The return line runs through a landscape of low moraine hills, fields and small woods, where the glaciers of the last Ice Age dumped their load and left hollows that have filled with water. The roads dip and rise in a pleasant rhythm, with sharp but forgiving bends. At twenty-two metres above the sea, the point is hardly high, but the views can be wide. In May the rapeseed fields flare yellow, and in autumn the beech woods turn gold.

Schellhorn, a small village on the edge, and Raisdorf, a larger one with shops, are close by. Fuel and supermarkets are right in Preetz. If you want a place to sit and catch your breath, the lakeside is only a few minutes' walk from the centre, and swans are always on the water. The light in the evening is soft here, and the whole district takes on a gentle, tired glow. Kiel is half an hour on, and you will find the traffic lighter if you wait until after the evening rush.
t.eutin castle@54.1,10.6:
Eutin's castle is easier to enjoy from the water side. Walk through the gardens at the back and the park slopes down to the shore of the Great Eutin Lake, with an avenue of old trees, a curving gravel path, and swans sliding across the surface in a V. The landscape garden was laid out in the English style in the early nineteenth century and is still planted with fine old trees, among them oaks and beeches that are well over a century old. On summer evenings an open-air opera festival is staged on a stage at the water's edge, and the sound carries across the lake.

The castle's moat and its low, brick-and-stucco front give it a gentle, domestic look, more country house than fortress, and the whole thing sits on what was once an island. It is only a short walk from the town centre, with its rose beds, its market square and its half-timbered houses, and a few good places for coffee. Rose growers in the area have given Eutin its nickname, and in June and July the town's gardens are in bloom.

The road to Eutin from the south, from Hamburg and the Segeberg country, runs through quiet farmland with big skies, past thatched farms and lakes glimmering between the trees. As you approach the lake district the countryside grows more rolling, and the road begins to bend. The surfaces are generally good, and there are many pleasant little lanes to explore. Traffic is light on weekdays, but summer weekends bring crowds heading for the beaches on the Baltic.

Eutin has about seventeen thousand people and plenty of filling stations, shops and cafés, while Malente has a spa-town feel and a long lakeside promenade. This is a good place to stop for lunch, with a choice of cafés on the market square. Kasseedorf, seven kilometres off, is a tiny village with a small manor house. If you can, stay until late afternoon, when the light on the water turns gold and the day-trippers leave for home.
t.ahrensburg@53.7,10.2:
Ahrensburg owes its character to a single building, the castle. Schloss Ahrensburg is a Renaissance moated residence of pale rose-pink stucco, built in the late sixteenth century by the Rantzau family, one of the great noble houses of Holstein, and it stands in a green park beside a mirror-like pond. The house has a fairytale shape, with gables, turrets and a drawbridge, and it is now a museum. Behind it stretch lawns and an avenue of ancient limes, and the town's coffee houses and bakeries cluster nearby.

The area has a far older claim to fame. About twelve thousand years ago, reindeer hunters roamed the tundra of what is now Stormarn, and the remains of their camps were found in the Ahrensburg tunnel valley, a long, glacial channel just north of the town. The culture is now known to archaeologists as the Ahrensburgian, named for the town, and it is one of the best-known late Ice Age hunter cultures in northern Europe. A walk through the wooded valley gives a hint of that wild past.

Ahrensburg is a town of thirty thousand, a prosperous commuter place on the northeastern edge of Hamburg, and it has the comforts you would expect: filling stations, supermarkets, good bakeries and a pleasant pedestrian zone. It is an easy place to take a break, because it is close to the city and has easy parking. Großhansdorf, three kilometres to the north-east, is a woodland suburb with a large nature reserve of beech forest, where the ground rises into low hills.

For the rider, the coffee stop is a gentle pause between the city and the lakes beyond. The roads east of Ahrensburg wind through woods and fields, with sandy lanes lined with oaks, and the traffic thins quickly once you pass the last roundabouts. In spring the beech woods are a fresh, bright green. Take your coffee in the castle park if the weather allows, and watch the ducks on the moat. It is a calm place to start the day.
t.hamburg north east edge@53.6,10.1:
Hamburg's north-eastern fringe, where the city gives way to fields, is a district of long avenues, brick housing blocks and green corridors. The Wandse, a small river that runs through the area, has been tamed into a chain of ponds and parks, and the path along it is popular with walkers and cyclists. Farmsen-Berne and Steilshoop, the two large districts nearby, are residential neighbourhoods built mostly in the twentieth century, with rows of apartment buildings, shopping centres and tree-lined streets. Wandsbek, a little further south, is the big local hub.

For a motorcyclist, a start here has a clear advantage: it is on the right side of the city for a run out to the north and east, avoiding the harbour and the tunnels and the Elbe bridges. You can pick up the roads towards the lakes of Holstein or the heaths of the Lüneburg country without crossing the centre. Commuter traffic on weekday mornings is heavy, so early on a weekend or after nine on a weekday are better.

Hamburg itself deserves a moment of thought as you leave. It is Germany's second city, with a harbour that has been central to its life for over eight hundred years, and its wealth is visible in the red-brick warehouses of the Speicherstadt, the grand merchant houses and the lakes of the Alster in the heart of town. The city has always seen itself as a free city of merchants, independent and outward-looking, and people there still say they are Hamburgers first and Germans second.

Fuel is plentiful in all the surrounding districts, with stations on the main roads and supermarkets on every other corner, so fill up before you go. A bakery breakfast of rolls and coffee is the local way to start. The wind from the west, off the North Sea, will usually push you along on the way out.
t.hamburg@53.6,10.1:
The Wandsbek and Farmsen end of Hamburg is the quiet side of the city, and it makes a gentle landing at the end of a day. After the traffic of the autobahn, the streets are slow and tree-lined, with low brick buildings and the soft glow of shop windows. The district is not on any tourist list, but it has the unhurried feel of a place where people actually live, with weekly markets, small cafés and corner bakeries, and a long stretch of park beside the Wandse where dog walkers and joggers pass in the evening.

If you have arrived back with energy to spare, Hamburg is a city that rewards an evening. Head for the water: the Alster lakes in the centre are ringed with paths and cafés, with white excursion boats gliding across the surface. Or take the ferry across the Elbe, which is part of the city's ordinary public transport and gives a fine view of the harbour cranes, the container ships and the grand shape of the concert hall on the quay. The city's signature snack, a fish roll with pickled herring or fried fish, can be bought at a stall near the landing stage.

The weather in Hamburg is famously changeable, and the saying goes that you can have four seasons in an afternoon. Rain, wind and sunshine pass over the flat land in quick succession, so a layer of waterproofs is always useful. Autumn and spring tend to be the most pleasant, with the low light of evening turning the brick red and the canals silver. If it rains, shelter in the doorway of a café and wait; it will pass.

There is no worry about fuel here, because the district is thick with stations and supermarkets, and the nearest big shops are in Wandsbek, a few minutes away. Park the bike somewhere safe, take off your helmet, and give your legs a moment to remember how to walk. Then decide whether to go straight to bed or to find a late supper. Either is a perfectly good way to end a ride.
t.hamburg south east edge@53.5,10.1:
The Vier- und Marschlande, the Four Lands and the Marsh Lands, spread out to the south-east of Hamburg, and this starting point at the edge of the city is the doorway to them. For several centuries this has been the garden of Hamburg: a low, fertile floodplain of the Elbe where farmers grow vegetables, flowers and fruit under glass and in the open, and send them into the city's markets. The land is protected by dikes and drained by a network of ditches, and the old farmhouses, thatched and half-timbered, sit on mounds at the edge of the fields.

Rothenburgsort, the district just to the north, is one of the places where the city's industrial past is most visible. A neo-Gothic water tower, built in the nineteenth century and now empty, stands among the warehouses, and the old workers' quarter, almost entirely destroyed in the firestorm of 1943, has been rebuilt with plain, sensible blocks. The Elbe's many channels and locks run through the area, and boats work them day and night.

The ride begins in a tangle of bridges, railway lines and slip roads, and the first quarter hour demands attention. Once you are through, the road opens out on the dike, and it's a long, flat run through the marshes towards Bergedorf and the edge of the Sachsenwald. Corners are rare, but the views are wide, with great skies, grazing cattle and, in spring, fields of tulips and rape. The wind is the main player, and on the dike you feel every gust.

There is no shortage of fuel at the start, because the city has stations in every direction. Once in the marsh, the choice narrows, so fill up here and carry on. Bergedorf, a few kilometres to the east, has a castle, an old centre and plenty of cafés for a first coffee. Start early on a weekend, when the traffic on the city's exits is light, and the market gardens are just waking up. By the time you reach the Elbe's tidal banks, the city will already feel far behind.
t.sachsenwald forest road@53.5,10.3:
The Sachsenwald is the largest forest in Schleswig-Holstein, a broad sweep of beech, oak and spruce on sandy ground just east of Hamburg, and it has an unusually personal history. In 1871 Kaiser Wilhelm I gave it to Otto von Bismarck, the Chancellor who had united Germany, as a reward for his services, and Bismarck made his home on its edge, in Friedrichsruh. He lived there for much of his later life, entertained statesmen and walked the forest paths, and he is buried in a mausoleum a short distance from the old house, in a simple chapel in the trees.

The forest road runs at about fifty-five metres above sea level, across a gently rolling surface of glacial sand and gravel. The corners are soft, the surface is mostly smooth and the trees press close on both sides, giving the ride a rhythmic, tunnel-like quality. In autumn the leaves of the old beeches turn bronze and fall in drifts on the verges, and in spring the forest floor is carpeted with wood anemones. Deer and wild boar are common, and the forest has a reputation for fine mushrooms.

Because the Sachsenwald is a working forest, you will meet timber lorries, cyclists, walkers and horse riders, so slow down on blind bends. Weekends can be busy near the car parks. The villages on the edge, Witzhave, Wohltorf and Dassendorf, are small, with quiet streets and a handful of bakeries. Aumühle, a short ride away, is where Bismarck's estate lay, and the local museum tells his story.

Reinbek, a town of twenty-five thousand about seven kilometres off, has a Renaissance castle, a mill, and plenty of fuel and food. It is the sensible place to refuel, since the forest villages have few pumps. A good approach is to ride the forest on a weekday morning, when it is quiet, and to bring a little water. When the sun comes through the high trees and the light falls in shafts on the road, it is hard to want to be anywhere else.
t.lauenburg old elbe town@53.4,10.6:
Lauenburg sits on a steep bank above the Elbe, a small town with an old centre that tumbles down the hill in two levels, the upper town and the lower town, joined by narrow alleys. For centuries it was a toll station on one of the most important trade routes in northern Europe. Salt from Lüneburg went by barge and cart up the old Salt Road to Lübeck, and the Stecknitz Canal, an early artificial waterway, linked the Elbe to the Baltic. Boats, merchants and customs men all passed through Lauenburg, which is why the old houses are so good.

The town stands where the Elbe-Lübeck Canal begins, a waterway of 1900 that replaced the old route, and it is also the capital of what was once the Duchy of Lauenburg. The Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck was given the title of Duke of Lauenburg on his dismissal in 1890, a rather odd consolation prize. The little museum of Elbe shipping, in the lower town, tells the story of the river and its boats.

The Elbe has also been a destroyer here. In the floods of 2013 the river rose to record levels, swamped the lower town and left mud in the streets and cellars, and the townspeople are justly proud of the way they cleaned up. At twenty metres above sea level, the point is high enough to be safe, but you can see the flood marks on the walls of the old houses.

A motorcycle ride here is a delight, with an old river road winding along the Elbe through villages like Artlenburg and Echem, past dikes and meadows where cattle graze. The surface is mostly good, the corners long and easy, and the traffic light outside the summer weekends. Lauenburg is a town of nearly twelve thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a few cafés in the old town. Climb the steep alleys on foot, and look back at the river from the top. It is a good view of a working river.
t.hamburg@53.5,10.1:
At the end of a ride from the east, the road drops into Hamburg's old industrial quarters, and the city seems to gather itself in. Rothenburgsort and Hammerbrook are the districts around the point, and they carry a darker history than most. In July 1943, during the bombing of the city, a firestorm swept through these streets, killing tens of thousands and flattening whole neighbourhoods. Rebuilding came in the plain, practical style of the 1950s, and little of the older city survives. A few ruined walls and one or two memorial plaques remain.

Just to the west lies the HafenCity, one of the largest urban redevelopment projects in Europe, where old warehouses and new glass blocks sit side by side along the harbour. The Elbphilharmonie, the concert hall opened in 2017 on top of an old brick warehouse, is the showpiece, and from its public plaza you can look across the whole port. The Speicherstadt, the red-brick warehouse district, was listed by UNESCO in 2015 and is at its best in the evening, when the lights come on and are reflected in the canals.

The ride in is a mixture of dike road and urban motorway. After the open marshes and the quiet of the Vier- und Marschlande, the last stretch is tight and busy, with bridges, ramps, tunnel mouths and a lot of trucks. Take it slowly, keep your lane and watch the signs, because it is easy to take the wrong exit and end up in the port. Weekday evenings are heavy, and Sundays are far easier.

At twenty metres above sea level, the point is on the edge of the old floodplain, near the Elbe's bridges. Fuel is easily found, with stations along the main roads and bigger supermarkets nearby. Park near the harbour and walk for twenty minutes, because the city's best view is on foot. The ships sound their horns as they come and go, the gulls cry, and the day winds down to the smell of salt water and diesel.
t.berlin@52.5,13.4:
The tower, finished in 1969 and 368 metres high, is the tallest structure in Germany and can be seen from nearly everywhere in the city. It was built by the East German government as a showpiece of socialist engineering, and when the sun hits its steel sphere, it throws a cross of light that Berliners cheekily called the Pope's revenge.

The neighbourhood is a mix of the grand and the plain, and it tells the whole story of the city. Nearby is the Nikolaiviertel, a reconstructed medieval quarter on the site where Berlin began, and the huge brick Marienkirche, one of the oldest churches in the city. A few minutes away is Museum Island, whose five museums on an island in the Spree were listed by UNESCO in 1999. Across the river the great boulevards lead to the Brandenburg Gate, and along the way you pass the remains of the Wall, a strip of cobbles in the road marking where it ran.

As a place to start a ride, Berlin is demanding. The streets are wide but busy, with trams whose rails can catch a thin tyre in the wet, cobbles in the older quarters, and a great many cyclists, scooters and delivery vans. Traffic lights are everywhere. Early on a Sunday morning the centre is almost empty and a pleasure, but at rush hour it is slow and stressful. Once you are beyond the ring road the landscape opens into forests and lakes, and the riding gets better quickly.

Fuel in the centre is limited, because the stations are mostly on the outer roads, so fill up on the way in or on the way out. Parking a bike in Mitte is easy to do and hard to do well, and a locked chain through the frame is sensible. Berlin eats late and stays up later, so there is no need to hurry.
t.iwami jo site@35.1,132.4:
The Iwami Ginzan silver mine lies in a narrow, forested valley in Shimane Prefecture, on the Sea of Japan side of western Honshu, and the site called Iwami-jo is a reminder that the silver here was worth fighting for. Iwami-jo, also known as Yamabuki Castle, was a mountain fortress perched on a ridge above the mining district, and for much of the sixteenth century the great regional clans, first the Ouchi, then the Amago and finally the Mori, struggled to control it. The mine was a source of wealth and power, and whoever held the castle held the silver.

The silver itself transformed this part of Japan. Large-scale mining began in the 1520s, when new refining techniques from Korea made it possible to extract silver more efficiently, and by the early seventeenth century the mine was producing a huge share of Japan's output, and Japan in turn supplied a notable fraction of the world's silver. European mapmakers of the time marked this region as the silver mines. The site was listed by UNESCO in 2007, partly because the mine left so little scar on the landscape; the forest has grown back over the workings.

The riding here is a calm affair. Approaches to the mining district are narrow country roads through cedar forest, with a few tight bends and a lot of shade, and the speed limits are low. The town of Oda, about ten kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and it is the place to fill up before heading into the valley. In the old district, car access is limited, and you are expected to park at a visitor lot and walk or cycle.

The ride goes on from here toward Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, a long day across the Chugoku mountains, so plan for an early start. Autumn is spectacular, with red maples against dark cedar, and spring brings fresh green. Summer is humid, and the winter coast can be grey and wet. Take a rain jacket in any season, since the weather off the Sea of Japan changes fast.
t.daikansho site@35.1,132.4:
Daikansho was the administrative heart of the Iwami Ginzan silver mine, the place where the magistrate sent by the shogun ruled the district. After the Tokugawa took over the mine in 1600, they appointed a daikan, a magistrate, to oversee production, collect the silver and govern the people, and the office, in the town of Omori, became the centre of power in the valley. The surviving gate and the long white-walled building that now houses a museum were rebuilt in the nineteenth century, and they give a sense of the weight of officialdom in this remote place.

The first magistrate is the most famous. Okubo Nagayasu, a man of unusual talent who started his career as a Noh performer's son and rose to become a mining engineer, was appointed to Iwami and later to Sado Island, another great source of silver. He reorganised the workings, improved drainage and ventilation, and stabilised the district, and he is remembered as the man who made the mine efficient. The silver was carried by pack horse over roads to the coast and then shipped to the capital, and some was exported through Hakata and Nagasaki.

For motorcyclists, the approach is simple. The valley road from Oda leads in along the river, with a single lane in places and a few passing bays. Visitors are encouraged to park in the lots at the edge of the old town and walk the long street, which is lined with wooden houses, temples and shops, and a small shop selling local sweets and stone-ground flour is a good stop. The surface is generally good, but it is narrow and shaded, and leaves can be slick in autumn.

Fuel is in Oda, eleven kilometres away, and there is little in the valley itself. Rain is frequent here, so a waterproof layer is wise in any month. If you want to see more of the district, rent a bicycle in the village, since the best way to feel the scale of the old town is slowly. Come early in the morning, before the tour groups, and the street is empty and quiet.
t.house of the kumagai family@35.1,132.4:
The Kumagai family house stands on the main street of Omori, the little town that grew up around the Iwami Ginzan silver mine, and it is a rare case of a merchant house that looks as it did two centuries ago. The Kumagai were among the leading merchants of the district, trading in goods, and dealing with money and the officials of the magistrate's office, and the house was rebuilt in the early nineteenth century after a fire swept the town. It is now an Important Cultural Property, and the care given to its restoration is obvious.

What strikes you inside is the practicality. A long earthen corridor runs the length of the house from the street to the back, with a big kitchen at one end, an open hearth, and a series of rooms for living, receiving guests and storing goods. The wooden pillars are dark with age, and there is a small garden at the back with a storehouse. A system of strongboxes and hiding places recalls the importance of security in a mining town that handled silver. The house shows how prosperity and discretion went together here.

Riding in is easy enough, if you accept the rules. The roads into the valley from the coast at Oda are narrow country lanes, shaded by cedar, and the old street of Omori is closed to most traffic, so you park at a visitor lot at the edge and walk up the gentle slope. It is about a ten-minute walk, and a small shop selling local goods and a cafe or two break the journey. The pavement is uneven, so wear sensible boots rather than your riding armour.

Fuel is down in Oda, about eleven kilometres away, and that is the place to fill before heading back toward the long ride to Miyajima. Rain is frequent, and the wet slate and red tile roofs shine nicely after a shower. Try to arrive early, since the house is open at limited hours, and many visitors come in the middle of the day.
t.iwami ginzan kaido yunotsu okidomarido@3:
The old road from the Iwami Ginzan mine to the sea at Yunotsu and Okidomari was the route silver took to the world. For centuries, ore and then refined silver were carried on the backs of porters and pack horses along a mountain track that dropped from the mine to the Sea of Japan, a distance of several hours on foot. At the coast, ships collected the cargo and carried it to the markets and ports of the country. Yunotsu was a harbour town with a deep inlet; Okidomari, the name of which means something like moorage offshore, was where the boats waited in the bay.

Yunotsu is an unusual place. It is a hot-spring town of old wooden inns and bath houses, with red-tiled roofs, a narrow main street of stone paving, and a small beach, and its hot springs are said to be some thirteen centuries old. The red roof tiles are typical of the Iwami region, glazed in a local iron-rich clay that gives a deep rust colour and withstands the salt and the snow. Walking through the town is like stepping into a quieter century, with the smell of sea and sulphur.

The coast road here, Route 9 and the local lanes, runs along the edge of the sea in a mix of gentle bends and long straights, with tunnels and views of rocky bays, and the traffic is light, so it is a pleasure on a clear day. The old mine road itself is a walking trail, not for motorcycles. In winter, storms from the north bring huge waves and sometimes close the road, and in summer the beaches are lively but not crowded.

Gotsu, the nearest sizeable town with fuel and shops, is about sixteen kilometres away, and that is where to fill. The seafood is a draw: look for fish grilled on the spot, and for the local sweet made from rice. A hot bath at the end of a coastal ride is a perfect reward, and many inns offer day use, so ask. Go in spring or autumn when the air is mild, and watch for sudden showers.
t.miyanomae@35.1,132.4:
Miyanomae is a name that looks mysterious but means something simple: in front of the shrine. It is a neighbourhood in the old mining town of Omori, in the valley of the Iwami Ginzan silver mine, and the name tells you how the town was arranged. Shrines and temples were scattered through the valley, and the houses of miners, officials and merchants gathered around them along the narrow, curving road that is the spine of Omori.

The town today is a preserved district, listed in the 1980s as an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, and walking through it is a gentle experience. The houses are low, wooden, plastered in white and brown, with dark tile roofs and latticed windows, and the lane is lined with small shops, cafes and galleries in restored buildings. A stream runs beside the road, and the hills rise steeply on both sides, covered in cedar and bamboo.
