Life here is slow, and on a quiet weekday morning you will hear birds and water more than engines.

For riders the approach is through the valley from Oda, along narrow roads under thick forest, with some tight bends and little traffic. You must park at the visitor lot at the edge of the district and walk in; bikes are not welcome on the old street itself. It is about ten minutes on foot to the heart of the town, and the walk is a pleasure, past bridges and moss-covered walls. In rain, the cobbles and stones are slippery, so take care.

Fuel and food come from Oda, some eleven kilometres away, and there are only a few simple cafes in the valley. This stop belongs to a long ride toward Itsukushima Shrine at Miyajima, a very long way south-east across the Chugoku mountains, so an early start and a full tank are important. Autumn leaves colour the valley beautifully, and spring brings fresh green and the sound of frogs from the little paddies.
t.tomogaura@35.1,132.4:
Tomogaura is a tiny port on the Sea of Japan coast, a deep, narrow bay in the rocky shoreline of Shimane Prefecture, and it has an important place in the story of Iwami Ginzan. In the early years of the silver rush, in the sixteenth century, this was one of the harbours where ore and silver left the district for the outside world. The natural shelter was valuable: steep, wooded hills on three sides, and a narrow mouth facing the sea, so that small ships could anchor safely out of the winter storms.

The port also has a defensive history, since the clans that fought for control of the mine needed to protect their supply line to the coast. A road led up from the harbour to the mining district, the Tomogaura Kaido, and the whole sequence of mine, road and port forms the cultural landscape that UNESCO listed in 2007. What you see now is a quiet fishing village, with a few houses on the shore, boats pulled up on the slipway, nets drying and the smell of seaweed and salt. It is easy to imagine how different it must have looked when silver was loaded here.

The riding is the reward. The coast road along this part of Shimane runs through a series of tunnels, headlands and small bays, with the grey sea on one side and wooded hills on the other. The bends are gentle and the surface is generally good, and in good weather the views of cliffs and islands are fine. In winter, northerly gales make it a rough, cold place, with wave spray over the road in storms, and the best months are May and June, and September and October.

Bring a snack and water, and, if you are lucky, buy fish directly from a boat. In the evening the light on the water is lovely, particularly when the sun sets over the sea and the lamps of the fishing boats come on.
t.rakan ji gohyakurakan@35.1,132.4:
Rakan-ji is a small Buddhist temple in the Omori valley with an extraordinary secret in the rock behind it. Cut into the cliff are three caves, and inside them sit about five hundred stone figures, the Gohyakurakan, the five hundred disciples of the Buddha, each carved from the soft local tuff and each with a different face. Some laugh, some frown, some seem to be talking to their neighbours, and some are asleep. They were made in the eighteenth century, over a few decades, by a master carver and his helpers, and they were commissioned to console the spirits of the miners who died in the silver workings.

The mine was a deadly place. Digging in the tunnels filled the lungs with fine dust, and many miners died young, and the people of the valley responded with religious devotion. A pilgrim's tradition says you will find a figure with the face of someone you have lost, and the visitors who walk slowly through the caves, searching the faces, are rarely noisy. A stone bridge over the stream leads to the temple, and the setting among cedar trees is quiet and cool.

Getting there takes some effort, but it is worth it. The road into the valley from Oda is narrow and shaded, with a few tight bends, and the final approach is on foot from the visitor parking area, over uneven stone paths. The temple is open at limited times and there is a small entrance fee, so check beforehand. Moss makes the stones slippery in wet weather, and the caves are damp, so wear shoes with good grip.

Fuel is available in Oda, around eleven kilometres away, and there is little in the valley, so fill before you ride in. Spring is gentle, with fresh leaves, and autumn colours the hillsides, but even on a grey, wet day the temple has a special atmosphere. The silence here is its own reward, and a few minutes spent among the figures leaves a lasting impression. Allow a leisurely hour on the site.
t.omori ginzan@35.1,132.4:
Omori Ginzan is the town that silver built, and it is one of the most appealing historic places in western Japan. It stretches for about two kilometres along a narrow valley, a single winding street lined with merchant houses, samurai residences, temples and shrines, and a stream that tumbles beside it. At the height of the mining boom, thousands of people lived in this valley, but now it is a quiet place of a few hundred residents, and the contrast with its busy past is part of the charm.

The history is large. A merchant from Hakata is said to have started the mining in the 1520s, and a new refining method, brought from Korea, made production soar. By the early seventeenth century, Iwami silver was a major part of the world's supply, and the Tokugawa shogunate took direct control of the mine in 1600, sending a magistrate to run it. When the silver ran low, the mine declined, and it finally closed in 1923. The forest returned and covered the old workings, so that the valley looks like a normal mountain landscape, which is one reason why UNESCO praised it as an example of low-impact mining.

The town is a pleasure to walk. Old houses with white plaster walls and dark roof tiles now hold small shops, cafes and guesthouses, and a few young families have moved in to run them, giving the street a gentle life. Local bread, pottery and cloth are good buys. The street is closed to most vehicles in the day, so park at the visitor lot at the edge and walk, or rent a bicycle.

Getting here by motorbike means a narrow, wooded road up from Oda, with a few tight bends and light traffic, so take it steadily. Fuel is available in Oda, about eleven kilometres away, and there is none in the valley. The weather can be wet in any season, with fog in the early morning, so carry waterproofs. The best light is early, before the coaches arrive, when the street is quiet and the stream is audible.
The Tomogaura road is a mountain path, and it is one of the best ways to understand how silver left the mine. It climbs out of the valley at Omori, crosses a ridge, and drops down to the coast at the small harbour of Tomogaura, a journey of a few hours on foot, and for centuries it was walked by porters carrying ore on their backs and by pack horses with straw sandals. The whole route has been preserved, and sections of old stone paving, shrine gates and wayside markers survive in the forest.

The trail goes through beautiful woods, tall cedar and cypress, and, in the damp shade, a thick carpet of ferns and moss. Streams cross the path, and in places you can see the old stone steps worn smooth by centuries of feet. It is a quiet, cool walk, particularly in summer, and one of the few places in western Japan where you can feel the old road under your boots. Wildlife is part of it: monkeys, deer and wild boar live in the hills, and birdsong fills the forest.

On a motorbike, you cannot ride the old path itself, and you should not try. The paved roads around it, however, are good for riding. The valley road from Oda to Omori is narrow and winding, with a few tight bends, and the coast road along the Sea of Japan is a pleasure, running through tunnels and past headlands with views of grey water. Traffic is light, and rain is frequent, so take care on wet surfaces and fallen leaves in autumn.

If you want to walk the path, allow a half day, take water and a rain jacket, and wear proper shoes, since the ground can be slippery. Check at the visitor centre in Omori for the current state of the trail, because storms sometimes close sections. The reward is quiet, and a feel for the silver road.
t.ginzan sakunouchi@35.1,132.4:
Sakunouchi is the heart of the Iwami Ginzan mining district, the area where the silver was dug, and the name roughly means inside the fence. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the mining area was enclosed and controlled, and the people who worked within it were registered and monitored, so that nothing valuable left without notice. Today the site is a quiet forested valley with a footpath, a stream and the openings of many old tunnels, some of them hundreds of years old.

The tunnels are called mabu, and the best known, Ryugenji Mabu, is open to visitors for a short walk. It is a narrow, damp passage dug by hand, with chisel marks still visible on the walls, side shafts leading off into darkness and small niches where lamps were placed. The air is cool and still, and the sound of dripping water is constant. It gives an immediate and unvarnished sense of how hard the work was, and how small the miners were by the standards of today. A short way along the valley stand the remains of a refining site, with terraces and foundations in the trees.

Getting here by bike means leaving the machine behind. The valley road from Oda is narrow, wooded and shaded, with a few tight bends and light traffic, and visitors park at the lots at the edge of the district, then walk or cycle in. The paths are well made but wet and slippery in rain, so bring sensible shoes and a light waterproof. The tunnel is cool even in summer, so a thin extra layer is welcome.

Fuel is in Oda, about eleven kilometres away, with little available in the valley itself. There are a few modest cafes and shops in Omori, but come with water and a snack. Visit early in the day, before the coaches, and you may have the tunnel to yourself. The ride from here continues on a long road toward Itsukushima, so keep an eye on time, and leave plenty of daylight for the journey.
t.yunotsu@35.1,132.3:
Yunotsu is a town that could have been built for people who like to walk slowly. It lies on the Sea of Japan coast of Shimane Prefecture, in the municipality of Gotsu, squeezed into a narrow ravine between hills and sea, with one main street of wooden inns and bathhouses, red roof tiles glowing in the light and a small bay at the end. The hot springs here are said to be thirteen centuries old, and some of the bathhouses are small, plain, communal places where the water comes straight from the ground and the locals soak before work.

The town's other claim is that it was the port of the silver. The Iwami Ginzan mine lies in the hills behind, and the old road, the Yunotsu-Okidomari Kaido, brought ore and silver down to this coast, where ships took it away. Yunotsu is part of the UNESCO listing of the mine and its cultural landscape, and the harbour, with its sheltered cove and the old warehouse lanes, still has the feel of a place built for loading. The red roof tiles, glazed with local clay, are typical of the Iwami region and have survived centuries of salt and snow. Some of the buildings are of an old style with shingled walls and latticed upper floors, and there are also unusual pale bathhouses with elegant tiled facades.

The ride in is the Shimane coast, a quiet piece of Japan: tunnels, headlands, small harbours and cliffs, with the grey Sea of Japan beside you and the road running up and down along the shore. The curves are gentle and the surface is generally good, and you will often have it to yourself. Winter brings northern storms with high waves, and fog sometimes comes in from the sea, so watch the forecast. Gotsu, sixteen kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and it is sensible to fill there, since the town itself is small.

Try fresh fish at one of the small restaurants, and consider a short bath before you ride on. The light in the evening, when the sun goes down over the water and the lamps come on along the alley, is the best moment of the day. A night here is better than a stop.
t.iwami ginzan silver mine and its cultura:
Under the forest that covers Iwami Ginzan is one of the great silver mines of the world, and it is a kind of miracle that you can hardly see it. The silver was dug here from the 1520s to 1923, in narrow hand-cut tunnels, and the district grew into a complex of mine, refineries, a mining town, roads and harbours, all of which were listed by UNESCO in 2007 as a single cultural landscape. What the committee praised was the lightness of the touch. Unlike so many mining regions, this one was not ripped apart, and the forest simply grew back.

The silver rush began when a Hakata merchant brought refining specialists from Korea, and production boomed. By the early seventeenth century Japan was among the major silver producers in the world, and Iwami was its greatest mine. European mapmakers of the time labelled the region as silver mines. The Tokugawa shogunate took control in 1600, and the magistrate they sent, Okubo Nagayasu, put the district in order. The silver was carried down mountain roads to the coast and shipped away, and the mine's long decline ended in closure in 1923.

The valley is a delight for a quiet rider. The approach from the town of Oda, about eleven kilometres away, is a narrow, wooded road, with a few tight bends and little traffic. Cars are limited in the old town, so you park at the edge and walk, past mossy walls, wooden houses, temples and a stream. A short stretch of tunnel is open to visitors, and the Rakan-ji temple with its five hundred stone figures in the cliff caves is worth a visit.

Fuel is in Oda and the coastal towns, not in the valley. The journey continues toward Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, a long day across the Chugoku mountains and down to the Inland Sea, so start early and keep an eye on the clock. The best seasons are autumn, with red maples against dark cedar, and spring, with fresh leaves. In summer it is humid, and the Sea of Japan coast brings rain in any season.
t.batopilas@27.0,-107.7:
Batopilas sits at the bottom of the Copper Canyon, in a gorge so deep that tropical fruit grows where the rim above is covered with pine forest. The town was founded in 1708 as a silver mining settlement, and its fortunes surged in the 1880s, when an American, Alexander Shepherd, a former governor of the District of Columbia, bought the mines and made a fortune. He brought in machinery and electricity, and Batopilas had electric light before Mexico City did, a fact the locals tell with pride. The old stone houses, the aqueduct and the plaza with its bandstand recall the boom, and the remains of the hacienda are still there.

The canyon is the home of the Raramuri, also known as the Tarahumara, a people who have lived in the sierra for centuries and are famous for their long-distance running, covering enormous distances over rough terrain in sandals made of old tyre tread. Their villages are scattered through the hills, and a few women sell baskets and woven goods by the road. Not far from the town is the mission church of Satevo, built in the eighteenth century, often called the cathedral of the sierra, a solid, whitewashed building in a quiet valley.

The road from Creel to Batopilas is one of the great descents in Mexico, dropping from about 2,300 metres to roughly 500 in a series of hairpins on the canyon walls, with huge drops, blind bends and sections of gravel. It is long, slow and demanding, not a road to hurry, with trucks and buses squeezing past on the narrow parts. Landslides happen in the rainy months, from July to September, and the drive back up is just as slow. Early morning gives you the best light on the canyon walls.

Fuel is in Creel, and there is no station to rely on along the way, so fill the tank and carry a spare can. Batopilas has small guesthouses, simple restaurants and a modest supply of petrol, but confirm before relying on it. It is hot down here, so shed layers as you descend, and swim in the river if you have time.
t.plon lake@54.2,10.4:
Plon is a small town on a tongue of land between two lakes, and the biggest of them, the Grosser Ploner See, is the largest lake in Schleswig-Holstein, a broad, shining sheet of water dotted with islands and fringed with beech woods and reeds. The ride begins at the lakeside, a few minutes from the old town, with the pale Baroque castle on its hill above the water, and that sense of space and light sets the tone for the day. About thirteen thousand people live in Plon itself, with Ascheberg, a village on the lake's western shore, a short way off.

The landscape here is called the Holsteinische Schweiz, Holstein Switzerland, a name that makes locals smile and visitors raise an eyebrow, since the highest point is little more than a hill. But the glacial landscape of lakes, hummocks and valleys is lovely, and it makes good motorcycle country for people who like gentle, rolling roads instead of mountains. The lanes wind between fields and woods, through villages with brick churches and thatched barns, with a surface that is mostly good and bends that flow. The route toward Malente, Bungsberg and Eutin gathers pace through the hills, and at 168 metres, Bungsberg is the highest point in the state, where you can top it with a flourish. Traffic is light outside summer weekends, when cyclists, sailors and day trippers fill the roads.

The castle in Plon was built in the seventeenth century for the dukes of Holstein-Plon, and it later served as a military academy and is now a boarding school. The town itself began as a Slavic fortress on an island in the lake, and it later became a trading centre of the region, with a small, pretty centre of brick houses and a harbour. Eutin, farther east, was the birthplace of the composer Carl Maria von Weber, and its castle and rose gardens are worth a stop.

The lakes are a haven for birds, with cranes, grebes and white-tailed eagles nesting around the shores, and in autumn migrating geese fill the sky. Beech forest covers the hills, and in May the rapeseed fields glow yellow. The air smells of water, cut grass and, sometimes, a smoked fish stand by the quay, where eel and herring are sold.

Fuel is easy to find in Plon and the larger villages, and the cafes by the lake serve excellent cake. Bring a light waterproof, since the weather in northern Germany changes quickly, and take your time.
t.danish wohld lanes@54.4,10.0:
The Danish Wohld is a rolling peninsula of farmland and beech woods between Kiel Fjord and the Bay of Eckernforde, an unassuming corner of Schleswig-Holstein that rewards a motorcyclist with exactly what a short evening ride should offer: quiet lanes, long views and the smell of the sea on the breeze. The name is old, with Wohld meaning forest, and it recalls the days when this land formed a border region between the Danish and German worlds. The ride starts in the lanes near Osdorf, a village of a couple of thousand people, with Felm a little farther on, and Kiel's busy fuel stations and cafes a short ride behind you.

The roads here are narrow and flowing, running between the hedgerow banks known as Knicks, which divide the fields and give the landscape a tidy, patchwork look. The surface is generally good, though farm vehicles, mud from tractors and sudden blind bends need attention, and in harvest season dust and straw collect on the corners. The land rolls in gentle waves, with just enough ups and downs to keep things interesting. Late afternoon and early evening are the best times, when the light turns golden and the farm traffic fades, and May, when the rapeseed blooms bright yellow, is especially lovely. Coastal lanes along the bay add sea views, with sailing boats and wind-bent trees.

Gettorf, the main village on the route, is a quiet place of old brick houses and a stately church, and nearby are manor houses, such as Gut Knoop, that recall the days of the great estates, when noble families owned most of the land and farm labourers lived in rows of tied cottages. The Baltic coast here was a theatre of Danish and German conflict in the nineteenth century, with the region changing hands after the war of 1864. Today it is peaceful farming country, with cows, wheat and fields of maize.

The nature is soft and cultivated. Hedgerows shelter hares, partridges and songbirds, and the beech woods are carpeted with wood anemones in spring. On the coast, reeds and meadows give way to pebble beaches, where seabirds gather, and the air smells of salt, manure and cut hay. The wind off the Baltic is a constant companion, and in autumn the light is low and golden.

Bring a light jacket for the evening, and watch for deer at dusk, which are common on these lanes. Fuel is easy to find in Kiel and Gettorf. Take your time.
t.prague@50.1,14.4:
Prague does not need introduction, but it does need a plan if you are leaving it by motorcycle. The city lies on the Vltava river in the heart of Bohemia, with a skyline of spires and towers climbing the hill to the castle, and a medieval centre that survived the twentieth century better than most. The Charles Bridge, begun in 1357 under Emperor Charles IV, is lined with baroque statues and almost always full of people. The Old Town Square has its astronomical clock, dating back to the fifteenth century, and Vyšehrad, the rock above the river, holds an old church and a quiet cemetery where Dvořák and Smetana are buried.

Beer is the unofficial national religion, and Prague is its cathedral. Czechs drink more beer per head than any other nation, and the pubs serve it fresh, cold and cheap, with pork knuckle, dumplings and sauerkraut. The pilsner style was born in Plzeň, not far west, in 1842, and a glass of unfiltered lager in a cellar pub is the way to start. If you are riding, stick to the coffee and save the beer for the evening.

Leaving the city is the hard part. Traffic is heavy, trams run on cobbled streets, and the rails and wet stones can be treacherous for a motorcycle, so take care. Fuel is easy and cheap, and there are many large stations on the ring road. Motorcycles do not need the motorway vignette in the Czech Republic, though rules change, so check. Heading northeast toward Bohemian Paradise, the road crosses farmland and small towns, past Mladá Boleslav, where the Škoda car factory has been making vehicles since the 1890s.

Beyond, the landscape rises into sandstone rock towers and forested ridges, with castles perched on volcanic rocks, and the quiet roads are a fine contrast to the capital. Start early, avoid the morning rush, and enjoy the moment when the city falls behind and the fields open. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the light is soft and the crowds thinner.
t.pirna@51.0,13.9:
Pirna is the front door of Saxon Switzerland, the sandstone country of the upper Elbe, and the town has a long memory of being looked at. In the 1750s the Venetian painter Bernardo Bellotto, nephew of Canaletto and working under his uncle's name, painted Pirna in a series of sharp, luminous views, and you can still recognise the town hall and the market square from his canvases. The old centre is compact, with a steep-roofed Rathaus, a Gothic hall church above the roofs and rows of pastel houses, and the whole place feels pleasantly unhurried. It has about forty thousand people, so fuel and food are easy.

The Elbe runs past just north of the old town, wide, grey-green and slow, and it is a working river with barges and paddle steamers. Above the town the Sonnenstein fortress stands on a rock, with a complicated history that includes a dark chapter in the Nazi period, and the rocky hills of Saxon Switzerland begin to rise immediately to the south. The sandstone here, pale and easily worked, was quarried for centuries and shipped down the Elbe to build Dresden, and much of that city's grandeur was cut from the cliffs you are about to ride beside.

The Saxon Wine Route starts here, running northwest along the Elbe valley to Dresden, Radebeul and Meissen, about fifty-five kilometres of gentle road. It is not a place of dramatic bends but of rhythm and scenery, with vineyards on south-facing slopes, small wine estates, castles and the Elbe on one side. Saxony is one of Germany's smallest and most northerly wine regions, and its wines, mostly dry whites like Müller-Thurgau, Riesling and Weissburgunder, are rarely exported, so you drink them here or not at all. Traffic around Dresden can be heavy, especially at rush hour, so plan accordingly.

Spring brings blossom in the orchards and early green on the vines, summer is warm and busy, and the best time for riding is September, when the harvest begins and the terraces turn gold. The Elbe valley can be misty in the morning, and in winter cold air settles in the river basin. A last coffee in Pirna's market square, with the old painter's view in front of you, is a nice way to begin.
t.diesbar seusslitz@51.2,13.4:
Diesbar-Seußlitz is a very small place at the far northern end of the Saxon Wine Route, in a bend of the Elbe where the hills soften and the valley widens. The village, made of two older villages joined together, sits between the river and a slope of vineyards, and above the roofs stands the baroque palace of Seußlitz, once a convent for noble ladies and later a country estate, with a terraced garden stepping down toward the water. The population is only a few hundred, so do not expect much beyond the essentials, and plan your supplies in advance.

The wine here is the point. Saxony's vineyards lie on the Elbe at around fifty-one degrees north, about as far north as commercial wine growing goes in Germany, and the vines survive thanks to the river, which holds heat, and the steep south-facing terraces. The soil is a mix of granite, loess and sandy loam, and the white wines, particularly Riesling, Weissburgunder and Müller-Thurgau, are dry and crisp, with good acidity. Production is tiny, and most of it is drunk within Saxony, which is a reason to stop at a small estate and ask what is open.

The riding is easy and gentle, a pleasant coda to the route. The road follows the river between fields and orchards, with a few low bends and views across to the far bank, and in autumn the vines glow yellow and red. It is bike country in a modest way, with a lot of cyclists on the Elbe path alongside, so go carefully on summer afternoons. There are ferries across the river in places, small cable ferries that carry a few vehicles, which are a good way to change the pace.

Fuel is not in the village. Nünchritz, about seven kilometres off, is the nearest town of any size, with a petrol station and shops, and Meissen, farther up the river, has larger supply and the famous porcelain works. Between September and October, young wine, called Federweisser, appears in the cellars, cloudy and sweet and slightly fizzy, and it goes with onion tart. A walk through the palace garden at sunset is a small reward for the end of the road.
t.bergen auf rugen@54.4,13.4:
Bergen sits at the middle of Rügen, Germany's biggest island, on a low hill called the Rugard where a Slavic stronghold once stood. The Slavs, the Rani, ruled the island until the Danes took it in 1168, and the small hill-top fort fell to King Valdemar's men, who then converted the people by force. A short walk from the market square you find St Mary's church, one of the oldest on the island, built in brick in the twelfth century, with a plain, sturdy shape and a few faded medieval paintings inside. A tower on the Rugard, named after the writer Ernst Moritz Arndt, gives a view across the island.

With about fifteen thousand people, Bergen is the island's main town and has fuel, supermarkets and the other services that the villages lack. It is not a resort, which is part of its appeal: it is a working market town, a bit grey in the Eastern German way, with solid streets and a pleasant pedestrian zone. Visitors going to the seaside resorts pass through without stopping, so you can have a coffee in peace.

The riding on Rügen is a pleasure of a quiet kind. The roads are flat or gently rolling, often lined with old avenues of lime and chestnut trees whose branches meet overhead, and the whole island has a luminous, low-lying light, with the sea often visible at the end of a field. The famous chalk cliffs of Jasmund, with the Königsstuhl, lie to the northeast, and the white, tree-crowned cliffs, which inspired Caspar David Friedrich, are best seen from the beach path. Putbus, to the south, is a classicist town of white houses built for a prince, with a small steam railway nearby nicknamed the Raging Roland.

Summer is busy, and the roads fill with holiday traffic, bicycles and slow campers, so if you can, come in late spring or September. The wind is constant, and the weather is changeable, with sudden showers coming off the Baltic. Local food is fish: smoked herring, pan-fried flounder and the ubiquitous fish roll, along with sea buckthorn juice and liqueur, tart and orange. The bridge across the Strelasund will bring you back to the mainland, and the island will stay in your mind.
t.gabes@33.9,10.1:
Gabès is a port town on the south-eastern coast of Tunisia, and it has a trick up its sleeve: a palm oasis that runs right down to the sea. People say it is the only coastal oasis in the Mediterranean, and when you stand under the date palms with pomegranates and bananas growing beneath and the sound of irrigation water in the channels, you can believe it. The oasis is also the source of henna, which has been grown and sold here for a very long time, and the stalls of the souq are packed with the dried leaves, powdered and bagged.

It is a hard-working city, not a tourist one. There is a large industrial zone with phosphate processing on the shore, and the air and sea have suffered, which is a serious local issue. The centre has a lively market, a long avenue, cheap cafes, and shops that sell everything from spices to scooters. Fuel stations are everywhere, as are cash machines and places to eat grilled fish, so it is an easy start. Fill the tank and take water before you leave, because the road into the interior thins out quickly.

The ride from here goes inland and up into the Dahar hills, a rocky tableland of ochre and grey that rises from the coastal plain. After a short run through olive groves, the road starts to climb in loose bends towards the Berber village of Matmata, famous for its underground houses, dug into pits in the soft rock to escape the heat. One of these houses was used as a film location for Luke Skywalker's home on Tatooine in Star Wars, and visitors still arrive to see it. Real families still live in some of the underground rooms.

Tarmac is generally decent, but sand can blow across the road, and there can be loose gravel on the shoulders and goats in the middle of it. In summer, heat can reach well over forty degrees, so start early. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with clear skies and long visibility. Ride with a good hydration plan, wear light but protective gear, and watch for the police checkpoints that are common on Tunisian roads, where a polite greeting and your documents will usually do the job.
t.tataouine@32.9,10.5:
Tataouine is where the Sahara starts to feel close. The town of some sixty thousand people sits on a dry plain south of the Dahar hills, in the middle of the southern Tunisian steppe, and beyond it to the south and west the dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental stretch toward Algeria and Libya. Its name will already be familiar to anyone who has watched Star Wars, since George Lucas borrowed it, with a small spelling change, for Luke Skywalker's desert home. The film crews shot around here, and the fans have kept coming.

The real attraction lies in the ksour, the fortified granaries of the Berber people. These are stacked, vaulted storerooms built of mud and stone, arranged around courtyards, where families kept grain and olive oil safe from raiders and drought. Some are clearly ruined and some have been restored, and a few hill villages such as Chenini and Douiret cling to the ridges nearby, with cave dwellings cut into the rock and a white mosque on the crest. Chenini has a legend about the Seven Sleepers, a story shared by both Christian and Muslim tradition, with a shrine said to mark their resting place.

Riding here is about space and light. The roads cross open country in long, straight runs and gentle rises, with sudden bends where the land folds into hills, and the colours range from pale yellow to rust-red. The scenery is dramatic, but the surface may include patches of sand and gravel. Wind can be strong, so keep a firm grip, and camels sometimes cross the road without warning. Summer is fiercely hot, with temperatures well above forty degrees, and the best months are from October to April.

Tataouine is a proper regional town, so it has fuel, cash and food in good supply. The main road has plenty of stations, but stock up whenever you see one, since the distance between towns can be large. Try the local dishes: lamb or chicken cooked slowly with spices, fresh bread baked in clay ovens, and sweet mint tea served hot and strong. It is a friendly place, and a few words of French or Arabic go a long way with locals.
t.red lodge@45.2,-109.2:
Red Lodge is the doorstep of the Beartooth Highway, and it knows it. A small town of just over two thousand people in south-central Montana, it sits at around five and a half thousand feet where the Beartooth Mountains meet the plains, and its main street of brick buildings, saloons, outfitters and cafes is lined with flower baskets in summer. Behind it, the huge granite wall of the range rises in a ragged line, still carrying snow in July.

The town began as a coal mining centre, and the mines drew immigrants from Finland, Italy, Scotland and Eastern Europe, so the place still has Scandinavian bakeries, Italian restaurants, and an annual festival of nations. The mines are long closed, and tourism and skiing have taken over, plus a rodeo that is still a local institution. It is a friendly and unpretentious place, and bikers are common on summer weekends.

The Beartooth Highway, US 212, is one of the most celebrated mountain roads in America, and the television journalist Charles Kuralt called it the most beautiful drive in the country. It leaves the town in a series of switchbacks, climbs across a high plateau scattered with lakes and boulders, and tops out at Beartooth Pass at almost eleven thousand feet. The air is thin, the temperature can drop by twenty degrees, and snow can fall in any month. The road is typically closed from mid-October until around Memorial Day, and it may shut temporarily at other times, so check conditions before you set out.

Fuel in Red Lodge before you go, because the highway and the little settlements beyond have limited supplies. Wear warm gear and rain protection, and make an early start to avoid the afternoon thunderstorms that build over the peaks. You may see mountain goats, marmots and pika on the rocks, and in the valleys, moose and elk. Pull off at the viewpoints to take in the glacial cirques and the long, wild drop toward Wyoming. In the evenings, a cold beer on Main Street feels like a reward.
t.yellowstone northeast entrance@45.0,-110:
The northeast entrance to Yellowstone is a quiet gate on a quiet road, a small log-framed sign among spruce and meadow near the Montana-Wyoming border, a few miles beyond the two tiny settlements of Silver Gate and Cooke City. Most visitors enter Yellowstone through other gates, so this one feels like a back door, and that is part of its charm. At well over seven thousand feet, it is cool even in summer, and the air smells of pine and cold water.

What lies beyond is Lamar Valley, often called the Serengeti of North America. It is a broad, grassy valley where bison, elk, pronghorn and coyotes graze, and wolves, reintroduced to the park in the mid-1990s, are watched through spotting scopes by dedicated enthusiasts at dawn and dusk. Grizzly bears wander the hillsides. The animals move on their own timetable, and on a motorbike you should keep your distance, never approach or feed them, and stop only at pull-outs. Bison can block the road entirely, and a wait is part of the experience.

The road from the Beartooth Pass descends toward the gate in long, loping bends, through high plateaus of rock and tundra and then into forest, with the jagged peaks of the Absaroka range crowding the horizon. Between here and the interior, the road follows Soda Butte Creek and the Lamar River, with easy curves, a good surface and scenery that is gentle after the drama of the pass. Speed limits in the park are low, and rangers enforce them, so take your time. Weather changes quickly, with snow possible even in summer.

This is the only road in the park that stays open to wheeled traffic all winter, since it links the park with Cooke City, which makes it a lifeline for the small communities beyond. Cooke City and Silver Gate have basic services, but supplies are limited and prices are high, so take fuel and snacks with you. The park charges an entrance fee, which covers a motorcycle for several days. Mosquitoes in June can be fierce, so carry repellent, and bring a good camera with a long lens.
t.luneburg old town@53.2,10.4:
Lüneburg got rich on salt. Beneath the old town lies a salt dome, and from about the tenth century until the 1980s, brine from it was boiled into the white stuff that Hanseatic ships carried across the Baltic to salt herring in Scandinavia. The wealth that flowed back paid for a town of high red-brick gables, stepped roofs and ornate town hall, and the result, intact to a rare degree after the war, is one of the loveliest old towns in northern Germany. With about seventy thousand people, it is a city, but the old centre feels like a village in places.

The salt has left its mark in another way. Because the mining and pumping hollowed out the ground, many buildings have sunk unevenly over the centuries, and houses lean at alarming angles, with floors, walls and windows out of true. Some streets look as if they are leaning into each other for support. Around the harbour on the Ilmenau river, an old wooden crane stands on the quay, a reminder of the barges that once loaded salt here. The market square, Am Sande, has fine gabled houses, and the town hall has medieval chambers that are open to visitors.

Riding to Lüneburg from Hamburg is a gentle run through farmland, and the best part comes after the town, in the Lüneburg Heath, the great region of sandy heather moor and juniper stretching south and west. The roads here are flat and quiet, with long, easy bends, avenues of oak and birch, and occasional villages with thatched roofs. Late August and September are the best time, when the heather blooms purple, and bees hum in the fields. Out of season it is a subdued landscape, and mist often lies in the hollows.

In the old town, you can find everything. There are cafes in the courtyards, small bakeries and bars, and fuel stations on the ring road. Cobbles in the centre are slippery after rain, so ride slowly and park at the edge of the pedestrian zone. Try a Heidschnucken lamb dish, from the heath's own sheep breed, or a slice of buckwheat cake, and walk along the river in the evening. Lüneburg is a place to slow down and look up.
t.goslar overnight option@51.9,10.4:
Goslar is a place that makes you want to stay the night. The town lies on the northern edge of the Harz mountains, in Lower Saxony, with a medieval centre of timber-framed houses, slate roofs and crooked lanes that is on the UNESCO World Heritage list together with the nearby Rammelsberg mine. About forty-three thousand people live here, but the old town feels much smaller, and in the evening, when the day-trippers have gone, the cobbled lanes are quiet.

Wealth came from the mountain. At Rammelsberg, just outside the town, miners dug silver, copper, lead and zinc for around a thousand years, until the mine closed in 1988, and the ore paid for the town's churches and merchant houses. The emperors noticed. In the eleventh century, the Salian rulers built a great imperial palace, the Kaiserpfalz, which was restored in the nineteenth century, and the town became a favourite place for imperial assemblies. The market square has a glockenspiel on the town hall, with a mechanical show in which scenes from the mining past revolve at set hours.

For a rider, the Harz is a joy. The roads climb from Goslar through spruce forest toward Bad Harzburg and the Oker valley, with good surfaces, long curves and gentle gradients, and with a view back across the plain. In recent years, many of the spruce forests have been devastated by drought and bark beetles, and the hillsides are scarred with grey stands of dead trees, a sobering sight. Weather can change fast in the mountains, with fog and drizzle on the ridge, and in winter the roads can be icy.

As a place to sleep, Goslar offers a wide range, from small guesthouses in half-timbered houses to modern hotels outside the centre, and most can find a place for a motorcycle in a yard or garage. Fuel is easy to find on the main roads at the edge of town, with Langelsheim a short ride away. Evening meals of Harz specialities include game, mushrooms and the region's sausages, followed by a local beer. After a long day, an early night in an old room with creaking floors is hard to beat.
t.wienhausen abbey road@52.6,10.2:
Wienhausen is a village on the River Aller, a few kilometres from Celle, and it has something remarkable behind its walls: a medieval convent that never really stopped being a convent. Kloster Wienhausen was founded in the thirteenth century as a Cistercian nunnery, and when the Reformation arrived in the sixteenth, it turned Lutheran but carried on as a community of women. A group of Protestant sisters still lives there today. The brick Gothic buildings, with their stepped gables and cloister, are among the best preserved of their kind in northern Germany.

What makes the abbey famous is its textile collection. Inside are medieval embroideries and tapestries, some of them very large and very old, that survived because the nuns never threw anything away. They show scenes of saints, legends and daily devotion, and some are among the oldest of their type in Germany. Because they are fragile, they are displayed only at limited times, and the abbey is generally open for guided visits in the warmer months, so check hours before you go. The garden and the cloister, in summer, are extremely peaceful.

The road to the abbey is a country lane through fields and woods, along the Aller, with a flat landscape of meadows, pine and birch, with a few half-timbered farmhouses. It is easy, slow riding, best done on a quiet weekday morning, when you might pass only a tractor or a cyclist. The Aller is a lazy river here, with willows and herons, and in spring the meadows flood. A stop at the abbey is a chance to leave the engine silent and listen to the birds.

Wienhausen is small, with about four thousand people, so services are modest. Celle, a larger and beautiful town of half-timbered houses a short ride away, has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and is the sensible place to eat. Near the abbey, there may be a cafe or two, though opening hours vary. Respect the quiet of the place; it is a living community, not just a museum, and helmets and loud boots are best left at the gate. It is a gentle, reflective stop on a ride.
t.kiel canal view@54.3,10.0:
The Kiel Canal is one of the busiest artificial waterways in the world, and you can stand beside it on a quiet country lane and feel entirely alone, until a container ship the size of an apartment block slides past at head height, a few metres from the bank. Opened in 1895 as the Kaiser Wilhelm Canal, it cuts across the base of the Jutland peninsula from the Elbe estuary to the Baltic at Kiel, a distance of about ninety-eight kilometres, saving ships a long and stormy trip around Denmark. Today, thousands of ships use it each year.

The view from the bank is a strange mix of pastoral and industrial. Cows graze in meadows right up to the water, cyclists and walkers use the towpaths, and the ships are huge and silent, almost seeming to float through the fields. Car and passenger ferries cross the canal at numerous points, many of them free of charge, and they run at set intervals, though they stop when large vessels pass. High bridges, built tall enough for sea-going ships, carry the main roads. Ship-spotters bring thermoses and binoculars, and some sites have signs listing the name, origin and cargo of each passing ship.

The roads along the canal are flat, quiet and pleasant, with long straight stretches, tree-lined lanes and low traffic, and the surrounding area, the Danish Wohld, is an undulating landscape of fields and woods with small villages. The wind is typically from the west and fresh, and weather changes quickly, with sun, showers and a rainbow within an hour. Late afternoon and early evening are lovely, with long shadows and golden light, and in summer the sun sets late, giving plenty of time for riding.

Services are modest on the immediate bank, with a few cafes and kiosks near the ferries, but the village of Gettorf, about six kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket and a bakery, and Kiel itself is not far. Check the ferry timetable, because a missed crossing can add a long detour. Bring a layer for the wind, and a bit of patience: watching a giant ship pass slowly by is a surprisingly good way to unwind after a day of corners.
t.beartooth highway point 2@45.0,-109.5:
At the top of the Beartooth Pass, the world drops away. You stand at about 10,950 feet on a broad, treeless plateau of granite, tundra and tiny lakes, with snowfields clinging to the shaded slopes even in midsummer. The air is thin enough that you will notice it when you walk, and the sky is a deep, dark blue. In every direction, the rock is old: the Beartooth range is made of some of the oldest rock in North America, nearly three and a half billion years old in places, and the landscape has the bare, scoured look of something that has seen a very long time pass.

The plateau supports a fragile alpine ecosystem. Low cushions of flowers, sedges and dwarf willow cling to the ground, mountain goats graze on the slopes, and marmots and pikas watch from the rocks. In summer, the wildflowers are astonishing, and short as the season is, the colours are intense. Hikers set out from pullouts along the road, though at this altitude any walk is slow and demanding, and the weather can change in minutes.

The highway crosses the border between Montana and Wyoming here, and in fact it dips in and out of both states along this high stretch. The pass is closed in winter, usually from mid-October, and a fall of snow can come any month of the year, so be ready for cold, wet conditions. Thunderstorms build on summer afternoons and lightning is a real danger on the exposed ridge, so make a point of crossing early and be off the top by noon.

On the bike, the experience is exhilarating and demanding. The road is wide and well engineered, with big, open corners and a surface that is generally smooth, but it has steep drops, little in the way of guardrail in places and frost damage that appears each spring. Wind can be fierce on the plateau. Tourists and drivers of large vehicles often drive slowly and stop abruptly, so keep your distance.

There are no services at the summit, and the nearest fuel is a long way off in either direction. Carry water, a warm layer and gloves, and take your time. Do not be surprised if you find yourself pulling over every few minutes, because the views are enormous, and the sense of height is hard to describe until you are there.
t.beartooth highway point 3@45.0,-109.4:
This is the stretch where the Beartooth Highway shows off. After climbing out of the Rock Creek valley in a series of long switchbacks, the road emerges onto a vantage point with a big, open view back down the canyon. The Rock Creek Vista Point sits a little over nine thousand feet up, and from the railing you look down a deep glacial trough, a U-shaped valley carved by ice, with the road you have just climbed threading up its side and a tangle of peaks beyond.

The geology here is on a grand scale. The valley was gouged out by glaciers during the Ice Age, and the walls show the smooth, polished look of ice-scoured granite. Streams tumble from the snowfields above, and the meadows below are dotted with small lakes. The view is especially good in the morning, when the low sun picks out the ridges, and in the evening, when the rock glows orange.

The ride up to this point is among the most exciting in the country. The highway ascends the mountainside in a series of hairpins and long sweeping bends, with views opening at every turn, and a large, looping switchback known simply as the Hairpin is the most dramatic. The road is well surfaced, but the drops are steep, so ride within your limits and keep your eyes up. Cyclists labour up the slope, and you will meet motorhomes taking the bends wide.

There are no services here, just a small viewpoint with a toilet, so make sure you have fuel and water. The weather can change in minutes, with cloud coming down over the road and a drop in temperature that catches the unprepared. If it is cold, enjoy the view from the viewpoint while the clouds lift, rather than pressing on in poor visibility.

Look out for marmots and pikas among the rocks beside the car park, and for the occasional bighorn sheep on the cliff. Allow time for photographs, because this is one of those places where you want to linger. The best light is in the morning, and the crowds thin out after sunset, though the road is hardly the place to be after dark.
t.beartooth highway point 4@45.0,-109.9:
Cooke City is a tiny community at the end of the world, or so it can feel, wedged into a mountain valley just outside the north-east corner of Yellowstone National Park. It began as a mining camp in the 1880s, when prospectors found gold, silver and lead in the surrounding hills, and it was named for Jay Cooke, a financier who backed the Northern Pacific Railroad. The railway never came, however, and the boom faded, leaving a handful of log buildings and a small, hardy population.

Today, the town survives on summer tourism and winter snowmobiling. Visitors pour through in high season, and its main street has the wooden storefronts, cafes, motels and gift shops of a classic mountain outpost. Its neighbour, Silver Gate, a short way east, is smaller still and has a rustic charm of its own, with log cabins and quiet lanes. Both lie in grizzly bear country, and locals take bear safety seriously.

One strange fact: in winter, Cooke City is cut off from the rest of Montana, because the Beartooth Highway closes under deep snow. The only way in is through Yellowstone, along the park road that runs through the Lamar Valley, which is kept open year-round. It makes the town one of the most remote communities in the lower forty-eight states, and winter here is a serious business.

For the rider, Cooke City is the practical hub. It has fuel, which is the first you will see after Red Lodge if you have come over the pass, and a few restaurants and places to stay. Prices are higher than in the lowlands, and opening hours can be limited outside summer, so plan ahead. The road east over the Beartooth Pass is just behind you, while to the west the park road leads into the Lamar Valley.

Moose, elk and bears wander through the valley, and you may meet them on the road, especially at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down and your eyes open. The air smells of pine and woodsmoke, and the stars at night are astonishing. If you can, stay a night and watch the light fade over the peaks before you move on.
t.beartooth highway point 5@45.0,-110.0:
The northeast entrance to Yellowstone is one of the quietest of the park's five gates, a small station on a road that runs west along Soda Butte Creek into the Lamar Valley. Here you leave the high, bare country of the Beartooths and enter a land of rolling sagebrush, cottonwood and wide meadows, with mountains rising on every side. It feels very different from the crowded geyser basins to the south, and many visitors say it is the best part of the park.

The Lamar Valley is known as the American Serengeti, a name earned by the huge numbers of animals that live there. Bison graze in herds of hundreds, pronghorn bound over the sage, elk and bighorn sheep move through the hills, and wolves, reintroduced to the park in 1995, hunt across the valley floor. Dawn and dusk are the best times to see them, and you will often notice groups of wildlife watchers with spotting scopes lined up at the roadside. Grizzlies and black bears also roam here, and a sighting can cause a lengthy queue.

Riding in Yellowstone is a pleasure, if you accept the pace. The speed limit is low, usually forty-five miles an hour or less, and enforced, and the roads are often interrupted by wildlife, so you cannot hurry. The surface is generally good, with occasional patches of frost damage, and the bends are gentle. A bison herd crossing the road can stop traffic for half an hour, and it is unwise to challenge a bison for the right of way. Keep at least twenty-five yards from large animals and a hundred yards from bears and wolves.

There is a park entry fee, payable at the gate, and the entrance stations can have queues in summer. Fuel is limited: Cooke City, just before the entrance, is the last stop on this side, and the next fuel inside the park is some distance away, around Tower-Roosevelt or Mammoth, so fill up before you go in. There are basic facilities at Tower Junction, including a rustic lodge, but check their seasons.

Weather in the park can change quickly, with summer thunderstorms and snow in the shoulder seasons. The best time to ride is early morning, when animals are active and the light is gold on the hills, and the smell of sage and wet grass hangs in the air.
t.chief joseph scenic byway point 4@45.0,-:
Cooke City is a one-street mountain town in the far corner of Montana, and nobody drives to it by accident. It sits at around 7,600 feet beside Soda Butte Creek, just outside the northeast entrance to Yellowstone, and its twin, Silver Gate, lies a mile to the east. Together they are home to a few hundred people in summer and fewer than a hundred in the long winters, when the snow can be deep enough to bury the ground floor of the buildings.

The town began with gold. Prospectors came here in the 1860s and 1870s, and mining claims spread across the surrounding mountains, but the remote location and the difficulty of moving ore made it a hard place to get rich. The main street still has wooden false fronts and a few old buildings, and it has the character of a place that has outlived its original purpose and found a second life with visitors.

For riders, it is one of the best bases in the northern Rockies. The Beartooth Highway starts a few miles east, climbing to almost 11,000 feet before dropping into Red Lodge, Montana, in a series of broad switchbacks that many call one of the most beautiful roads in America. West of town, the road runs through Lamar Valley, in Yellowstone, where bison and wolves are often seen. The Beartooth is closed by snow for much of the year, normally opening in late May and closing in mid October, so check the dates.

Cooke City has fuel, motels, a few restaurants and a general store. Supplies are limited and prices are higher than in Cody, as everything has to be brought a long way. The pumps are small and may close early, so fill up when you can. Expect cold nights even in July, and be ready for rain or snow in any month.

Wildlife is abundant. Grizzlies and black bears roam the valleys, moose feed in the willows, and mountain goats and bighorn sheep appear on the cliffs above. Take bear precautions seriously. The sky at night is very dark and, with luck, filled with stars. After a long ride from Cody over the pass, a hot meal here is as welcome as anything you will eat on the trip.
t.elbe@52.1,10.3:
Despite the name, there is no great river here. This Elbe is a village in the rolling farmland of southeastern Lower Saxony, between Salzgitter and Hildesheim, and the river that shares its name flows more than a hundred kilometres to the east. It is a quiet place of brick farmhouses, a church, fields of sugar beet, wheat and rapeseed, and gentle hills, close to the small towns of Baddeckenstedt and Holle in the valley of the Innerste.

The landscape is the northern foreland of the Harz. On a clear day you can see the dark, wooded hills of the Harz on the southern horizon, and the low ridges around here, the Salzgitter hills and the Hainberg, give the roads a pleasant rhythm of short climbs, gentle descents and long views over the fields. In May the rapeseed turns the slopes bright yellow, and in autumn the beet harvest fills the lanes with tractors and mud, so watch the surface.

The region has a strong industrial history hidden beneath the farmland. Iron ore found around Salzgitter led to the creation of huge steelworks in the 1930s, and the town grew rapidly around them, with some of its industry still active today. Hildesheim to the northwest is an old bishop's city with a cathedral and St Michael's Church, both on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and Wolfenbüttel to the east has a large ducal palace and one of the oldest libraries in Europe.

The riding is easygoing: quiet country roads, some well surfaced, others patched and narrow, linking villages through fields and woods. There is little traffic outside rush hour, but watch for farm machinery and wildlife at dawn and dusk. The real curves are a short ride away, in the Harz around Goslar and the hills of the Innerste valley, where the roads climb through forest to dams and reservoirs.

Elbe itself is small, so for fuel and shops head to Holle, Baddeckenstedt or Salzgitter, all within a few kilometres. Village bakeries and inns are found in the area, and a slice of cake and a coffee is a fine excuse to stop. If you were expecting to see the Elbe river, check the route: the Prignitz rides along that river lie far to the northeast, beyond Wolfsburg and Magdeburg.
t.near modrany@50.0,14.4:
South of Prague, the Vltava leaves the city through a deep, wooded valley, and the suburbs give way to villages, orchards and cliffs. It is a place of transition: the city's traffic behind you, the Bohemian countryside ahead.

The Vltava is the river of Smetana's famous symphonic poem, and its course south of Prague is a chain of dams and reservoirs, beginning at Vrané with a small dam and power station, then rising toward the larger lakes at Slapy and Orlík. The valley is lined with weekend cottages, a Czech institution: under communism many families built small chatas in the countryside, and the tradition of leaving the city on Friday evening is still strong. Zbraslav, on the river nearby, has a former Cistercian monastery turned chateau.

The rides from here head west to Karlštejn and the Berounka. Karlštejn Castle, built by Emperor Charles IV in the fourteenth century to protect the crown jewels and his collection of holy relics, rises from a wooded hill above a narrow valley, with towers stepping up to the Great Tower and its chapel decorated with gold and precious stones. The surrounding Bohemian Karst is a landscape of limestone cliffs, caves and quarries, including the flooded quarry known as Velká Amerika, sometimes called the Czech Grand Canyon, and the Koněprusy Caves. The Berounka valley itself winds through forest, with roads following the river in long curves.

The roads around here are mostly narrow, with variable surfaces, cobbled sections in some villages, and tight bends through the woods. Weekends bring cyclists and day-trippers, and the road to Karlštejn can be crowded. Remember the Czech rules: dipped headlights are required at all times, and the legal alcohol limit for drivers is zero. Prague itself has trams, cobbles and congestion, so leave early to avoid the city's traffic.

For fuel and supplies, Modřany and Zbraslav are close, as are the larger towns along the main roads. Village pubs serve hearty Czech food, such as goulash, roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, and of course excellent beer, which is for the evening, not the ride. Bring a jacket, as the river valleys can be cool and damp in the morning, even in summer.
t.near lubbenau on the way back@51.8,13.9:
The Spree river does something strange in the Spreewald: instead of running in one channel, it splits into hundreds of small streams and canals that thread through a low, forested wetland southeast of Berlin. This spot lies near Lübbenau, the main town on the edge of this watery labyrinth, which has been a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1991. For centuries, people here lived on small islands of dry land, travelling by flat-bottomed punts, and some farms are still reached only by water.

The Spreewald is also home to the Sorbs, a Slavic minority who have lived in Lusatia for over a thousand years, with their own language, traditions and colourful costumes. Signs in the area are bilingual, in German and Lower Sorbian. And it is famous for gherkins: Spreewald pickles, marinated in vinegar, dill and spices, are sold everywhere, and they were one of the few East German products that survived reunification as a favourite brand.

For the swim, the canals of the Spreewald are not really for swimming; they are shallow, slow and busy with boats. But to the south lies the Lusatian Lake District, a chain of lakes created by flooding old open-cast lignite mines, and many of them now have sandy beaches and clear water. Lakes near Lübbenau and toward Senftenberg are popular on hot days, with bathing areas and cafes. The water is clean, though some lakes still have restrictions while the banks settle.

Riding here is flat, gentle and green. The roads cross fields, forests and small villages, with long, straight stretches and occasional cobbled sections in the villages. Traffic is light except on summer weekends, when tourists flock to the Spreewald. Watch for cyclists, as the area has excellent cycle paths, and for tractors and deer. The A13 motorway runs close by toward Berlin, but the smaller roads are more pleasant.

Lübbenau has fuel, cafes, restaurants and boat trips through the canals. A punt ride, with a picnic of pickles and local beer, is a classic Spreewald experience. Lübben, Luckau and Cottbus, all nearby, have more services. Then follow the quiet roads north toward Berlin, past the Scharmützelsee and the lakes of the Dahme valley.
t.konradshohe@52.6,13.2:
At the northwestern edge of Berlin, where the city gives way to forest and water, Konradshöhe is a quiet residential area in the district of Reinickendorf, on a gentle rise above the Havel river and the Tegeler See. It feels more like a village than part of a capital: tree-lined streets of villas and small houses, sailing clubs and boathouses along the water, and the Tegeler Forst, a large forest of pine and oak, on its doorstep.

The Tegeler See is the loveliest of Berlin's big lakes, with wooded islands and sailing boats, and a promenade along the shore in Tegel. Nearby, Schloss Tegel was the home of the Humboldt brothers, Wilhelm and Alexander, the scholar and the explorer, and the family still owns the house and park. The Havel flows south toward Spandau, with its citadel, one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortresses in Europe.

Riding into Konradshöhe is easy and green. The roads from the north pass through forests and fields in Brandenburg, then enter the city through Heiligensee or Hennigsdorf, with the Havel and lakes alongside. The roads are generally good, though some streets have cobbles. Traffic is light compared to the city centre, but you will meet cyclists, buses and the occasional tractor near the edge of town. The ferry across the Havel from Konradshöhe to Spandau is a pleasant way to cross by foot or bicycle.

Fuel, supermarkets and cafes are close by in Tegel and Heiligensee. There are beer gardens and restaurants along the water, perfect for a drink in the evening sun after a long day on the Scharmützelsee loop. The lakeside paths are great for an evening walk, with views of the sunset over the water.

You come back to Berlin from the Scharmützelsee, a long lake in the Brandenburg woods southeast of the city, known as the Märkisches Meer, the sea of the Mark, and the contrast between that open water and this sheltered corner of the Havel is pleasing. Both are reminders of how much water and forest surround Berlin, and how quickly you can leave the city behind.
t.near beelitz on the way back@52.3,13.0:
Asparagus is a serious business in Beelitz. Every spring, from April to late June, the sandy fields around this small Brandenburg town southwest of Potsdam produce white asparagus, Spargel, which Germans adore, and roadside stalls, farms and restaurants all over the area sell it fresh, served with butter, hollandaise sauce, potatoes and ham. The season ends traditionally on 24 June, St John's Day, and people come from Berlin just for the asparagus.

Beelitz is also known for the Beelitz-Heilstätten, a huge sanatorium complex built in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries for tuberculosis patients from Berlin. In the First World War it served as a military hospital, and a young Adolf Hitler was treated there after being wounded in 1916. Later it was a Soviet military hospital, where the East German leader Erich Honecker was briefly treated in 1990. Many buildings were abandoned after the Soviets left, and their ghostly ruins became popular with photographers. Today a treetop walkway lets you look down on the overgrown rooftops.

For a swim, the lakes around here are the answer. The Seddiner See, near Michendorf, and the larger Schwielowsee near Caputh and Ferch, both have bathing areas and clear water, and on a hot day they are full of Berliners. The water is clean and warm by midsummer, and there are cafes and beer gardens along the shores.

The riding is gentle and green, with flat or slightly rolling roads through pine forests, fields and villages. The roads are generally good, though some village streets are cobbled, and you will meet cyclists, tractors and the occasional deer. The A9 and A10 motorways run nearby, but the backroads are more pleasant. The landscape is quiet, with big skies and the smell of pine resin in summer.

Beelitz has fuel, shops and places to eat, and in season, of course, asparagus everywhere. From here, the way back to Berlin runs through Potsdam, with its palaces and parks, including Sanssouci, the summer palace of Frederick the Great, which is worth a stop if you have time, before the final stretch into the city.
t.glienicke@52.6,13.3:
Glienicke/Nordbahn is a small town just outside Berlin's northern edge, in Brandenburg, and during the decades of the Berlin Wall it found itself in one of the strangest positions in divided Germany. The town was in East Germany, but it pushed into West Berlin on three sides, and one narrow part of it, known as the Entenschnabel, the duck's bill, was enclosed by the Wall on almost every side, so that residents of a few streets lived inside a corridor of concrete and barbed wire, with West Berlin just over their back fences.

Today the Wall is gone, and the Berliner Mauerweg, a path for walkers and cyclists that follows the old border, passes through the area, with information boards telling the stories of those years. Glienicke itself is a quiet, green suburb of houses and gardens, with a growing population of commuters. The nearby Berlin districts of Hermsdorf, Frohnau and Lübars are leafy and calm, and Lübars still has a village green, a church and farmhouses, an old village swallowed by the city.

The riding into Glienicke is easy: roads through forests and fields from the north, then quiet suburban streets. Some streets are cobbled, and traffic is light except at peak hours. Watch for cyclists, as this is a popular area for bike rides along the Mauerweg and through the forests of the Tegeler Fließ, a small stream with meadows and wetlands.

Fuel, supermarkets and cafes are close by in Glienicke, Hermsdorf and Frohnau. After a long day out to the Müritz National Park, with its lakes, forests and ospreys, or across the wide open landscape of the Oderbruch, this quiet finish is a gentle way to end the ride.

For a final reflection, walk a few minutes along the Mauerweg and imagine the Wall standing here, with watchtowers and floodlights, and the families who lived so close to the other side. It is hard to picture now, among the gardens and quiet streets, but it is only a generation ago.
t.maple creek@49.9,-109.5:
They call Maple Creek the Old Cow Town, and the nickname fits. This small Saskatchewan town of about two thousand people grew up in the 1880s as a ranching centre when the Canadian Pacific Railway came through, and cattle are still the backbone of the local economy. The main street has old brick buildings, a western-wear store and a museum full of ranching history, and on a quiet afternoon it feels like the place has not changed much in a century.

South of town rise the Cypress Hills, a plateau that stands several hundred metres above the surrounding prairie and was never covered by the glaciers that flattened the rest of the plains. The highest point, on the Alberta side, is the highest ground between the Rockies and Labrador. The hills are covered in lodgepole pine, aspen and fescue grassland, and they are home to elk, moose, deer and many birds that seem out of place on the prairie. The Cypress Hills Interprovincial Park straddles the Alberta and Saskatchewan border, and Highway 21 from Maple Creek leads up into the Centre Block in a series of gentle climbs with growing views over the plains.

The hills have a dark chapter. In 1873, American wolf hunters and traders killed a group of Assiniboine people in the Cypress Hills Massacre, an event that pushed the Canadian government to send the newly formed North-West Mounted Police west. They built Fort Walsh in the hills in 1875, and the rebuilt fort, now a national historic site, can be reached from the park on a road through the forest. The story of the Mounties, the whiskey traders and the Indigenous people is told well there.

For riders, the roads around Maple Creek are about space rather than corners: long, straight prairie highways with huge skies and few cars, broken by the climb into the hills. The Gap Road between the park blocks is gravel and can be slippery when wet. Maple Creek has fuel, food and basic accommodation, but Medicine Hat, about an hour west, is the nearest city with full services. Wind can be strong and storms build quickly in summer, so keep an eye on the sky.
t.cottbus@51.8,14.3:
Cottbus is the capital of Lower Lusatia, a city on the Spree about 120 kilometres south-east of Berlin, and it is a better lunch stop than its reputation outside Brandenburg suggests. The street signs are bilingual, German and Lower Sorbian, a reminder that the Slavic Wends have lived in this region for well over a thousand years. The old market square is handsome after careful restoration, and the Art Nouveau state theatre ranks among the finest buildings of its kind in eastern Germany.

The real reason to linger, if you have time, is Branitz Park on the south-eastern edge of town. It was laid out by Prince Hermann von Pückler-Muskau, the restless nineteenth-century traveller, writer and landscape gardener, who reshaped flat sandy fields into a rolling English-style park. He is buried inside an earth pyramid that rises out of a small lake, which is exactly as strange and memorable as it sounds. A slow walk round the park after a morning in the saddle is a fine way to reset.

The countryside around Cottbus is flat, so the riding is about atmosphere rather than lean angles. To the north and west lies the Spreewald, a maze of river channels, alder woods and villages like Burg where people still move hay and goods by punt. To the south and east, the landscape tells a different story: decades of open-cast lignite mining have left huge scars, and some of them are being flooded into new lakes. The Cottbuser Ostsee, created from the former Cottbus-Nord mine, is turning into one of the largest artificial lakes in Germany. Riding past these half-finished landscapes is oddly fascinating.

Food here leans hearty and local. Spreewald gherkins are everywhere, and a classic Lusatian plate is boiled potatoes with quark and a splash of linseed oil, simple but good on a hot day. You will find fuel and every kind of shop in town. Roads in the region are generally smooth and quiet, but expect cobbles in older village centres and straight tree-lined avenues where the light flickers and the wind from the open fields can push you around.
t.rheinsberg@53.1,12.9:
In 1736, Crown Prince Frederick of Prussia, the future Frederick the Great, moved into the palace at Rheinsberg with his wife, and he later said the years he spent here were the happiest of his life. Away from the stern court of his father, he read philosophy, played the flute, corresponded with Voltaire and surrounded himself with friends. The palace, rebuilt for him in an elegant Rococo style on the shore of the Grienericksee, is still the jewel of this small town, and the park around it, with its avenues, sculptures and views across the water, is perfect for a slow walk.

Rheinsberg has literary associations too. In 1912 Kurt Tucholsky published a light, witty novella called Rheinsberg: A Picture Book for Lovers, about a young couple's weekend trip to the town, and it became a bestseller. The town also has a tradition of ceramics, and you can find local pottery in shops near the palace.

There is one more surprising piece of history. Just north of town, in the forest by the Stechlinsee, stood the first nuclear power station of the GDR, which operated from 1966 until 1990 and has been in the process of being dismantled ever since. It is a strange contrast to the Rococo elegance of the palace, but it says something about the twentieth century in this quiet corner of Brandenburg.

The landscape around Rheinsberg is a world of lakes and forests. The land here was shaped by the glaciers of the last ice age, which left behind hundreds of lakes, sandy soils and gentle hills, and the area merges seamlessly into the Mecklenburg Lake District to the north. The roads are quiet, winding between lakes and through pine and beech forests, often lined with old trees. Some village streets still have cobbles, and the sandy verges can be soft. Rheinsberg has fuel, cafés and restaurants, including fish from the lakes. Summer is the busiest time; spring and autumn are quieter and very pretty.
t.lichterfelde@52.4,13.3:
In 1881, Werner von Siemens opened the world's first electric tram line in Lichterfelde, a short track connecting the railway station with the cadet academy. Thirteen years later, Otto Lilienthal, the pioneer of human flight, had an artificial hill built in the same suburb so that he could launch his gliders from it, whatever the wind direction. The mound is still there, now a small park with a memorial. For a quiet residential district in south-western Berlin, Lichterfelde has a surprising place in the history of technology.

Today it is a green, leafy area of villas, apartment blocks and gardens, part of the borough of Steglitz-Zehlendorf. The Botanical Garden, one of the largest in the world, lies on its northern edge, with greenhouses full of tropical plants and gardens arranged by region. The former Prussian cadet academy, a vast complex of brick buildings, later served as an SS barracks and then, after the war, as a US Army base, and its history is a microcosm of Berlin's twentieth century.

As a starting point for a ride to the Oderbruch, Lichterfelde has the advantage of being on the edge of the city, with good access to the motorway ring. The ride east crosses Berlin's outer suburbs and then the flat, sandy plains of Brandenburg, before reaching the Oderbruch, the wide valley of the Oder river on the Polish border. The Oderbruch was a vast marshland until Frederick the Great had it drained and settled in the eighteenth century; it is now a flat, fertile landscape of fields, dykes and villages, under an enormous sky.

There is plenty of fuel, food and coffee in Lichterfelde and the surrounding districts. Berlin rush hours are best avoided, so plan your departure accordingly. The city streets are often cobbled in places, and tram tracks can be slippery in the rain. The Oderbruch roads are flat and straight, with long avenues of trees, and on a windy day crosswinds can be tiring. Spring, when the fields are green and the storks are nesting, is a lovely time to go.
t.neuruppin@52.9,12.8:
Two of the most important figures in Prussian culture were born in Neuruppin: the architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel in 1781 and the novelist Theodor Fontane in 1819. Fontane went on to write the Wanderungen durch die Mark Brandenburg, a multi-volume account of his travels through the region, and the first volume opens with the county of Ruppin. Reading even a few pages before riding these roads gives them a depth they might otherwise lack.

The town was almost completely destroyed by fire in 1787 and rebuilt to a strict, classical plan, with straight streets, wide squares and uniform houses. The result is unusually elegant for a small Brandenburg town. Neuruppin lies on the shore of the Ruppiner See, a long, narrow lake formed by glacial meltwater, and the lakeside promenade invites a slow amble. In the nineteenth century, the town was famous for the Neuruppiner Bilderbogen, cheap, colourful prints depicting news, stories and morals, which were sold all over Germany.

North of the town lies the Ruppiner Schweiz, a small area of wooded hills and deep valleys with lakes, streams and old mills. The name, like many Swiss references in German landscapes, is a romantic exaggeration; there are no mountains here. But it is a beautiful area, with quiet roads through beech forests, along lakes and past small villages. The roads are narrow and winding, sometimes with cobbled sections, and the forests are cool and shady on hot days.

Neuruppin is a good place for lunch. There are restaurants and cafés in the old town and along the lakeshore, serving local fish and Brandenburg specialities. Fuel and other services are easy to find. The Ruppin area is popular with day-trippers from Berlin, especially on summer weekends, but on weekdays it is quiet and peaceful. In spring the forests are bright green, and in autumn the beeches turn gold and copper, making it one of the most beautiful times to visit.
t.burg bei magdeburg@52.3,11.9:
Burg likes to call itself the town of towers, and as you approach across the flat Elbe plain, you can see why: medieval church spires and the remnants of old fortifications rise above the rooftops. It is a market town of some twenty-five thousand people, east of Magdeburg, and for most riders on the Prignitz ride it is simply a convenient place to refuel. But it has a few surprises.

The military theorist Carl von Clausewitz, author of On War, was born here in 1780, and a small museum in the town commemorates him.
