Burg also has an industrial tradition; it was known for its shoe and glove making, and the town lends its name to a well-known brand of crispbread that has been produced here for generations.

A few kilometres west of Burg, at Hohenwarthe, lies one of the most remarkable feats of engineering in Germany: the Magdeburg Water Bridge, which carries the Mittelland Canal over the Elbe on a steel trough almost a kilometre long. Barges sail across the river above the river, and you can walk or cycle along the towpath to watch them. It is a strange and wonderful sight, and it is well worth a short detour if you have time. The Elbe–Havel Canal also passes through Burg itself.

The landscape around Burg is flat and agricultural, with large fields, forests and the floodplains of the Elbe. The roads are generally good, straight and quiet, with occasional cobbles in the villages. The A2 motorway passes just south of town, connecting Berlin and the Ruhr. To the north, the roads lead towards the Altmark and Prignitz, with their vast open spaces, small villages and the dykes of the Elbe. Burg handles fuel, groceries and lunch without fuss. The weather is typical of central Germany: warm summers, cold winters and often windy on the open plains.
t.near trebotov@50.0,14.3:
Just beyond Prague's south-western edge, the landscape changes abruptly. The city's apartment blocks give way to wooded hills and limestone cliffs, and the Berounka river winds through a valley lined with summer cottages, villages and the occasional factory. You start and finish on the plateau above the valley, near Třebotov and Černošice, a pleasant, practical place to start and finish rides without fighting through the centre of the capital.

This is the edge of the Bohemian Karst, an area of limestone hills, caves and gorges that stretches west towards Karlštejn. The rock has been quarried for centuries, and some of the old quarries, now flooded and overgrown, are surprisingly beautiful; the most famous, nicknamed Velká Amerika, has sheer walls dropping to a turquoise lake and is sometimes called the Czech Grand Canyon. Karlštejn Castle, built by Emperor Charles IV in the fourteenth century to protect the crown jewels, stands on a hill above the Berounka a short ride away.

The rides that start here head far to the north-east, to the Krkonoše and the Orlické Mountains near the Polish border, so the first part of the day is about covering distance. The Prague ring road will take you around the city, but on weekdays it clogs easily. The local roads in the Berounka valley are narrow and winding, with tight bends, railway crossings and cyclists, and they make a pleasant warm-up or cool-down at either end of the day.

There are fuel stations in the surrounding villages and on the main roads towards Prague, and pubs and restaurants in Černošice and the other valley towns. Czech pubs are a fine place to end a ride, with cheap, hearty food and excellent beer, though remember that the legal blood alcohol limit for riding is zero. On summer weekends, the valley fills with Praguers heading to their cottages and to the river, so traffic can be slow. Early mornings, with mist rising from the river, are the most atmospheric time to ride.
t.hermannsburg@52.8,10.1:
In the middle of the nineteenth century, a pastor named Ludwig Harms founded a missionary seminary in Hermannsburg, a small village in the Lüneburg Heath, and sent farmers and craftsmen as missionaries to Africa and beyond. Their influence spread far further than anyone could have expected: there is a Hermannsburg in South Africa, and another in the Australian outback, founded by Lutheran missionaries from here. The mission still exists, and the village has kept a quiet, slightly pious charm, with half-timbered farmhouses and old oak trees.

The landscape around Hermannsburg is the classic Lüneburg Heath: sandy soils, pine forests, juniper bushes, birch trees and, in late summer, vast purple carpets of flowering heather. The heath is not a natural wilderness but a cultural landscape, created over centuries by grazing sheep, especially the local breed known as Heidschnucken, and it is maintained the same way today. The Örtze, a clear, fast-flowing little river, runs through the village, and it is popular with canoeists.

There is also darker history close by. A few kilometres west, near Bergen, lies the site of the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where tens of thousands of prisoners died, Anne Frank among them. The memorial is a sombre, important place to visit if you have the time and the frame of mind. To the east, the airfield at Faßberg played a major role in the Berlin Airlift of 1948 and 1949, when Western aircraft supplied the blockaded city by air.

For riders, Hermannsburg is a practical fuel stop with a supermarket, bakeries and cafés. The roads through the heath are generally quiet, flat to gently rolling, and pleasant rather than challenging, with long straights through the forests and gentle curves between the villages. Watch out for military vehicles, deer and the occasional tank crossing near the training areas, and for sand on the road surface. The heather blooms from about August to September, and that is the best time to visit, though the heath is beautiful in every season.
t.near grunewald@52.5,13.2:
Berlin has a racetrack hidden in plain sight. The AVUS, which opened in 1921 through the Grunewald forest, was both one of the first motorways in the world and a racing circuit, where drivers and riders competed at astonishing speeds on its long straights and steep, banked north curve. Racing ended long ago and the banking is gone, but the road is still there, now part of the A115 motorway, and the old grandstand and timing tower survive by the roadside. Passing them on the way into the city is a nod to history.

You end on the edge of the Grunewald, Berlin's largest forest, a vast area of pine and oak woods on the western side of the city, bordered by the Havel river and dotted with lakes. Berliners come here to walk, cycle, swim and escape the city, and on summer weekends the lakes, like the Krumme Lanke and the Schlachtensee, are full of swimmers. In the middle of the forest, the Teufelsberg, a hill built from the rubble of wartime Berlin, is crowned by the ruined domes of an American listening station from the Cold War.

There is also a sombre memorial. At Grunewald station, Platform 17 was one of the main departure points for the deportation of Berlin's Jews to the ghettos and death camps during the Second World War, and steel plates along the platform record the dates, numbers and destinations of the transports. It is a quiet, powerful place.

The rides that end here come back from the Harz mountains and Saxon Switzerland, long days that finish with motorway miles into Berlin. The Grunewald and the western suburbs offer a calm end to the ride, with tree-lined avenues and villas, but Sunday evenings bring the whole city home at once. Fuel and restaurants line the main roads, and the beer gardens by the lakes are a fine place to unwind.
t.near breddin on the way back@52.8,12.3:
In August 1896, on a hill called the Gollenberg near the village of Stölln, a few kilometres south-east of the point, Otto Lilienthal lost control of his glider, fell about fifteen metres, and died of his injuries the next day. He had made hundreds of flights from these slopes, and his experiments laid the groundwork for the Wright brothers. Nearly a century later, in 1989, an Interflug Ilyushin airliner was landed on the grassy meadow at the foot of the same hill as a tribute, and it is still there, a strange and wonderful sight in the open countryside, now a small museum.

All around is the Rhinluch, a flat, open landscape of wet meadows, drainage ditches and small villages between Breddin, Rhinow and Dreetz, in the north-west of Brandenburg. It is a land of big skies, storks and cranes, where the horizon seems endless and the wind blows freely. In autumn, thousands of cranes gather on the fields, filling the air with their calls.

For a swim on the way back, the area has lakes and slow rivers, and the Havel and its side lakes lie to the south. Not every stretch of water is suitable: some lakes are bird reserves where swimming is not allowed, and others have muddy, reedy shores, so look for the local bathing spots, marked with signs and often with a small beach or jetty. The water is soft and often a little brown from the peat, and in summer it warms up nicely.

The roads in the Rhinluch are flat, quiet and often straight, lined with old trees, with cobbled sections in some villages and the occasional tractor. Watch out for crosswinds on the open stretches. Breddin and the surrounding villages are small, with limited services, so fuel is best found in larger towns like Kyritz, Neustadt or Wusterhausen. On the way back to Berlin, the roads through the Havelland are pleasant and easy, with little traffic.
t.near buch@52.6,13.5:
Buch, on the far northern edge of Berlin, is a district shaped by medicine. In the early twentieth century, the city architect Ludwig Hoffmann built a series of large hospital complexes here, in a park-like setting outside the crowded city, and Buch has been a centre of hospitals and medical research ever since. Today it is home to the Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine and a cluster of biotech companies, as well as a large hospital campus, and the old Hoffmann buildings, with their red-brick and stone façades, are still impressive.

Around the institutes, Buch has a surprisingly rural feel, with forests, fields and lakes stretching north into Brandenburg. The Bucher Forst is a large wooded area crossed by walking and cycling paths, and the Karower Teiche, a series of ponds, are a nature reserve, home to many birds. The Panke, a small river, flows south from here through the city to the Spree. In the old village centre, a Baroque church stands next to the park of a castle that was demolished in the 1960s.

As a finish point for rides back from Lusatia, with its lakes formed from old open-cast mines and its strange, scarred landscapes, Buch offers a quiet end to the day. The ride back into Berlin from the south and east involves crossing the city or using the motorway ring, and weekday evenings are the slowest time to try it. Once in the northern suburbs, the roads become quieter, lined with trees and houses.

There are fuel stations and supermarkets in Buch and the neighbouring districts, and a few restaurants and cafés. The Barnim plateau to the north, with its forests and lakes, is a pleasant area for short rides, with quiet roads and cobbled villages. Berlin's weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters, and the north-east of the city often feels a little breezier and cooler than the centre.
t.near gerswalde on the way back@53.2,13.8:
The Uckermark, in the far north-east of Brandenburg, is one of the emptiest regions in Germany, and that is precisely its charm: rolling hills, endless fields of grain and rapeseed, beech forests, villages with brick churches and, scattered everywhere, lakes left behind by the glaciers of the last ice age. Gerswalde sits between some of the largest of these lakes, and on a hot day on the way back to Berlin, it is a wonderful place for a swim.

The lakes here are often remarkably clear, with sandy bottoms and reedy shores, and many villages have small bathing spots with a jetty or a patch of grass. A few kilometres to the east, the Oberuckersee and the Unteruckersee stretch north towards Prenzlau, whose huge brick Gothic church of St. Mary, rebuilt after wartime destruction, rises above the town and the lake. Gerswalde itself has the ruins of a medieval moated castle.

The landscape of the Uckermark was shaped by the ice, which left behind a series of moraines, kettle holes and lakes, giving the land its gentle, rolling character. The region is a stronghold for birds: cranes nest in the wetlands, white-tailed eagles hunt over the lakes, and in autumn thousands of cranes and geese gather on the fields. The air smells of cut hay and lake water in summer.

The roads in the Uckermark are a delight for riders who appreciate quiet, scenic routes. They wind gently through the hills, past lakes and fields, often lined with avenues of old trees, with little traffic. Some village streets still have cobbles, and the surface on the minor roads can be patchy. Services are sparse, so fill up in Prenzlau or Templin. The ride back to Berlin is straightforward, either on the A11 motorway or on the quieter roads through the Schorfheide forest, a vast area of woodland that was once a royal hunting ground.
t.marienfelde@52.4,13.4:
Between 1953 and 1990, more than a million people who had fled or left East Germany passed through a camp in Marienfelde, in the far south of West Berlin. The Notaufnahmelager, the emergency reception centre, was where they were registered, questioned by Western intelligence services, housed and sent on to new lives in the West. Part of it is now a museum, with exhibits and personal stories that bring the divided city vividly to life, and it is one of the more moving places in Berlin to spend an hour.

Marienfelde has older roots too. The village church, a sturdy fieldstone building from the early thirteenth century, is considered the oldest surviving village church in Berlin, still standing on its green among the trees. And the district has a long industrial tradition: the Mercedes-Benz plant here is often described as the oldest still-operating production site of the Daimler group, and has been making components for more than a century.

Today Marienfelde is a quiet residential area on the southern edge of the city, with housing estates, allotments and fields, and on its southern side, the line of the former Berlin Wall, now a cycle path, the Mauerweg, which you can follow through woods and meadows. For rides south into Brandenburg it is convenient, because it lies right on the city boundary.

The Spreewald ride heads south from here, through the sandy forests and villages of the Teltow and Dahme areas, towards the maze of channels and alder woods around Lübbenau and Lehde, where the river splits into hundreds of waterways and boatmen pole flat-bottomed punts through the forest. Roads in that direction are flat and mostly quiet, lined with trees, with occasional cobbles in the villages and long, straight stretches through pine forests. Fuel, bakeries and supermarkets are easy to find in Marienfelde and the surrounding districts.
t.near konradshohe@52.6,13.3:
On the north-western edge of Berlin, the city dissolves into water and woods. Around Konradshöhe and Heiligensee, villas and gardens run down to the shores of the Havel and the Tegeler See, Berlin's second-largest lake, with islands, sailing boats and a long promenade at Alt-Tegel. Across the water, the Tegel forest stretches away, a dense area of pine and oak that hides walking paths and small lakes.

Schloss Tegel, on the southern shore of the lake, was the family home of the Humboldt brothers, Wilhelm, the linguist and educational reformer, and Alexander, the naturalist and explorer, whose travels in South America changed the way people saw the natural world. The house, remodelled by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, is still privately owned by descendants, and the family burial ground lies in the park. On the other side of the forest, the old Tegel airport, closed in 2020, is slowly being transformed into a new urban quarter.

The rides that finish here come back from the Barnim and the Märkische Schweiz, regions of forests, lakes and rolling hills north-east of Berlin. The Werbellinsee, a long, clear lake in the Schorfheide forest, may be the loveliest lake in Brandenburg, and the Märkische Schweiz around Buckow is a small area of hills, valleys and lakes, where Bertolt Brecht and Helene Weigel had a summer house that is now a museum. The roads there are winding and quiet, with cobbled sections and avenues of old trees.

Coming back into Berlin, the northern suburbs are generally calmer than the south and east, and the roads along the Havel are pleasant, lined with trees and houses. Fuel is on the main roads, and beer gardens and restaurants along the lake shores, where you can sit with a cold drink and watch the boats. Summer evenings by the Havel are long and gentle, a very Berlin way to finish a ride.
t.near schlieben on the way back@51.7,13.4:
The Elbe-Elster district, in the far south of Brandenburg, is a quiet, sparsely populated land of forests, heath, farmland and small towns, between the Elbe and the Black Elster rivers. Schlieben, a small town on a low hill, stands in the middle of this landscape, and the countryside near it is a place to pause on the way back towards Berlin, especially on a hot day.

To the east lies the former lignite mining area of Lusatia, where decades of open-cast mining left vast craters that are now being flooded to create new lakes. At Lichterfeld, near Finsterwalde, the Bergheider See was formed from one of these mines, and on its shore stands the F60, a gigantic overburden conveyor bridge, more than five hundred metres long, which has been preserved as a visitor attraction and is sometimes called the lying Eiffel Tower. The lake has bathing spots, and the contrast between the clean water and the massive steel structure is surreal. Other former mining lakes in the area have also been opened for swimming, though some are still off-limits because the banks are unstable, so always obey the signs.

To the south-west, Doberlug-Kirchhain has a Cistercian monastery church founded in the twelfth century and a Renaissance castle, both beautifully restored, and they make a worthwhile stop if you have time. The forests around Schlieben are mostly pine, on sandy soils, with heathland in places, and they smell of resin in the heat.

The roads here are quiet and flat to gently rolling, often lined with trees, with long, straight stretches through the forests and cobbled sections in some villages. Schlieben itself is small, so services are limited; fuel and supermarkets are easier to find in Doberlug-Kirchhain, Herzberg or Finsterwalde. The ride back to Berlin is long but easy, through the forests of the Dahme-Spreewald region, with little traffic outside the main roads.
t.near wilhelmstadt@52.5,13.2:
Spandau was a town in its own right for centuries before it became part of Berlin in 1920, and its people still sometimes say they are going into Berlin when they head for the centre. The finish is near Wilhelmstadt, a district on the western bank of the Havel, south of Spandau's old town, and it is a calm place to finish rides that have spent the day in the lakes of the Uckermark or around Bad Saarow.

The Spandau Citadel, a few kilometres north, is one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortresses in Europe, a star-shaped stronghold surrounded by water, built in the sixteenth century around an older castle. Its medieval Julius Tower once held the imperial war treasure, a hoard of gold coins from French war reparations. The citadel is now a museum and cultural venue, with exhibitions, concerts and a large colony of bats wintering in its vaults. Spandau Prison, where Rudolf Hess was the last inmate, was demolished after his death in 1987 to prevent it becoming a shrine.

The old town of Spandau has a pleasant market square, a Gothic church and narrow streets, and the Havel, here wide and slow, is lined with boats, houses and green spaces. To the south, the river widens into a chain of lakes, the Havelseen, bordered by forests, with beaches and footpaths along the shores.

Coming back into Berlin from the west and north, Spandau is often your first contact with the city, and the roads can be busy, especially on Sunday evenings. The Heerstraße and other main roads are wide and fast, while the side streets are quieter, with cobbles in places. There are fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants throughout Spandau. A walk along the Havel at dusk, with the light reflecting off the water and the boats coming home, is a fine way to end the day.
t.berkenbruck on the way back@52.3,14.2:
Berkenbrück is a small village on the Spree, between Fürstenwalde and Frankfurt an der Oder, in the east of Brandenburg. The river here winds slowly through meadows and forests, and the village, with its houses scattered along the water and among the pines, has a sleepy, summer-holiday feel. On the way back towards Berlin, it earns its place with a swim in the river or in one of the small lakes nearby, such as the Dehmsee.

The Spree is gentle here, with sandy banks and reedy shores, and the water is soft and slightly brown from the peat. It is popular with canoeists and anglers, and on hot days families from the surrounding villages come to swim. The lakes are calmer and warmer, with small beaches and jetties. As always with natural waters, check the depth and the current before diving in, and swim only at designated spots where possible.

A few kilometres west, Fürstenwalde has a Gothic cathedral, St. Mary's, whose interior was rebuilt after the war with a striking modern design inside the old brick shell. South of Fürstenwalde, in the forested Rauen Hills, lie the Markgrafensteine, two huge granite boulders carried here by the glaciers of the ice age from Scandinavia. In the nineteenth century, a giant granite bowl was carved from one of them and transported to Berlin, where it still stands in front of the Altes Museum in the Lustgarten.

The roads around Berkenbrück are quiet and flat, winding through forests and along the river, with occasional cobbles and sandy verges. Fürstenwalde, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The ride back to Berlin follows the Spree valley or the A12 motorway; the old country roads through the villages are slower but far more interesting. In summer, the forests smell of pine and the evenings are long and warm.
t.near jablonne v podjestedi on the way ba:
The long ridge of Ještěd rises to the east, and on its summit stands one of the most unusual buildings in Central Europe: a hyperboloid tower that combines a television transmitter and a hotel, designed by the architect Karel Hubáček and completed in 1973, its silver cone visible for miles around. This stop is on the western side of the ridge, near the small town of Jablonné v Podještědí, in a landscape of hills, forests, ponds and villages on the way back from the Krkonoše.

Jablonné is a quiet town, but it has a large Baroque basilica dedicated to St. Lawrence and St. Zdislava, a thirteenth-century noblewoman known for her charity, who was canonised in 1995. Just outside the town stands Lemberk Castle, where Zdislava lived, a Renaissance château on a rocky outcrop above the valley. To the north rise the Lusatian Mountains, a range of volcanic hills and sandstone rocks along the German border, with forests and good roads.

For a swim, the area south-west of the point, around Stráž pod Ralskem and Hamr na Jezeře, has lakes and reservoirs with bathing spots, popular in summer. The landscape there has an unusual history: for decades, uranium was extracted underground by chemical leaching, and the clean-up is still going on, while the large military area of Ralsko, used by the Soviet army until 1991, has slowly been returned to nature. Swim only at official bathing spots, where the water quality is monitored.

The roads around Jablonné are quiet and winding, passing through forests, over hills and through villages with old timber houses, typical of the region. The surface can be patchy on the minor roads, with potholes and gravel. Jablonné has a few shops and pubs, but for fuel, the larger towns of Česká Lípa, Liberec or Hrádek nad Nisou are more reliable. Remember the Czech rule of dipped headlights at all times.
t.near lovosice on the way back@50.5,14.1:
On 1 October 1756, on the fields around Lovosice, Frederick the Great's Prussian army fought an Austrian force in the first battle of the Seven Years' War, a conflict that would spread across Europe and around the world. The battle was indecisive, but the Austrians withdrew, and the war went on for seven long years. Today the battlefield is farmland and vineyards, with a few memorials, and the town of Lovosice is a modest industrial place on the Elbe.

The landscape around it is anything but modest. The České středohoří, the Central Bohemian Uplands, is a range of volcanic hills, cones and domes rising steeply from the Elbe valley, with forests, orchards and vineyards on their slopes. The Lovoš, a cone-shaped hill just north of town, offers wide views, and Milešovka, a little further west, is known as one of the windiest places in the country. The Elbe winds through a gorge between the hills, and the views from the roads are spectacular.

A few kilometres away, Litoměřice is a beautiful old town, the seat of a bishop, with a large main square, Baroque churches and a wine-growing tradition. Terezín, just across the river, is a fortress town built by Emperor Joseph II at the end of the eighteenth century, which the Nazis turned into the Theresienstadt ghetto and concentration camp; the memorial is a deeply moving place to visit.

For a swim on the way back, there are flooded gravel pits along the Elbe plain, some with bathing spots and kiosks, and the water is clear and refreshing in summer. Choose a designated spot, as some lakes are private or used for fishing. The roads through the uplands are winding and scenic, with good surfaces and little traffic. Lovosice and Litoměřice have fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The ride from Bohemian Switzerland, with its sandstone cliffs and the great natural arch of Pravčická brána, follows the Elbe valley south.
t.near lindow on the way back@53.0,13.0:
North of Berlin the Brandenburg countryside dissolves into lakes, and Lindow sits between three of them, a small town of cobbled streets, brick houses and old trees. The ruins of a Cistercian nunnery stand on the shore, and Theodor Fontane, the great chronicler of the Mark Brandenburg, wrote about the nuns of Lindow in his travels through the region. It is a quiet, slightly melancholy place, and on a summer evening, with the light on the water, very beautiful.

The stop itself is a short way from the town, among the lakes and forests of the Ruppiner Land. Swimming is the main attraction here: the lakes have sandy beaches, reed beds and wooden jetties, and the water is clean and warm in summer. The Gudelacksee, next to Lindow, is one of the larger lakes, with an island and a camping ground.

Gransee, a few kilometres east, has a fine Gothic church and a memorial to Queen Louise of Prussia, whose coffin rested in the town overnight on its way to Berlin in 1810. The monument, designed by Schinkel, is a delicate cast-iron canopy over a sarcophagus.

The riding in Brandenburg is famous for its tree-lined avenues, the Alleen, where old lime, oak and chestnut trees arch over the road, creating tunnels of green. They are beautiful but unforgiving: the trees stand close to the edge, and accidents are often fatal. Ride within your limits, and watch for cobbles in the villages, which can be slippery when wet.

Gransee is where to fill the tank and buy groceries. Lindow is the place to stay put: buy a piece of smoked fish from a lakeside stall if you find one open, sit on the jetty and let the reeds rustle.
t.zehlendorf@52.4,13.3:
Before it was a motorway, the A115 that runs past Zehlendorf was the AVUS, a dead-straight test and racing road opened in 1921, where Mercedes and Auto Union raced in the 1930s on a steeply banked curve that terrified drivers. The banking is gone, and the road is just a busy stretch of the Berlin motorway network, but its history adds a little spice to finishing a ride here.

Zehlendorf is the green, leafy south-west of Berlin, a district of villas, gardens and forests. The Grunewald, a large forest, stretches to the north, and the lakes of the Havel and the Grunewald chain, Schlachtensee, Krumme Lanke and Wannsee, are within easy reach. In summer they are packed with swimmers, and the paths around them are busy with walkers and cyclists.

Dahlem, next door, is home to the Free University and the Botanical Garden, one of the largest in the world. The Onkel Toms Hütte estate, designed by Bruno Taut in the 1920s, is one of the modernist housing estates listed as a World Heritage site, with colourful facades and gardens.

Coming back from the Fläming, the final stretch into Berlin follows the motorway or the old roads through Potsdam. Traffic can be heavy, especially on Sunday evenings, and Berlin's speed cameras are numerous.

On a hot evening the lakes win over everything else. Park near the Schlachtensee, swim out from the wooded shore, and then find a beer garden; fuel and food in Zehlendorf are only a few minutes away when you are ready.
t.trossin on the way back@51.6,12.8:
Pine, sand and silence: the Dübener Heide is one of the larger forests of central Germany, a broad plateau of heath and woodland between the Elbe and the Mulde. Trossin lies on its eastern edge, a small village surrounded by fields and forest, a few kilometres from Dommitzsch, where the Elbe flows slowly past meadows and old willows.

Torgau, a short ride north-east, is where American and Soviet troops met on the Elbe on 25 April 1945, cutting Germany in two. The meeting, known as Elbe Day, was celebrated as a symbol of Allied unity, and a monument on the riverbank commemorates it. Torgau also has a fine Renaissance castle, Schloss Hartenfels, with a famous spiral staircase.

Swimming here is a matter of choice. The Elbe is tempting on a hot day, but the current is strong, the river is used by boats and the banks can be steep and muddy. Local lakes and ponds in the Dübener Heide offer safer options, and some have designated bathing areas in summer. Ask locally or look for signs.

The riding is quiet and easy, with straight roads through forest and fields. Grip is usually fine, yet watch for cobbles in the villages, sand on the edges of forest roads and wildlife, especially deer and wild boar. Traffic is light, and the forests are cool and shady on hot days.

Near Kossa, in the forest, a Cold War command bunker of the East German army has been preserved and opened as a museum on certain days, a reminder that this quiet heath was once a military zone. Mockrehna and Dommitzsch have fuel and shops, and Torgau has restaurants and cafés.
t.spandau@52.5,13.2:
Spandau is older than Berlin. It was granted town rights in the thirteenth century, and its people still say they are going to Berlin when they cross into the city centre. The old town sits at the confluence of the Havel and the Spree, and its great fortress, the Zitadelle, is one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortifications in Europe, a star-shaped stronghold with bastions, a moat and the medieval Juliusturm, where the German imperial war treasure was once stored.

The name Spandau also recalls a darker chapter. The Allied prison here held Nazi war criminals after the Nuremberg trials, and Rudolf Hess, Hitler's deputy, was its last inmate. After his death in 1987, the prison was demolished to prevent it becoming a shrine.

This finish lies in the northern part of the district, near Hakenfelde and Haselhorst, where the Havel widens into lakes and forests line the shore. The Spandau forest, to the north, is a large area of pine and oak, and the riverbanks are popular with walkers and anglers.

Coming back from Potsdam and the Havelland, the roads run along the Havel through forests and villages, with fine views of the river. The final stretch into Spandau can be slow, with traffic lights, cobbles and tram lines in places.

Do not just skirt the place. Ride into the old town, leave the bike near the market square and walk the few lanes of half-timbered and baroque houses, then across to the citadel moat as the light goes. Fuel and food are plentiful; atmosphere, in Berlin's suburbs, is rarer.
t.near kloster lehnin on the way back@52.3:
Lehnin Abbey was founded in 1180 by Margrave Otto I of Brandenburg, who, according to legend, fell asleep under an oak while hunting, dreamed that a white stag was attacking him, and drove it off by calling on Christ. The Cistercian monks who came from the Harz cleared the forests, drained the marshes and built a great brick church, one of the earliest examples of the north German Brick Gothic. It still stands, restored, in a quiet village surrounded by lakes and forests.

The abbey is also linked to a mysterious prophecy, the Vaticinium Lehninense, a medieval poem that seemed to predict the fate of the Hohenzollern dynasty. It was probably written much later, but it caused a stir in the nineteenth century and is still debated by historians.

You are a few minutes' ride from Lehnin, in the Zauche, a plateau of sandy soil, pine forests and lakes south-west of Potsdam. The lakes are many and varied, from small forest ponds to larger lakes with beaches and jetties. Swimming is popular in summer, and the water is generally clean.

The riding is quiet and gentle, with tree-lined avenues, forest roads and village streets. Most of the asphalt is in fair shape, but cobbles appear in the villages and on some old roads. Watch for wildlife, especially deer and boar, and for slow farm traffic.

For more than a swim, Brandenburg an der Havel lies to the north-west, an old town of churches and waterways whose cathedral island is the cradle of the whole Mark. Kloster Lehnin itself can sort out fuel and a coffee, and in early summer the farm stands along the roads sell strawberries by the basket.
t.near glienicke@52.6,13.4:
Until 1989 the Berlin Wall ran right past here. Glienicke/Nordbahn, just across the boundary in Brandenburg, was home to the Entenschnabel, the duck's bill, a narrow strip of East German territory that poked into West Berlin, with houses whose gardens backed onto the Wall. Today the Mauerweg, a walking and cycling path, follows the old border line, and a few traces remain.

This finish lies in the far north of Berlin, near Lübars and Blankenfelde, where the city gives way to fields and farms. Lübars is a real village, with a green, a church, farmhouses and horses, and it feels miles from the city centre. The Tegeler Fließ, a small stream, winds through meadows and woods nearby, and the area is popular with walkers and riders on horseback.

It is an odd landscape to finish in. You ride in through ordinary suburban streets, and suddenly there are paddocks, a pond and a church tower, with the tower blocks of the Märkisches Viertel standing on the horizon like a reminder of where you are. The contrast says a lot about West Berlin, a walled city that had to keep its last farms because it had nowhere else to go.

Coming back from Lehnin and the Zauche, the final kilometres follow the ring or cut through the northern suburbs, with traffic lights, buses and stretches of cobbles that rattle the mirrors. Approach the old border slowly; the roads here were never built for through traffic.

Glienicke has shops and fuel on its main street. Lübars has a couple of places to eat around the green, and on a warm evening there is no better reward than sitting there, boots off, listening to horses instead of engines.
t.near chorin@52.9,13.9:
Chorin Abbey rises out of the trees like a red brick cathedral that someone forgot to finish. Cistercian monks founded it in the thirteenth century as part of the German settlement of Brandenburg, and its towering west front is one of the finest examples of north German brick Gothic. After the Reformation it fell into ruin, and the Prussian architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel was among those who campaigned to save it in the nineteenth century. Today it hosts a well-known summer concert season and has a gentle, almost romantic air.

The surroundings are part of the Schorfheide-Chorin biosphere reserve, one of the largest protected areas in Germany. The landscape here was formed by the last glaciation: moraine hills, kettle lakes, beech forests and peat bogs. It is unusually hilly by Brandenburg standards, so the roads actually rise and fall, curving between lakes and through cathedral-like stands of beech. Cranes, sea eagles and beavers live here, and in autumn the sound of migrating geese fills the sky.

The riding is relaxed rather than demanding. Many minor roads are avenues lined with old trees, beautiful but unforgiving if you run wide, and some village streets are still paved with cobbles that get slick in rain. Agricultural traffic and cyclists share the roads. A few kilometres east, at Niederfinow, the ship lifts raise barges up the edge of the Oder valley; the old 1930s steel structure and the new lift beside it are an engineering spectacle worth a short detour.

Chorin itself is a small village, so for fuel head into Eberswalde, the nearest proper town, which also has supermarkets and bakeries. Near the abbey there are cafés catering to visitors, especially on weekends and concert days. Park, walk under the brick arches, and enjoy one of the quietest corners within an hour of Berlin.
t.near grunheide@52.4,13.9:
For most of its history, Grünheide was a sleepy village of lakes and pine forests on the south-eastern edge of Berlin. Then Tesla arrived. The enormous electric car factory that opened here in 2022 transformed the place into a symbol of industrial change, controversy over water and forests, and new traffic. Even so, the countryside around it still offers some of the nicest lake landscapes near the capital.

The area is threaded with water: the Werlsee, the Peetzsee and the little Löcknitz river, whose valley is a nature reserve with alder woods and wet meadows. The lakes are glacial, left behind by the last Ice Age, and their shores are lined with holiday cottages and bathing spots. In summer, Berliners come out for swimming and boating, and the air smells of pine resin and warm sand.

The roads around Grünheide are typical Brandenburg: flat or gently undulating, often straight through forest, with the occasional curve around a lake. Avenues of old trees line many of them, and some village streets are still cobbled. Traffic can be heavy near the factory and the A10 motorway junctions, especially at shift changes, but the minor roads east and south quickly become quiet. Watch for wild boar and deer, particularly at dawn and dusk.

Fuel is available along the main roads and in nearby Erkner, which is also the place to find a proper selection of shops. There are lakeside cafés and inns around the villages, especially busy on summer weekends. From here, routes lead east towards the Oderbruch and the Polish border, or south towards the Spreewald and Saxon Switzerland, making Grünheide a convenient pause on the way out of the city.
t.near kourim@50.0,14.9:
Long before Prague dominated Bohemia, Kouřim was one of its centres of power. On a promontory above the Kouřimka stream lie the earthworks of Stará Kouřim, a vast early medieval Slavic hillfort that archaeologists consider one of the most important in the country. The later town, founded in the thirteenth century, still has stretches of its walls, a Gothic gate and the sturdy church of St Stephen, which together give this small place a strong sense of age.

Kouřim also hosts an open-air museum of rural architecture, where timber farmhouses, barns and mills from across central Bohemia have been rebuilt, a pleasant stroll if you want a break from the saddle. The surrounding landscape is gently rolling farmland, with fields of wheat and rapeseed, orchards and small woods, and villages with baroque chapels and ponds.

The roads are typical of central Bohemia: narrow, winding, and of variable quality. Some stretches are smooth new asphalt; others are patched and bumpy. Traffic is light, but tractors and local drivers can surprise you, and village speed limits are often enforced. To the east lies Kolín, a larger town on the Elbe with a Gothic cathedral, and Kutná Hora, the old silver-mining town with its famous bone chapel, is within easy reach for a detour.

Kouřim is small, so for a wide choice of fuel head for Kolín or Český Brod, where stations and supermarkets are plentiful. Kouřim has a few pubs and cafés around its square, serving Czech staples like goulash, svíčková and of course beer. Stop, walk to the old walls, and enjoy one of the quieter historical towns of the region before continuing towards the mountains in the north.
t.near brandys nad labem stara boleslav@50:
The twin town of Brandýs nad Labem and Stará Boleslav faces itself across the Elbe, and each half carries a different kind of history. Stará Boleslav is where Wenceslas, the duke later venerated as Saint Wenceslas, was murdered by his brother Boleslav in the tenth century. Its basilica became one of the oldest pilgrimage sites in the Czech lands, and on 28 September, the national holiday, pilgrims still arrive in large numbers.

Brandýs, on the other bank, is dominated by its Renaissance château, a favourite hunting seat of the Habsburgs, decorated with sgraffito and surrounded by gardens. The last Austrian emperor, Karl, lived here as a young officer. The old town square, with its arcades and colourful houses, is a lovely place for a break.

The riding nearby is easy-going. The Elbe plain is flat, with long stretches of road between fields and riverside forests. The river is lined with floodplain woods and old meanders, home to herons and beavers, and in summer the air smells of grass and water. Further north, the land rises towards the sandstone country around Mělník and Kokořín, where the roads start to wind among rocks and pine forests.

Traffic can be heavy on the main roads towards Prague, especially at rush hour, and the D10 motorway nearby is a fast but dull option. Prefer the minor roads, but watch for cobbles in the towns and uneven surfaces in villages. The town has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, as you would expect from a place of almost twenty thousand people. Stop for a coffee on the square in Brandýs, cross the river to the basilica, and then head north towards the rocks and castles.
t.near gransee@52.9,13.2:
Gransee is one of the best-kept medieval towns in Brandenburg, still enclosed by almost the full ring of its brick walls, with gate towers and defensive turrets. In the middle stands the great brick Gothic church of St Mary, and on the market square a curious cast-iron monument designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel marks the spot where the coffin of Queen Louise of Prussia rested overnight in 1810 on its way to Berlin. Louise was hugely popular, and her early death caused national mourning.

The countryside around Gransee is typical of northern Brandenburg: gently rolling farmland, pine and oak forests, and countless lakes left by the glaciers of the last Ice Age. To the north lie the Stechlin and Ruppin lake districts, beloved of the writer Theodor Fontane, who described the region in his famous travel writings. The lakes are clear and quiet, perfect for a summer swim.

The riding here is relaxed. Roads run through forests and fields, often lined with avenues of old trees, which are beautiful but leave no room for error. Some villages still have cobblestone streets. Traffic is light, apart from the B96 main road, which runs north from Berlin towards the Baltic coast and can be busy, especially in summer. Wildlife is abundant, so watch for deer and wild boar, particularly at dawn and dusk.

Gransee has fuel stations, supermarkets and a few cafés and restaurants. It is a good place for a break: walk around the walls, visit the church and the Louise monument, and enjoy the calm of a small town that has kept its character. Next, the road continues towards the Lusatian lakes, a very different landscape shaped by mining.
t.near golzow@52.3,12.5:
South of Brandenburg an der Havel the land breaks into a quiet patchwork of pine forest, heath, small lakes and farm villages, the transition between the Havel lowlands and the Fläming hills. Golzow is one of those villages, a cluster of farmhouses and a church where you will rarely see more than a few cars. It is the sort of place where you stop because it is peaceful rather than because of any particular attraction.

This country was shaped by glaciers. The ice sheets of the last cold period left sand, gravel and lakes, and the result is a landscape of sandy soils, dry pine forests and wet hollows. The forests smell of resin on warm days, and in late summer heather blooms on open areas, some of which were military training grounds during the Cold War. Lakes in the area offer clear water for a swim on hot days, and the shores are often lined with reeds and alders.

History is never far away. Not far north is Lehnin, with a Cistercian monastery founded in the twelfth century, one of the oldest in the region and an important site in the early history of Brandenburg. To the south, the town of Bad Belzig has a medieval castle and a thermal spa. The roads between them are quiet and pleasant, with gentle curves and long straights through forests, but some are narrow, lined with trees, or paved with old cobbles.

Golzow itself has no real services, so plan fuel and food in Brandenburg an der Havel, Lehnin or Bad Belzig. A picnic by one of the lakes is a good alternative. From here, routes lead south-east towards the Lusatian lakes, where former opencast mines have been flooded to create a new landscape of water and sand.
t.near furstenberg@53.2,13.2:
Three lakes wrap around Fürstenberg/Havel, and the town calls itself a water town with good reason: bridges, boat hire, and the Havel threading between the Röblinsee, the Baalensee and the Schwedtsee. It sits right on the border with Mecklenburg, at the southern edge of the great lake district that runs north towards Neustrelitz and the Müritz, and in summer the waterways are full of houseboats and canoes.

There is a heavier story here too, and it deserves a stop. On the far shore of the Schwedtsee lies the memorial of Ravensbrück, the largest Nazi concentration camp for women, where tens of thousands of prisoners from across Europe were held between 1939 and 1945. The site is sober and well presented, with an exhibition in the former guard buildings. Looking back across the water at the pretty town afterwards is an unsettling experience, and an important one.

The riding around Fürstenberg is easy and green. Roads run through beech and pine forests, past lakes glimpsed between the trunks, with gentle curves and very little elevation. The B96 is the main artery and fills up with holiday traffic on summer weekends; the side roads towards Himmelpfort and Lychen are calmer and lovelier, though some are narrow, tree-lined and cobbled in the villages. Cranes and sea eagles are common sights.

Fürstenberg has fuel, supermarkets and several places to eat, including cafés near the water where smoked fish from the lakes is a local speciality. It is a good lunch halt on a long day north of Berlin. If time allows, Himmelpfort a few kilometres east, with its ruined monastery, is famous in Germany as the Christmas post office where children's letters to Father Christmas are answered.
t.near wendisch rietz@52.2,14.1:
Brandenburg likes to call the Scharmützelsee its sea, the Märkisches Meer, and from the southern shore at Wendisch Rietz you can see why. The lake stretches away for about ten kilometres towards Bad Saarow, wide enough that on a windy day it throws up proper waves. Wendisch Rietz sits at the southern tip, with a harbour, a beach, holiday homes and a channel linking the lake to the Glubigsee and the waterways beyond. The name hints at the Slavic Wends who lived here before German settlement.

The riding around the lake is a favourite with Berlin bikers on summer weekends. The road along the western shore runs through pine forest with glimpses of water, and the roads north towards the Rauen hills add a little rise and fall, rare in this flat region. Up in those hills lie the Markgrafensteine, two huge granite boulders dragged here from Scandinavia by Ice Age glaciers; one of them was split in the nineteenth century to make the enormous granite bowl that now stands in front of the Altes Museum in Berlin.

Weekends bring traffic, cyclists and police checks, so the busiest stretches are best taken calmly. Weekdays are far quieter. Watch for sand blown onto the road at forest edges and for wild boar at dusk. In the villages, cobbles still appear.

Wendisch Rietz has cafés, ice cream and fish restaurants by the harbour in season. For fuel and a wider choice, Storkow, Bad Saarow and Beeskow are all within easy reach. Bad Saarow, at the other end of the lake, is an elegant old spa town where Maxim Gorky and other writers stayed in the 1920s, and its thermal baths remain a draw.
t.near ziesar@52.3,12.2:
Ziesar was once the home of bishops. For several centuries, the Bishops of Brandenburg made the castle here their main residence, and the brick keep and the chapel with its medieval wall paintings still stand. The castle now houses a museum on medieval Christianity and episcopal life, a surprising treasure for a small town of a couple of thousand people on the edge of the Fläming.

The landscape around Ziesar is the transition between the flat Havel lowlands and the low, forested hills of the Fläming to the south. The Fläming takes its name from Flemish settlers who came in the twelfth century to farm the land and drain the marshes, and their villages, with brick churches and fieldstone walls, still dot the countryside. The forests are mainly pine, with some oak and beech, and in spring the fields are bright yellow with rapeseed.

Riding here is gentle and relaxing. The roads are quiet, with long straights and gentle bends, and the occasional hill gives a view over the surrounding countryside. Some country roads are narrow and lined with trees, and cobbles still appear in villages. The A2 motorway passes nearby, convenient for a fast return to Berlin or a quick escape west towards Magdeburg.

Ziesar has a few shops and places to eat, but it is small, so for a full range of services the larger towns of Brandenburg an der Havel or Genthin are the reliable choice. A visit to the castle makes a good break, and the town has the quiet air of a place that once mattered more than it does now, which is part of its charm. From here, routes lead north towards the Barnim forests and the Werbellinsee, a very different landscape of beech woods and deep lakes.
t.near rhinow@52.7,12.3:
Human flight has a claim to begin in the hills above Rhinow. On the Gollenberg near Stölln, Otto Lilienthal made many of his glider flights in the 1890s, launching himself from the slope in his bat-winged contraptions, and it was here in 1896 that he crashed and died of his injuries. The hill is now a memorial and a popular site for paragliders, and in a nice twist, in 1989 a large Interflug Ilyushin airliner was landed on the grass airfield at its foot, where it now stands as a museum and wedding venue.

The Rhinow hills are a small island of high ground in the flat, wet landscape of the Havelland. Around them stretch meadows, marshes and peat bogs, the Havelländisches Luch, home to one of the last populations of great bustards in Germany, heavy birds that strut across the fields and are protected with great care. The Havel and Rhin rivers meander through the region, with floodplains that attract cranes and geese in spring and autumn.

The roads here are flat and quiet, crossing open meadows and passing through small villages with brick churches. They are pleasant to ride, with long views and big skies, but wind can be strong on the open plain. Some roads are narrow, and the villages may have cobblestones. Traffic is light, apart from farm machinery.

Rhinow is a small town with limited services. For fuel and supplies, head to Rathenow, a larger town known for its optical industry, or Friesack. From the top of the Gollenberg, the view over the Havelland is surprisingly wide, a rare vantage point in this flat land. Take a moment to think of Lilienthal and his dream of flight before riding on.
t.near marienwerder@52.9,13.5:
Marienwerder is a small village north of Berlin, set among forests and canals in the Barnim district. The landscape here is shaped by water, both natural and man-made. The Oder-Havel Canal, which links the two rivers, passes close by, as does the older Finow Canal, built in the early seventeenth century and often described as the oldest artificial waterway in Germany that is still navigable. Its locks and towpaths are a charming reminder of the past.

The forests around Marienwerder are part of the Barnim plateau, a region of moraines and lakes left by the last Ice Age. Pine dominates, but there are also stands of beech and oak, and the lakes are clear and quiet. To the north, the Schorfheide, once a royal and later a political hunting ground, is a vast forest home to deer, wild boar and eagles. In autumn, the trees turn gold and the air is filled with the calls of cranes.

Riding in this area is peaceful. The roads are quiet, winding through forests and along canals, with occasional gentle hills. Some of the smaller roads are narrow and tree-lined, and cobbles still appear in villages. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays. Be careful at dawn and dusk, when wildlife is most active.

Marienwerder has limited services, so plan to get fuel and supplies in Eberswalde, the nearest larger town, or in Bernau to the south. The canal locks make good photo spots, and a picnic by the water is a fine way to spend a break. Onward, the way continues north towards the Uckermark, a region of rolling hills and lakes that is among the most sparsely populated in Germany.
t.near rakovnik@50.1,13.8:
Rakovník guards its old centre with a pair of Gothic gate towers, and the taller of them, the Prague Gate, looks as if it has been borrowed from the capital's skyline. The town is the centre of a rural district west of Prague, known for its hops and beer, and the surrounding countryside is a gentle mix of fields, orchards and wooded hills. It has a calm, slightly sleepy atmosphere that suits a lunch stop well.

The real attraction lies to the south and east, in the Křivoklátsko, one of the largest continuous forests in central Bohemia and a UNESCO biosphere reserve. The Berounka river winds through a deep valley here, and the royal castle of Křivoklát, once a hunting seat of Czech kings, stands on a rocky spur above the forest. The roads through the forest and along the river are a delight, with tight curves, changes in elevation and very little traffic.

Riding in this area requires attention, as roads can be narrow and surfaces variable. Watch for wildlife, especially deer and wild boar, and for local drivers who know the roads better than you do. In summer, the river valley is popular with canoeists and campers, and some roads may be busier. In autumn, the forests turn gold and red, making for a spectacular ride.

Rakovník has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, so it is a good place to fill up before heading into the forest, where services are limited. Local pubs serve Czech food and beer from nearby breweries. From here, the route follows the Berounka towards Karlštejn, the great Gothic castle built by Emperor Charles IV to house the crown jewels.
t.near benesov nad ploucnici@50.7,14.3:
Few small towns can boast two Renaissance châteaux, but Benešov nad Ploučnicí has both, an upper and a lower castle standing side by side above the Ploučnice river. They were built in the sixteenth century by the Wartenberg and Salhausen families, and their gables, painted rooms and courtyards make a surprising sight in a town of a few thousand people. Guided tours run in season.

The town sits in the valley of the Ploučnice, a winding river that flows west towards the Elbe at Děčín. The surrounding landscape is hilly and wooded, part of the volcanic uplands of northern Bohemia, with conical hills, basalt outcrops and small villages. To the north lies Bohemian Switzerland, a national park of sandstone towers, gorges and the famous Pravčická brána, the largest natural sandstone arch in Europe.

The roads around Benešov are narrow and winding, following valleys and climbing over hills. They offer a satisfying ride, with plenty of curves and changing scenery, but the surfaces can be uneven and some villages have cobblestones. Traffic is light, apart from the main road through the valley. Watch for cyclists and hikers, especially near the national park.

Benešov nad Ploučnicí has a few shops and pubs, and fuel can be found in the area, though the nearest large town is Děčín, on the Elbe, which has a wide range of services and a big château of its own. A stop in Benešov to see the castles is well worthwhile. Next, the road continues towards the Krkonoše, the highest mountains in the Czech Republic, through a succession of valleys, hills and forests.
t.near wittstock@53.1,12.5:
In October 1636, on the hills south of Wittstock, a Swedish army crushed the combined forces of the Holy Roman Emperor and Saxony in one of the bloodiest battles of the Thirty Years' War. Archaeologists later found a mass grave of soldiers on the battlefield, and a museum in the tower of the old bishop's castle in Wittstock tells the story of the war and its brutal impact on ordinary people. The town itself is enclosed by one of the most complete medieval brick walls in Germany, with towers and a gate.

Wittstock lies in the Prignitz, the north-western corner of Brandenburg, a region of farmland, forests and small rivers, sparsely populated and quiet. To the south-east stretches the Kyritz-Ruppiner Heide, a vast heathland that was used by the Soviet army as a bombing range during the Cold War. A long campaign by locals prevented the German military from taking it over after reunification, and today it is a protected landscape of heather, sand and pine, glowing purple in late summer.

The riding here is relaxed, with long, straight roads through fields and forests, and occasional gentle curves. Traffic is light, apart from the motorway junction, where the A24 and A19 meet near the town. The roads can be windy on the open fields, and wildlife is a hazard at dawn and dusk. Some villages still have cobbled streets.

Wittstock has fuel, a supermarket or two and places to eat, and the old town has cafés where you can sit near the walls. The Harz mountains are still far to the south-west, a long ride across the plain, so this is a good place for a solid meal and a full tank.
t.near kropstadt@52.0,12.8:
Kropstädt is a small village in the forests north of Lutherstadt Wittenberg, on the southern slopes of the Fläming, a low ridge of sand and gravel left by the glaciers of the penultimate Ice Age. The village is quiet, with farmhouses, a church and fields stretching to the edge of the forest. It is the kind of place you pass through on your way to somewhere else, but the surrounding area is full of interest.

Wittenberg, a short ride south, is where Martin Luther is said to have posted his ninety-five theses on the door of the Castle Church in 1517, sparking the Reformation that changed Europe. The town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Luther's house, the town church where he preached, and the house of his colleague Philipp Melanchthon. The painter Lucas Cranach also lived and worked here, and his workshop produced many of the famous portraits of Luther.

The Fläming itself is a gentle landscape of forests, heaths and fields, with villages of fieldstone churches built by the Flemish settlers who gave the region its name in the twelfth century. The roads here are quiet, with long straights through the forests and gentle curves through the villages. Watch for sand on the road at the forest edges, for wildlife at dawn and dusk, and for cobbles in the villages.

Kropstädt has next to nothing for travellers; fuel, groceries and restaurants wait in Wittenberg, which has plenty of choice. A meal in one of the old town's restaurants, perhaps with a local beer for the evening, is a fine way to round off a visit. The Scharmützelsee lies to the north-east, a long ride across the forests of Brandenburg.
t.buckow@52.6,14.1:
Bertolt Brecht and Helene Weigel spent their summers in Buckow in the 1950s, in a house by the lake, and it was here that Brecht wrote the Buckow Elegies, a series of short poems tinged with disillusion. The house is now a small museum, with Weigel's old covered wagon from Mother Courage in the barn. The playwright was not the first to fall for Buckow; the novelist Theodor Fontane praised the area, and the doctors of the nineteenth century prescribed its air for the nerves.

Buckow is the heart of the Märkische Schweiz, the Brandenburg Switzerland, a name that makes Swiss visitors smile but captures something real. After the flat lands around Berlin, the landscape here is surprisingly hilly, with steep wooded slopes, ravines, streams and clear lakes, all left by the glaciers of the last Ice Age. The Schermützelsee, on which Buckow sits, is surrounded by beech forests, and walking trails lead through the hills to viewpoints and springs.

The riding here is a delight by Brandenburg standards. The roads climb and descend through the forests, with real curves and gradients, and the views over the lakes and hills are lovely. They are narrow in places, with tree-lined avenues and cobbled village streets, and they can be busy with cyclists and walkers on weekends. Watch for wildlife and for leaves on the road in autumn.

Buckow has cafés, restaurants and a few shops, but fuel is more easily found in Müncheberg or Strausberg. A cake on a lakeside terrace, followed by a short walk to the Brecht-Weigel house, makes a perfect break. The Scharmützelsee, a larger and busier lake, lies to the south.
t.spreenhagen@52.3,13.9:
Spreenhagen is a scattered rural municipality south-east of Berlin, where the River Spree winds through forests and meadows between Fürstenwalde and the capital. The villages here are small and quiet, with old churches, farmhouses and modern homes for commuters, and the landscape is a typical Brandenburg mix of pine forests, wet meadows and lakes.

The Spree is the river of Berlin, flowing through the heart of the city, but here it is a quieter stream, meandering through a broad valley with alder woods and reeds. The forests around Spreenhagen are part of a large wooded area that stretches south towards the Dahme lakes and east towards the Scharmützelsee, and they are where deer, boar and many birds. In summer, the lakes are popular for swimming and boating, and the air smells of pine and warm sand.

The roads are mostly flat, running dead straight through pine forest and only bending where a lake or a village gets in the way. Traffic is light, apart from the main roads near the motorway, which can be busy with commuters and trucks. The A12 motorway to Frankfurt an der Oder and Poland runs nearby, providing a fast route east or back to Berlin. Watch for wildlife, especially at dawn and dusk, and for sand on the road at forest edges.

Fuel and supplies are most reliably found in Fürstenwalde, the nearest larger town, a few minutes away. Fürstenwalde has a cathedral and a pleasant centre on the Spree. Spreenhagen itself works well for a rest in the forest before heading south towards the Lusatian lakes, where former opencast mines have been flooded to create a new landscape.
t.near letschin@52.7,14.5:
Frederick the Great stands on a pedestal in Letschin, and the people of the Oderbruch have good reason to remember him. In the mid-eighteenth century, the Prussian king ordered the draining of this vast marshy floodplain of the Oder, a huge engineering project that created new farmland and villages for thousands of settlers. He is said to have declared that he had conquered a province in peace. The landscape today is a flat, fertile plain of fields, ditches and dykes, stretching to the Polish border.

The Oderbruch has a dramatic modern history too. In April 1945, the Soviet army launched its final offensive on Berlin from the bridgeheads across the Oder, and the battle of the Seelow Heights, on the ridge at the western edge of the plain, was one of the bloodiest of the war. A memorial and museum at Seelow tell the story, and the landscape still bears traces of the fighting.

The riding here is flat and open, with long straight roads across the fields and big skies overhead. The views are wide, and the light is beautiful in the evening. The roads can be windy, and agricultural traffic is common, especially at harvest time. Some roads are lined with trees, and the villages may have cobbled streets. The Oder dyke offers a fine ride along the river, with views into Poland.

The nearest dependable fuel and food are in Seelow or the larger villages along the main roads; Letschin is a place to look, not to shop. A local inn may offer hearty Brandenburg dishes, such as potatoes with quark and linseed oil. The Lusatian lakes lie far to the south, a long ride along the eastern edge of the country.
t.near brandenburg an der havel@52.4,12.5:
Brandenburg an der Havel gave its name to the whole state, and its cathedral on an island in the Havel was founded in the tenth century, when this was a frontier between Germans and Slavs. The town is a maze of water, with the Havel splitting into channels and lakes, and its old centre is spread across three historic towns, the Old Town, the New Town and the Cathedral Island, linked by bridges. Brick Gothic churches, gates and towers rise above the rooftops.

The town has a proud industrial past. The Brennabor works once made bicycles, prams and cars here, and the steelworks were among the largest in East Germany; the industrial museum in the old steel mill tells the story. The humorist Loriot, much loved in Germany, was born here in 1923, and a few bronze figures of his characters dot the town centre.

The surrounding landscape is full of water, with the Havel and its lakes forming a chain of blue through forests and meadows. The riding here is relaxed, with roads following the lakes and winding through villages, and some gentle hills to the south. The roads in the town can be busy and cobbled, and the bridges can be narrow. To the west, the Havel lowlands stretch towards the Elbe, with wide meadows and big skies, home to storks and cranes.

Brandenburg an der Havel has plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants. A coffee by the river, watching the boats pass, is a pleasant break, and the cathedral is worth a visit for its crypt and its treasures. The Oderbruch, a very different landscape, lies far to the east.
t.near sperenberg@52.1,13.4:
South of Berlin, the forests around Sperenberg hide a strange history. In the early 1930s, at the nearby Kummersdorf army testing ground, a young Wernher von Braun began his rocket experiments for the German military, the first step towards the V-2 and, eventually, the Saturn V. After the war, the Soviets built a large air base at Sperenberg, which remained in use until the last Russian troops left in 1994. The old runway and buildings are now abandoned, slowly being reclaimed by forest.

Sperenberg itself is an old village known for its gypsum, which was quarried here for centuries. The old quarries have filled with water, creating clear lakes surrounded by white cliffs, an unusual sight in Brandenburg. The surrounding landscape is mostly pine forest, with lakes, meadows and small villages, and the Mellensee and other lakes to the north are popular for swimming and boating in summer.

As for the riding, it is relaxed and quiet. The roads are flat or gently rolling, long forest straights broken by the odd bend at a lakeshore. Traffic is light, apart from weekends, when Berliners come out to the lakes. Sand drifts onto the asphalt where forest meets field, deer and boar keep their own timetable, and village cobbles get greasy in the wet. Some of the old military areas are still closed, so follow the signs.

Sperenberg is too small to count on for fuel; Zossen and the larger villages along the main roads are where to fill the tank and find a proper meal. A picnic by one of the gypsum lakes is a nice alternative. The Oderbruch lies to the north-east, a long ride around the edge of Berlin.
t.near baruth@52.0,13.6:
Glassblowers once worked in the forest just outside Baruth. In the eighteenth century, the counts of Solms-Baruth founded a glassworks here, using the local sand and the wood of the surrounding forests, and a village grew up around it. Glashütte, as it is still called, is now a museum village, with workshops where you can watch glass being blown, old workers' houses, a café and craft shops, a charming stop deep among pine trees.

Baruth itself is a small town with a castle and a park, set in a broad valley that runs east to west across southern Brandenburg. This is the Baruther Urstromtal, an ancient glacial valley carved by meltwater from the ice sheets, and it is lined to the south by the gentle hills of the Fläming. From the higher ground, the views stretch over the forests and fields, a rare vantage point in this flat land. The forests are mostly pine, with heaths and dunes in places, and they are sheltering deer, wild pigs and wolves, which have returned to Brandenburg in recent decades.

The roads are flat or gently rolling, ruler-straight through the trees, kinking only at village corners. Traffic is light, apart from the B96, which runs north and south through the town. Blown sand, crossing game and the odd cobbled village street are the only real hazards. On hot summer days, the smell of pine resin fills the air.

Baruth has fuel, a few shops and restaurants, and the museum village has a café serving cakes. Luckenwalde, the nearest larger town, has more services. A visit to the glassworks, followed by a coffee, makes a pleasant break before the long, flat run east towards the Oderbruch.
t.near nauen@52.6,12.7:
Tall masts rising out of the flat Havelland meadows mark Nauen's claim to fame. The transmitting station here, founded in 1906, is considered the oldest radio station in the world still in operation, and in its early days it sent messages to German colonies and ships across the oceans. Its main building, designed by the architect Hermann Muthesius in the 1920s, is a fine example of brick modernism. Guided tours are offered occasionally.

Nauen itself is a small market town with a church and a pleasant old centre, set in the Havelland, a region of meadows, fields and wetlands west of Berlin. The landscape is flat and open, with big skies and wide views, and in spring and autumn, cranes and geese gather in huge numbers on the fields. To the west, the Havelländisches Luch is one of the last refuges of the great bustard, a heavy bird that struts across the fields, carefully protected by conservationists.

From the saddle it is relaxed. The roads are flat and straight, crossing the meadows and fields, with gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is light, apart from the main roads near the town and the motorway. The roads can be windy, and agricultural traffic is common. Some villages still have cobbled streets, and many roads are lined with old trees.

Nauen has pumps, groceries and restaurants, making it a convenient stop. A local bakery or café is a good place for a break. The Spreewald, with its canals and forests, lies to the south-east, a long ride around the edge of Berlin, so a full tank here is sensible.
t.near kremmen@52.8,13.0:
In 1412, on a causeway through the marshes near Kremmen, the forces of the new Hohenzollern rulers of Brandenburg fought the Dukes of Pomerania in a battle that marked the beginning of the Hohenzollern era, which would eventually lead to Prussia and the German Empire. The causeway, the Kremmer Damm, still crosses the wetland, and a memorial cross marks the site of the battle. Fontane described it in his travels, and the story is part of Brandenburg folklore.

Kremmen is a small town on the edge of the Rhinluch, a vast wetland of meadows, ditches and peat bogs that stretches west towards the Ruppin lakes. The town's most charming feature is its barn quarter, the Scheunenviertel, a street of old timber-framed barns on the edge of town, built outside the walls to protect the town from fire. Many of the barns have been converted into restaurants, cafés and craft shops, making them a lovely place for a break.

The riding here is relaxed and peaceful. The roads are flat, with long straights across the wetlands and gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is light, but the roads can be windy, and agricultural vehicles are common. In spring and autumn, cranes and geese gather in the wetlands, and the sound of their calls fills the air. Watch for cobbles in the villages and for trees close to the road.

Fuel is most reliably found in Oranienburg or Velten, a short ride to the east and south. The Scheunenviertel offers coffee, cake and hearty Brandenburg dishes. The Barnim forests and the Werbellinsee lie to the north-east, with beech woods and clear lakes.
t.near s ubice@52.4,14.5:
Until 1945, Słubice was the Dammvorstadt, the suburb of Frankfurt an der Oder on the east bank of the river. When the border was redrawn along the Oder after the war, the town became Polish, its German population was expelled, and it was resettled by Poles, many of them themselves displaced from lands further east. Today, a bridge links the two towns, and the border is open, with people crossing freely to shop, work and study. The Collegium Polonicum, a joint institution of the European University Viadrina in Frankfurt and a Polish university, stands near the bridge as a symbol of reconciliation.

For many Germans, Słubice is a shopping destination. The bazaar near the border sells cheap cigarettes, clothes and souvenirs, and fuel is usually cheaper on the Polish side, so many riders fill up here. The town also has restaurants serving Polish dishes, such as pierogi, żurek soup and bigos, at prices lower than in Germany.

The Oder itself is a wide, slow river, with meadows and floodplain forests on both banks, and the views from the bridge are lovely, especially in the evening. The riding around Słubice is flat and open, with roads along the river and through the fields and forests. Traffic can be heavy near the border crossing, and the roads in Poland may have different speed limits and rules, including the requirement to ride with dipped headlights at all times.

Słubice has plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants. A stop for a meal and a full tank is a classic part of a ride to the Oder. The Barnim forests and the Werbellinsee lie to the north-west, back across the border in Germany.
t.near storkow@52.2,13.8:
Storkow's castle, rebuilt after years of decay, stands by a canal that links the Storkower See with the waterways towards Berlin and the Scharmützelsee. The town is small and quiet, with a church, a market square and a lock where boats wait to pass. It is a gateway to the Dahme-Heideseen nature park, a region of lakes, forests and heathland south-east of Berlin.

The Storkower See is a long, narrow lake, surrounded by forests and reeds, and it is popular for swimming, sailing and canoeing in summer. The nature park stretches south, with dozens of lakes of all sizes, many of them clear and quiet, and forests of pine and oak. Wolves have returned to the area in recent years, and sea eagles, cranes and beavers are common.

On the bike, things are relaxed. The roads wind through the forests and along the lakes, with gentle curves and occasional hills. Traffic is light, apart from weekends, when Berliners come out to the lakes. Mind the sandy verges, the deer at twilight and the bumpy cobbles that still pave some village centres. The roads around the Scharmützelsee, to the east, are a popular weekend ride, with more curves and views over the water.

Storkow has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, making it a good stop. A coffee by the canal, watching the boats pass through the lock, is a pleasant break. The Fläming, with its forests and villages, lies to the south-west, and the inline skating trails there are famous across Germany.
t.near dahme@51.9,13.3:
Dahme/Mark sits at the eastern end of the Fläming, where the low hills meet the lowlands of Lusatia, and its castle ruins and old town walls hint at a more important past. The town is small and quiet, with a church, a market square and a park around the ruins of the castle, which burned in the early twentieth century. The surrounding landscape is a mix of forests, fields and small villages, with gentle hills that offer views over the plain.

The Fläming is known across Germany for the Fläming-Skate, a network of smooth asphalt paths for inline skaters and cyclists, over two hundred kilometres long, winding through the forests and villages. The paths are closed to motor vehicles, but you will see skaters and cyclists on the roads nearby, especially on weekends. The villages of the Fläming have fieldstone churches, built by the Flemish settlers who came here in the twelfth century, and the landscape is peaceful and green.

The roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, with long straights through the forests and gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is light, but watch for skaters and cyclists, sand on the road, and wildlife at dawn and dusk. Some villages still have cobbled streets, and many roads are lined with old trees.

Dahme has fuel, shops and a few restaurants, and Luckau, to the east, is a lovely old town with a fine market square. Golßen, to the north, is famous for its pickled gherkins, a speciality of the Spreewald region. The Spreewald itself, with its canals and forests, lies to the east.
t.near bruck@52.2,12.8:
The wet meadows west of Brück are one of the last places in Germany where the great bustard still lives. These heavy, turkey-sized birds, among the heaviest flying birds in the world, strut across the fields of the Belziger Landschaftswiesen, and conservationists have worked for decades to protect them, with observation towers where visitors can watch them display in spring. Even if you do not see one, the meadows, with their big skies and wide horizons, are worth a pause.

Brück is a small town on the edge of the meadows, with a church and a few shops. The surrounding landscape is a mix of wet grassland, fields and forests, crossed by the little Plane river. To the south-west lies Bad Belzig, with its castle, Burg Eisenhardt, and its thermal spa, and beyond it the hills of the Hoher Fläming, the highest part of the Fläming ridge, with forests, valleys and villages.

As for the riding, it is relaxed and peaceful. The roads are flat or gently rolling, with long straights across the meadows and gentle curves through the villages and forests. Traffic is light, but the roads can be windy, and agricultural vehicles are common. Watch for wildlife, sand on the road and cobbles in the villages. In spring and autumn, cranes and geese gather in the meadows, and their calls fill the air.

For fuel and a sit-down meal, head for Bad Belzig or Beelitz, because Brück itself offers very little. Beelitz, to the east, is famous for its asparagus, harvested in spring and sold at roadside stalls. The Fläming forests lie to the south, with quiet roads and skating trails.
t.near gramzow@53.2,14.0:
A ruined gable of red brick is all that remains of the church of the Premonstratensian monastery at Gramzow, founded in the twelfth century and one of the oldest in the Uckermark.
