It stands alone on a rise, framed by trees and sky, a striking reminder of the medieval colonisation of this land. The village around it is small and quiet, and it also houses a museum devoted to the small private railways that once crisscrossed the region.

The Uckermark is one of the most sparsely populated regions of Germany, a land of rolling hills, lakes, fields and forests in the north-east of Brandenburg, near the Polish border. The landscape was shaped by the glaciers of the last Ice Age, which left moraines, kettle lakes and boulders scattered across the fields. The villages have fieldstone churches, cobbled streets and old manor houses, some restored, others crumbling.

The roads roll over the hills and wind around the lakes, with gentle curves and long views. Traffic is very light, and the landscape is open and varied. Watch for agricultural vehicles, cobbles in the villages and trees close to the road. Wildlife is abundant, with deer, wild boar and cranes common, and sea eagles soaring over the lakes.

Do not expect a pump in Gramzow. Prenzlau, Angermünde or Schwedt covers fuel and food. Prenzlau has a huge brick Gothic church, and Angermünde has a lovely old town. The Fläming, with its forests and skating trails, lies far to the south, on the other side of Berlin.
t.near potsdam@52.4,13.1:
Frederick the Great wanted a place without cares, sans souci, and he built one in Potsdam: a summer palace on a terraced vineyard, surrounded by a vast park of gardens, temples, follies and more palaces. Sanssouci is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with the other palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin, and it draws visitors from all over the world. Frederick himself is buried on the terrace, and visitors still leave potatoes on his grave, a tribute to his promotion of the crop.

Potsdam has more history packed into it than almost any German city. In the summer of 1945, the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met at the Cecilienhof Palace to decide the future of Germany. During the Cold War, the Glienicke Bridge, between Potsdam and West Berlin, became known as the Bridge of Spies, where captured agents were exchanged. The city is surrounded by lakes and forests, and the Havel winds through it, forming a chain of blue.

The riding in Potsdam itself can be challenging, with heavy traffic, cobbled streets, tram lines and cyclists. But the roads around the city, along the lakes and through the forests, are pleasant and scenic. The roads towards Werder and the Havelland are popular with riders, with gentle curves and views over the water.

Potsdam has plenty of fuel stations, shops, cafés and restaurants. A coffee in the Dutch Quarter, a neighbourhood of red brick houses built for Dutch craftsmen in the eighteenth century, is a pleasant break. The Uckermark lakes lie to the north, a long ride around Berlin.
t.werder@52.4,12.9:
Every spring, when the fruit trees blossom, Werder throws one of the biggest parties in Brandenburg. The Baumblütenfest, the tree blossom festival, draws huge crowds to taste the local fruit wines, and the town on its island in the Havel becomes a sea of people, music and stalls. For the rest of the year, Werder is a pretty, quiet town, with an old centre on the island, a church, a windmill and views over the water.

The area around Werder has been a fruit-growing region for centuries, supplying Berlin with apples, cherries, pears and plums. The orchards cover the hills around the town, and in spring, the blossom is a wonderful sight. The town also has one of the northernmost vineyards in Germany, on the Wachtelberg, and its wines have a small but loyal following. From the hills above the town, the view stretches over the Havel and its lakes, with Potsdam and the towers of Berlin on the horizon.

From the saddle it is relaxed and pleasant. The roads wind through the orchards and along the lakes, with gentle curves and occasional hills. Traffic can be heavy in the town and during the festival, and the old centre has cobbled streets. The roads towards the Havelland and the Zauche, to the west and south, are quieter and offer more open riding.

Werder has fuel stations, shops, cafés and restaurants, and many places serve local fruit wines and juices. A coffee on the island, followed by a walk to the windmill, makes a lovely break. The Uckermark lakes lie far to the north, on the other side of Berlin.
t.near wandlitz@52.8,13.4:
During the years of East Germany, the name Wandlitz meant something sinister to many citizens. In a guarded estate in the forest near the lake lived the members of the ruling Politburo, Erich Honecker among them, cut off from the population behind walls and guard posts, with access to Western goods that ordinary people could only dream of. When the estate was opened after the fall of the Wall in 1989, people were surprised by its modest, almost petty privileges. Today, the houses are part of a clinic, and the forest has reclaimed its quiet.

Wandlitz itself is a pleasant lakeside community north of Berlin, set in the Barnim nature park, with the Wandlitzsee and other lakes surrounded by forests. The lakes are clear and popular for swimming in summer, with beaches, boat hire and cafés. The landscape is part of the Barnim plateau, shaped by the glaciers of the last Ice Age, with gentle hills, forests of pine and beech, and many lakes.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant. The roads wind through the forests and along the lakes, with gentle curves and occasional hills. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, when Berliners come out to the lakes, and the roads near the motorway can be busy. Keep an eye out for sand on bends, animals at the edges of the day and stretches of old cobblestone.

Wandlitz has fuel stations, shops, cafés and restaurants, making it a convenient stop. A swim in the lake or a coffee by the water makes a pleasant break on a hot day. The Uckermark lies to the north, a land of rolling hills, lakes and empty roads.
t.near storkow@52.2,13.9:
East of Storkow, a string of shallow lakes and reed beds known as the Groß Schauener Seen forms one of the most important bird sanctuaries in the region. Ospreys, sea eagles, cranes, bitterns and many ducks breed or rest here, and an observation tower gives a view over the water and the reeds. The lakes have been fished for centuries, and a traditional fishery on their shore still sells smoked fish, a delicious lunch for anyone passing through.

The landscape around here is classic eastern Brandenburg: pine forests, small fields, quiet villages and lakes of all sizes. The soils are sandy, left by the glaciers and their meltwaters, and in places there are dunes, now covered in pine. The Dahme-Heideseen nature park stretches to the south and west, with dozens of lakes and few people. To the east, the Scharmützelsee and the Rauen hills offer a more lively scene, with spa towns, beaches and restaurants.

The riding here is quiet and relaxed. The roads are mostly flat, running dead straight through pine forest and only bending where a lake gets in the way. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays. Watch for sand on the road at forest edges, for wildlife, and for cobbles in the villages. On summer weekends, the roads near the Scharmützelsee can be busy with motorcycles and cars.

Fuel is available in Storkow, and the fishery and the villages offer simple meals. Smoked eel, trout or whitefish with bread and a salad is the local speciality. The Uckermark lies far to the north, on the other side of Berlin.
t.near sandau@52.8,12.0:
Sandau is one of the smallest towns in Germany, a cluster of houses and a big Romanesque brick church on the east bank of the Elbe in Saxony-Anhalt, opposite the meadows that stretch towards Havelberg. A cable ferry crosses the river here, a slow and peaceful way to reach the other bank, and the experience of standing on the deck with your bike, watching the broad, brown river slide past, is a fine reason to come.

The Elbe here is one of the most natural large rivers in central Europe, with wide floodplains, meadows, oxbow lakes and riverside forests, protected as part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve. White storks nest on the roofs of the villages, and in spring and autumn, huge flocks of geese and cranes gather on the meadows. The river floods regularly, and the dykes that protect the villages are a reminder of its power; in 2013, a dyke broke nearby, flooding a wide area.

The riding here is flat and open, with roads along the dykes and through the meadows and villages. Traffic is very light, and the views over the river and the floodplain are wide and beautiful. The roads can be windy, and agricultural vehicles are common. Some roads are narrow, and the villages may have cobbled streets. Check the ferry schedule before planning a crossing, as it can be suspended during high water.

Services in Sandau are thin, so plan the tank and lunch around Havelberg, a short ride north, which has a magnificent cathedral on a hill above the town. A meal in Havelberg, with a view over the river, is a fine reward. The Dahme lakes lie far to the east, across the whole of Brandenburg.
t.near lieberose@52.0,14.4:
South of Lieberose, a wide expanse of open sand and heath stretches away under the sky, so bare in places that it has been nicknamed the Lieberose desert. For decades, this was a Soviet military training area, where tanks churned the ground and fires burned the forest. After the troops left in the 1990s, the land was left to nature, and it has become a refuge for wildlife, including wolves, which returned to Germany around the turn of the millennium and have established packs in the region.

The area has a darker history too. At Jamlitz, near Lieberose, a satellite camp of the Sachsenhausen concentration camp held thousands of Jewish prisoners in the last years of the war, many of whom were murdered or died in the camp. After the war, the Soviets used the site as a special camp for prisoners. A memorial and a small exhibition remember the victims.

Lieberose itself is a small town with a castle and a ruined church, set in a landscape of forests, heaths and lakes on the edge of the Spreewald. The riding here is relaxed and quiet, with long straight roads through the forests and gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is very light, and the landscape is wild and empty. Sand drifts onto the asphalt where forest meets field, deer and boar keep their own timetable, and village cobbles get greasy in the wet. Some areas of the former training ground remain closed due to unexploded munitions, so stick to the marked roads.

Lieberose has next to nothing for travellers; fuel, groceries and restaurants wait in Lübben, Beeskow or Cottbus. Lübben, at the edge of the Spreewald, is a good place for lunch, with its canals and boats. The Dahme lakes lie to the west, with forests and quiet roads.
t.near werder@52.4,13.0:
Albert Einstein spent his summers in Caputh, on the shore of the Templiner See between Werder and Potsdam, in a wooden house he had built in 1929. He loved sailing on the lakes and called the house his paradise. When the Nazis came to power in 1933, he left Germany and never returned. The house, a modern timber building on a hill above the village, can be visited, and it is a fascinating glimpse into the private life of a genius.

The landscape between Werder and Potsdam is a chain of lakes and forests, with the Havel widening into the Schwielowsee and the Templiner See. The villages along the shores, Caputh, Ferch and Petzow, are pretty and quiet, with old houses, churches and boat moorings. At Petzow, a castle designed in the style of Schinkel stands in a park laid out by Peter Joseph Lenné, the great Prussian landscape gardener, and Ferch has a small museum of the Havelland painters who worked here.

On the bike, things are a pleasure. The roads wind along the lakes and through the forests, with gentle curves and views over the water. A small ferry crosses the narrows at Caputh, a charming shortcut. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the roads in the villages can be narrow and cobbled. Watch for cyclists, who are numerous on the lakeside paths and roads.

There are cafés and restaurants in the villages, often with lakeside terraces, and fuel is available in Werder and Potsdam. A fish lunch by the Schwielowsee, followed by a visit to the Einstein house, makes a memorable break. The road to Lehnin Abbey continues south-west through the forests of the Zauche.
t.near sperenberg@52.1,13.3:
The Soviets called it the Forbidden City. At Wünsdorf, east of Sperenberg, the high command of the Soviet forces in Germany had its headquarters until 1994, a vast garrison town hidden in the forest, home to tens of thousands of soldiers and their families, with schools, shops and theatres, closed to ordinary Germans. Before that, the German army had its own headquarters here, with huge bunkers built in the 1930s. Guided tours of the bunkers and the old garrison offer a fascinating glimpse into the military history of the twentieth century.

Today, Wünsdorf is slowly being reinvented, with new homes, a book town of second-hand bookshops and a museum. The surrounding landscape is a mix of pine forests, lakes and villages, with the Mellensee and the Großer Wünsdorfer See popular for swimming and boating in summer. The forests are quiet and empty, home to deer, wild boar and birds.

The roads are flat or gently rolling, long forest straights broken by the odd bend at a lakeshore. Traffic is light, apart from the B96, which runs north and south through the area and can be busy with commuters. Blown sand, crossing game and the odd cobbled village street are the only real hazards. Some former military areas are still closed or contain unexploded munitions, so stay on the marked roads.

Fuel and food are available in Zossen and Wünsdorf, and a café in the book town makes a pleasant break. The ride towards Lehnin Abbey continues west through the forests, past more lakes and villages.
t.near litvinov@50.6,13.6:
Litvínov lies at the foot of the Ore Mountains, the Krušné hory, in north-western Bohemia, and it is a town of contrasts. Below it stretches the Most basin, scarred by decades of open-cast brown coal mining and dominated by the chimneys of a large chemical works. Above it, the mountains rise steeply in a wall of forest, and a few kilometres up you are in a different world of beech and spruce woods, high meadows and small villages near the German border.

The history here is complicated. The coal basin was heavily industrialised in the twentieth century, and many villages were destroyed to make way for mines, including the old town of Most, which was demolished in the 1960s and 70s. Its Gothic church was famously moved several hundred metres on rails to save it. The Ore Mountains themselves suffered badly from acid rain in the late twentieth century, but the forests have been recovering, and the region's mining heritage is now recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site shared with Germany.

The riding is the main reason to come. The roads climbing from Litvínov into the mountains are steep and winding, with hairpins and sharp bends, and they lead up to the ridge, where you can ride along the plateau with views over the basin below. Surfaces vary, and in winter the mountains can be snowy and icy. Watch for logging trucks and cyclists.

Litvínov has fuel and food. For a photo, the views from the mountain roads over the basin are dramatic, especially in the evening light, when the industrial landscape takes on a strange beauty.
t.near cesky brod@50.0,14.9:
Český Brod means Czech Ford, and the name tells you why the town exists: a crossing on the old trade road running east from Prague towards Kolín and the Elbe lowlands. Merchants, armies and pilgrims all came this way, and the town grew fat enough on the traffic to build walls. A stretch of fortification and a stout gate tower survive, and the long square, with its church and arcaded houses, is a calm place to sit for ten minutes at the end of a ride.

The bigger story lies a few kilometres east, on a low rise above the fields. At Lipany in 1434 the radical Hussite field armies, the Taborites and Orphans who had beaten crusade after crusade for fifteen years, were finally crushed by an alliance of moderate Hussites and Catholic lords. A memorial mound marks the battlefield. There is not much to see beyond the monument and the wide horizon, but standing there with the wind in the wheat you get a sense of how open and exposed this country is, and why cavalry and wagon forts mattered so much.

The landscape is gentle: big arable fields, orchards along the lanes, copses of oak and pine, and a scattering of fishponds. Some of the ponds and small reservoirs in the area are used for swimming in summer, especially around Klučov and the woods towards Kounice. Water quality varies with the season and a hot August can turn ponds green, so look at what locals are doing before you jump in.

As a finishing stretch the riding is easy-going. The roads roll over shallow hills with long sightlines, and the minor routes between villages are quiet if patchy in places. The main road back towards Prague can be busy at commuting times. Fuel, a supermarket and a few pubs serving svíčková and cold Bohemian lager are in town, which is about all a tired rider could ask for.
t.near bilina@50.5,13.8:
Bílina sits in the valley of the Bílina river in north-west Bohemia, between the industrial basin around Most and Teplice and the volcanic cones of the České středohoří, the Bohemian Central Uplands. Look up from almost anywhere in town and you will see the Bořeň, a massive dome of phonolite rock rising abruptly from the woods. Climbers love its crags, and walkers make the climb for the views across the basin and the uplands.

The town has been known for its mineral water for centuries. Bílinská kyselka, a naturally sparkling water from local springs, has been bottled here since the eighteenth century and is still sold across the country, along with Zaječická hořká, a famously bitter mineral water with a reputation as a remedy for digestion. The spa park and pump room are a short stroll from the centre. The chateau of the Lobkowicz family stands above the old town.

For riding, the location is excellent. To the east and north, the České středohoří offers some of the most interesting roads in Bohemia, winding between steep volcanic hills, through orchards and vineyards, and down into the Elbe valley. To the west, the Ore Mountains rise along the German border. The basin itself is less attractive, with open-cast mines and power stations, but even that has a strange, raw grandeur.

As a food stop, Bílina is modest but adequate. There are pubs and restaurants in the centre serving solid Czech food: goulash, roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, fried cheese. Fuel is available in town. Bring an appetite, then head for the hills.
t.tunisia matmata and tataouine route poin:
Chenini sits on a ridge like something the hill has grown. Flat-roofed houses and cave dwellings climb the slope in steps, the colours are the same pale ochre as the rock, and above the village a white-domed mosque stands on the crest, easy to spot from the road below.

This is one of the best-known Berber villages of the Dahar, and a place where the old way of life is still partly visible. Many of the houses are cut into the rock itself, with rooms opening off narrow lanes, and the older part of the village includes granaries and an underground mosque. The people here have a reputation for adapting to hard terrain, and their language, Tamazight, has survived in small communities of the south for centuries. Some families still live in the village; others have moved to newer houses down the hill, leaving the old quarter to visitors and a few stubborn residents.

A short distance away is Douiret, another hill village, with its own hill-top ksar and a handful of restored guesthouses in former cave dwellings. Both are on the ridge that gave the district its name, and the walk between them offers views across a landscape of dry valleys and distant escarpments.

The ride is a pleasure, if a quiet one. The road winds through low hills, with the road surface generally good and the bends tight enough to keep you concentrating but rarely difficult. Heat is the main enemy in summer, and wind can fill the air with dust, so a clear visor and a bottle of water are useful companions. Goats cross at their own convenience, and locals are happy to wave you on or warn you of what lies ahead.

The village has a few small cafés and shops that cater to visitors, but Tataouine, a lively town of more than sixty thousand, offers the main supplies, fuel and accommodation. Come for the light in the early morning or late afternoon, when the stone glows and the shadows are long.
t.near baruth@52.1,13.5:
Glassblowers once worked in the forest just outside Baruth. In the eighteenth century, the counts of Solms-Baruth founded a glassworks here, using the local sand and the wood of the surrounding forests, and a village grew up around it. Glashütte, as it is still called, is now a museum village, with workshops where you can watch glass being blown, old workers' houses, a café and craft shops, a charming stop deep among pine trees.

Baruth itself is a small town with a castle and a park, set in a broad valley that runs east to west across southern Brandenburg. This is the Baruther Urstromtal, an ancient glacial valley carved by meltwater from the ice sheets, and it is lined to the south by the gentle hills of the Fläming. From the higher ground, the views stretch over the forests and fields, a rare vantage point in this flat land. The forests are mostly pine, with heaths and dunes in places, and they are sheltering deer, wild pigs and wolves, which have returned to Brandenburg in recent decades.

The roads are flat or gently rolling, ruler-straight through the trees, kinking only at village corners. Traffic is light, apart from the B96, which runs north and south through the town. Blown sand, crossing game and the odd cobbled village street are the only real hazards. On hot summer days, the smell of pine resin fills the air.

Baruth has fuel, a few shops and restaurants, and the museum village has a café serving cakes. Luckenwalde, the nearest larger town, has more services. A visit to the glassworks, followed by a coffee, makes a pleasant break before the long, flat run east towards the Oderbruch.
t.near kremmen@52.8,13.1:
In 1412, on a causeway through the marshes near Kremmen, the forces of the new Hohenzollern rulers of Brandenburg fought the Dukes of Pomerania in a battle that marked the beginning of the Hohenzollern era, which would eventually lead to Prussia and the German Empire. The causeway, the Kremmer Damm, still crosses the wetland, and a memorial cross marks the site of the battle. Fontane described it in his travels, and the story is part of Brandenburg folklore.

Kremmen is a small town on the edge of the Rhinluch, a vast wetland of meadows, ditches and peat bogs that stretches west towards the Ruppin lakes. The town's most charming feature is its barn quarter, the Scheunenviertel, a street of old timber-framed barns on the edge of town, built outside the walls to protect the town from fire. Many of the barns have been converted into restaurants, cafés and craft shops, making them a lovely place for a break.

The riding here is relaxed and peaceful. The roads are flat, with long straights across the wetlands and gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is light, but the roads can be windy, and agricultural vehicles are common. In spring and autumn, cranes and geese gather in the wetlands, and the sound of their calls fills the air. Watch for cobbles in the villages and for trees close to the road.

Fuel is most reliably found in Oranienburg or Velten, a short ride to the east and south. The Scheunenviertel offers coffee, cake and hearty Brandenburg dishes. The Barnim forests and the Werbellinsee lie to the north-east, with beech woods and clear lakes.
t.near dahme@52.0,13.5:
Dahme/Mark sits at the eastern end of the Fläming, where the low hills meet the lowlands of Lusatia, and its castle ruins and old town walls hint at a more important past. The town is small and quiet, with a church, a market square and a park around the ruins of the castle, which burned in the early twentieth century. The surrounding landscape is a mix of forests, fields and small villages, with gentle hills that offer views over the plain.

The Fläming is known across Germany for the Fläming-Skate, a network of smooth asphalt paths for inline skaters and cyclists, over two hundred kilometres long, winding through the forests and villages. The paths are closed to motor vehicles, but you will see skaters and cyclists on the roads nearby, especially on weekends. The villages of the Fläming have fieldstone churches, built by the Flemish settlers who came here in the twelfth century, and the landscape is peaceful and green.

The roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, with long straights through the forests and gentle curves through the villages. Traffic is light, but watch for skaters and cyclists, sand on the road, and wildlife at dawn and dusk. Some villages still have cobbled streets, and many roads are lined with old trees.

Dahme has fuel, shops and a few restaurants, and Luckau, to the east, is a lovely old town with a fine market square. Golßen, to the north, is famous for its pickled gherkins, a speciality of the Spreewald region. The Spreewald itself, with its canals and forests, lies to the east.
t.near cesky brod@50.1,14.9:
Český Brod means Czech Ford, and the name tells you why the town exists: a crossing on the old trade road running east from Prague towards Kolín and the Elbe lowlands. Merchants, armies and pilgrims all came this way, and the town grew fat enough on the traffic to build walls. A stretch of fortification and a stout gate tower survive, and the long square, with its church and arcaded houses, is a calm place to sit for ten minutes at the end of a ride.

The bigger story lies a few kilometres east, on a low rise above the fields. At Lipany in 1434 the radical Hussite field armies, the Taborites and Orphans who had beaten crusade after crusade for fifteen years, were finally crushed by an alliance of moderate Hussites and Catholic lords. A memorial mound marks the battlefield. There is not much to see beyond the monument and the wide horizon, but standing there with the wind in the wheat you get a sense of how open and exposed this country is, and why cavalry and wagon forts mattered so much.

The landscape is gentle: big arable fields, orchards along the lanes, copses of oak and pine, and a scattering of fishponds. Some of the ponds and small reservoirs in the area are used for swimming in summer, especially around Klučov and the woods towards Kounice. Water quality varies with the season and a hot August can turn ponds green, so look at what locals are doing before you jump in.

As a finishing stretch the riding is easy-going. The roads roll over shallow hills with long sightlines, and the minor routes between villages are quiet if patchy in places. The main road back towards Prague can be busy at commuting times. Fuel, a supermarket and a few pubs serving svíčková and cold Bohemian lager are in town, which is about all a tired rider could ask for.
t.near buch@52.7,13.5:
Buch, on the far northern edge of Berlin, is a district shaped by medicine. In the early twentieth century, the city architect Ludwig Hoffmann built a series of large hospital complexes here, in a park-like setting outside the crowded city, and Buch has been a centre of hospitals and medical research ever since. Today it is home to the Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine and a cluster of biotech companies, as well as a large hospital campus, and the old Hoffmann buildings, with their red-brick and stone façades, are still impressive.

Around the institutes, Buch has a surprisingly rural feel, with forests, fields and lakes stretching north into Brandenburg. The Bucher Forst is a large wooded area crossed by walking and cycling paths, and the Karower Teiche, a series of ponds, are a nature reserve, home to many birds. The Panke, a small river, flows south from here through the city to the Spree. In the old village centre, a Baroque church stands next to the park of a castle that was demolished in the 1960s.

As a finish point for rides back from Lusatia, with its lakes formed from old open-cast mines and its strange, scarred landscapes, Buch offers a quiet end to the day. The ride back into Berlin from the south and east involves crossing the city or using the motorway ring, and weekday evenings are the slowest time to try it. Once in the northern suburbs, the roads become quieter, lined with trees and houses.

There are fuel stations and supermarkets in Buch and the neighbouring districts, and a few restaurants and cafés. The Barnim plateau to the north, with its forests and lakes, is a pleasant area for short rides, with quiet roads and cobbled villages. Berlin's weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters, and the north-east of the city often feels a little breezier and cooler than the centre.
t.near werder@52.4,12.9:
Albert Einstein spent his summers in Caputh, on the shore of the Templiner See between Werder and Potsdam, in a wooden house he had built in 1929. He loved sailing on the lakes and called the house his paradise. When the Nazis came to power in 1933, he left Germany and never returned. The house, a modern timber building on a hill above the village, can be visited, and it is a fascinating glimpse into the private life of a genius.

The landscape between Werder and Potsdam is a chain of lakes and forests, with the Havel widening into the Schwielowsee and the Templiner See. The villages along the shores, Caputh, Ferch and Petzow, are pretty and quiet, with old houses, churches and boat moorings. At Petzow, a castle designed in the style of Schinkel stands in a park laid out by Peter Joseph Lenné, the great Prussian landscape gardener, and Ferch has a small museum of the Havelland painters who worked here.

On the bike, things are a pleasure. The roads wind along the lakes and through the forests, with gentle curves and views over the water. A small ferry crosses the narrows at Caputh, a charming shortcut. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the roads in the villages can be narrow and cobbled. Watch for cyclists, who are numerous on the lakeside paths and roads.

There are cafés and restaurants in the villages, often with lakeside terraces, and fuel is available in Werder and Potsdam. A fish lunch by the Schwielowsee, followed by a visit to the Einstein house, makes a memorable break. The road to Lehnin Abbey continues south-west through the forests of the Zauche.
t.quedlinburg@51.8,11.2:
Quedlinburg is one of the best preserved medieval towns in Germany, with roughly thirteen hundred half-timbered houses, a number that is hard to believe until you have walked its streets. The whole old town, with the castle hill and the abbey church, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1994. The houses date from the fourteenth to the nineteenth centuries, and many have been restored with care.

The history is older than the houses. In the tenth century, Quedlinburg was a favourite residence of the early German kings of the Ottonian dynasty, and Henry I, who founded the dynasty, is said to be buried in the crypt of the collegiate church of St Servatius, on the hill above the town. For centuries an abbey for noble women stood here, with powerful abbesses who sometimes ruled as princesses. The Romanesque church, with its massive twin towers, is a fine example of the style, and the church treasury holds a few precious relics.

The old town is a delight to walk, with cobbled lanes, a handsome market square with the town hall and a statue of Roland, and a number of small museums. Among them is a museum devoted to Lyonel Feininger, an American-German painter and Bauhaus teacher who loved the town. Quedlinburg was also known for seed growing, and a huge acreage of flowers and vegetables once surrounded the town. The poet Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock was born here in 1724.

For riders, Quedlinburg is the end of a day in the Harz, reached by quiet roads along the northern edge of the hills, through farmland and small villages. The roads are gentle, with a surface that is mostly good and traffic that is light, apart from the tourist season. Fuel is on the edge of town, and it is best to leave the bike in one of the car parks outside the historic core. In the evening, the old streets are lit by lamps, and the sound of church bells carries across the roofs. Weddersleben, four and a half kilometres away, is a village with little for a visitor.
t.near widuchowa on the way back@53.2,14.4:
This is the Lower Oder Valley National Park, the only floodplain national park in Germany, and one of the wildest corners of the country. In spring the river floods the meadows, turning them into a shallow, glittering lake, and the dykes become islands. Birds arrive in huge numbers: cranes, geese, white-tailed eagles, black storks and corncrakes, whose rasping call is heard on summer nights, and beavers have returned to the channels.

The old town of Gartz, on the western bank, has a medieval gate and a church with a tall tower, and a quiet, unspoilt air. A few kilometres south, Schwedt, a larger town of about thirty-eight thousand people, has a more industrial story. It grew in the 1960s around an oil refinery at the end of the Druzhba pipeline, which supplied much of eastern Germany with fuel, and its wide boulevards and tall blocks are a legacy of that period. Before that, Schwedt was a centre of tobacco growing, thanks to Huguenot refugees who planted tobacco in the Uckermark in the seventeenth century, and some old drying barns still stand in the villages.

The riding here is gentle and spacious. The roads run along the dykes and through the polders, with long, open views of the river and Poland beyond, and the atmosphere is calm. The surface varies from smooth asphalt to old, bumpy brick and patchy repairs, and in places the road narrows and becomes a single track. Wind from the east can be strong, and mist often hangs over the meadows in the morning and evening. The border with Poland is open, and a bridge or ferry crossing is easy, with a different landscape on the other side, though you should carry your papers.

Schwedt has fuel, supermarkets, cafes and everything else a rider might need, and it is the best place to fill the tank, because the villages along the river are small and have few services. Gartz has a bakery and a couple of simple places to eat. Try a plate of smoked fish or a serving of local potato dishes, and give yourself time for a stop at one of the dyke-top viewpoints in the evening, when the cranes come in to roost.
t.near tauche on the way back@52.1,14.1:
The Spree flows through here on its way from the Spreewald to Berlin, and its slow brown water, edged with reeds and willows, shapes everything. Along its banks stand the usual boathouses, jetties and campsites that tell you the river is used for paddling and fishing.

Beeskow has a medieval castle, one of the oldest in the region, and a surviving ring of town walls. The castle houses a cultural centre and, unexpectedly, a large archive of art from East Germany, with thousands of paintings and sculptures made under the socialist state, many of which were once displayed in factories and public buildings. For anyone interested in how art was produced under a dictatorship, it is a fascinating place. The old town has a quiet, slightly faded charm, with a market square and a handful of cafes.

The land around is a mix of pine forest, meadow and farmland, with a scattering of small lakes. Roads are flat to gently rolling, mostly good, and lined with trees in many places. Corners are mild, and traffic is light, with the main hazards being tractors and the occasional deer. Spring brings the smell of blossom and cut grass, and in autumn mist lies over the river valley in the morning.

This is a sensible start and finish point because the area is easy to reach from Berlin by the A12 motorway, and the quiet roads begin almost at once. Fuel and supermarkets are available in Beeskow, and the smaller villages have little. A swim in the river or one of the small lakes is possible, but look for signed bathing places, as banks can be steep and muddy. Late afternoon in summer, with warm light on the water and the smell of hay, is a lovely time to arrive.
t.near zandov on the way back@50.7,14.4:
The country is one of volcanic hills, sandstone rocks and mixed woods, the western edge of the Lusatian region. Cone-shaped basalt peaks rise from the farmland, and the lower slopes are patched with orchards and small fields. It is lovely and little visited, and you will often have the roads to yourself.

Česká Lípa, with nearly forty thousand people, has plenty of fuel and food, and a neat old centre with a Gothic Augustinian monastery and a handsome square. The town sits at the edge of the Kokořín and Lusatian landscapes, and it is a natural base for a few days of exploring. The nearby Máchovo lake, near Doksy, is a famous spot for swimming and boating, and the sandstone rocks and forests around it have a romantic, mysterious character.

For a rider, the roads here are enjoyable and varied. They wind through the foothills of the Central Uplands, climbing to small passes and descending to quiet villages, with views of volcanic cones and distant ridges. The surface can be patchy, and bends are often tight and blind, with farm traffic and cyclists. In summer the hills are green and the air is warm, and in autumn the beeches and oaks are a blaze of colour. Fog fills the valleys on cold mornings and burns off by midday.

The area was long home to a mixed Czech and German population, and the old half-timbered houses, known as Umgebinde, are a distinctive feature of the region. Many have been restored, and a few small museums tell the story of the weavers and glassmakers who once lived here. Fuel is easy to find in Česká Lípa, but the smaller villages have little, so fill up beforehand. A bowl of garlic soup and a dark beer in a village pub is a good way to end a day.
t.near spreenhagen@52.3,13.8:
Spreenhagen is a scattered rural municipality south-east of Berlin, where the River Spree winds through forests and meadows between Fürstenwalde and the capital. The villages here are small and quiet, with old churches, farmhouses and modern homes for commuters, and the landscape is a typical Brandenburg mix of pine forests, wet meadows and lakes.

The Spree is the river of Berlin, flowing through the heart of the city, but here it is a quieter stream, meandering through a broad valley with alder woods and reeds. The forests around Spreenhagen are part of a large wooded area that stretches south towards the Dahme lakes and east towards the Scharmützelsee, and they are where deer, boar and many birds. In summer, the lakes are popular for swimming and boating, and the air smells of pine and warm sand.

The roads are mostly flat, running dead straight through pine forest and only bending where a lake or a village gets in the way. Traffic is light, apart from the main roads near the motorway, which can be busy with commuters and trucks. The A12 motorway to Frankfurt an der Oder and Poland runs nearby, providing a fast route east or back to Berlin. Watch for wildlife, especially at dawn and dusk, and for sand on the road at forest edges.

Fuel and supplies are most reliably found in Fürstenwalde, the nearest larger town, a few minutes away. Fürstenwalde has a cathedral and a pleasant centre on the Spree. Spreenhagen itself works well for a rest in the forest before heading south towards the Lusatian lakes, where former opencast mines have been flooded to create a new landscape.
t.near neuruppin@53.0,12.7:
Two of the most important figures in Prussian culture were born in Neuruppin: the architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel in 1781 and the novelist Theodor Fontane in 1819. Fontane went on to write the Wanderungen durch die Mark Brandenburg, a multi-volume account of his travels through the region, and the first volume opens with the county of Ruppin. Reading even a few pages before riding these roads gives them a depth they might otherwise lack.

The town was almost completely destroyed by fire in 1787 and rebuilt to a strict, classical plan, with straight streets, wide squares and uniform houses. The result is unusually elegant for a small Brandenburg town. Neuruppin lies on the shore of the Ruppiner See, a long, narrow lake formed by glacial meltwater, and the lakeside promenade invites a slow amble. In the nineteenth century, the town was famous for the Neuruppiner Bilderbogen, cheap, colourful prints depicting news, stories and morals, which were sold all over Germany.

North of the town lies the Ruppiner Schweiz, a small area of wooded hills and deep valleys with lakes, streams and old mills. The name, like many Swiss references in German landscapes, is a romantic exaggeration; there are no mountains here. But it is a beautiful area, with quiet roads through beech forests, along lakes and past small villages. The roads are narrow and winding, sometimes with cobbled sections, and the forests are cool and shady on hot days.

Neuruppin is a good place for lunch. There are restaurants and cafés in the old town and along the lakeshore, serving local fish and Brandenburg specialities. Fuel and other services are easy to find. The Ruppin area is popular with day-trippers from Berlin, especially on summer weekends, but on weekdays it is quiet and peaceful. In spring the forests are bright green, and in autumn the beeches turn gold and copper, making it one of the most beautiful times to visit.
t.near oranienburg@52.8,13.3:
Oranienburg is a town on the Havel river, a short way north of Berlin, and it carries two very different histories side by side. On one side there is the palace, built in the seventeenth century for Louise Henriette of Orange, the Dutch-born wife of the Elector of Brandenburg, who gave the town its name. It was the first baroque palace in Brandenburg, and its Dutch influence is seen in the proportions and brick. The town became known as Oranienburg, the castle of Orange, and the palace now houses a museum and gardens.

On the other side is a darker chapter. In 1936 the Nazi regime opened the Sachsenhausen concentration camp at the town's edge, and tens of thousands of prisoners died there. The site is now a memorial and museum, and a visit is sober, serious and well worth the time. Many people combine it with a trip from Berlin, and the surrounding town carries the memory in quiet ways. Allow a few hours and treat the visit with the gravity it deserves.

As a starting point for a ride into the Ruppiner Land, this is a handy exit from the capital. North of the town, the roads fall into a rhythm of straight, tree-lined avenues, a typical feature of Brandenburg, with old chestnuts, limes and cherries standing at the roadside. Sandy soil, pine plantations and glittering lakes fill the landscape, and the pace is calm. Surfaces are generally good, though some are patched, and avenues can be dappled with light that hides potholes. Traffic is light on weekdays and busy on summer weekends as Berliners head for the water. Spring and early autumn are pleasantly mild.

The ride continues to Neuruppin, the home town of the writer Theodor Fontane, and on to Rheinsberg, where Frederick the Great spent happy years as crown prince in a small lakeside palace. Oranienburg has fuel stations, a supermarket and cafes, and the suburban train line to Berlin makes it easy to leave a car. Leegebruch, a smaller town nearby, has basic services. Top up here before heading out, as pumps thin out in the forest.

t.near lichterfelde@52.4,13.3:
In 1881, Werner von Siemens opened the world's first electric tram line in Lichterfelde, a short track connecting the railway station with the cadet academy. Thirteen years later, Otto Lilienthal, the pioneer of human flight, had an artificial hill built in the same suburb so that he could launch his gliders from it, whatever the wind direction. The mound is still there, now a small park with a memorial. For a quiet residential district in south-western Berlin, Lichterfelde has a surprising place in the history of technology.

Today it is a green, leafy area of villas, apartment blocks and gardens, part of the borough of Steglitz-Zehlendorf. The Botanical Garden, one of the largest in the world, lies on its northern edge, with greenhouses full of tropical plants and gardens arranged by region. The former Prussian cadet academy, a vast complex of brick buildings, later served as an SS barracks and then, after the war, as a US Army base, and its history is a microcosm of Berlin's twentieth century.

As a starting point for a ride to the Oderbruch, Lichterfelde has the advantage of being on the edge of the city, with good access to the motorway ring. The ride east crosses Berlin's outer suburbs and then the flat, sandy plains of Brandenburg, before reaching the Oderbruch, the wide valley of the Oder river on the Polish border. The Oderbruch was a vast marshland until Frederick the Great had it drained and settled in the eighteenth century; it is now a flat, fertile landscape of fields, dykes and villages, under an enormous sky.

There is plenty of fuel, food and coffee in Lichterfelde and the surrounding districts. Berlin rush hours are best avoided, so plan your departure accordingly. The city streets are often cobbled in places, and tram tracks can be slippery in the rain. The Oderbruch roads are flat and straight, with long avenues of trees, and on a windy day crosswinds can be tiring. Spring, when the fields are green and the storks are nesting, is a lovely time to go.

t.near bad harzburg@51.8,10.5:
Bad Harzburg is a spa town at the northern gate of the Harz, a place of grand villas, a Kurpark, a casino and, on the hill behind it, a cable car that carries visitors to the ruins of a medieval castle. The castle, called the Harzburg, was built in the eleventh century by Emperor Henry the Fourth as part of his campaign to control the Saxon lands, and when the Saxon nobles rebelled in 1074 they destroyed it. The ruin is mostly a few walls and a tower stump now, but the place has a dramatic position, and a viewing area gives a wide look over the plain to the north.

On the same hill stands the Canossa Column, a granite pillar put up in 1877 by order of Bismarck, who wanted to remind everyone of the moment when his chancellorship refused to bend to Rome. It carries a line from his speech, famous in German politics: we will not go to Canossa. You do not have to share his views to enjoy the quiet woods around it, and the walk up is short and easy.

The town's other claim is its water. Brine springs have been used here since the nineteenth century, and the spa buildings, pump rooms and promenades speak of the age when doctors prescribed walks and mineral water for almost everything. The centre today is lively and a bit old-fashioned in a pleasant way, with cafés serving cake, restaurants with Harz specialities such as game and trout, and shops selling local sausages. A little waterfall called the Radau falls in a ravine near the edge of town and is an easy walk.

As a food stop it is a good one, with about twenty-three thousand people, fuel stations, supermarkets and many places to sit down. Parking a motorbike near the pedestrian zone is straightforward, and the cobbles in the centre are short. Weekends in good weather are busy, as riders from Hanover, Brunswick and Hamburg arrive in numbers, and the town can be filled with the sound of engines, so a weekday gives more room to breathe. After a meal, the climb into the hills begins at once, and the road toward Torfhaus and the high Harz gets steep and bendy within minutes.
